Transmissions: Element 120 is a very short mod said to be set in the Half-Life universe. It's very short, taking me just under an hour to finish.
If you've played Portal or Portal 2 recently, you may be aware of several mods that alter one or more aspects of the game to provide a new experience. This is like that; Transmissions uses a new type of Portal gun called the gravity gun and it acts like a type of grenade launcher. With this and your trusty Half-Life weaponry, you battle your way through a city filled with the combine and headcrab/headcrab zombies.
As far as I saw in my playthrough, there is no definitive story. It's really just four chapters of hallways and creepy, dark, tunnels.
This is more like a proof-of-concept game in my opinion. There's not much in it to really discuss outside of this new gravity gun and even then it only has one multi-use function.
Obligatory Score: 6/10
Note: There is a weird sound issue in the game where sound doesn't go to the one side of the earphone. At times you can strike the ground in front of you but the sound will only play in one ear.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
It was okay.  Not as good as Smash.
This game can't compete with standard 2D fighting games like Street Fighter or Soul Calibur.  The only use for this game is if you need a good 3 or 4 player game, and I would rather you not look here.
IN RESPONSE TO DEVELOPER:
A member of the development team posted in the comments and asked for more feedback on why I thought what I thought of the game.  I was going to post the following as a comment reply, but apparently those can't be longer than 1k characters.
In no particular order:
1)  One of the biggest mechanics in the game is that there's a universal weapon pickup that each character can grab and it turns into either one of two weapons a particular character has available to them.  A couple reasons I don't like this design decision:
1a)  Any character who has their weapon is always more powerful than a character who does not.  Effectively, you *must* pick up a weapon in order to be viable in combat.  It doesn't introduce player choice; it means I always rush to the nearest unguarded weapon before entering a fight.  I would rather just always have a weapon and never need to pick one up.
1b)  Each character has two weapons.  I usually like one of the character's weapons better than the other.  I would much rather a character always use a single weapon so that I know what I'm getting.  I want to feel like I have mastery over a given character because I have the same moveset every time I play; for example, with Hattori I always discard the polearm because I like the katana better.  (If you want a single character to have different moves, I'd rather see a character with a stance change mechanic; see Nightwing's appearance in Injustice.)
2)  I got really confused when I found out that there were only three heavy attacks:  Neutral, Side, and Down.  I guess this is because keyboard players jump with the up key, so they can't use an up special.  If there's only three, I'd prefer specials on Up, Down, and Neutral/Side sharing the same special a la Smash 64.  Partly, the neutral heavy attacks feel a lot like conventional "up" attacks in Smash.
2b)  Also, there's only two mid-air heavy attacks?  Would it be weird if I wanted to be able to use my ground specials in the air instead?
2c)  Some of the specials seem redundant.  Most specials either move you forward or upward.  The down and right specials seem like they're usually forward-moving; these seem redundant, and I'd rather have the better attack on right and some kind of utility on down.
3)  I'd love to have more projectile options for use while zoning with your opponent.  Right now the only way to get a projectile attack is to throw your weapon, which I do all the time.  If you can't throw your weapon because you take out the weapon equip mechanic (which I suggest), I'd love to see some special attacks built for zoning at long ranges, like projectile attacks or reflection shields.
4)  I'd like to duck through platforms by pressing down+jump, rather than just down.
5)  Monetization isn't a gameplay design thing, so it doesn't make-or-break the first impression, but like, in the context of the Steam economy...  $5 for a character?  I picked up Injustice for $5.  I got Sanctum 2 and all the DLC for $3.20 total.  For TF2, a Rescue Ranger goes for $0.40 on the community market.  I don't know if I'd ever spend $5 on a single character in Brawlhalla when I can get an entire game for the same amount.
Oh, and as for the "It's not as good as Soul Calibur comment".  I play a decent amount of Soul Calibur, and the entire game is about pressuring your opponent to make  a stupid choice and then punishing them for it by countering whatever they chose.  I don't know if the Brawlhalla team is big into 2D fighters at all, but there's a free PDF introduction to fighting game mechanics here:
I only read the first few chapters, but it was an interesting read.
In Brawlhalla, I just want more options for what I can do to an opponent.  I feel like the extent of the game is just running at an opponent and trying to pick an attack that happens to hit them instead of having their attack hit you.

Hello, gamers! I decided to write a review for this game because, well, it needs the recognition it deserves and any game that is good enough to make me purchase it twice for 2 different platforms is pretty damn good to me! This review will be pretty long and detailed, so you're in for a read!
First off, I said that I had purchased this game twice now. Indeed, I have! I had bought it for PS3 a good while back and when I upgraded to PS4, I was devastated that I could no longer play it anymore. Once fateful (ha!) day, I saw it for sale on Steam. I was so stoked because I had really been missing it at that time! To the best of my recollection, the studio primarily responsible for this game went under because the game sadly didn't get enough publicity or support, but I would have loved to see what else the makers of this game could have produced.
You start the game as a deceased person, who comes back to life and has the never-before-seen ability to affect fate and has no fate yourself. You begin a journey to save Amalur from evil, while at the same time trying to understand the mystery of why you were able to change the fates of those around you and find out why you don't have a fate yourself. And so begins your easily 100+ hour long journey through this MASSIVE world laid out before you.
THE GOOD STUFF:
THE WORLD OF AMALUR
First, you can easily sink 100 hours into this game and even way more depending on how completionist you play. This game is a great price for the content and is also loaded with the DLC too, adding more content. The world is massive and lush with color. There were no colors left untouched on the pallette by the designers. It's huge, vibrant and bright. There are tons of quests, from your main quest to side quests scattered throughout the world that you can get from NPC's, job boards and by finding a ket item that opens up the quest line for you. Such a large world is of course inhabited by a large and diverse set of enemies, all of which are many of the classic fantasy style enemies we've all come to know and love.
There are towns and settlements scattered throughout the world, which, upon finding them opens up a fast travel option to quckly get back to them from across the vast expanse of game you have set out for you. There are hundreds of NPC's to see and talk to, some of which actually have some very interesting things to say. And what RPG would be complete without some collectibles? There are "Lorestones" scattered throughout the regions of the game that, when activated, play a bard's song in the background while someone tells a story, sharing with some lore from within the world. It's a great way to learn about the game world that you are in and each Lorestone is part of a set. When you complete a set, ranging from 3-6 or more stones, you recieve an XP bonus for completing the set, as well as another bonus specific to that set. For example, there is a set of Lorestones called the "Webwood Stones" and upon completing the set, you gain a damage bonus against spider enemies. Some stones offer defensive bonuses, some damage bonuses and others give HP or MP bonuses, all of which are permanent.
COMBAT AND GAMEPLAY
KoA:R has some of the BEST, fluid and most fun combat I've ever experienced in ANY Game! Even Angry Joe Vargas, a popular YouTuber, praised much about this game, the combat definitely being one of the big ones he focused on. You can choose between 3 main classes: Mage, Warrior and Rogue. Each has its preferred weapons, but if you have the stats for it, you can use ANY weapon or wear ANY armor you want! Daggers, wands, staves, talismans, daggers, longswords, greatswords, faeblades, chakrams, bows, all are weapon types you can find and I'm sure I've forgotten a few. You know what chakrams are, right? Zena used chakrams, bruh! Each class has its preferred weapons, and at higher levels (I believe that the level cap is 40) you gain bonuses from those weapons, provided you have the skills to use them and are using the class that gets the most from them. The same goes for armor as well. Light armor, such as mage robes, medium armor for the rogues and heavy plate armor for the warriors.
You can chain attacks together between different weapons in your primary and secondary slots that is each assigned to a spscific button, allowing you to switch between primary and secondary weapons with a simple button press. All characters can use magic spells at the beginning of the game and can unlock more specific to that class and even put skill points in other branches of the skill tree to use those skills. So even if you chose a rogue, as I usually do, you can put points into the mage tree as well and use those spells with the same character! Combat is fast, fluid and looks stunning! Even more variety is added with "Reckoning Mode."
By killing an enemy, you have your fate meter charged with a little fate each time you do so. When it's fully charged and you activate Reckoning Mode, your character slams their fists into the ground, knocking back and damaging all nearby enemies. After this, your meter begins to drain. While it's draining, all enemies move in slow motion and your attacks do insane damage. When you have nearly killed your enemy, they will have a small amount of HP left, and a button prompt will appear over them. If you are able to get all nearby enemies into this state, then acticate the prompt above one of their heads, you then perform an awesome and flashy QTE finishing move that kills all of them at the same time. During the QTE, you can rapidly press the indicated button to get up to a 200% XP bonus!
I couldn't possibly type all of the information regarding weapons and armor and the way skills work with them and so on, but it's one of the deeper systems I've ever seen! Also, you have "Fate Cards" based on the stats of your character through leveling and skill point allocation, you can choose one of these cards after each level-up that create sub classes for your character. Such as a "mage-rogue" type character that gets bonuses to stealth and mana or magic damage and so on. The game encourages you to blend your character types, making combat more seamless and fun!
THE BAD STUFF:
As great as the game is, there are some shortcomings. While the world is big and beautiful, it can at times, seem a bit dead. Large areas that contain nothing much at all can be boring. It's not quite an open world game, but it is at the same time. The game world is split into zones separated by loading screens. You can freely explore each zone, which is large but has invisible walls or something to that effect. You CANNOT jump. Also, some NPC's show strange expressions that don't always fit their dialogue. Sometimes, they appear to have no expression at all. The game can also get a bit repetitive. Having such a large world, it is easy to assume that many of the side quests become "samey" and boil down to simple fetch quests. If you assume this, then you are correct, but they still aren't terrible boring.
The story is also typical of a large game like this. While you know what the idea is because it's told to you at the beginning, since there is so much random questiong done, there is often a lot of time in between important story mission and plot, leaving you feeling confused about what you're doing sometimes and not remebering what the last conversation in the story of the game was. It's also not written by the best writers. It can feel bland and poorly written sometimes, with the dialogue feeling boring and unengaging. As much fun as the game is, you get the feeling that you don't REALLY care about the world that you're trying to save, and that sucks. But overall, a great game!

Brawlhalla is in short, a simple Smash Bros, albeit much more frusterating. I'd recommend Rivals of Aether over this.
Cons:
After playing and getting into the top 150 rankings, the problems really became apparent as to why this game is so annoying to play. Most of the games turn into a campfest, in where the player who gets bored the quickest and makes a move is punished by the god awful design which is extremely active hitboxes. Most of the heavy attacks have around 3 seconds of active hitboxes in which if you touch them, you will take damage and be thrown away, which is terrible for a fighting game. It's also notable that guns are probably the best weapon because edgeguarding becomes pathetically easy with them and their Sair, which is again, a very active hitbox. Sometimes when you hit people and they barely dodge the attack, the hitsound will play, but no damage or knockback is dealt, causing me to get confused because I don't know to follow up the combo or not. Also, the servers are god awful and will cause you to lose stocks.
Pros:
The game feels nice, and landing attacks (that they don't dodge and the hitsound still plays) feels rewarding, and comboes are fun and interesting. Dodging is nice, but the hitboxes make it annoying.
Overall, I'd say to try this game, but do not buy it. In it's current state, spamming is hard to punish (active hitboxes are a part of that too), and some weapons are considerably stronger than some.

Trine 2 is a fairly enjoyable game and worth the discounted price tag during a sale (same can be said with the first Trine). If you don't have anyone to play with, this game probably not worth your time. If you do have friends to play with (locally or online), make sure everyone can cooperate well, otherwise you'll take forever to get past a simple section in the game.
For a platformer, Trine definitely has it's own feel to it and I really wish I enjoyed the platforming in this game more than I actually do. Maybe it's the lack of forward momentum that kills it for me, or at least the 'feel' of it. That forward momentum is there, but I don't know... Something about the movement is a little off-putting to me. Then again I do have different standards than the typical gamer when it comes to platformers, so you probably won't mind - it's not that bad, but anyway... Puzzles are relatively simple yet vary in difficulty of executing (depending on the skills of the players), but, in my opinion, the game begins to feel a bit too repetitive fairly quickly. This may be because I had already played through the original Trine and didn't find the game mechanics in Trine 2 to be much different than the first, but uh-uh.
On the positive side, this game's audio and visuals are very nice - the environments are detailed and varied, the colors are well-saturated and pleasing to look at, and the overall 3D side-scrolling presentation is done beautifully. The combat in this game takes advantage of a skill tree to help you defeat enemies faster and upgrading your skills opens up new approaches to various combat situations. The actual flow of the combat is fairly simple - there's no complicated control scheme or combo system and most player actions can be done with no more than two buttons, making the game fairly accessible for new players.
Overall, Trine 2 does have a unique feel to it and I think there's something in the game that you're bound to enjoy. So have at it. Or not.

Holdfast: Nations at War is the spiritual successor to Mount and Muskets and M&B: Warband's Napoleonic Wars. It's basically the same game mechanics with a different engine and more fleshed out player interactions. Eveyone is now capable of individual proxmity voice chat, which Mount and Blade lacked. There's only the French and English nations playable with a handful of maps. Although, Prussia is being added in the next update.
For someone who played during the late days of Mount and Musket and then on to Napoleonic Wars, this game has the potential to surpass Warband's limitations. Right now the only unsatifactory element is the melee. Bayonet attacks do lack the refined coordination and hit boxes that the Warband engine had. But Overall the game is fun, the community is superb, and the presentation is above average for an early access game.

Let me just say that Winter Wolves is a company who ought to get much more in the way of support- because this game is essentially one of the greatest visual novel games I've ever been able to play.
Loren the Amazon Princess is a game that is actually worth the full price- a rarity in these times, but if you like fantasy or adventure games, you'll want to grab this.  For once, you don't even play as the title character- instead, you play the second banana- either a human male slave, or an elven female.  The character you choose may have different observations about certain scenarios, and they may have a different set of people they might start a relationship with, but to be quite obvious, that's all the difference between them.  Both the male or female characters can get the same moves and the same classes, so really the only thing you're getting is a different view of the world.
Combat is actually very well-handled- you just place your characters, and go.  Their turn comes up, you pick a skill or an item to use, and then you repeat until the combat is done.  You'll always have a healer on hand, because whatever you pick for your character- gender or class- you get a class of Healer right off the bat.
As far as the story, it's actually well-written, and the characters have their own personalities.   You can talk to them in camp, you can flirt with a certain few of them, and if your scores are high enough, you'll even end up having to make a choice in a lovers' triangle between two party members- or maybe even more. There are both gay and straight options for both male and female characters- even more than Dragon Age, for crying out loud, and that's saying something.
There's even a bit of DLC, which unlocks four more party members and expands the third chapter with an entire new area.  It is completely worth it, no matter what.
Finally, a bit of warning:  Yes, the Steam version is the toned-down version.  There's a wokaround that you can use, but fair warning- this does create some NSFW scenes in the story, and changes some of the outfits on characters.  Take it as you will.
All in all, I would play this again and again and again, unlike some full-price console games and the like.  Go buy this game!

"Loren The Amazon Princess"'s game mechanics reminded me of the very simple games I played as a kid, such as the original (think 1980s) Bard's Tale or Wasteland that you could play on the old Apple II.  I liked it. Not every gamer is a twitch player, so this was a non-frustrating game to play.
I liked that the player had a ton of different romanceable companions, and endings, depending on the pc's gender and personality style.  (Hence the many play throughs to see all the different endings.)  Some of the relationships, however, felt creepy/abusive - the kind where you'd tell a girlfriend to WALK AWAY THIS GUY IS BAD NEWS sort of thing.
About a quarter of the writing fell into the "purple prose" category.  I could have done without all the internal musings by my character; it felt that the amazing dialogue between certain characters and reparte was written by one author and the internal musings was written by the author's angsty emo younger sibling.
That being said, I really enjoyed the game and the dlcs. Played "Loren" for at least 39 hours, so I got my money's worth.  Hoping the developer's next game - Season of the Wolf (?) when it comes out is equally good.  And now that I've written a review of the game, I'll probably poke my nose into it some more.

Loren has the distinction of being the first game ever where I picked the male PC to use over a female PC for a first playthrough. As a woman gamer, this is really rare! But Loren presents two interesting backstories to choose from and those backstories really do influence how others treat your character and the dialogue options you have.
So, to back up: this is basically a low-fi version of Dragon Age. It's heavily story driven, with several interesting characters, tons of dialogue and interaction, huge amounts of world-building, lots of really cool and diverse types of female characters, realistic conflict between characters, and Loren manages to do it all without BioWare's budget or AAA status. The character designs are really cool (Dora and Chambara are probably my favorites) and once I realized (about 5 hours into the game, whoops!) there was a "fast combat" option in the menu to speed things up, the classic turn-based combat made me fairly nostalic. My big complaint with the game would probably be the skill trees, partially because for strength-based (warriors) characters most of the skills were useless and for will (mages) and skill-based (thieves) the skills were often unbalanced and there's never a marker to tell you when/how you can gain certain skills (is it progression? A certain level of will? What? Why can I NEVER pick that skill?). It gets frustrating, particularly at higher levels, as the skill points you receive are minimal throughout the game.
Regardless of my frustration with the skill trees (and by about hour 7 I just gave up and started auto-assigning), Loren's definitely one of the better RPGs I've played recently. I'm looking forward to the other playthroughs I intend to do to see alternate paths, romances, and endings.

First off, I played the entire game using just the keyboard, no controller like it states you need on the store page. I can't imagine it playing better with a controller, anyway. The gameplay may be a little awkward to begin with as you control the movement of both characters simultaneously (one brother is controlled by the WASD keys and the other, using the arrow keys). Yet, what was initially awkward only became increasingly enjoyable once I began to appreciate what the developers were trying to achieve.
The unique gameplay, detailed sense of atmosphere and a few interesting puzzles is really what is on offer here. The story is relatively straightforward and is mainly conveyed through action rather than dialogue, as the game displaces verbal speech with exchanges of gibberish between its characters, similar to way language is used in say, The Sims. The effect is something exotic and unfamiliar if not distancing, but it is successful in conveying a sense of belonging and place for its main characters.
There's quite a fun journey to be had here and a few surprises throughout even if nothing is explained but more to evoke a sense of atmosphere and history more than anything else. Oh, and be ready for a good time, just not a long time.

I'm writing this review specifically for M&B: Warband : Viking Conquest
One of the best games I've ever played, easily in the top 5, this experience is like no other and the most complete gameplay  I've ever enjoyed. Every game has its genre and can shine in those areas but M&B: VC just shines in everything.
Strategy on so many levels: micro in real-time battles, macro in gathering and directing your personal and follower forces, city management, interdependent economies, relationship building in-faction, building allies and diplomacy with enemies, assigning leadership roles and lords to protect forts, directing allies in battle and to strategic points on the map... this list goes on as this game is primarily a strategy game but each of those that come to mind can be talked about for hours. Each choice has a geniune impact ex: do you spend your time your protecting your single village from bandits and cultivate its economy so you earn enough gold to field a larger army or hunt down your king's enemies to build stonger relationships in-faction, reknown and reputation so you can one day stop taking orders and start giving them. You can't say its RTS or Turn-Based given that everything moves and changes as you move your character or camp out but if you stop moving the world stops with you so you have all the time you need to plan out your next moves.
RPG on so many levels: Unique traits that develop based on how you choose to fight your battles, 20+ unique character skills that you can spend literally 100's of hours building and not master the skill tree. Gear that you can loot from battles, buy from towns, find in unique areas of the map or search out the best craftsmen across the map to have created. Some gear you can only find from specific tribes so you're constantly working your way towards something better/different. You can add complexity to the rpg elements with injuries that change you from battle to battle and gear that loses durability. Even your troops have promotion trees and can provide morale boosts or change roles as they survive battles alongside you. And you have to put in work to get them to the highest levels and keep them alive. Even in 2000 person battles you will cringe when one of your Briton Nobles or Norse Bodyguard dies. Best of all you start with absolutely nothing and have to work your way up, not with gimmicky quests but through the best of your rpg skills put to use.
War on so many levels: From field battles to seiges your choices make a significant difference and each fight is unique because of that. You can parley with the enemy lord before battle, decide on a skirmish attack pre-battle or give a speech to boost morale, choose your troop position at the beginning and throughout battle, very quickly and fluidly I might add. Then's there's your personal contribution to the battle which was one area I was worried would be Dynasty Warrior-esque but was so happy to find the quite opposite. Yes the skills you build through the RPG aspects matter but you are still human and it shows. You can fall (unconcious) in battle just as easily as your other troops if you're not careful or not skillful or just unlucky and caught a javelin to the face. And that's it, the battle goes on without you because git gud. Sieges from outside or in are also unique experiences and can feel like storming the beaches of Normandy (with swords) or holding the Alamo (bows... you get it). You can take 1000 troops with you into a seige and count each one of them as they die by your side as you break into a fort of 500 that fights to the last man. Positioning, and tactics play a part throughout or at least will save you troops you don't have to retrain. War.... its FANTASTIC.
Fighting on so many levels: Each weapon you pick up will require you without equivocation to understand the mechanics of that specific weapon. Some are easier than others, some can be used on horseback and some you will hate because you can't get the hang of them. Depending on if you choose to play with weapon durability, you might find yourself mid battle scrambling to pick up whatever the last dead guy dropped to fight off attackers and you better know how to use whatever you just picked up. Siege defense against 500 and your quiver of 30 arrows just ran out? Learn to throw a javelin or hell use a rock sling. There are occasional tournaments events in major cities that force you to use different weapons at random for worthwhile prizes. None of your movements are predetermined either, meaning if you want to swing your sword from left to right you have to direct you character to do so. If you would like to thrust, block high, block right, swing left and overhead stab with your spear then you you have to do it all yourself. No button-mashing Assassin's Creed-like 30 hit combos, that'll get you killed. Just hardcore vikings fighting for their lives.
Soundtrack: There aren't many songs in VC, just over 20 mins of soundtrack.... and it is glorious. Go to youtube before you buy the game and check it out. The game transports you away and you're completely absorbed 5 hours later.
Okay so this review has gotten insanely long so I'll end on saying that the best part is the game stays challenging from beginning to end. Like you could literally be 1 faction city away from complete conquest and be more worried about if you have enough gold to pay your troops or enough food to last a seige. One sandbox campaign of Viking Conquest had over 1300 saves.....
Time. Well. Spent.

So the game is cute and all and it boasts a charming low poly aesthetic but there are a lot of things wrong with it that are kind of detrimental to its replay value.
It has a distinct lack of purpose. You have a shop. You grow your shop. That's it. If you want something more engaging than that, probably don't get this game. There are no distinct characters to keep you company, there's no story, there aren't any cool modes to play in and I'm sorry to say it, the base gameplay really doesn't hold up on its own. There's also no challenge to making money. Everything sells itself and you end up with a hella lot of money that you don't even know what to spend on. The "deep mechanics" that this game is supposed to feature are interesting because despite there being some interesting ones present, they're never actually explained in the game but more on that later.
Holy mother of game design is the UI atrocious. Ordering stuff is ok but then you go to stock the shelves and you have to scroll through your inventory one item at a time to get to the one you need. It's not organized in any way either and it doesn't have its own dedicated screen like the order form menu does as far as I know. It slows down gameplay and makes it tedious to do the things you have to do to maintain your shop. Instructions are never presented at the right times either. Like when I come up to the machinery in the back, it doesn't prompt any kind of explanation as to what it is or how to use it. Either get left in the dark or google it. Also, man, why do I manually have to get rid of unneeded tutorials? Why is that a thing? Devs, please find a way to present the tutorial messages once and never show them to me again. Tutorial menus are meant to be an optional read, not a mandatory one. I shouldn't have to c;lick through the tutorial menu to deactivate annoying prompts that the game gives me throughout gameplay. Y'all obviously wired something weird there.
I will say that Shoppe Keep is a pretty good game for things like streaming since you can chat with your audience and not have to worry about much aside from the occasional barbarian but that's as far as I'll go.
Other than that, 3/10. Maybe get it when it's on sale for a dollar or less. Or better yet, play Recettear instead. That's a game that's infinitely less brainless.

This game is old enough that I don't feel like a particularly detailed review is called for. All you really need to know is that it's a fantasy RPG in the general realm of Skyrim, but not quite as high-budget, with a combat system similar to Dark Souls, but MUCH more fun and playable. You could also say it's a less dark and less ambitious version of Shadows of Mordor. Like Skyrim, it could definitely have benefited from mods to fix some bugs and balance some of the mechanics, but it's still a very fun game with multiple ways to play, pretty good writing (which happens when you hire an actual fantasy author and not your intern), good voice acting, decent graphics, and again, it's just a very pick-up-and-play type of game that still manages to hold your attention for dozens of hours (and it has two DLC that are not bad, though not fantastic either). It's the kind of game where you can tell that a sequel with more time in development would have just been amazing; all the potential is here, it just needed some more tweaking, some more unique enemies and environments, and so on. I recommend any fan of action game or fantasy titles to pick this up (I bought it on 360 and PC, if that tells you how much I like it).

No use mincing words. If you've ever had an interest in Picross, but don't have the wallet to buy a dedicated game to it like the ones on the Nintendo eShop, then this game will deliver exactly what you expect it will. It's barebones, so you aren't getting any flashy extravagance like the binary image suddenly turning into colored pixelart or animating itself. And you're not getting anything more involved that a 15 by 15 grid. You solve the puzzle and reveal the image. That's it. If you run out of puzzles, there's load of flash games online out there labeled 'picross', 'nonogram', or 'paint-by-numbers' to help you sate your thirst for more.
Other than that, the game is free, gives you what you want, and gives what you pay for. It's got workshop compatibility, so if you want to see other people's fan-made puzzles (likely copied whole ham from Mario Picross for the GameBoy) or just distribute puzzles that you made yourself, this is the platform to do so without even spending a dime.

After seeing Flik's "Let's look at: Picross Touch" on YouTube, I decided to give this a try. It's free, so there really was no harm in doing so. 30 hours later, I'm still playing and enjoying the game.
The interface and controls are easy to understand, and there is a lot to solve. People new to Picross (like I was) will easily start learning the strategies just by progressing through the different puzzles and difficulties. You may see some familiar faces in later puzzles, and it's fun to have that moment of "I know what this is!" when solving a puzzle.

Discussing the Final release here.
I bought the game when it was first released on Early Access at it's original 15 dollar price range.
Price - Currently at 25, anyone who had been following the game without purchase, I feel have no real right to complain. A few sales have come and gone and developers have done a great job to let people know of price changes before the end of a sale. It was easy to obtain this game for 10-15 dollars, which is a much better range for the current level of content.
Combat - Not much to say or expect out of a hack and slash game. Similar games such as God of War, Devil May Cry, etc have more complex styles due to the characters having multiple weapons and abilities.
Visuals - Not a terrible looking game, but not the best i've seen. I understand the concern with player models, though I personally make the point that if you spend most of your time fighting and moving forward, you wouldn't be staring that often at the character's faces, though I do agree they should be point to point of the show's models.
Sound - Attacks, Enemies and Voice actors are on point, pretty much from the source material.
Story - Considering this is a side story that can't have any major bearing on the show, I did not come into this game expecting it to be amazing, more so since the original concept of the game was just a horde mode style game. I doesn't have the same charm as the show, a weak villian and a terrible final boss.
Content - A simple 10 mission story with Horde mode on the way, It isn't great (more so if you paid 25 for the game) but when horde mode is released, it should give something more to the game.
As for the Paid DLC for Team JNPR, I understand the concern with the path of DLC, but I will hold back my torch until I see a price range, It might not be expensive at all, or it should be.
OVERALL - It is a fun game and worth a try (maybe wait for it to go on sale before buying it?) I feel the expectation of fans did not match the path the game was going and people reacted to it as such.

I want to defend this game, but that pricetag doesn't really help.

Now it may seem like im hopping onto a bandwagon here, but I truly dont recommend this game to people who haven't played it in its earlier stages, or back on console. The game is deeply flawed in several ways that only complete overhaul would fix.
Unless you plan on grinding for weeks, dont expect to get any of the higher tier commodities. But hey, if you're down for microtransactions you can buy $20 worth of virtual cash that wont even cover half of the price for some of the newer additions to the lineup of ridiculously overpriced luxuries. Missions quickly become stale and stressful, and while heists are a way to swoon you into thinking that you'll be able to fund so many ill minded activities, they usually end up being a carnival of salt for you and your friends the third time you fail the heist due to some aspect that requires ridiculous amounts of experience in the game.
Rockstar truly ♥♥♥♥ed themselves with this whole anti-modding philosophy as well. It isn't negative in any way, shape, or form yet people get the worst sorts of backlash for things they had no control over. Hell, people who even got their gains "legally" ended up getting characters reset, with the usual no response after explaining that they weren't hacking. Even with this system in place, exploiters run rampid in nearly every online server, and the only way you are truly, 100% safe is through the single player. Which, by the way, has been absurdly watered down thanks to the folks down at Take-Two deciding that OpenIV didn't deserve to be a part of their game, even though it was a down right improvement.
To recap, across three systems I have well over 2k hours in this game. I was expecting a different experience on PC but just found the same♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a fuller experience when it came to the modding community. The game was fun with friends while it lasted, but after a few months of play it becomes stale and obsolete. There really isn't much to do in Los Santos, and even with the addition of SecuroServ, and even the gunrunning update, the place still remains a barren wasteland. If you have enough friends, then maybe you can make something worthwhile of a memory.
But then you have the community. The community is one of the worst in any online game I've ever seen. I have seen so many toxic players, people who take the game waaaay too seriously, and those who abuse the power they can receive through higher cost goods that most players dont have access to. Back in the beginning, the only thing you had to worry about was if someone had a tank, and that wasn't a common sight. Then the insurgent came out. Then the Hydra. Now three, nearly four years later we see ourselves with vehicles like the Oppressor and the APC, which were complete ♥♥♥♥ing mistakes to introduce to a community like the one that GTA Online harbors.
So yeah. While I have fun with this game on the off occasion, I usually find myself cycling through the same motions to fulfill the braindead quests, killing people over and over again to send a message of some sort over a game where you can basically pay to win, and dealing with the same, all blacked out characters that will gat you down if you come within a mile radius of them with you and your friends.
I really hope you can fix some of this in GTA VI, Rockstar. But I get the strong feeling that you won't.

While I’ll admit I was initially a bit bristled at the fan-service in Loren the Amazon Princess, (even with the censor option turned on) it’s worth overlooking as the battle system is well arranged and challenging and the overall story of a young man or woman rising from slavery to become second in command of an army that will save the world is very well done, as is the secondary elements of the story.
I especially liked how each party member character has a lot of character development that can be encouraged by the player, through talking to them and completing optional quests. The most obvious example is the well done way Loren herself can gradually becomes less sexist and conservative, eventually becoming a truly enlightened Queen upon the end of the game IF the player argued with and challenged her preconceptions, presented evidence of the flaws in the Amazon system, proved the worth of men, made her realize the cruelty of slavery ect ect.
While it may be a bit expensive and is definitely only for mature audiences, it’s well made, tells an interesting tale about interesting people and I could honestly see playing through it a second time to see what effect different choices would have on the story.
I would definitely recomend buying this game during a Sale, or full price if you are a fan of the Visual Novel/Party Tactics RPG genre.

To sum it up shortly, I'd call this game "poor man's LOTR"; but despite how negative that sounds, it's actually quite decent, surprisingly so.
You start with your own character (with the choices of a dude and an elf girl) serving as the right-hand person for the main hero throughout the game, farm and grind your way (rather easily) into power, and gather more interesting people into your party along the way. The classic 'good guys vs evil powerful king' kind of story, it's pretty enjoyable if you're into that. My only gripe with the general storytelling and the social progression of the game was how often my party proved to be naive, optimistic and painfully altruistic everytime they engaged... anyone really. But maybe that's because I've built up my character to be "friendly" rather than "forceful" or "joking". If that is why, then that's awesome.
Some more freedom and a variety of choices would've been very welcome, but alas, the only choices you get mainly revolve around "romance between the characters" which is pretty SFW and mild while excessively flirty and LGBT-friendly if I may add - merely fillers much like in Mass Effect franchise and not too focused on as it would be in a "dating sim".
The art style is very simplistic yet just as pleasing to the eye, well.. my eye at least. The backgrounds and music is well done (most of the time) and the general atmosphere is just great.. and again, very LOTR-ish (but not as massive and majestic perhaps).
As for the gameplay, it pretty much consists of navigating through a map, picking some choices that rarely affects the main storyline (I suppose they focused on character development more than interactivity) and the rest is pretty much JRPG style turn-based battles.
I'd say it's quite good for a visual novel game, it's worth the money and I'd recommend it. But if you're not into visual novels, I doubt you'll enjoy this one bit.
Edit: Forgot to add, it's pretty lengthy too, can't really finish the whole thing in one go unless you skip every dialogue and such, and the game does have some replayability thanks to the character development, but not a huge factor in that on it's own.

Short: 6/10  A decent story based RPG with strong Date-Sim elements.
Long:   Loren is a heavily story driven RPG with an emphasis on romance and dating elements. You take the place of a second in command whom is send to complete the adventures and perhaps find love (it's not that hard). The story length of the game will depend almost solely on your reading speed, as it follows a "Text-Fight-Text-Travel Etc" formula.
Story: 8/10   Good, classic a little cliche. It makes sense and is touching (for those of you with emotions..)
Sound: 5/10  Average, it's what you would expect, the music fits the setting.
Gameplay: 4/10  It is simple, pretty easy to use. I have some issues regarding item comparison (or lack of). As well as inability to re-spec. I also encountered a minor bug while on the "Equip" screen. All in all more attention was needed here.
Graphics: 7/10  Animation pretty much doesn't exist, which is sad. The world is fairly well drawn and fits the story. The characters are presented in such a way, and have enough "Stills" as to give them a wide enough range of difference. On the downside, I found it pretty silly that my dwarf holds an axe in his picture while being equipped with a sword in the game.
+1:  I've not played many games in the Visual Novel genre, but Loren has made me want to take a closer look at some of them. It deserves a +1 for that alone.

I'm writing this review specifically for M&B: Warband : Viking Conquest
One of the best games I've ever played, easily in the top 5, this experience is like no other and the most complete gameplay  I've ever enjoyed. Every game has its genre and can shine in those areas but M&B: VC just shines in everything.
Strategy on so many levels: micro in real-time battles, macro in gathering and directing your personal and follower forces, city management, interdependent economies, relationship building in-faction, building allies and diplomacy with enemies, assigning leadership roles and lords to protect forts, directing allies in battle and to strategic points on the map... this list goes on as this game is primarily a strategy game but each of those that come to mind can be talked about for hours. Each choice has a geniune impact ex: do you spend your time your protecting your single village from bandits and cultivate its economy so you earn enough gold to field a larger army or hunt down your king's enemies to build stonger relationships in-faction, reknown and reputation so you can one day stop taking orders and start giving them. You can't say its RTS or Turn-Based given that everything moves and changes as you move your character or camp out but if you stop moving the world stops with you so you have all the time you need to plan out your next moves.
RPG on so many levels: Unique traits that develop based on how you choose to fight your battles, 20+ unique character skills that you can spend literally 100's of hours building and not master the skill tree. Gear that you can loot from battles, buy from towns, find in unique areas of the map or search out the best craftsmen across the map to have created. Some gear you can only find from specific tribes so you're constantly working your way towards something better/different. You can add complexity to the rpg elements with injuries that change you from battle to battle and gear that loses durability. Even your troops have promotion trees and can provide morale boosts or change roles as they survive battles alongside you. And you have to put in work to get them to the highest levels and keep them alive. Even in 2000 person battles you will cringe when one of your Briton Nobles or Norse Bodyguard dies. Best of all you start with absolutely nothing and have to work your way up, not with gimmicky quests but through the best of your rpg skills put to use.
War on so many levels: From field battles to seiges your choices make a significant difference and each fight is unique because of that. You can parley with the enemy lord before battle, decide on a skirmish attack pre-battle or give a speech to boost morale, choose your troop position at the beginning and throughout battle, very quickly and fluidly I might add. Then's there's your personal contribution to the battle which was one area I was worried would be Dynasty Warrior-esque but was so happy to find the quite opposite. Yes the skills you build through the RPG aspects matter but you are still human and it shows. You can fall (unconcious) in battle just as easily as your other troops if you're not careful or not skillful or just unlucky and caught a javelin to the face. And that's it, the battle goes on without you because git gud. Sieges from outside or in are also unique experiences and can feel like storming the beaches of Normandy (with swords) or holding the Alamo (bows... you get it). You can take 1000 troops with you into a seige and count each one of them as they die by your side as you break into a fort of 500 that fights to the last man. Positioning, and tactics play a part throughout or at least will save you troops you don't have to retrain. War.... its FANTASTIC.
Fighting on so many levels: Each weapon you pick up will require you without equivocation to understand the mechanics of that specific weapon. Some are easier than others, some can be used on horseback and some you will hate because you can't get the hang of them. Depending on if you choose to play with weapon durability, you might find yourself mid battle scrambling to pick up whatever the last dead guy dropped to fight off attackers and you better know how to use whatever you just picked up. Siege defense against 500 and your quiver of 30 arrows just ran out? Learn to throw a javelin or hell use a rock sling. There are occasional tournaments events in major cities that force you to use different weapons at random for worthwhile prizes. None of your movements are predetermined either, meaning if you want to swing your sword from left to right you have to direct you character to do so. If you would like to thrust, block high, block right, swing left and overhead stab with your spear then you you have to do it all yourself. No button-mashing Assassin's Creed-like 30 hit combos, that'll get you killed. Just hardcore vikings fighting for their lives.
Soundtrack: There aren't many songs in VC, just over 20 mins of soundtrack.... and it is glorious. Go to youtube before you buy the game and check it out. The game transports you away and you're completely absorbed 5 hours later.
Okay so this review has gotten insanely long so I'll end on saying that the best part is the game stays challenging from beginning to end. Like you could literally be 1 faction city away from complete conquest and be more worried about if you have enough gold to pay your troops or enough food to last a seige. One sandbox campaign of Viking Conquest had over 1300 saves.....
Time. Well. Spent.

I didn't play this game for very long before coming to my conclusions, and really, you don't have to play the game long at all to know what it's about. Time of Dragons was a pretty fun and clever concept, with dragons carrying turrets on their back and blazing into an all-out war with other dragon species. It seems like a rare breed. However, it's spoiled by one fatal flaw: it's multiplayer PvP
.
1) Engaging, action-filled combat. It's fun to see stuff explode.
2) The dragons, while kind of blocky and mushy-looking, have cool designs, and they're all unique from each other.
3) The game is free to play, and there's no P2W system of any kind.
1) It was fun for five minutes, then started getting boring really fast, mostly because of your lack of options. Do you want to PvP in this way or
way? It's all the same thing: kill the other players and win. There was no variety whatsoever, and the few choices you do have aren't very interesting.
2) I couldn't really get a leg-up in terms of experience since everyone who was playing seemed to be higher and better than me. Again, this made the game boring pretty quickly, because there is no skill scaling. What's the point of fighting if I can't win anything? Not fun. Moving on.
3) The abilities don't seem to do anything. I've hit my special ability several times on enemies and tried like hell to get it to land on them. It doesn't seem to hurt them. Even if it did, they usually managed to kill me before I could tell. I tried the fire blast with Tiamat and vampirism thing that drains health with Vampire, and neither seemed to hurt the enemy. Maybe I just couldn't land it right, but should it really be that hard to land? Especially in a high-action environment where I don't have a lot of time to swoop in and hump the enemy before using my ability?
4) Almost the entire playerbase was Russian for some reason. So I couldn't even chat with people. Even if I could, it's not like I'd have anything to say except "Hey, can you help me kill this dragon so I don't die again?" I'm sure if I banged my head on the keyboard a bunch of times, it'd have the same effect.
5) There's no single-player or PvE options, so if you enter a battleground and see no other players... that's it. You have to leave and join another one and hope you have other people to play with. And if you're on at the wrong time of day, no one at all will be around. Unless they're Russians, I guess. Which is fine, if you're Russian.
6) Turning is slow as hell and has gotten me killed more than once. Even when using an evasive maneuver, it was impossible to avoid an attack if the dragon was already on your♥♥♥♥♥
7) It says each dragon has a "role" but they don't come into play at all. Players don't really stick together (because the teams are usually 2 or 3 people), so roles are pointless. It's pretty much what you think works best for keeping your♥♥♥♥♥alive. So pick a dragon with high health and high damage every time so you have a fighting chance.
There's nothing special about it. It's just mundane multiplayer PvP with players you can't understand. Skip this one and move on. Unless you like to be frustrated. Then be my guest.
It could very well be that I played the game at "the wrong time of day" and maybe more US players join in the evening, but that still shouldn't matter. Whether you're playing in the morning of evening, you should still see more than ten players at a time.

If you're not concerned about manufactured outrage about irrelevant microtransactions(People with too much money on their hands can buy singleplayer currency - The horror!) and you liked the previous Deus Ex, than you'll probably be reasonably happy with this game.
Granted, the microtransactions are fairly silly, but they really are completely irrelevant. You have to go to the store page in-game to find them, and none of them are in any way required to beat the singleplayer.
People complaining that it has less story depth than Human Revolution have managed to construct some industrial-strength rose tinted glasses in the few years since the last game. It's very similar in quality, and most people that aren't looking for a reason to be mad will likely enjoy this game. I certainly did, at least.
It's not a perfect game by any means, (I've run into my share of minor bugs) but it's hardly deserving of the negative steam reviews it's been getting.

Path Of Exile has been my primary ARPG for a while, but I wanted to try Torchlight 2 to see what it was like.
After playing a few hours in the demo I HAD to buy it, and the Steam Holiday Sale made that possible for 50% off.
I enjoy the simple, gold-based currency system, and so far my luck hasn't been too bad regarding drop rates for lock box keys.
I enjoy the ability to select the gender of my character, although I do wish there were a couple more classes, as sometimes it feels like the potential skills force you too much into one archetype (i.e. sword-and-board versus two-handed, with skills you've invested points in that do NOT translate from one or the other).
The gameplay is fast-paced but still fairly relaxing on Normal mode, and the cartoony-style  monsters make it where I could see young children playing on the easy mode without being scared.
Overall I can definitely see why this game is so popular, and I'll be playing more!

Very enjoyable on the whole. This is a high fantasy rpg/choose your own adventure mix and for the most part it pulls it off.  The combat consist of your party versus an enemy party with both sides selecting abilities and targets in a turn-based manner. It ranges from serviceable to enjoyable depending on how long you've been playing but by the time your done you'll be edging toward boredom with the combat. That's not to say there's aren't tactic elements but the bare graphics and simplistic but perfectly functional U.I eventually get old. It also has some romance elements that are entirely optional and not a core part of the story.
Other minor things to note. The basic sound effects aren't terribly good and I found myself listening to music within the first couple of hours. Characters are for the most enjoyable but one of my biggest issues is how the best one is part of the DLC. In fact, the DLC feels incredibly core to the main game to the point where I wouldn't recommend it without it. It adds much to the ending, a large side-quest and a significant number of characters to your party.
Pros
-Cool Characters and enjoyable story.
-Choose your own adventure style decision trees.
-Function core gameplay.
Cons
-DLC feels very much part of the main game. Would not recommend playing without.
-Combat can become tedious after many hours.
-Lack of animated graphics.
-Bad audio effects.
Closing Thoughts: The time I spent playing the game was very enjoyable but the price might be slightly too high all things considered. Would absolutely recommend picking it up if it ever goes on sale and purchasing at full price if this game's core elements sound appealing to you.

The only thing I do like about this game however, is the characters themselves and the relationship system. Other than that this game is pretty boring to play.

Overall, I found this to be a very enjoyable RPG. The combat system may be difficult for some people who haven't used that sort of grid-style before, but it's easy to get the hang of, & may appeal to people who find regular turn-based combat a bit slow. The art style was nice, though I would've liked to see more stills from special scenes in the game. While the story isn't that original, I did like that it tells the story from the point of view of someone other than the "Chosen One." The characters were interested, & I found the writing particularly compelling in the last two chapters. I also have to give the writers credit for doing a good job of writing a romance that actually adds to the story development rather than just feeling tacked on... on least in the romance option I picked. Overall, great game for someone looking for an old-school RPG who isn't afraid of using their imagination.
While the combat is a little more simplistic than I would like, overall this game was really fun and fairly well written.

I absolutely loved this game, and kudos to the developer for making this available for macs too!  I've made it through one playthrough and have to stop so I can get caught up on a bunch of work :P
I really enjoyed the story, and just how many options there are (that whole replayability factor) for dramatically altering the storyline.  The battles also were not tedious, and there was no pointless grinding--unless you wanted to do so.
There were a few things that could have been fine-tuned a bit more, but while they were slightly annoying, they weren't enough to keep me from enjoying the game.  These included:
1) Buying equipment for the party, especially when it gets big, is a little tedious.  You have little checks that appear above each character's head if they can equip a piece.  However, you have to click on each character, then hover over each piece of equipment before you can see whether it's worth the investment.  On top of that, it's hard to keep the names of different pieces of equipment straight, so you're constantly checking the same pieces on the same characters.  A few things that would help with this are: a) no checks above a character if they have a piece equipped, b) something like a plus or minus indicator above a character's head, instead of the check, to show whether or not the piece of equipment is an improvement on what they already have, and c) stores that have set pieces of equipment.  Half the time, you exit out of a store, go back in, and hey, totally different equipment--and guess, what?  It's better than what you just bought.
2) Some sort of indicator that shows, when you camp, whether or not someone has something to say to you.  I don't know how many times I clicked through every character only to have them give me the standard reply.
3) The skill point system.  Sure, I'd love to have more points, like a point on every level, but that's probably not realistic :P  The bigger issue was the interconnectedness of leveling up skills.  I don't know how many times I wanted the next level of X skill, but it wasn't available until i unlocked Y & Z skills, which were skills I didn't want.  So essentially, you end up wasting those valuable skill points in order to finally get the skill you really wanted.
But really, this is a fantastic game for those who love the story part of rpgs, but can't do the action combat that so many of them have turned to.   Now, if only they could figure out how to port the old-school jrpgs into mac verstions :P

Video Review:
Shoppe Keep is a strange game. It’s a first person store management game where you can design and stock your store, fill your shelves, hire robots to do your job for you, and fight and endless army of thieves that think stealing from you is a good idea. The gameplay routine revolves around stocking your displays, setting new displays, pricing your items, and paying attention to the current trends of what’s selling. Once the store opens up it’s all about guarding your items from thieves, barbarians, and trying to keep your shelves stocked at the same time. At first this a lot of engaging work, but the moment you unlock engineering and can hire bots to do all of this for you? (Which you really need to do in order to manage it all) It becomes so easy that you’ll find yourself literally running around jumping because you have literally nothing else to do. You can’t speed up time or pass a day. Every time you start a day you are committing to 15 minutes of watching everything flow once you unlock automation (Which you can do very early on.)
The creators of the game injected their sense of humor into the game. All the names in the game are just random combinations of a list of generated words. You’ll find plenty of silly names, my favorite being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Butthead”. In the beginning you’re also restricted from jumping until you spam spacebar enough to “break” the restriction. There’s also a sort of unlockable tree that allows you to unlock new items to sell and new customers to buy your things that is used as progression. You can even unlock a tavern to make some extra coin on the side or a garden to do some planting if you so choose.
The graphics are honestly pretty bad but if you’re this far into this review I’d hope that doesn’t bother you. You’ve already seen the screenshots yourself probably. What does bother me is the horrible animations. Your character holds his weapons up above his head like an idiot with the first person view; which covers half your screen. And when you look in the mirror you can see that the devs literally did not bother to actually animate anything outside of the first person perspective. They thankfully remembered to render a body for your first person view, which more devs forget to do, but they really didn’t put much effort into that either. The animation of your feet and the sound of them are completely desynced and there literally isn’t a jumping animation to be spoken of.
The game doesn’t have a tutorial to speak of either. It has a bunch of help menus and early notifications saying “We won’t stop showing you this notification until you read the help menus”. But walls of text on help menus are one of the most boring ways to teach a game in existence so I’m willing to bet most people just click through them and don’t read them as a result. The big problem about this game is just that there’s so much missing, so little effort in some areas, and so many problems with the game design itself that it feels incomplete. As if it was released in an early build and was abandoned. Sitting 15 minutes while you watch bots do everything for you isn’t fun. Having to do everything yourself to avoid using bots is too much micromanagement. There’s no way to speed up time though, and time pauses when you alt tab. This means after eight hours or so you’ll probably find yourself getting bored with nothing to do.
Shoppe Keep is fun to start, but after you get past the start you realize just how shallow and underdeveloped it really is. And it really has been abandoned. No additions or updates are planned. And with the current pricing of it? It’s not really worth your time. I wouldn’t recommend it. It gets a 4/10 from me. I had fun with it. It was almost an average game, but it was incomplete and abandoned.

I got this game on sale for $4.99. At this point, I've put 40 hours into it, and I can honestly say that it is a very solid hack-and-slash RPG.
Kingdoms of Amalur has the three standard RPG classes: mage, warrior, and rogue. Unlike in many other games, though, the player can mix these classes and the game actually rewards that. You are rewarded for mixing up your style of combat. One of the easiest ways to do this is to use a spell from one class, then use one from another. In addition, there are "fate" cards that grant bonuses for any possible variation of the three classes. "Do you want to be a tank that uses magic? Awesome! Have some elemental and physical damage resistance. Oh, and let's go ahead and make your dodge into a short-range teleport!"
The mixing of classes is where this game really shines.
My one major gripe with the game is that it can quickly become very easy. A mage/warrior may not deal as much damage as a simple warrior would, but he will also not take nearly the same amount of damage. At the time I'm writing this, I have a character up to level 18, and he is absolutely unstoppable. There are very few enemies who have a chance at killing this character, and I have tried to find them.
Between his health regeneration rate and his damage resistance (both physical and elemental), I haven't used a health potion in almost 3 hours of gameplay.
That said, this game has a lot to offer. It is certainly worth the $5 that I paid, and it's probably worth quite a bit more than that. There is a lot of replay value just because of the variety of ways that the game can be played. I've played a rogue and a warrior/mage, and I really have enjoyed every bit of it. I haven't even begun to delve into the alchemy or the "heavy weapons" thing, but I really should try it out. (Maybe a warrior/mage who wears robes and carries a warhammer? I dunno.)
In any case! If you're at all into hack-and-slash, dungeon-crawler type RPGs, then this game will surely satisfy that craving at least for a while.
Hope this helps, and have fun!

I enjoyed this game so much. Everything from art to music was positively delightful. The way that the game gives you choices and options makes it very inviting, and allows anyone to find a playstyle that works for them. You want to play a battlemage, swinging swords and slinging spells? Done. You want a standard rogue, daggers and bow? Done. A combination of all three archetypes? You can do that too!
As for flaws? KoA:R suffers from standard inventory management hassles. Additionally, I would personally like more options in the character creator (But I love spending stupid amounts of time in character creation). Besides that, the only other major flaw is that the ability to customize the game makes it hard to find what -exactly- you want. There's just so much there, it's a bit hard to decide how to play. While the "fateweavers" allow you to respec, it will cost you, and the cost will increase as you respec again and again. While money is plentiful enough in the game, it still disincentivizes changing your playstyle. It's a little offputting; you want to try everything, and the game seems to limit you.
In Summary, Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a great game, offering a crazy amount of content and flexibility, while accepting the shortcomings that follow those traits. Great fun, much recommended,

Kingdoms of Amalur: The Reckoning is so fantastical that it may as well have been written by R.A. Salvatore.
Oh wait...It was?  Oh, okay.
You start the game as a corpse, being corpsey on top of a big ol' corpse pile. Frankly at this point you're just happy to have company. But suddenly you wake up and you're no longer a corpse. Disheartened, you leave the pile and set off on an adventure. A very, very long adventure.
Kingdoms of Amalur is a fast paced, action RPG based more around dodging, blocking, and combos then it is stats and things like status effects. Instead of choosing a class at the beginning of the game you instead choose your class depending on what you put your points into. For example, putting all your points into Might unlocks nothing but warrior classes, all your points into finesse makes you a super good rogue, and all points into magic makes you a giga wizard.
Or you can mix it up and instead get a class card that's a mix of two or even all three class types. So yes, you can build Might and Magic and create a muscle wizard.
Combat is fairly arcadey and fast pace, you still do damage depending on your stats, but I haven't found an enemy you couldn't take out at any level if you were good enough. You can equip two weapons, a primary and secondary weapon, and can switch in between them freely. This leads to opportunities to extend combos and maximize damage as well as adding whatever spells or powers you have on your character for some ludicrous Devil May Cry looking stuff.
It also gives you an opportunity to counter an enemy attack instead of blocking or dodging, since human enemies usually go into a stun animation when you hit them, while you need to start dealing some damage on larger foes before they start to waver.
So if someone is readying an attack, you can switch to your faster weapon and cut them off instead of dodging or blocking/parrying. It's actually really neat just how many combat options they managed to fit into this game.
I would suggest playing on hard, however. Even normal difficulty is far too easy unless you're looking for the most casual experience possible. But at that point just. You know, watch a movie.
Amalur itself is so high fantasy it starts throwing DnD Campaign setting books at you. As said before R.A. Salvatore wrote the backstory for Amalur, spanning some 10,000 years or so of a bunch of info you won't bother to learn. That's not to say that the setting is boring, but it reeks of Salvatore, so much so that you could probably see Drizzt hiding around the corner.
Gadflow, a corrupted Fae, seized control of the winter court and waged war against the younger races with his army, the Tuatha. The big problem for the mortals is that the Fae have immortal souls, and will come back and continue warring against the mortals after they're killed. So yes, they won't die even if we killed them.
All mortals are tied to the weaves of fate, your life and death are predestined and you can't do anything to change it. EXCEPT YOUUUUUUUU
See, as stated before, your character died, and they met their fate. But they're brought back to life by Hughes and his well of souls, something that shouldn't happen. So since your character was already dead, they met their fate and are now fateless. Not only does that mean your not tied to fate, but you can change other peoples fates, kill those who weren't supposed to die there, and change a predetermined future entirely, you're completely free from the cycle. But much like my ex-wife you can also ruin other people's lives entirely. Because your character can break the cycle, he can change the fate of the people around him, maybe even remove Fae from the cycle and essentially kill them as well. Now if you were a big stinky idiot fairy, that sounds kind of scary.
Amalur's world is surprisingly bright and colorful, considering the subject matter. The War between the Tuatha and mortals still rages in far off lands, disease is spreading and you constantly run into injured and broken veterans that have been fighting the Tuatha, sometimes for years. But Kingdoms of Amalur doesn't saturate colors or anything to represent the fact that all mortals may be killed in the near future, the world still goes on, uncaring of the events around it.
Also this game is long, like really long. I'm 21 hours in and don't see an end in sight. I'm pretty sure though, if I just went along the main story I'd be done in no time, but there are a good number of side quests that may as well be their own main quest.
Everything in Amalur screams fantasy, from the creatures to the locations to even your weapons and armor, it's like a tabletop game got out of hand.

The game is still pretty good though, surprisingly good. It just came out at the wrong time, considering it came out in between some high profile games like Skyrim and Dragon's Dogma with very little fanfare. Can you believe Rhode Island funded this game, though? That's kind of crazy. Oh god, the frame rate...
Gameplay:
This is the BIGGEST problem I have with the game! When you're walking around, slaying hoards of enemies it's perfectly fine, hitting max frame rate and everything, but the moment you hop into any vehicle it's nearly halved when there is any enemies on the screen with you. This makes missions where you need the vehicles nearly impossible nad vomit endusing, like it literally will make you nauseous. Note that all the controls are still functioning normally and are extremely slick, but that's also when the frame rate has been decreased so sometimes you just have to press the button and hop it activates on time. Again this makes the driving sections a pain and nearly unplayable, and to put a nice cherry on top, you can't skip them (not that I think you should be able to if you are able to handle it, keyword being able). That being said running around the demonic metal overworld is a blast, and zapping and slashing enemies is exetremely fun. The controls are smooth and make sense for the most part (though sometimes instead of dodging your character will just stand there gaurding instead, but it isn't as bad as it sounds). All this being said, users with older computers beware (and maybe even newer ones).
Story:
Though I'm not exactly the target demographic for the game and several references go straight over my head, the story is fun and awesome. Jack Black, Ozzy Osbourne, and all the other voice talents do a splendid job! Though the previously mentioned frame rate issue hasn't allowed me to actually finish the story so more on this later on in the future.
Graphics:
The Overworld is amazing, with it's metal aesthetic and all. And although it's no Tamriel, it's sure to be a blast exploring. The overworld also doesn't suffer from things that open world games usually do either, there's plenty to explore in the game, and you'll be rewarded for doing so nearly everytime you decide to, whether it's by the overworld itself or the collectables. The game also looks great for the time it was released. Biggest gripes about it are that some of the characters and enemies just look out of place (i.e. the big fist guys), lack of any HUD (i.e. health or a mini map), and THE FRAME RATE!
Music:
The game features several liscened songs that are certainly great, however I much prefer the ambience, which is a mix between the heavy metal rock and soothing ambience. So the best thing is that you have music that matches any mood you're in.
Overall:
Very enjoyable game IF you have the right hardware. If not then this game isn't for you.

Let me start by saying two things: I love this game (it's one of my favorites), but it's not a game for everyone.
I say that for several reasons.
First of all, this is an otome/visual novel and RPG hybrid, so while there's a good bit of fighting and grinding to be had, there's a definite emphasis on character relationships. You have your choice of 6 potential mates--that's 3 men and 3 women for both Soren (the male MC) and Elenor (the female MC), or you always have the option of going it alone by ignoring any romantic dialogue. While you can trigger special subquests and dialogue, there isn't really a way to "build" friendships with other characters outside of this romantic interaction. Obviously, the otome element isn't ideal for everyone.
You also have the choice of what personality you'd like to have (joking, tough, or nice) depending on the dialogue choices you make in the early phase of the game. That said, there's no other customization available for the MCs besides your choice of one of two classes and a selection of armor and weapons. You cannot modify their name, appearance, or personality beyond these elements.
It's also an older style RPG, which means turn-based and a heavy focus on AoE (area of effect) spells and attacks. While you do have the ability in later chapters to roam the world map freely, several chapters prevent you from doing this and force you to follow the linear plot.
While there also is a strong, central plot with some subplots and quests (many of which can be unlocked along with 3 additional party members on the Castle of N'Mar expansion pack), and decent quality writing, I do admit the game can drag out at times, both with the fighting and the plot elements.
Despite its faults, however, this quickly became one of my favorite games due to both the nostalgic love of older-style games and high replay value, given the many different endings that can be unlocked both through character romance and different versions of the ending. No spoilers, but some of those endings can definitely be pyrrhic and deliciously, heart-wretchingly tragic.
Ultimately, if you like old-style RPGs and you have patience and time to kill, it's worth the cost (though, admittedly, I got mine on sale half-off and felt it was definitely worth that). However, for those looking for a fast-paced game or stronger emphasis on the battle elements of the game, this probably isn't for you.
