One of the more fun indie games I've played recently, with nice 2D art and fun, albeit not incredibly original, RPG story and gameplay. This is a hybrid visual novel and RPG, which is an unusual combination and not for everyone; however, if either of those genres appeals to you, or you enjoy character-driven RPGs with romance options (such as Bioware's RPGs), it's definitely worth a try.
Winter Wolves clearly takes bits and pieces from other game series they like; the game it is perhaps most indebted to is Dragon Age: Origins, as the camp system holds definite parallels, and the ability icons look like they could have been taken directly from that game. The story is fairly pedestrian high-fantasy, though with a few twists (such as playing not the destined hero, but her sidekick), and while the turn-based combat system is quite polished for an indie RPG, it offers nothing incredibly new.
That said, while Loren is not the most innovative game in gameplay or plot, its mixture of VN and RPG is much rarer and works for the game. While it's not bringing a ton of new stuff to the table, what it does bring is executed well. The battle system is quite enjoyable (and has adjustable difficulty, which is always nice!) and the characters are overall fairly likable, though any party members you don't romance on a given playthrough - with a few exceptions, such as dwarves Dora and Ramas - will mostly remain ciphers until you do. The romance system is fairly nice, though, giving you a good amount of insight into your chosen character(s); it's also fairly inclusive in its options, with each protagonist (the male human Saren and the female elf Elenor) having four to six potential romance options (in the basegame, one heterosexual, one homosexual, and two bisexual options, divided evenly among genders; the expansion offers two more bisexual romances, one of each gender).
Is it worth it? You can easily finish your first run through the game, doing everything it is possible to do (including DLC) in 15-20 hours, but Loren offers replay value through its multiple endings and romance routes. (It also offers cheats to help speed up replays once you've beaten it once, which is handy.) $20 would be fair for the deluxe version (especially as indie game development can't pay that well), but for just the basegame and no DLC, it's a bit steep. If you do get it, I would definitely recommend getting it via Steam just because it is a little cheaper than buying it from the developer's website. (And if you do buy it via Steam, the version from Winter Wolves' website will unlock itself with everything you have bought here, including DLC.) And the deluxe version of Loren is certainly worth picking up on a Steam sale, at the very least.
P.S. One thing I should probably address is the fanservice outfits. The original version of the game included some rather scanty outfits for several of the main characters that could be changed to more modest covering through a Preferences setting. (Endgame romance scenes also came in near-nude/clothed versions.) The Steam version does not have this enabled, so you will by default be playing the covered-up version. That said, if you want the fanservice outfits, it's fairly simple; just download the demo from the developers' website, which will automatically unlock the full game and/or DLC if you've bought them through Steam, and then use that version to change the settings and save. Since the Steam and WW versions both share the location for saves and settings, changing the one will affect the other, and your Steam install will now have the fanservice outfits. (You'll have to go back to the WW version if you want to change back to the modesty outfits, but as you'll see, it's a fairly minor thing to have to do.)

I love stealth games. I love having the power, to theoretically, get in and out of any place and it seem like nothing ever happened. Thief is sometimes viewed as the epitome of the genre- It's brutal, okay? This game isn't training wheels just because it's the first entry. Hell, I beat the first level after about 90~ minutes of gameplay. Is that a bad thing? Absolutely not. At least in my books.
The game's really strong in its presentation. It might look terrible today (there's no denying that) but back in '98, it would really shine. The animations really caught my attention for some reason (not the one's of Garret using weapons in first person) the guards had a really oddly satisfying looking way of sneaking around to me. Of course, their running animation is pretty weird, no denying, but I rest my case.
Thief has this weird way of presenting lore. You can learn about these people's everyday lives just by reading a note or a book they had left around, and it makes it feel like you're actually stealing from a real rich family or something. I personally loved the touch of detail that was required in order to put that together, and it obviously wasn't an afterthought- these things are prominent right from the beginning.
Last but not least, the controls. It's hard to talk about controls in a review, since everyone has a different 'feel' for things. The vanilla controls were fine for me, except for A and D making you turn instead of just sliding. After a little bit of fiddling in the controls menu, I was all set. The jumping felt a little floaty at first, but I grew to like it. It feels realistic, but if Garret was a worldwide-level gymnist.
Overall, I think this game would be a fine addition to any retro steam gamer, like myself. It's cheap, and lasts a really long time. Some people in the reviews have hundreds of hours! Thief Gold earns itself a 8.5/10. Get it.

Thief is not only one of the best stealth games I have ever played, but also one of the best games in general I have played. While the game is severely outdated in terms of graphics, the feeling and quality of the gameplay is just outstanding and it really is fun to go through.
The stealth mechanics are very good, and I imagine they were an incredible innovation at the time. The soundtrack also fits the game greatly and immerses you into the experience very well.
But the one thing that really makes me love this game is the absolute atmosphere and overall feeling of truly being a thief you get while playing. While the universe presented from the game at first looks very traditional and boring, it is actually very interesting to explore and look into the lore of it all. I was honestly suprised to learn that the setting which the game takes place in is not just some bare Tolkien ripoff, but a truly authentic fantasy playground that greatly immerses you.
The game succeeds to make you actually feel like a thief, it doesn't just say that you're a thief and give you the toys to do it, it really gives you a sense of place. It's a little tough to explain but once you play the game for yourself you will know what I'm talking about.
But when you do actually get into the sword fighting mechanics sooner or later it actually isn't that bad. While slightly clunky to get used to, it is actually innovative and it mirrors some sword fighting systems from certain games we have today.
During potentially scary sections of the game, you will feel despair and helplesness because of it. The soundtrack reinforces that too.
The people in the game, even guards feel like real people and not just cardboard cutouts walking around the place for players to simply pass by. Most of the time you can hear guards talking to each other about events happening in their lives or even recent stuff you pulled off in your thieving spree in the previous mission.
While the game is a little tough to get into at first because of its age, the time you will get from putting effort and patience into it will be kindly rewarded from the fun you get later.
I would reccomend this for absolutely anyone to try, especially if you're a stealth fan, because this is one of those games that really brought attention to the genre. Reccomended at any price, especially on sale. Feel free to pick this up at any time.
Will break your heart, in the best way.

This game is simply amazing. It seems like nothing great at first glance and I was unsure before buying it, but it was worth it. By worth it I mean the 1.49€ I payed, I don't think I'd recommend buying it for the full price.
"Brothers" is a very short game and I'd recommend playing it in one long session because the story really sucks you into the environment and it also takes a bit to get used to the unique gameplay mechanics. It took me just about 3h to finish the game, but I derped two or three times. If I knew what to do at every little bit I would have been able to do it in 2.5h.
It's really not a special setting. Having to complete a far dangerous journey to save a relative is nothing new. But the way it's done is just mind-boggling! The emotions I felt for these characters living through lows and highs (especially the highs are normally rare and hard to implement in sad games!) of their lives really don't compare to anything I have felt in a video game before.
The only thing that isn't great about the story is that it is very linear. But that's okay.
The graphics are really nothing special. The boys look kind of cute (not in that way! ;D) but the textures are boring. But that's not really the main focus of the game so that's okay.
The physics do bug out rather often to the point where it get's a little annoying. For instance right at the start you have to push a cart with both brothers. To pick up the handles of the cart you will have to stand at very specific places with the brothers otherwise it doesn't work. They also move rather jittery sometimes.
They just don't make bears like the use too.

I'm writing this review specifically for M&B: Warband : Viking Conquest
One of the best games I've ever played, easily in the top 5, this experience is like no other and the most complete gameplay  I've ever enjoyed. Every game has its genre and can shine in those areas but M&B: VC just shines in everything.
Strategy on so many levels: micro in real-time battles, macro in gathering and directing your personal and follower forces, city management, interdependent economies, relationship building in-faction, building allies and diplomacy with enemies, assigning leadership roles and lords to protect forts, directing allies in battle and to strategic points on the map... this list goes on as this game is primarily a strategy game but each of those that come to mind can be talked about for hours. Each choice has a geniune impact ex: do you spend your time your protecting your single village from bandits and cultivate its economy so you earn enough gold to field a larger army or hunt down your king's enemies to build stonger relationships in-faction, reknown and reputation so you can one day stop taking orders and start giving them. You can't say its RTS or Turn-Based given that everything moves and changes as you move your character or camp out but if you stop moving the world stops with you so you have all the time you need to plan out your next moves.
RPG on so many levels: Unique traits that develop based on how you choose to fight your battles, 20+ unique character skills that you can spend literally 100's of hours building and not master the skill tree. Gear that you can loot from battles, buy from towns, find in unique areas of the map or search out the best craftsmen across the map to have created. Some gear you can only find from specific tribes so you're constantly working your way towards something better/different. You can add complexity to the rpg elements with injuries that change you from battle to battle and gear that loses durability. Even your troops have promotion trees and can provide morale boosts or change roles as they survive battles alongside you. And you have to put in work to get them to the highest levels and keep them alive. Even in 2000 person battles you will cringe when one of your Briton Nobles or Norse Bodyguard dies. Best of all you start with absolutely nothing and have to work your way up, not with gimmicky quests but through the best of your rpg skills put to use.
War on so many levels: From field battles to seiges your choices make a significant difference and each fight is unique because of that. You can parley with the enemy lord before battle, decide on a skirmish attack pre-battle or give a speech to boost morale, choose your troop position at the beginning and throughout battle, very quickly and fluidly I might add. Then's there's your personal contribution to the battle which was one area I was worried would be Dynasty Warrior-esque but was so happy to find the quite opposite. Yes the skills you build through the RPG aspects matter but you are still human and it shows. You can fall (unconcious) in battle just as easily as your other troops if you're not careful or not skillful or just unlucky and caught a javelin to the face. And that's it, the battle goes on without you because git gud. Sieges from outside or in are also unique experiences and can feel like storming the beaches of Normandy (with swords) or holding the Alamo (bows... you get it). You can take 1000 troops with you into a seige and count each one of them as they die by your side as you break into a fort of 500 that fights to the last man. Positioning, and tactics play a part throughout or at least will save you troops you don't have to retrain. War.... its FANTASTIC.
Fighting on so many levels: Each weapon you pick up will require you without equivocation to understand the mechanics of that specific weapon. Some are easier than others, some can be used on horseback and some you will hate because you can't get the hang of them. Depending on if you choose to play with weapon durability, you might find yourself mid battle scrambling to pick up whatever the last dead guy dropped to fight off attackers and you better know how to use whatever you just picked up. Siege defense against 500 and your quiver of 30 arrows just ran out? Learn to throw a javelin or hell use a rock sling. There are occasional tournaments events in major cities that force you to use different weapons at random for worthwhile prizes. None of your movements are predetermined either, meaning if you want to swing your sword from left to right you have to direct you character to do so. If you would like to thrust, block high, block right, swing left and overhead stab with your spear then you you have to do it all yourself. No button-mashing Assassin's Creed-like 30 hit combos, that'll get you killed. Just hardcore vikings fighting for their lives.
Soundtrack: There aren't many songs in VC, just over 20 mins of soundtrack.... and it is glorious. Go to youtube before you buy the game and check it out. The game transports you away and you're completely absorbed 5 hours later.
Okay so this review has gotten insanely long so I'll end on saying that the best part is the game stays challenging from beginning to end. Like you could literally be 1 faction city away from complete conquest and be more worried about if you have enough gold to pay your troops or enough food to last a seige. One sandbox campaign of Viking Conquest had over 1300 saves.....
Time. Well. Spent.

Now unlike last time where I outlined all the pros and cons of this game in a neat and organized manner, I will now be doing this quickly and poorly made as I am frustrated that I have to write this a second time.
Let's get into it, the gameplay is awful. (I played with a controller so the keys will be different but) this is a hack-and-slash where almost every combo (besides maybe one or two with the shoot button, although I tried and I couldn't find any) consists of one of these below:
x x x x
x y
x x y
x x x y
y
The game is made for fighting waves of enemies and that's it. That's all you do. I did look online to confirm this and every review I read pointed to the exact same thing. Almost (ALMOST) every enemy is similar, except with different amounts of damage, defense and movement speed. Now of course you're probably thinking: "Well that dosen't sound too bad, some of the best games I have ever played sound just like that", and I don't judge you cause that was exactly what I thought when I bought this pre-early access school project (the only title it's worthy of). This is a hack-and-slash that seems to be single-target-based (if you don't know what I'm talking about, play some Arkham Asylum), where the enemies come at you as if you are supposed to be playing it like a multi-target HaS (basically they all attack you at once trying to bring you down with pure force). Now what made the Arkham games fighting so good was not just that you had multiple combos using equipment (which this game is severly lacking mind you) but you also had seemless transition between enemies, you could easily go from beating down one enemy to countering the one behind you (if you want to dash to an enemy, you have to do it manually and the dash can easily go to far because collision detection). This does not work when the counter button is inconsistent (which it is, in RWBY) and they are all trying to attack you at once. If this were a multi-target-based game with basic AoE attacks the fighting could at least be semi-interesting but alas, it is complete♥♥♥♥♥♥ and as I said before the fighting is all you do in this game. The game is wave fighting and defending (with I believe one escort). THAT'S IT. UNDER THESE CIRCUMSTANCES, I'M GLAD THAT THIS GAME IS SHORT (I hear it's about 2-4 hours).
The sound, I was told by one friend that the music in this game was "Basically RWBY music for hack-and-slash" (-_-). Now, before I played this game I was a big fan of RWBY, (would it made people angry if they knew that my favourite episode was
?) and after this game, while I am still very excited for Volume 4 I no longer regularly watch RWBY episodes. The music for RWBY (the cartoon) is absolutly excellent, it rivals GoT for me (or at least, almost). While the music from the game isn't half bad (I actually had to re-listen to the 25 minute soundtrack after writing a line that I would have prefered screaming as the music) but the music becomes so terrible because it's not in line with anything. The music is simply for a faster paced game, while this game is slower than traffic in New York on the I-95 (I know, I've been there, it took about two hours to get through into normal traffic). The music is just so out of place that it's hurts, it almost gives me motion sickness from the distance between the two speeds. And please don't get me started on the sound effects. Between the stupid lines of the characters (who never interact with each other) who talk about how "Hey! We should open that door", the combat sound effects are atrocious. The weapons, and the enemies both have one sound effect each. THAT'S IT. ONE.
General: the game is ♥♥♥♥ing awful. I consider the GoT: the RPG to be better and the combat in that game was a turn-based system of attacking and blocking which took forever. I would rather walk across a 30 meter (32.8 yard) pool of Lego barefoot than complete this..."game".
As one of the Youtubers who put out a video explaining the problems of this game once said "The biggest joke about this game is the price tag, and I didn't even have to write that one".
Ps: I still can't believe I have to save this review in Word to make sure that it stays up.
Edit: Now, I know it's been a while since I played RWBY: GE and I have calmed down a bit since then (I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at the missed oppertunity, this is such a good IP and would make a tremendous game under the right conditions). This is both a good and a bad game. The big problem is that it's pretending to be something it's not. I made completely valid points for an important reason, the price. The price allows me to put a certain amount of expectation on this game. If this game were five dollars then maybe I would begin to favour it and maybe even stick with it until the end of the game. This game is competing in a market it has no right to be in. They got the cast to do voice work for this game (although I still get nightmares about the sound design) and they really did try to innovate (although I'm still coonfused about what this game wants to be).
To end this I will say this: I always compare this game to Game of Thrones: the RPG. Because while I am a huge fan of Game of Thrones, the game is missing too much for me to enjoy it. But, It's a game for super-fans. RWBY: GE is a game for all those who buy all the keychains, all the shirts, all those who would riot if Rooster Teeth were to shut down production of the show. So I guess what I am saying is this: I am looking at this from a gamer's perspective, if you are like me and you will review or recommend a game simply based on the game then you will not enjoy this. But if you see this game as a piece of RWBY and you have 27.99 to spare then go ahead, I don't intend to stop you. But know this; if you go through the first and second level and you aren't enjoying the game then you will not enjoy the rest.
Thank you and have a nice day

As a person whom is easily bored of games, I think this game is great.
I read all the negative reviews and was well prepared to find the game boring. (but at least support the creators or rwby).
Instead, I found I quite enjoyed it.  Admittedly, you can finish the campaign in a few hours, but if you get your multiplayer on with some friends you can still have a lot of fun ranking up!
Since all the negative reviews made a habbit of going through all the aspects of the game, I'll do the same.
Balance:  While some attacks are less useful than others, I think they're well balanced.  While a single hit combo is usually pretty weak, i've used it when trying not to kill something for a team mate, I'm glad it's there.  Most charaters have attacks that are more splash damage intensive, and there's usually a few attacks that are more useful in certain situations.  I wish you could increase the difficulty in multiplayer though, so you could increase the degree of the challenge... at the same time I still die from time to time anyway (because I can be quite careless).  Though I will say, I don't love blake's attacks.  I usually end up just using her two hit combo over and over, as well as her ranged from time to time and it gets kind of boring.
Graphics:  I think the game looks great.  Of higher what I'd call higher quality to most of theoriginal series, so I couldn't have expected more.  I suppose if I had one critisism it's the ship that picks you up at the end.  the inside looks pretty bad, and the metal for the entire thing looks odd and plasticy.
Audio:  I don't think it's especially repetitive.  I suppose more taunts would be cool, but the one present is good.  I LOVE yang's humorous puns through out the campaign so much you have no idea.  Even asside from that, they each have a few different terms they'll use during or after combat.  Ex. Yang will say (the things I can think of off the top of my head) "Taste my fists", "Did that tickle?", "Didn't even break a sweat".  When finding a realicks, she'll say "hello", "I found a thingy", and a couple other things I don't remember.  So I'd say there's sufficient variety and I'm quite very happy with the voice acting.  I suppose weis's talk of "Perfect form" gets old, as her taunt says it, and a couple of her battle dialogs do as well.
Content:  There's at least 12 unique opponents you fight, and there's 10 chapters to the campaign.  That's not the most ideal quantity of content; however, the game is still being developed, as you can see if you read their feed.  They're working on a new game mode, adding turrns, and also adding team JNPR.  The ranking system is a decent way to prolong gameplay as well, I myself am only half way through earning rank 3, though I think it'd be cool if you gained a small advantage for each rank.  Or perhaps you could earn an extra starting skillpoint for each character every 2 ranks, I'd like to beable to get a few more abilities, but realisically speaking, i don't think that would make you EXCEEDINGLY more powerful.
So there you have it.  Overall, I think it's a great game.  If the devs never realsed another update, I'm sure I won't get as many hours out of it as I have out of some games; however, I'd say it was worth the money and if you're a fan of the series, then I'd say it's definately worth the money... unless you know 25$ was like a years worth of income, then maybe not.
EDIT:  Now that I think about it I do have one issue, my shift key doesn't work so i can't sprint and stuff.  Windows 10, logitec keyboard.  I'd love it if that could be fixed.

For a free, early access game this is looking pretty good so far. I enjoy flying around and defeating other dragons with the use of missiles and plasma cannons. I even went through a phase of playing this game often and in doing so, I noticed I was playing with the same players over and over. Even the leaderboards contain mostly players I have seen and played with before. After playing against some of the same people a few times, it can actually feel like two players have something against each other and begin trying to kill each other more than the other players. As with many games, you can hurt players on your team which can lead to you being betrayed (this normally only happens when there are no enemies and your team seems to get bored easily) or accidentally hit. Of course this problem lies within player attitude and not the game itself. I can say though, that the lack of enemies (or teammates for that matter) seems to be down to the game seemingly having no team balancing which results in a lot of unfair matches.
The flight feels quite nice and fluid for the most part but it can be hard to determine the scale and distance of certain objects in the environment. So when you are flying around and you notice you're coming quite close to something large, you usually try to turn sharply or pull up which is difficult sometimes as the dragon seems to want to almost drift and keep moving forward as opposed to just sharply and swiftly pulling up. Most of the time you end up crashing into said object which makes you more vulnerable to attack.
The turret/weapon system is great. It features a number of weapons and items to help you in battle such as plasma turrets (default weapon/fire type), missiles and a special attack that is performed with the R key if I can remember correctly. Most of the special attacks are short range and have what seems to be a spherical radius. In my opinion, the Ogre's (big green, tank-like dragon) special attack is overpowered, since he can stun you and keep you in one spot then use his vast amount of health and firepower to quickly dispose of you.
Anyway, my next point about the turret and weapons system is that the crosshair seems to take a very long time to catch up with where your dragon is looking which can be annoying when you have a clear shot ready but your crosshair is nowhere to be seen. Earlier I mentioned items. These items include stamina refill, weapon cooldown, mines (that float in the air) and a smoke screen (I may have missed something from the list). These also have a cooldown period but can give you an edge in battle and instantly regenerate upon respawning after death. The mines and smoke screen can be good items to use and can make a great combo as you can drop a mine if you're being followed, then drop the smoke screen which will blind your enemy and lead them to fly into the mine. The smoke screen can also hide you when you're on low health and allow you to escape. Your dragon can be given a speed boost (shift key) which takes stamina rather quickly but (if you have it equipped) you can use your stamina refill to give your dragon a second boost.
I did notice that the models and sounds seem to be based off other games/movies...
The Inara - Ikran (Avatar) (Similar sounds too)
The Fury - Toothless (HTTYD/2) (Also similar sounds)
The Vampire (mainly it's head) reminds me of creatures from the old game Altered Beast but may just be a coincidence.
Tiamat is given the same name as the bat queen from Darksiders (perhaps this dragon was given this name instead of the vampire since it would have looked too close to Tiamat). Again, perhaps it's just coincidence or I'm just looking into it too much.
This game is very team based with nice graphics and a great idea behind it. It's a great game for passing the time and having fun and can actually be quite competitive. When you have balanced teams, it can be very enjoyable. If you enjoy team based, dragon flying, weapon firing action then this game is for you. I recommend trying this game and seeing what you think. I may have written a bunch of bad points (which I seem to find it hard not to with most things) but I do really like this game.

This game is amazing. (edit since first writing this review: Loved this game. I'm back for another round and currently playing it again. I still haven't purchased anything extra - not a single "micro-transaction". Seriously great game!)
I've been enjoying this series since the original, way back in the early 00's. I only have 10 hours in Mankind Divided thus far, but I have been enjoying it thoroughly. One thing that I'm super impressed with is the fact that there are no load screens in between areas. Deus Ex has always been notorious for long loading screens. Apparently that is a thing of the past.
I enjoyed the previous title, but I feel like the story telling in this one is much more interesting - at the very least, more immersive. It's still pretty heavy-handed with the naturals vs augs theme, but it does a much better job of drawing you into the story, so you actually care about the characters you meet, and the story as a whole. For example, I spent a good amount of time on a side quest, which dealt with forged papers that augs need to traverse the city. That side quest alone was multi-faceted, and I feel like there were many ways to go about dealing with the situation (or it could be ignored all together).
I've read a lot of "interesting" reviews on here with people talking about the end of the game, and they only have like 22 hours in on it. I don't feel like it's possible to fully enjoy this game if you just run through it from beginning to end like that. There are so many things to explore and people to talk to and side quests to complete. Do yourself a favor and take your time with this game. Explore the world, and find every item out there.
The aug system in Mankind Divided is pretty damn cool too. It's basically like it always has been, but with a little twist. I would say that describes the game as a whole honestly. They've tweaked and streamlined the game perfectly, without dumbing it down or changing it all together (I have my finger pointed at you Bethesda).
To address the "elephant in the room". I hate the idea of micro transactions. pay to win games upset the hell out of me. I did not pre-order this game. I don't do that ever. I have not and will not pay for anything in-game. With that said; I haven't felt the need to either. It's absolutely not pushed upon you in any way at all. There is a shop button on the main menu, which can be completely ignored. I have looked at it, and it seems to me like paid cheating. If there is someone out there foolish and lazy enough to buy in-game items with real money, that is just something I just don't understand. Either way, I can't see giving this amazing game a bad review for something you can completely ignore with no ill effects.
Edit since completing the game: The ending is more of a cliffhanger than I would like, but it's pretty intriguing nevertheless. I enjoyed this installment thoroughly though, and it is absolutely worthy of the Deus Ex name. I do not say that lightly either. The original is quite possibly my favorite video game of all time. I still have no idea what folks are talking about with micro-transactions. There was no time where I had to buy anything in game (nor would I). I would say the only thing that I found annoying at all were the cut scenes in between major areas. They were repetetive and lazy at best, but that is a very minor gripe.

I'm really enjoying the playthrough thus far, but I do have some gripes to mention.
I commend them for releasing two patches before the weekend hit — I really do.  However, I would've highly preferred they just push the release date back a couple weeks.  Game developers in general are really starting to forget what the term "finished product" means, and such forgetfulness has been an absolute plague within the industry as of late.  Of particular note, Eidos should know intimately well by now — from past exposure and pronounced player sentiment over the years — that people DO NOT want game developers making their mouse x-y sensitivity choices for them.  This was inexcusable, and since they were obviously capable of adding separate X and Y sensitivity sliders to the menu less than a week after launch, it seems super-sloppy to me that they just weren't in there to begin with.  Also, DX12 support should have been included AT LAUNCH.  It's just another reason why the release date should've been September 5th.
Additionally..  I had some Day One Edition items (Praxis kit, Elite combat rifle) simply VANISH because I loaded a past save.  Seriously Eidos?  You need to re-tool that little gem of a concept, because it's half-baked and flat-out sh*tty.
Other than that, it's typical Deus Ex fare, which is a good thing.  Respectable visuals, great cinematics, highly story-driven..  These are the things I expect from a Deus Ex release, and Eidos has done a great job of sating those expectations thus far.

Even though I can vouch that this game was balanced as if the shop didn't exist it's still a slippery slope towards terrible gameplay design we can expect in future products. You can bet that the next entry in the series will make praxis points impossible to get or worse... you might find that Jensen has limited "daily energy" that you can replenish by buying 'gems/cells' for real money.
Do not be fooled, it happened countless times before on the mobile market and if we don't let our voices be heard it will happen on PC as well.

This game was amazing when it came. Way ahead of its time then. Now, several years later it still holds its ground and is in my humble opinion still THE BEST stealth game available today. However, that is a standpoint that may not be shared by everyone. I will try to tell you below, why I think it is and explain my thoughts around that.
Lets not ignore the elephant in the room here. The games graphics ARE outdated by todays standards. But I believe that graphics isn't everything. Not that I prefer "ugly games". I'm just saying that a game can be absolutely amazing despite not having 4K high res modern graphics. If it has a story that holds true to the world the game takes place in, and that story is interesting enough, I won't be able to actually tell you how the graphics were without starting the game only to take a closer look at the graphics. Thief gold is that kind of game.
But there is a partial cure for that and that cure is called Tfix 1.25c and is an unofficial patch for Thief 1/ Thief gold that uses the NewDark engine. It enables higher resolutions among other things. If paired with the HD texture mod you end up with something that looks less dated than the original, but at the cost of the vibrant colours the original textures have.
However graphics and visual is but a small part of a game. It's in the story and characters where Thief gold really shines. The story and game world feels very authentic and the mood of the game world is solid throughout the game. When the game was first released, such imersive story was unheard of outside role playing games. The story really draws you in.
This is a really hard game and it really doesn't hold your hand with things like mission icons and flashing direction arrow in the HUD telling you where to go. YOU play the game and YOU need to know what to do and remember where to go in a map. The map function in game shows you Garrets own hand drawn map with field notes on.
I think that plays a really big role in why I love this game to death. It is meant to be hard and challenging. If you have a mission pointer á la skyrim hanging in mid air in front of you, telling you where to go, you really don't need to explore to get from point A to B.
If you like hard games with a steep learning curve that is rewarding to those who manage to get over the difficulty hump, then this game is for you. If you don't have pationece to stop and consult your map in game to plan the route to take by yourself, then you will most likely not like this game.

After hundres of hours both in the FPS and the RTS (=the strategic) war map game as a German, I have to rewrite my review.
When I started, I grinded together with my brother for good equipment and first RTS units. It took very long, but as we had some aims, we did it. We wanted to have enough troops to start own battles, also some recon vehicles (nice team vehicle). The grinding itself was not always fun, as often in F2P games. YOu can get things much faster by paying.
Now I have about 15 soldiers and 10 RTS units - but the last 3 months the game collapsed. Most German clans stopped playing, thus each war round lasts about 2 days, with the US crushing Germany. Only on the eastern front, there is still german activity.
Main reason for this is imho a very unbalanced game. Three factions (GE, US, SU) play against each other, but Germany is placed in the middle, with the same ressources as all other factions. The weapons of GE were nerfed often in the last years (to compensate for on average more skilled players in the GE faction?). Both US and SU have superior, medium range full auto weapons that actually were hardly ever or never used in WWII. On top, GE has more players active in the war game, therefore by a so-called "underdog bonus" both US and especially SU receive a massive bonus on ressources gain. Of course thats not fun as GE player, and many clans just stopped playing. When I started, GE was doing well but lost always in the end. Now there is no resistance anymore and US just steamrolls to victory with ease.
Last but not least, the game lacks WWII feeling. The more experienced the players in a battle, the more the game looks like a battle ISIS vs ISIS: a handful of jeeps with MGs rush at a base, all players with full auto weapons jump off, capture the point. Repeat. Nobody (except snipers) use bolt action rifles, no trenches or bunker battles, no artillery...

Good game all in all. Rather short, even with the expansion, as two playthtoughs have only been 16 hours, but I thuroughly enjoyed those playthroughs. The game feels more like a story than a game, and if that's your thing, then you're in luck. You get plenty of choices to keep you on your toes, and I'll admit, I cried a few times in some of the romance options. What can I say, I'm a softie.
Art: 8/10 - Beautiful game, especially for the kind of game. Kind of sucks that there's no animations, as in some situations they would be alot better than character portraits standing there with text, but it's all really well drawn.
Characters: 8/10 - Solid characters with believable motives.
Gamplay: 7/10 - Basic gameplay, but manages to be strategic.
Sound: 5/10 - I'll admit, 90% of the time I played muted. The songs aren't bad, but they're repeated frequently.
Story: 9/10 - Enthralling story, kind of predictable at some points, but ends up being really well done. Not to mention all of the choices you get.
All in all, I give it an 8/10. If they make a sequel, I'll buy it in a heart beat.

The comparisons to Dragon Age are what made me buy this game. However, it isn't nearly as polished and lacks the twists and depth of DAO had. I wasn't expecting it to be perfect, but it certainly fell short of expectations.
Most of the characters in this game don't have varied dialogue styles. As a result, they come off as having been written by the same person. Rather than having distinguishing characteristics, they seem very archetype based and lack further depth. Dialogue choices don't really give the player a feeling of control or influence in the game, unlike in DA:O.
The gameplay is largely uninteresting. The game has two parts: dialogue and encounters. The former tends to feel forced-- some of the dialogue scenes are better written than others, but overall one tends to feel railroaded and loses very little skipping through dialogue scenes to the end.
Encounters are largely predictable, especially once having settled into a routine. Turn based dice rolling with few animations makes encounters a matter of how fast you can spam commands to get through them. There is no overhead positioning strategy, simply front and back rows and a few types of combination attacks.
For the price, I would say this game is not worth it. If it came down, it might be.

I hate overly positive reviews. The entire review scale on most websites has been shifted because these incarnations of Pollyanna insist on giving everything 10s. Just the thought that 3/5 or 5/10 isn't considered "average" makes me want to extract vengeance on the endless parade of perfect scores. Now that I have adequately set myself up as hypocrite of the year, let's begin the review.
This game is about Loren, who happens to be the princess of the Amazons (yes, I am Captain Obvious, and I'm going for promotion - I like the sound of "Major Obvious"). Going against all gaming tropes, she doesn't get kidnapped, nor do you play as her. Loren: The Amazon Princess begins with the titular character decapitating some training dummies, then berating her slaves for failing to provide more. She is then quickly informed that her mother (the Queen) did not return and is presumed dead. Loren rejects this and embarks on a mission to save her mother, but the captain manages to force Loren to take the Amazon's most prized slave - that's you.
This game's greatest strength is its characters. Sure, Loren may be a terrifying-dual-sword-wielding-badass, but she's also never left the citadel before, and it shows. Within an hour of starting the game, she will have demanded to speak to the Queen of a republic, choked a bartender for the crime of ignoring her, and referred to the Amazons as better than all other nations. Other characters are no less entertaining, as you meet characters like Draco Firestarter - a fire mage who likes to start fires (am I a major yet?) and manages to cause the rest of the party to burst out laughing every time he talks, or Dora the
nicest thief in town - she teaches that the best way to make friends is to give them money.
This does lead me to one of this game's few flaws - while the dialogue is well written all around, you have little insight into what your character will say. Every dialogue choice you make is one of four options - Joking, Friendly, or Forceful - and occasionally Romance. While the latter always progresses that character's romance, the first three aren't very clear on what you're about to say. For example, early in the game you arrive in a nearby city and Loren insults it. Your response? Joking, Friendly, or Forceful, without any indication on whether an option agrees with Loren or not. The only surefire way is to save before you choose, then pick every option and see which you'd prefer.
The graphics are a matter of taste - this game isn't meant to melt your GPU to your motherboard. Many of the reviews seem to hate the graphics, I personally enjoy the graphics. The only graphical issue is with a few of the backgrounds - I noticed stairs leading up to a castle tower looked exactly the same as stairs to an inn's rooms. Minor, but a little strange. Overall though, I'd suggest looking at screenshots and seeing for yourself if you like the graphics. I really don't suggest deciding to purchase (or not) a game based on graphics.
The gameplay is fairly straightforward if you've played RPGs before - everyone is either a warrior, a thief, or a mage, and you've got Strength, Skill, and Will to put points in. Certain enemies might be weak against or resistant to certain elements (you used typhoon on fire demon! It's Super Effective!). However, there are a few gameplay elements that aren't self-explanatory, and they aren't explained to you either. For example - dual-wielding carries a penalty (except on Loren, who has a skill to remove this penalty). However, if you wield a dagger in the offhand, you aren't penalized - the game never actually tells you this. It also doesn't bother clarifying stats such as "Attack" , "Damage" (aren't they the same thing?) and "threshold" (I still have no clue that this does).
The vast majority of modern games have a few places at which you can choose a different path - and it almost always comes across as a failed attempt to get the player to play the game again. This is one of the few games where it actually works - once I finished the game, I was ready to start over with another character right then and there. Very few games have such replay value, but many of the choices you make actually give you a different story for a while.
This is one of those rare titles that actually appeals to gamers that care about characters and story, rather than running 4096x2160 at 120fps, or shooting everything you see with generic guns and getting racial slurs in return. If this type of game doesn't appeal to you, then go download
. But if you care the slightest about deep characters or a game that can pull you into its world, then I can't recommend this more.

I wished for a 'thumb to side' as this game actually has some moments of enjoyment but they just can't outweight the disappointment, all here is just to basic to be seen good like the stats:
You have 3 stats:
Strength
Skill
Will

Then this priced thing of you being the servant (read: slave) of the hero... well again it changes exactly... nothing
Oh exept that instead of '[PLAYERNAME] takes the party to X' it is 'Loran (your mistress) says that you go there', on most occasions you can just choose what -she- says, so there again is no real change exept for the change in the dialogues...
Which brings me to the next point: The text, in a game that is half a visual novel you would expect its text part to be the strong point of the game, this text is mediocre maybe, but not more.
The story initself is as clichee as it can get, read some other reviews, when you want to know more about this, because i find that they describe the story pretty well, in short:
As clichee as it can get,
'Kill X to make me trust you' like quests for progression
'Hardcore role-playing games with replay value are becoming rarer in today's age of simplification for the masses. There's fundamentaly no depth in it, just choose the attack with most damage and start killing the baddies.
Again this is not a bad game per se but its not worth its money as is, haven't the DLC hence I don't know if this changes some of this.
EDIT: Forgot to add that the dialogue choices are annoying at best since there are only three... in every dialogue... remember those old games where your character seemingly hadn't enough brain to say anything other than variations of 'yes' or 'no' with no room for something like 'well cool but could we instead do [OPTION 3]' or something like that? Now you've got 'Joking' 'Friendly' and 'Forceful' which are sometimes totally unintuitive. Imagine: You see your master arguing with someone, then both for some reason turn to the slave to ask for his/her opinion, since the argument started to get very heated you should think that 'Joking' brings your character to do something funny to loose up the situation... well no it could be that you just joke ABOUT either of the persons involved in the argument (read: A your master... probably not a good idea, or B: For example a major of some town... also not a good idea to provoke him... as a slave), I'm not saying that this happens everytime you cllick on joking its just that sometimes the result is just so far away from what you'd expect from that option.
Ofcourse you can just use your mousewheel to scroll back in the conversation but still this seems so annoying.
Lastly the 'romance scenes' for that you should read abundantgrace's or Striker Eureka's reviews as I think they describe them pretty good.
TL:DR:
Is it a good game? Hardly albeit quite enjoyable at moments
Is it a decent game then? Pretty much so, expect nothing to write home about but still you should be able to enjoy it somewhat
Is it worth the money? Thats a though question depending if its your cup of tea, if you are curious about buying iti wait for a sale and grab it there.

Moderately fun, but in no way worth $25--it's just too amateurishly done.  Buy it when it goes to 40% off or better.
Good points:
- The combat system is pretty good for its type, and I enjoyed trying to figure out the best abilities, combos, and strategies.  Don't believe the bit that says to choose Moderate Difficulty if you have RPG experience--crank it to Hard.  A good number of the battles seem to be scaled to average party level, so you don't have to worry about swapping in someone underpowered.
- A bunch of the character dialogue is really amusing, mostly anything involving Draco or Dora.  Other dialogue was occasionally cheesy but usually good.  I wasn't bothered by the Joking-Friendly-Forceful choices not telling you what was actually going to be said, partly because they almost never affect the end result of a conversation and partly because I eventually figured out that you could use the mouse wheel to scroll back and pick a different option as many times as you like.
- You can save/load pretty much anywhere and there are a giant number of savegame slots.  Alas that you cannot tag descriptions onto them.
Bad points:
- The documentation/help is limited and in at least one instance (the combat help) is outright wrong.  Example that irritated me right off: if you play a Thief you're asked to choose among skills that inflict status ailments without any way to determine what the ailments actually do.
- It needs another pass or three of heavy editing.  The writing has a lot of grammar and phrasing and usage errors, and the storyline sometimes suffers from plot inconsistency and obvious logic issues.  In a story-driven game that relies so heavily on text, these were really annoying.   (It also has a lot of ridiculously unlikely things happen just because they're plot-convenient, but that's kind of par for the course in this genre.)
- Better branch tracking would be good too--there are two main ways to get through chapter one, but there are parts of chapter two that assume you went one way and were seriously confusing to me because I went the other.
- I am not sure why the game has gear with mage-only stats that mages can't wear.  Maybe to drain gold from the unwary?
- When you finally get to see a second drawing of a character in Ch 4, it's only 50/50 whether they look the same as the first drawing.  (As a related good-ish point, it's kind of amazing what they can do with only one drawing and some variant facial expressions.)
I could talk about the outfits, but...  If you've looked at any of the screenshots then you know exactly what you're getting.  Whether they're a good or bad point is up to you.

Loren is a shining example of how you don't need a massive budget or an overly complex system to create a wonderful game.  Even though the events are mainly text-based and combat is a simple as it gets, Loren managed to provide the user with hours upon hours of fun.
Mainly it does this through a combination of excellent characters with deep tactical combat.  The amount of sub-classes and skills sets are quite impressive.  Even though heavy grinding isn't a requirement, I found myself doing a lot of it just because I wanted to unlock higher level skills.  It also optimizes the team concept by forcing the player to utalize the best combination of characters on the battlefield that mutually support each other.  For example, the theif class has limited effectiveness against healthy enemies.  But inflict a negative status (like poison or confusion) on an enemy and suddenly your theif will a turn into top-quality killing machine against them.  As such, it's important to team them up with characters who specialize in status abnormality inflicting attacks.  Likewise, there are all sorts of ways to tip the odds in your favor, such as using your front line brutes to absorb damage aimed at your weak mages in the back row.
All this is aiding by outstanding enemy AI.  In fact, it's some of the best AI I've ever seen in a turn based, back row/front row RPG.  There is nothing random about the enemy attack or defense patterns.  They will target your weakest characters in the back row with consecutive waves of long range attacks, mercilessly pummel your most badly injured soldiers in the front row, and assign guards to absorb the damage their own mages and healers when you start to significantly hurt them.
And of course the main thing that makes this game work is the excellent amount of diverse characters.  They are all quite diverse and unique, and you'll find yourself caring about all of them.  They have a wide range of different skills on the battlefield and different personalities off it, keeping the game immersive and entertaining the whole way through.
There are a few key weak points.  One is that that amount of characters you get (14) is disproportionate to the number of troops who can take part in battle (6).  It is quite frustratining to have to leave over half your team on the "sidelines" in combat.  Not only that, but the fact that Loren and your playing character have to be involved in almost every fight besides random encounters meant I found myself doing a lot of extra grinding just to keep everyone's levels up to par.  Thankfully this is somewhat mitigated by a large number of "iron man" events where you face a series of consecutive battles without recovering stamina or health between each one, thus forcing you to use your "backup" characters as well as your primary ones.
Also, while the Amazon culture of Loren is quite unique and interesting, the rest of the game is just an endless series of fantasy cliches:  Dwarves with long beards and big axes, Wizards with long beards, white robes, and big staffs, Elven assasins, a dark lord returned from the dead who seeks to conquer the world for some obscure reason.  Don't ever think of starting a drinking game based on every cliche you find in this game that you've seen before, or you'll become an instant alcoholic.
Loren the Amazon Princess isn't for everyone.  You need to really be into turn based combat, have an active imaginatino to make up for the lack of animation and graphics, and have a high tolerance for generic fantasy worlds full of Elves, Dwarves, and Humans antagonizing each other.  But if those apply to you, then you really can't go wrong with this title.

As someone whose first Tekken experience was from Tekken 7; I just have to respond to all the reviews that do not recommend the game because it "lacks any sort of proper tutorial."
, but to say that there are zero resources that show you the mechanics, moves or techniques to play the game is a gross understatement. If we took at a look at the game itself, it gives you Practice Mode and Move Lists. You might say "That's it?...." Yup, you don't need ANYTHING else to learn the basics. It's got sparring CPU's, move recording, stage selection, side selection, damage data, simple "frame data" (a very simplified, not so accurate view), and a whole lot of move lists.
Ah, but you do want to be everyones punching bag.. That's where you friendly Tekken community comes in. There are multitudes of online videos and guides made by good, great and amazing Tekken players around the world. They'll teach you backdashing, crouch cancelling, move buffering, throws, throw breaks, and every other neat tip, trick, technique you never knew even existed. I've put over 150 hours into this game on steam, ps4 and arcade cabinet and I (sadly) still suck, BUT I at least know enough about the game to follow along with what professional players do in a match and I can say that I'm not the worst at it among my friends who play it.
Now about the actual game
If you've never played a fighting game, I'd suggest playing some on a PSP emulator and watchig some vids to see if it's right for you.

OMG.... Yes.  Simple easy goodness.  Choose your own adventure at its purest.  This game "is like an onion", it don't look great but omg is it good and what are all these layers?!  And like being on a quest with an ogre, there is no hand holding.  Well..maybe just i tiny bit ;)
Basically its an iron-age mercenary survival simulator.  Rogue-ish, it'll knock you down but don't give up cuz you're never out. My most successful playthrough started with me being beaten and captured 10 different times within my first week of being a freelance merc, then many more times the following weeks.  Then i escaped ran to the nearest city, happened to be a tournament in town, and i won it betting all my money on myself.  I then bought a bakery and have been a successful bussiness owner since, with two more shops in the works.....thats right, my story has evolved into 'Conan the barbarian bought a bread store' lol.  I travel the land 40 deep (ragtag group from all nations) buying bread supplies and killing people for money, ima badass breadmaker and adoring every second of it.
The graphics are from the late 90's but that's when i was coming up so i have zero issue with that, especially when there's hundreds of units on the field going berzerk and there's not even a hint of a blink of lag with settings at max.  The biggest turn off of PC gaming for me is lag, so i cherish games of this magnitude that run (period).
This scratches that Skyrim itch like when you scratch your back with an actual back-scratcher, nailed it.
DEVS wish i could outfit my units not just the named mercs but that just may be a way of making their leveling up more meaningful, so maybe answered my own lol.
As i said in essence its kind of a simulator so it can be 'grindy' even though that word has no real meaning any more.  The grind is the game and you do it almost however you want.
Combat is third person and surprisingly satisfying even though i normally hate mouse combat controls.  Although it does have that downfall of mouse control that is it can be over-intuitive to the point it feels under-intuitive with the micro direction changes from moving a mouse.  But everything else overshadows this to a point that I can't call it a negative.
Overworld travel is done with small markers on a huge map with the 'you move the rest of the world moves' dynamic, if you're standing still its paused.  It reminds me of traveling in Fallout 1 except you can see how the map looks and you can see others moving around you before you encounter them.
It successfully cuts down one of the worst grinds in video gaming, the in-town grind.  You just hit tab to go to the town menu and instant port to where you want to go like shops or your own business haha.  There are still important quest givers in the streets but as soon as you find them and talk to them you hit tab and jump to wherever you need to go from there.  The towns are minimalist so don't expect Fallout or Skyrim level of visual social interactivity, there's a handful of roamers and the rest are 'quest givers' or potential 'quest givers' or shop owners.

Two brothers. In a van. And then a meteor hit. And they ran as fast as they could...
All Rick and Morty references aside, this game is a great buy, especially at the current sale price of like... what, a dollar? Usually when I see 'overwhelmingly positive' at a price point like this it's sort of an auto-buy for me, so despite reading about a fairly short playthrough time (~3-4 hours) I picked it up and was very pleased. *(note: try to get a controller for playing this)*
So this game isn't technically demanding or particularly difficult at all, but its artwork/visuals and soundtrack are very artistically combined to create a unique experience that is very immersive. This was probably one of the biggest compliments regarding the game for me, so if these are things you don't care a lot about, take that into account. The game is linear, but the feeling of exploration was still largely intact for me via the attention to detail and diversity of environments you encounter. The unique two-character control scheme was also an interesting mechanic, and kept relatively fresh throughout the game.
The storyline was basic but adequate.  While the plot is not reliant on any actual dialogue (the language spoken is gibberish) it serves as the overarching motivation for a journey through an unknown, mountainous, fairy-tale world with progressively picturesque scenery and stylistic revelations.  The  journey's progression left me thinking almost a little of The Hobbit atmospherically, although your take my vary.
Lots of people say the story is very emotional - I agree, although there weren't any moments that made me cry, as some people have mentioned, because I'm a real rough & tough guy.
Tldr; Great buy if looking for short yet immersive/artistic/emotional experience that is technically forgiving, novel and easily accessable (although you will probably want to have a controller).

Thief, as a game, is the jumping off point from where many stealth games start. You've got it all. The Loveable Jerk that is your player character, Garrett, who's grim but not so much you feel like a modern Batman comic, and sarcastic but not annoying. You've got dark, dirty streets and polished noblehouses. You've got large, twisted maps and levels, but not so much you're constantly getting lost, if you're smart. You've got amusing conversations around the corner from this dumb guard or that oblivious servant. A lot of things that are tropes in more modern stealth games started off here.
Now, I've played Dishonored on the hardest difficulty, clean hands and ghost and all, so I'm already thoroughly experienced with the stealth genre. I thought I could just jump in at Expert and do my thing, right? Wrong. This game is much harder than modern stealth games. There is no minimap, the puzzles can sometimes be obtuse and vague, you're a weak and squishy thief who can barely carry a sword, and your enemies can slaughter you in four hits even on the easiest difficulty. Needless to say, play on Easy your first time around. Forgo your ego, trust me. Finishing a level doesn't lose its sense of accomplishment, even on the lowest difficulty.
So do I recommend this game? Absolutely, but with a few warnings:
~This game is difficult. Even if you think you're good at stealth games, at least play the first few levels on easy, just to at least get familiar with the games' method of going about its stealth.
~There are zombies in this game, and they are obscenely overpowered. Don't try to fight them, unless you like wasting valuable water arrows and expensive holy water.
~Most enemies will kill you extremely fast, even on Easy. You can't fight them. You should only fight when cornered, and Garrett has stated himself a few times he doesn't like killing.
~Speed potions are a waste of your time except on Expert.
~There is NO MINIMAP, and the map only highlights blue to show where you vaguely are. You'll have to manually determine where you are on the map, and that's if you have a detailed one. Sometimes all you get is Timmy's dinner table scrawlings.
~Wear headphones. I mean it.

The game reminds me of the Nippon Ichi SRPG's (only not strategy).  The interface is very bear-bones, and the whole game basically boils down to "fight battle" -> "read talking head story" -> "buy stuff in town" -> "grind a few subquests" -> "fight story battle" -> "dating sim."  Theres nothing other than "in town" screen, "in camp" screen, the battles, and the relationship game.
All this I'd be OK with normally.  I loved the old Nippon Ichi SRPG's.  The stripped down format can shed off some of the unneccessary drags from rpgs and let you focus on the core of the gameplay.  But with Loren TAP, that's not really such a good thing.  The battle system is a very generic RPG style "front row/back row" style fight, with nothing really new or interesting.  Not only is it unoriginal and is almost completely unanimated, but its fairly easy as well.  I beat the first three bosses, and all of the scrub fights in between, and only ever had someone die once, and they were ressurected by the next turn.  I never came anywhere close to losing a fight.... on hard.
The story line is mediocre, and the romance/dating sim is lame.  The whole point of a Dating sim/relationship system is to pick your dialog options carefully given what you know about the characters personality.  In this game, you only get the options "Joking", "Friendly", or "Forceful."  And since you don't know what is actually going to be said, its a total crapshoot.  I often picked what I thought would be the right option, only to have my character say something that was the total opposite of what I wanted him too.  To me, that makes the whole process of a Dating sim totally broken.

I have nearly 2 hours in so far. I would like to start by saying that I have never played a visual novel based game before, and I generally try to avoid reading a lot of dialogue in games. Usually, I just like going in for the action, the loot, etc.

Once you start playing the game you just cannot put it down. The story and character interaction brings a lot of curiosity and entertainment.
Despite the awesome story and great character interaction, the game also has a fun and simple combat system, a nice GUI, and a fun leveling system. Although I haven’t got far enough, the loot seems to look promising based on screenshots.
In conclusion, I rate Loren The Amazon Princess a 10/10 based on what I have experienced. There are very few games that will capture my interest enough to read all of the dialogue, and this game is one of them. Great story, great characters, and a fun rpg system. 10/10!

This is exactly everything I've always wanted out of a medieval fantasy salesman simulator. It does a million things I've always wanted to see happen in the same game, at least at a shallow level, and makes mundanity out of a striking fantasy world, where a Legendary Relic Weapon is just another item you can stock on your shelf for a marked up price.
Unfortunately the game, despite being "complete", isn't too detailed and doesn't have more than the bare minimum amount of variety in everything it offers you, so whether you enjoy it or not depends largely on how long you can put up with the painfully slow progression to unlock what little additional content the skill tree offers you. And how many times you can go around forcing weed on everyone who isn't a Warrior class before you get bored of it.
Here are some specifics:
+ You can badger everyone who passes by to buy something from you even when they weren't planning to stop by your shop.
+ Every night while your shop is closed you have unlimited time to make plans, spend your money, and fiddle with the details of your shop in any way you please.
+ You have a large variety of furnishings to lay your main wares out on and can set any price for each item.
+ If customers don't like your price, they'll misplace the items instead of putting them back nicely or resort to trying to steal it, rather than just ignoring your shop.
+ You gain skill points for completing sales quests and leveling up an exp bar that increases with every buying or selling transaction, and can apply those to dramatically extending the game with all kinds of independent modular add-ons:
• Want additional goods to sell to wizards, rogues, and druids? Unlock it!
• Want to grow your own vegetables for sale? You got it!
• Want to own a pub down the street? No problem!
• Is dealing with so many customers overwhelming? Unlock steampunk helper robots to handle all the basic tasks for you!
• Want to have to defend your shop against occasional barbarian assaults? That's an option too!
+ Your achievements are reflected in-game as little trophies and statues in your home. Some of the trophies from shop quests even grant permanent boons.
It still has some odd bugs and quirks still which you should know about. I haven't found anything game-breaking yet, but there's quite a bit to deal with.
- Some items dropped on the ground are invisible sometimes (ninja stars on the floor of your shop are rendered inside the floor, helper droids freshly dug out of the trash are invisible because of the way their model works or something)
But the GUI shows you when your crosshair is over something invisible like that anyway, so it's not a problem.
- The "I took your freedom" achievement didn't get awarded to me until it was awarded as part of the "Phat Loot" achievement for some reason. (Which wasn't until my third barbarian attack, unlike the achievement description...)
- Many GUI menus and interfaces will actually overlap each other and bug out, eg. you can accidentally open your order menu under item inspection, or misclick on the helper bot menu and end up with your mouse locked to aiming your camera around again with it still open.
But thankfully the escape menu clears all the in-game menus.
- Pressing the "save" button in the in-game escape menu unpauses the game with the menu still open for some reason.
- During barbarian attacks the civilians are continuously running in every direction (they don't just go hide somewhere like they should), making it exceedingly difficult to tell where most of the enemies are until they've already reached your shop entrance and begun attacking you.
- Customers who are in your shop while you're attacking a dead body (ex. a thief who is already dead and you swing your sword/axe one time too many) sort of freeze up in place playing the same scream sound like fifty times on top of itself before finally running in fear ??? Freaky.
- Helper bots moving through you lift you off the ground momentarily because they're solid I guess? Weird.
Again, these are all minor issues that are really easy to deal with, so if that's okay to you, it's a decent game.
Other nitpicks
- Planting crops requires extreme precision for some reason, making it difficult to do quickly.
- There's an extremely low amount of content to begin with and every major unlock grants only two or three new things to play with for absurd skill points requirements. There isn't really enough here to warrant taking more than 8 hours to play through, but you're stuck selling weed for a very long time to feel like you've moved beyond simply brushing the surface of the game.
- The crafting system is completely opaque and will eat your items every time you try randomly guessing a 4 item combination until you either look up a guide or pay an absurd amount of gold to an NPC who unlocks all the recipes for you.
- The combat system is shallow -- There is only one thing in the game that doesn't immediately fall over dead from any single hit from the shopkeeper. All alternate weapons are purely cosmetic. It's meant to be that way.
- Gardening is an active activity that consists of planting a seed, waiting 30 seconds and then immediately harvesting everything. It seems to be based on the same system used for grilling meat, so if you leave your garden for even one full minute, all of your crops will already be spoiled and  useless (somehow). So instead of taking several days to grow a hearty batch of crops, you just sort of end up doing it during build phase and avoid doing it if at all possible while customers are out and about causing havoc in your shop?

I feel like this game could be more than it is, but even as it exists currently it's a really enjoyable shop management game. There are other ones out there, but they're not really managing a shop, specifically. Others are more JRPG or just indirect management, like Recettear and Holy Potatoes! It definitely scratches a management itch that other games don't.

Let's Review Brutal Legend
This game surprised me in many ways, i always saw the game back in the day, but the Rock/Music based game never appealed to me. When i got Brutal Legend i decided to give it a try. And let me tell you, i cant stop playing it.
Pros : - Its has all the major Metal Rock songs in it, making a kickass soundtrack.
- You can raise armies of metalheads and other units to combat other Rock Deities, which was a huge surprise to me.
- It isnt a linear based game, its open world, another fact that was completly unknown to me.
- Ozzy Ozbourne as the Guardian of Metal, come on how great is that.
- Jack Black is a major player in the game, the main character is voiced by him, so it gets a thumbs up from me.
- It has allot of funny moments, relating to Rock which is awesome.
- Being a game from 2009 i thought it would a small game, but i was wrong, after many collectibles and side quests , and major army battles, it just opens into a second area where the adventure and fun continues.
- It actually develops the characters and the connections between them, making the you invested in the story and actually wanting to get to the end.
- You have to perform solos based on numerical keys, like 3 3 2 2 3 1 , to activate an ability or summon your car.
- Upon visiting the Guardian of Metal AKA Ozzy - You can buy upgrades for you car, weapon, clothes, statues and paint jobs. So its pretty badass.
- When activating "relics" in the game, you get as a bonus more soundtracks that you can hear in the background, songs from the greats like Anthrax, Black Sabbath, Cradle of Filth, Judas Priest, and this just to name a few, because the list is enormous, making Brutal Legend the game with the most Metal Soundtrack.
Cons : - The Quest selection is a bit cluncky, having to load the map each time so you can select which mission you want to do, i think it could have been improved somewhat.
- The army commands are tricky, taking a few tries to get the full potential of them, and even so, you spend so much time trying to run around trying to select and position your troops that you can hardly get in the fight.
- Block yes Dodge no! and because of it you will end up diying a few times.

Final Review : I give it a 8.5 out of 10 - I regret not playing this game sooner, and im being totally honest about that. Like myself most people that overlooked this game, judged it by the cover, and i cant figure out why, because once you play it, you'll love it. Could have been better? Yes. Is it a bad game? No, not at all. Is it worth it? YES ROCK ON YES
Any further questions about Brutal Legends, find my group - Curate This or even on Youtube.

They offer pretty unique weapons like dual daggers, dual faeblades, and chakrams with really impressive and fluid combos and enchantments.
The graphics (as you can tell) aren't the best, but they're definitely not a problem if you've played some older games in your time, and it actually kinda gives the games an old/classic feel.
All in all, this is definitely a game I would recommend if you want an adventurous, classic rpg that you can pick up pretty quickly, but is still pretty challenging, even when you have to run through a dungeon from the last save/checkpoint. I'd give it a solid 4.1/5.

Brawlhalla is similar to games like Super Smash Bros, Awesomenauts, Etc.
The overall concept of the game is excellent.  It removes a little of the casual feel of other games in it's genre, and I believe it will appeal to more technical gamers.
The characters are all available to play right now while it is in beta, but they will be purchasable with in-game earned gold upon release (I believe), similar to the way you'd buy champions in LoL, Dirty Bomb, and loads of other free to play games.
The characters themselves are pretty cool.  The art style is simple, effective, and in my opinion, beautiful.  Each one has a unique moveset and has 2 weapon pick-ups available for it.  The attacks feel clean and the hitboxes make sense, the dodge cooldown seems perfect to me and longer, skilled fights will make you break out in a sweat.
A few awesome modes, slight character customization, and a very solid 1v1 ranked system are all just toppings on an already delicious cake.
10/10 definitely recommend for any brawler fan.

Fantastic game. Relatively short (2-4 hours, depending on how quickly you make it through the various puzzles), but fantastically well written, especially considering the lack of dialogue.
The controls are well thought out, and feel much smoother with a controller, although it is perfectly playable with a keyboard - however you will regularly need to hold down 4-5 keys, so older keyboards may experience problems with certains keys getting stuck. I only had minor problems, and it never seriously impacted the gameplay.
I would say that it's a "must play" game if ever there was a must-play story-driven puzzle game. It's effectively single-player co-op and as such almost sits in a genre of its own.
---
If I were to criticise it, I would say that very few of the puzzles are difficult. They start off easy and get progressively harder, but even the puzzles at the end did not take long. However, that rarely feels like a negative, and it keeps the game flowing.
Another minor criticism is that several of the scripted events (e.g. floor falling away - a la Prince of Persia: Sands of Time) feels a little bit forced. Again, it's very minor.
---
Overall, if you've looked at the game and wondered if it is for you, it probably is. If the imagery turned you off, then maybe look at it a little further before pulling the trigger; but it's certainly worth another look.

This is one of the first games I ever played and it has lost nothing to time. Other people do better pros and cons than I, but simply put: this is one of the greatest video-games of all time, the only struggles I have had with it on Steam have been caused by it being designed for a much older computer, but most issues can be fixed up by the use of "Tafferpatcher", a fan-made bug-fixer for this and "Thief II: The Metal Age", or by fiddling with the .ini and config files.
One of the best things about this and T2 is the community: their community is still making fan-missons and improving/modifying original missions, and both games come with a mission-making software, so you can always have something to do in this game.
I can't recommend this game enough, it is a hard, stealth based game, if you get into combat, you've already lost, so keep to the shadows and be the master thief you secretly want to be.

If you purchase it be sure to download the texture mod and patch it (at bottom of review).
In short
pros:
- Immersive stealth experience
- interesting lore
- multiple ways  to approach objectives
- memorable levels
- little in the way of handholding
- lots of stealing to do
- subtle foreshadowing (good storytelling)
- difficulty done properly with more objectives and opening up of extra areas on higher difficulties
- protagonist is cool with badass voice
- soundscape is good
cons:
- Ai sometimes overly sensitive sometimes the opposite
- exploitable Ai bugs
- outdated graphics (ok if you mod it though)
- story linear
- some people might not like the otherworldly levels and zombies so much (I like them though)
conclusion:
Old but gold. If you are willing to forgive the flaws I mentioned it is worth the money (especially if on sale).
