Exploration is one of the finest core elements, and unlike Bethesda games, known for worlds with the depth of a puddle, the map is smaller but actually feels alive. Great level design is something to be espected nowadays after human revolution, and I would have to be a lying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to say this game didn't. Who knew breaking into an information bank would be so much fun?? I have enjoyed my time with Mankind Divided immensely but it’s a game that gets in the way of its own fun far too often. What worked in Human Revolution works better here and where the last game faltered, Mankind Divided falters deeper.
One man army cyborg Adam Jensen returns two years since the last game hot on the trail of some international terrorists and the Illuminati. Like, the actual Illuminati. It’s a very silly game. With a plot that gets little resolution, whose twists are entirely obvious far in advance and has an absolute whimpering fart of an ending. It talks a lot about “men in the shadows”, those who are really pulling the strings. Yet not once do you come into contact with them. Adam Jensen seemed closer to catching them in Human Revolution than he does here. Although honestly it’s hard to care either way, since our hero is a very dull videogame man.
Stripped of what little personal stakes he had in the last game (his previous relationships all too conveniently swept under the rug) he mumbles through this one completely bored by a conspiracy involving the ACTUAL ♥♥♥♥ING ILLUMINATI. He’s a two dimensional plank with a handsome and lovingly rendered beard scribbled on. Not that any of the other game’s characters fare any better, with the few memorable ones quickly shuffled off only moments after being introduced. The less said about the greatly varying quality of voice acting, the better.
For all the expanse of its branching story, which does offer a genuine sense of agency, Mankind Divided failed to conjure much in the way of emotion from me. I didn’t care about anyone, I didn’t feel the stakes and it’s hard to care much about the variety of outcomes when you don’t care about those involved. In the wake of The Witcher 3, which is simply the new benchmark for meaningful RPGs, where every inch of the world was packed with character and humanity, Deus Ex’s cold philosophizing feels even more hollow than it did in Human Revolution.
And what of the game’s much discussed conflict? An us and them premise where humans augmented by technology are oppressed, meant to parallel tensions of race in the real world? Absolute pants. Mankind Divided’s happy to put on the appearance of important science fiction but fails to plant anything beneath the surface. It’s window dressing. Crass and shallow attention grabbing that alternates between over simplifying the problems and politics surrounding oppressed minorities or completely ignoring them. Now and then someone calls you names. You got stopped at a checkpoint? Just wave your special papers. Never mind that the allegory makes no sense, the game barely spares the time to explore it anyway.
Make no mistake, Makind Divided is a b-plot. A middling chapter that seems intent on padding out the series till the next installment, failing to resolve a single plot thread left hanging after Human Revolution. Topics of racism and oppression are raised here only as an attempt to lend the game some importance that its bog standard plot most certainly does not have.
Which is a shame because get away from the story and Mankind Divided is a great time. Set now in Prague, the game’s sole hub, Mankind Divided offers a huge world to explore that is absolutely packed full of details and rife with missions. It’s mostly one continuous space now and the way it all interconnects is a joy to discover. You’ll still have to endure far too many loading screens, missions often requiring you to dart back and forth between the separate areas despite the massive inconvenience.
It’s a visually arresting location though, the old and new combining in ways far more interesting than any of the locations in Human Revolution, that nicely echo the themes of the game. The game as a whole is quite striking looking, carrying on the same style from the last game minus the obnoxious gold filter. Its sense of fashion and architecture breathes life into the world in a way that immersed me completely. I believed in its depiction of Prague in a way none of the games other locations compared. The story might be nonsense but the sense of place is top notch.
That it looks so good owes far more to the inspired art direction than it does the underlying technology, the graphics admirable in places but limping far behind the competition. The stiff animated faces of the last game linger and whilst the main characters are a significant upgrade over the character models of Human Revolution, everyone else is doomed to having their faces resemble limp rubber.
Yet I managed to overlook all that as I was completely hooked chasing mission after mission, poking my head into hidden rooms and sneaking through vents. There are bank heists, murder investigations and other varieties of jobs to keep you busy. The writing is mostly rubbish (and ♥♥♥♥ me the exposition sometimes seems endless) but Deus Ex still does the whole “complete missions however you want” thing better than most. There are numerous options, far more than you could find in Human Revolution. Few are ever telegraphed either, this is a game that rewards the curious and in that way, Mankind Divided remains a uniquely compelling kind of game.
Finding that secret entrance or hacking into that one computer with all the answers is an experience you don’t get from any other titles these days. On top of that, the expansion of Jensen’s abilities thanks to some hidden augmentations in his robo-body (there’s a sub-plot involving this that goes absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing nowhere) is a lot of fun, giving you lots of toys that aren’t just variations on “thing that kills henchmen”. It’s spoiled only by a rather odd system in which unlocking certain abilities requires you to permanently disable others that are yet to be unlocked. Before you can test them or see if you like the one you’ve chosen. Thankfully, most of them are rather useful.
The remote hacking ability for instance is a welcome addition, letting you mess about with dozens of different gadgets and objects from a distance. It speaks to the great detail and size of the areas, unlocking it early will expose you to the richness of the world. These gadgets also better facilitate the stealth side of the game, providing you ways to distract or move unseen instead of simply trying to find that one perfect route through a level. Pacifism too is encouraged and how pleasant it is to find a game that lets me find ways to avoid killing everything. And you can still drag bodies around to pose in completely inappropriate ways. See how many unconscious henchmen you can stuff into the one shower.
So on the one hand, Mankind Divided scratches a very particular itch. Freedom, exploration and immersion. On the other, a ham fisted story, weak non-ending and an array of obstacles all too happy to get in the way of your fun.
I enjoyed it far too much not to recommend it. It IS fun when you get right down to it, elaborate missions allowing you to both plan and improvise. Where your curiosity and exploration is often rewarded. Just so long as you leave you can set aside any hope that the game might live up to numerous promises littered throughout, of a more interesting world and story.
For all the talk prior to release, for all the lip service given throughout the game and for all its other loud successes, Mankind Divided is a game that in the end doesn’t manage to say anything worth hearing.
It’s bloody great fun though.

Shoppe Keep is just what the name tells - a phantasy shop simulator, where the goal is to sell as many items as possible to your customers, protect the shop and expand with time. There is no real goal in the game, so all you do in this game is managing your shop.
Since there is no story in Shoppe Keep and no end goal, you basically can consider the process itself as the goal of the game, but sadly since the process is not much fun, it makes you wonder all the time why you waste your time on this game at all. The management of the shop feels clunky, you need to refer often to the manual, that are simply written pages ingame; or figure the stuff out yourself by pressing tons of butons. It takes a while to get used to the controls and shop functions. Besides setting up your shop and protecting it from thieves or barbarians, you need to wait. A lot. The morning phase takes 5 real time minutes, then comes the day, then the evening. Afterwards you can modify your shop again, so basically especially at the start of the game you spend time simply watching phantasy characters run around town hoping one would visit your shop and buy something, so get yourself a nice book or some videos to watch during the wait time.
The combat in Shoppe Keep could not be more simple. Left mouse-button to attack melee, right to cast a spell. So far in my playtime the combat was more of a symbolic action, meaning you hit the enemy once and they are dead. It offers no challange, the attackers AI run in a straight line so you mostly can kill them by spamming spells before they reach the shop or kill the thief right in front of the shop with one click. It cant even be called combat and the biggest challange of the game itself is sitting duck in the shop waiting for customers.
The graphics are clunky fun style, but after few minutes you dont have any more fun watching it. Basically, its one of the easiest graphic forms and not an eye candy at all. The character customization before starting the game already shows the limitations of the engine and since you spend most of the time inside the shop, you basically watch brown bricks whole day. The interface in the menu is strangely ordered, inside the game it makes you wonder about the functions that pop up when you press some buttons. Basically the defs did a minimal job here, so they also receive a minimal rating.
The whole progress of the game is making some money, ordering more and better items to sell and waiting for the customers. There are some skills you can invest that help you increase your profit, but there are only few and mostly you have to wait for them aswell instead of being able to work somehow on them. You have to wait when you order or build something, you can have to wait for the customers, you can to wait for the skils, you have to wait...
The sound does not have any serious effect on the game. After few hours I switched it off because playing the wait game is far more fun with your own music running. You dont need any sound feedback for the gameplay, so the audio does not help any immersion here. Besides that, I didnt really feel well immersed into the game, not really as a shop keeper, but instead I felt all the time like playing a useless game simulating a shop. Not a great feeling while playing a game, as you can imagine.
Its hard to imagine when the game would be enjoyable for someone, especialy because there are much better management simulators aswell better introduced phantasy games in that style, that let you trade a lot. The waiting in Shoppe Keep is what simply kills it - without a possibility to speed up time, its just no fun waiting 15 minutes for an ingame day to pass, just to set up some more selling furniture and wait again.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

Forgive the unorganized mess of comments that constitutes my review :)
-Combat isn't a total drag, however the character-specific jobs are very similar, failing to add a different flare to combat when I choose a Necromancer over a Mage or even Archmage. Considering the older and free flash game Monster's Den series has more useful variations within the same style of conducting combat, it's very poor.
-Writing on average is good/tolerable with it occassionally resembling a bad anime or fanfiction, or making you genuinely feel for the characters.
-The story is good. It trivializes itself by coming to a boil so quickly, leaving you altogether lukewarm about the broader story elements.
-Romances are diverse as are the characters you romance, providing different events based on their personalities which makes it enticing to select the "Romance" conversation option for every character just for the good times.
-The lore and the world is not bad.
-The game is a little too aware of it's own morality, training you into a very neutral diplomat, which is all well and good but you never invest yourself. You'll never find yourself fervently championing a cause before gradually coming to question yourself or standing true in spite of the opposition's morality, making the moral battles essentially moot.
-Characters are fairly well made.
-I HAVE to hate on the scantily clad character models. One or two are justified in the story and it further contributes to their characters overall, but everyone rushing into battle in metal tankinis is just flat out rediculous. It cheapens romances, making you feel like you've lined up hookers that you would ♥♥♥♥, and are now hiring based on their life and personality, instead of discovering romance between your character and another. It's awkward and completely unncessary.
-Very cool and very enjoyable approach to same gender romance. In my playthrough I have seen nothing that has made it clear that it's just a cheap marketing ploy.
-The dialogue system is completely out of whack. Be ready to save before every dialogue, because you are going to get some weird responses with the obscure Joking, Friendly, Serious, motiff.

I had high hopes for this game. Really, I did. In Early Access, I thought it had the makings of a great game, and I still do. But it's not a complete game right now.
Sure, they've released all the levels. The characters are functionally different enough to make playing each one a slightly different experience (nerf Weiss/Blake and buff Yang pls), and the co-op elements are worked in a way that I admire (teamwork is not forced, but rewarded appropriately most of the time). These are all well and good, and why I still think the game will be great when it's finished.
So why is it not a full game? Well, it's still buggy, for starters. An achievement is awarded for acquiring an artifact at the end of a short but challenging jumping puzzle (the only one in the game). I attempted the platforming section twice before discovering (by myself, out of curiosity) that I could simply jump up the cliff to my right and dash over to the platform where the artifact was, netting it and the achievement.
In another incident, I dropped down into a square arena only to turn and find our Yang jumping seemingly futilely at a platform holding another artifact. Since we had just jumped down from there and it was fairly high up, we shouldn't have been able to get back up. It took me maybe ten seconds of experimentation before I figured out I could climb back up and get the artifact anyway, also providing me with a stupidly cheap way to cheese the incoming horde of Grimm.
The bugginess is the main issue here, though I have a few more minor complaints. Combat is a little repetitive; generally, I found one good combo for a character (X X Y or X X X Y, typically) and simply spammed it for the rest of the game. The music is mostly good, but in the tense battle against the game's final boss, where Red Like Roses Part II should provide an epic backdrop to the game's ultimate challenge, it simply stops after a verse or two, fades out, and then fades back in again. I'm loath to believe that of the staff who worked on the game, nobody detected or could have fixed such a thing. I could do it, for Christ's sake. And while the voice acting is generally alright, I find the subtitles are sometimes slightly incorrect (even when they were correct in Early Access), a few lines sound half-arsed, and some lines at the ends of chapters cut off prematurely (we no longer get to hear Professor Port exclaim "to victory!" at the end of chapter 2).
I still think that RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a decent enough game in its unfinished state, and that it has the potential to be lots better. If you'd like to help Rooster Teeth to help the game to achieve its potential, feel free to buy it. But if you are expecting a finished game with lots of polish, you will be disappointed. The game is still a beta and merely an undeclared Early Access title at this stage.
UPDATE: Having played the JNPR update for about 40 minutes (without the DLC itself), I can confirm that Professor Port once again exclaims "to victory!" at the end of chapter 2 and that a couple of improvements were made to the subtitles. So that's good. I'll talk about Horde Mode when I play it.

For a free game, this is very well done. The mechanics in the game are pretty fluid and there's no issues with marking/unmarking blocks on my part.
My one and only complaint is the puzzles. Most of them are simplistic in nature, usually some sort of identifiable internet/gaming related picture of one sort or another, which isn't a bad thing at all. The issue comes when the puzzle just doesn't flow the way it should. You get to the end of a puzzle and then it's time for you to look at the picture and try to figure out where things are supposed to go. Now some of these are intuitive for most people who enjoy these types of games. However, there should not be any intuition involved at all choosing where blocks should be marked. The flow should take you to the end of the puzzle, with you always going "Aha! This one goes here, which makes this one go here" etc. It's honestly my only gripe about the game so far.
That said, I would still recommend it for play for those it doesn't bother. There's over 300 puzzles in the game, and it's free. Even if it cost $1-2, I would still recommend it. $5 we're getting into iffy territory with the difficulty of the puzzles and the flow. $10 would be an outright no at this point. This is a "mechanically" fun game with some graphics issues that may or may not bother you and a terrible story.
------------------------
I'll start with the elephant in the room, which is the graphics problems people are having.  I'm on a GTX 980, i7 4790, 16 gigs of ram and a nice ssd.  The game runs at a solid 60 fps and looks quite good on "high" settings.  If I set *anything* above high the game immediately begins lurching.  Setting some options higher outright caues the game to crash, both in game and in the graphics option menu.
Like I said I think the game looks quite good on high, but at the same time it doesn't look better than anything else currently on the market.  This isn't an issue for me, but it might be an issue for you.
------------------------
Mechanically the game is quite fun.
Its a cover shooter that does a good job of offering you stealth and combat playstyles as well as a mixture of the two.  The levels are fairly expansive and do a good job of capturing the multiple, interconnecting routes within a large open area feel that the original Deus Ex had - something that no one else has really ever managed to get right.  There is also tons of hidden stuff to find, most of which provides you with actual meaningful rewards.
------------------------
The big downside to the game is the story.  I did everything in the game, and it took me about 32 hours to beat.  But a lot of the game's content comes in the form of sidequests - the main story is incredibly short.  If you ignored the sidequests and just blitzed the main quest you could easily finish the game in under 10 hours.  I honestly wouldn't be suprised if you could finish it in less than 5 (and a lot of that time would be spent in some very long, unskippable, semi-interactive cutscenes).
What this means is that the game just sort of ends.  None of the major or even minor plotpoints come anywhere close to getting resolved, and even some of the sidequest plotlines don't get resolved either.  If I had to compare it to the original Deus Ex, it would be like if you got to the airport where Lebedev is, and the game ended immediately after you made your choice on how to deal with him.  There is just so much plot still left in the game that I cannot imagine they plan to finish it with DLC, or even a sequel.  If future games in the franchise advance the plot as slowly as Mankind Divided does you can expect 4 or 5 games before the plot comes anywhere near close to completion.
The one good thing I will give it on the plot front is that despite ending so suddenly the plot is still better than Human Revolution, as you have a real motivation for advancing the plot this time - unlike in Human Revolution where your motivation was avenging/finding your friend who is a girl that is manipulating you to steal your DNA but who otherwise has no interest in you despite you being romantically interested in her.
------------------------
All in all its a fun game, and if you're just looking for something to burn time its worth your $60.  But that doesn't mean its a great game - or even a good game.  I'd say its on the lower end of an average game, but the quality of PC games this year has been so uniformly low that even an average game stands out.

First of all I'd like to apologise to the level designers - what you've built here is some of if not the best and most compelling map design I've ever seen. I've never spent so long poking around a map, and I still feel like I have so much more to explore.
The graphics are nice, and so far the writing is okay, too. All in all this game SHOULD be extremely enjoyable.
The trouble is that it fights against the player at every available opportunity to ruin or sour the experience. First of all, the optimisation of this game is awful. Microstatters every 10m, crashes, sounds issues. The engineers and testers should be ashamed of the state the game was released in. If I were one of the artists or level designers working on this game, I'd be furious that players of this were constantly being ripped out of the fantastic world I'd created because of crippling technical issues. Such an immersive world that can't help but remind you that it's a game held together by duct tape every 30 seconds.
Then we come to the bizarre save/install DRM that cheated me out of some of my redeemed preorder bonuses after relocating my game's install to my SSD in an unsuccessful attempt to mitigate the optimisation issues. Apparently after doing that I no longer had the DLC installed (according to the game) and I lost access to the saves with that content redeemed, so I had to go back to a previous save and lost three hours.
I can't express how much I hate having to give this game a "not recommended". It's actually a great game so far, but due to the many issues it has I absolutely cannot recommend it in its current state. How it was released with the number of issues it has is extremely disappointing.
I'll continue to play because it's too late for a refund now and it's enjoyable when it's not stuttering or crashing, but in the future I'll b very wary of Square releases.
Edit: 1st July 2017 - Decided to try for another playthrough, loud this time. Managed to load the game up once for about two minutes before a crash. "Video driver error", despite having the latest drivers for my GTX980 installed. It appears not much has changed.
I had every intention of amending this review, but I don't see how that will be possible given that the game still sufffers from the same issues almost a year after release.

There isn't really much good to say about this game.  It feels like a unfinished product and from the history of the game it seems that it most certainly is.   It doesn't even do the core aspect of the game well which is running the shop.   The very few side activites don't really add to the game much either.
But it's not just the poor game-play that plauges the game.  I've run into annoying bugs.   For example theives are a constant in the game you will get a bunch in a single game day.   The only real recourse is to murder them and take your item back.   This however sometimes  but oddly not always upset  innocent shoppers and passers on the street causing them to flee.   Except much of the time they will glitch out repeat their scared line over and over before finishing the line overlapping the audio.   But it doesn't stop there they also run in place which can last for sometime.     I've also had quite a few theives just run into a wall in my shop and continue running endlessly into it until I took care of them.
The game could also use some ease of use mechanics.  The game days are much longer than they need to be  and from what I can tell there is no way to speed up the game.  This makes every day a chore even more so in the early game where you have less customers and times where you just stare at your entrence with nothing to do.   Later when it gets too busy the problem reverses now you're dealing with constant restocking and being interrupted by constant theives.  Would it really be too much to be able to hire a stockboy?   The management part of having to reorder would still be on you.
I'm also not sure if this is even a glitch or not.  But the AI has some extremely odd behaviors.  I've seen many of them purchase a very expensive item and then turn around and try to steal the cheapest items like a health potion and try to run away.   This behavior makes no logical sense it's like buying a new car but stealing a pack of gum  and be willing to die over the pack of gum.   Glitch or not this  really shouldn't be present.
The town is also uninspiried and boring.   This would have been fine at first if there was advancement like relocating to a new location with actual meaningful events and characters.  But that doesn't seem to exist.  Which is a shame.    I can't recommend this game.  I can't even find reasons to give it any praise.    In its current and no doubt final state it feels like something I would get in a early build.

No one, and I mean No one, except crazy fans of the game, has ever played it as much as I did, (80h), so what I'm about to say is absolutely coming from the ultimate experience of the game world.
Note: I've ulocked almost everything except some art books and songs, played it for 80 hours, why?!, because I had fun looking for the collectables and buried things in the world not knowing that something will come up at the end of the game and tell me where to find them all, but even that didn't make me regrit the exploration fun I had.
I loved this game so much, and here is what I loved "specifically" :
1- The Story, It is great, and fun, with lots of funny jokes and being stupid and epic at the same time. I think that they rushed the story too fast, and it was supposed to be longer..., saying that because I wanted more.
2- The beautiful Fantasy Metal World, OMG, I mean sometimes I forget that this is just a game, and start to imagine that there was something like that in the past, LoL.
3- The absolutely fantastic art work of the creatures, vehicles, buildings, clothes, ...and so much more.
4- The enemy variety is amazing, and the difficulty is really good, you don't feel like you're dominating everything, but if you wanna, you can get better and be creative.
5- The enemy AI is amazing, they can put you to sleep if you're not careful enough.

Mortal Kombat X is the 10th installment in the iconic Mortal Kombat series, and probably the best game out of them all. It features 26 playable characters (35 if you include all the DLC) with each characters having 3 different variations that are designed to fulfill specific roles (zoning, trapping, rushdown and so on). The variations provide changes in terms of moves and combos, so in reality you're looking at a game with potentially 105 characters (DLC included), which is a lot. The characters are well balanced for the most part, which means whichever character you choose to main will probably also be tournament viable if you get good enough at the game.
The game is also very fast paced for a fighting game, and offers players tons of content, from a (good, but short) story mode; to traditional towers in which the player has to beat a series of AI opponents with a final boss at the top; to living towers (regular towers that get updated with new challenges every once in a while to mix things up) and more casual game modes such as test your might and test your luck. It also features a return of the Krypt, in which you can unlock various costumes, fatalities and other behind the scenes novelties.
This port had a rocky start when it first launched on PC, with people not being able to get past the main menu due to its many issues, but most of the issues it had are now fixed. All in all, the game continues Netherealm Studios' tradition of offering the player great value for money by showering him with tons of quality content - a lot more than what you'll find in any other fighting game out there.
So why am I not recommending this?
As of January 20th, Netherealm had announced that they are dropping support for Mortal Kombat X on the PC. This means that the Kombat Pack 2 DLC, featuring Triborg, Bo Rai Cho, Leatherface and Xenomorph, will not be released on PC at all. This also means that PC users will not get the updated netcode that is currently being developed for the console users, and will have to stick to the inferior (and quite horrible) netcode the game currently has. On top of all that, every new balance patch the game receives from now on will not make it to the PC. In sum, anyone who plays this game on PC is doomed to play an inferior and different game than the console version. You'll have less characters, worse online, and worst of all - the frame data on your moves list will not be compatible to the frame data of your console counterparts, which means that any effort of friendly competitive play between a PC user and a console user will automatically put the PC user at a disadvantage (if you had plans to play this game competitively in casual tournamens like I had, you might as well forget about it).
Now lets be clear: while I do hold Netherealm Studios responsible for this to some extent, in my book the main villain of this is Warner Brothers, who now demonstrate a pattern of releasing shoddy game ports on PC (Batman: Arkham Knight, anyone?) followed by quickly dropping support for said ports. That company proves time and time again that it doesn't care about PC consumers by outsourcing games to bad port developers and quickly dropping support for said ports in favor of making new DLC. This is quite embarrassing for the company, as it turns away from the few people still willing to give it money for its horrible PC releases.
If you're a fan of Mortal Kombat, consider buying it on console as it is indeed a good game. If you're strictly a PC user, however, don't bother. You'll be playing an inferior product that will be vastly different from the main game. Also, in the future, if you encounter a Warners Brothers game that is being ported to the PC - avoid it like the plague. I know I will.

From what I've been able to play, Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning seems like a decent enough RPG. Unfortunately the Steam version seems to be bugged, and it crashes every 10-15 minutes or so. It sucks because this game seems like something I would really enjoy, if I could actually play it. I'll do my best to review it based on the 5 or so hours I've played so far, but take it with a grain of salt.
Pros:
- Fun combat
- Interesting skill/level system, it seems like you can make very diverse builds which adds replayability
- From what I've played so far the story seems promising, and I know it was written by a NYT best selling author
- The armor and weapons have a very cool design
- Decent enough graphics
- Runs well on low-end systems
Cons:
- The fantasy setting of this game seems kind of generic and dull compared to other games I've played
- There doesn't seem to be much choice/consequence
- The NPCs outside of the main quest are boring cardboard cut outs
- The world design doesn't seem very good
- Every side quest I've done so far has been a boring fetch quest
- The game crashes every 10 minutes. From what I can gather this is because of a Windows 10 compatibility issue, and although I have tried various fixes, none have worked.
It really is a shame that I can't play this game, because it does seem pretty good. I tried to stick with it but constantly saving and rushing through things to avoid losing progress from a crash just isn't something I can continue to put up with.
TL:DR: A seemingly good game that, for me, was ruined by a bug that caused the game to crash every 10-15 minutes. I would recommend Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning, but unfortunately because of this bug I cannot. Not taking the bug into account, I could see this game falling somewhere in the range of 7.5-8/10

You'll see a great majority of negative reviews here describing how GunZ 2 is not GunZ 1, this is true (although I really do miss K-styling). It is cleary stated in the title that it is a different game. Now putting that aside and reviewing GunZ 2: The Second Duel.
I enjoyed the different modes of play available from ffa to sword only duels, the unique move sets depending on who you pick is actually quite interesting, and upgrading equipment to higher lvls isn't that bad if you don't mind farming a bit (and doing well).
So why the downvote? Hosting. As the game stands it runs each match via peer to peer, so whomever is the host gets a nice fluid fun rewarding game. If you're not the host, have fun even getting 1 kill. From the time something happens on screen, it's already been 3-5 seconds. Yes seconds. And this isn't just part of the match, not spikes, but the entire match.
To wrap it all up, I had a very fun time when it was I who was hosting, not because I could decimate due to the huge handicap being the host brings, but beacuse this game actually does have potential if it worked very all players in a match at the same time, not just one.
TLDR: Fun when you're host, enjoy getting slaughtered with lag if not.

Thief: The Dark Project is a stealth game made by looking glass studios, but it was something different before it was a stealth game. Thief was originally an action rpg called "dark camelot". It was a game where you fought against a tyranical King Arthur as Mordred, portrayed as an underdog hero. The story THEN changed to the "The Dark Project" where you crawled through dungeons, fight monsters, and collect loot in indiana jones fashion. And then, 2 months before the game released they made it a game about stealth.
But heres the problem, the maps were not redesigned with stealth in mind. The maps where originally meant to be like a first person shooter type thing, but with a sword and bow instead of guns. And despite this games greatness it kinda shows. Far too many times you're forced out of stealth to fight monsters in caverns, and unfortunately one of the reasons they made it a stealth game was because the combat was ♥♥♥♥ing awful. So some levels feel like a massive slog to get through.
Besides that major flaw, this is an immersive game with an amazing sequel, and its too bad that I couldn't muscle through it. The stealth is involving, fun, challenging, and incredibly tense, but every other level I get forced into combat when I just want to go back to stealing treasure. Thief 2 fixes this to a great degree, and its sequel deadly shadows is fantastic. There's a great game here, that I'd reccomend to people with the patience for it, but for now I'll stick with thief 2, its unofficial expansion, deadly shadows, and the dark mod.
If you only want to play the game for the story, Bobbin Threadbare (Threadbareinc on youtube) has an excellent lets play of the game on his channel. The game is as good as it is flawed, and I know thats sacrilege to say, but this game shows that it was meant to be something else.
I give it a 9/10 overall.

Well, Grimm Eclipse is finally off of Early Access. Sadly, I have to write a scathing review rather than give it the tongue bath I would have liked to. Let's get this out of the way: Even if you are a fan of RWBY, this game is not worth the money. If you aren't a fan of RWBY, you are excused. You have other Steam listings to look at in your search for a hacky/slashy fun run. For the RWBY fans who are still here, let me explain what seems to have gone wrong.
Grimm Eclipse was in early access for some time. And in that time, it came a long way from the launch, it really did. Combat was adjusted, sfx levels were adjusted, and the models that came straight out of the show got axed for some arcane reason. Then a few extra bland levels got stapled to the back half and it was deemed finished.
The game is short, the characters play very similarly to one another (smash heavy attack or DIE), and the writing is short on the charm you may have come to expect on the shore. The game puts in a couple jumping puzzles in a desperate bid to keep things varied, but it falls flat, even when a lampshade gets hung on the situation. The fact that this callout was less gentle ribbing and more being hit over the head in case you missed it did not help matters.
Spoilers from this point on. The worst part about this is the absolute waste of the villain, Dr. Merlot. He receives some slight foreshadowing in the first couple areas that the game began Early Access with, but after he starts talking to the characters, any hope of him being interesting or complex gets buried like the rest of my hope for this game. Ozpin is no better when he starts up his back and forth with Merlot. Good guys yay, bad guys boo, now go stop Dr Wily. I mean Merlot.
It probably seems like I'm harping on this point a bit, but Dr. Merlot's actions are the sum total of the plot. His mark is left all over security breaches in Beacon's network, and he breeds mutated Grimm. Neither of these points are ever explained, even at the end. The titular team investigates this, learns nothing, smashes up the lab and calls it a night. If RWBY was a monster of the week kind of show, this would be excusable. More so at least. But RWBY is a long term narrative, and if Merlot was at least painted as complex, or threatening, or if at any point we had some insight into why he was doing what he's doing, it might have worked a little better, and I wouldn't feel so cheated. Instead, we get a cartoonishly evil scientist with no desire beyond making monsters. What an absolute mess.
The gameplay isn't better. Early areas are alright. Smash up some Grimm of varying types, some are tougher than the rest, counter when they wind up, and anything but the most basic enemy you can use your Heavy attack to break their guard. Which is always up. So your light attack, which should probably be your main method of attack, becomes almost worthless. Ursa are a pain to fight, since even heavy attacks don't stagger them, so you instead have to wait for them to stagger themselves. Waiting should not be a key factor in a hack and slash. Things get worse in the late levels of the game which introduce robotic enemies, which I had to cheese with Ruby's stun bullet ability to get a chance to hurt. Their range is too long, they knock you out of your attacks even as they receive yours with unflinching determination, and have a nasty habit of coming in pairs for maximum annoyance. Their gunner friends that show up later are just as irritating, as they jump backwards and blast the ground you're standing in faster than you can cancel your combo and evade the attack.
And the last boss fight is an absolute joke. Stand in front of him, wait for the weak point to become apparent, smack it as fast as you can, repeat. There's no method to force the weak point out beyond waiting, and I already talked about why that's not good. Defeating the enemy somehow makes Merlot's plans fall apart. Oh, and Merlot contributes only tired dialogue to the end fight. He doesn't even escape, he just loses without ceremony or closure.
As for what's good about the game: The voice cast from the series reprise their roles here, and perform well. Even Merlot doesn't sound bad, he's just poorly scripted. Sadly, so is Ozpin. Everyone else makes it through more or less intact. Even with the updated models, the game looks good. The team's movements are well animated, attacks are flashy and cool, and the enemies at least look interesting, even if they themselves aren't. Environments are visually pleasing as well, and you're not likely to get lost. Unfortunately, that's all I can really praise about the game. Things that were brought over from the show.
TLDR: Wait for Volume 4 instead.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is great. It’s a simple yet addicting game where you play as one of the four main characters and hack and slash through hordes of enemies. Each character is fun and unique to play as, leaving lots of replay value to find your most suited and favorite playstyle. (For example as Ruby, I like to stun enemies with ranged attacks and then go in with a power attack) The locations are varied, beautifully designed, and shaded. Character models do not exactly resemble the show but still look fine. There is an enticing skill system you’ll find yourself coming back to in order to unlock new and powerful abilities. The game also features a funny and interesting dialogue, and you’ll enjoy hearing each and every one of Yang’s puns. In addition to all of this, there is also a ranking system, which allows you to increase your hunter’s rank after you’ve maxed every character’s level and completed select challenges. All in all this leaves for an immeasurable amount of playtime. So why a negative review? Because despite everything, this game is missing key features. Combat itself is okay but nothing notable. Generally speaking enemies are damage sponges. You continue to whack away at them until they die. For example the Beowolves. Although hits from these enemies will take a chunk of your health, it’s fairly easy to just spam the dodge button and escape from them, leaving no sense of actual challenge or skill. For the most part the enemies aren’t even difficult. They often stand around, wait a few seconds, and then execute a fairly easy to dodge attack. (I would add the android/robot type enemies as the sole exception) Therefore there’s no real sense of challenge. Most of the difficulty comes from trying to survive hordes as opposed to an enemy itself. Which is alright but definitely a bit lacking in substance. This game was supposed to release with a horde mode. As mentioned earlier, this would maybe rectify the games lack of challenging AI because most of the difficulty and substance of the game relies on hordes instead of individual enemies. However as of the day this review was posted, there is no horde mode. Furthermore, teamwork is virtually nonexistent. For a game that prides itself on being similar to L4D2, It really falls short. The most teamwork you’ll probably ever get out of this game is if one of your members dies and you’ll need to revive them. Oh, but that’s the thing. If your teammates chooses not to revive you, your character will just revive after a set amount of time. So there’s no actual consequence for not helping each other. Not to mention each character is set up in a way that they can all play independently of each other. So despite having a full team, you’ll find you often don’t need each other and can just go off and fight on your own. It really is disappointing. And finally, there is no Team JNPR. Yes Team RWBY is great, but eventually you’ll tire of the four characters. For a game with only about four hours of campaign, there’s only so much you can get out of a limited cast. Adding another team would definitely increase the value and playability. Supposedly JNPR is planned but is also not part of the game currently. With everything I’ve listed, I’d say this game is definitely not worth $25. It’s very much incomplete. $15 sure; it's simple, it’s fun, and it’s RWBY. But $25? No. The campaign is short, it’s missing a promised feature (horde mode), combat is flawed, and you only get four characters to play as. So my overall verdict is this. If you’re a huge fan of RWBY and don’t care about price, buy this game. You’ll love it. You get the main cast, some fun hack and slash combat, and an interesting side story. But otherwise avoid it until they at least add Horde Mode. Or buy it during a sale.

What. The Hell. Is This?
I'm going to be honest, it was enjoyable at first, but after a few hours later, I was already so bored that I could not take it anymore. I played the game since Early Access, and the game being tagged as "fully released" and out of Early Access is just plain bullsh!t. Literally almost nothing has changed after getting out of Early Access (except for the last few levels with a new enemy that... well just isn't really game changing, and the HUD that... well... I can hardly see why that needed changes), and this game takes only a few hours just to finish. They could have had the rest of the story done and over with before getting out of Early Access; it's the plain truth. They had this rushed out so they can show it at RTX 2016 as "the final product", and it's sloppy and completely disrespectful. They spent a year making the game (since the Summer of 2015), and THIS is what we get? Talk about a cash grab.
Combat is repetitive, dull, and terribly simplistic that it makes me think they didn't try to capture the overall feel of those amazing fight scenes we saw in the show itself.
Story is lackluster, uninspired, and cliche to the point that it hurts to call it original. Seriously, it's THAT BAD.
Characters have the crappiest dialogue lines and doesn't give a sort of dynamic to the game (literally hearing Ruby making explosion noises and gunshots constantly is an annoyance), no variety when it comes to their move set (seriously, you have close range attacks, ranged attacks that hardly work for sh!t, and an ultimate move. It is laughably simple for what the game is based on), and can be so unbalanced all over the place when it comes to the game's enemies and bosses that it seemed like they didn't even do much work. It feels like RT Games just wanted me to hate the RWBY characters, and that's terrifying (though let's be honest, they did a crappy job with developing them in the first place)!
The antagonist of the game is... well I can't really say anything about him, other than the fact that he doesn't really seem threatening, and is completely up to the player to imagine how he looks like. You might as well as not had an antagonist if you weren't going to properly develop him. He's just there... and is completely disappointing.
This game looked promising when I played the pre-pre-pre-alpha (it was literally in its rough stages back then... well... this game still looks rough as hell) back at RTX 2015, but now... I consider it a crappy hack n' slash game with a RWBY skin on it. That's also the reason why you see plenty of "Positive" reviews on the store page... it's because those reviews have to do with people loving RWBY and... well that's pretty much it. Sorry if I offend you (yeah you, the person reading this), but most people tend to just buy games they don't realize are half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and a complete ripoff; reminds me of people that buy COD games. If you look at this game as a normal hack n' slash game, then you would have a Negative experience with it. I'd say, either avoid Grimm Eclipse, or buy the game during a sale (if you can get on a sale that costs less than $15 -__-).
As a die hard fan and longtime fanfiction writer of RWBY, I would say that this is not the RWBY game we dreamed of. I feel terrible for being so hard on a game based on my favorite series, but I can't even bear this game. If they had put more time into the game, it could be half as decent as we hoped.
So for now, I'll repeat my first statement. It's not worth $25. Buy it on a sale, or steer clear of this pile of garbage that RT made to steal even more of your money. It's a complete waste of potential for the show itself.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a 3rd person Hack and Slash\Character action game like DMC, Bayonetta or God Of War. It's based on the popular web series of the same name and was initially a fan game but then officially given the stamp of approval by RoosterTeeth who produces the series on Youtube. The game signifies RT official step in games publishing. While it is an admirable step it doesn't escape its fan made nature as there are many prevalent issues, odd design choices and a heavy sprinkling of repetitive\boring combat.
+ For what they're worth, the Character models looks nice.
+ The audio's really pleasant. It's only instrumentals and no lyrics which may annoy some.
+ Environments looks really nice I must say albeit empty.
+ Combat for the most part, flows nice when utilising all available mechanics.
- There's no pause menu. That may be fine for multi-player but why doesn't the game pause for single player.
- Combat needs a lot of work and gets repetitive after about 30 minutes of play. You have a light (square) and a heavy (tri) attack, counter, range and ultimate attacks.
- You never get different moves you just improve the starting skills to make them more powerful.
- Combat is repetitive, you'll rely on the same sequences over and over rather than trying something new e.g square (x2), triangle \ square (x3), triangle \ square (x4) triangle.
- The enemy variety is quite low. There are about 5 main types of enemies with 2-3 different versions of each but they all act roughly the same.
- The damage output you deal feels rather minuscule even with your skills fully maxed out. This can be seen when fighting against late game enemies where you could be stuck in combat against non boss types for quite a while.
- Arenas are just survive this wave or protect this thing. I wouldn't have mind this if there was some variety to break up the monotony.
- Your ranged attack is damned near useless, what's the point of having a ranged attack if you can't aim at or hit anything precisely.
- You'll attempt to aim at something and when you shoot, the player will lock on to something far in the distance rather than the enemy right in front of you.
- Enemies can seemingly break free from your combo hit stun and counter attack immediately without any warning signs.
- Enemies can hit you from what seems to be long a$$ distances either that or the hit boxes are either wonky or huge as hell.
- You can get stun locked in a combo sequence without any means of breaking free. This is apparent in later sections after the introductions of the robots.
- Camera is abysmal. It gets caught by scenery whereby it zooms all the way up inside the player model thus leaving you open to be attacked.
- Camera is passive rather than active and requires you to baby sit it the entire game.
- Final boss highlights everything wrong with this game. It's in an arena with one tanky enemy, it has absurdly large hit boxes, it spawns tanky respawning mobs which take a while to take down and takes forever to take down itself. Does this sound found to you because it doesn't for me and was not for me.
+/- Considering the $25 price tag, the level of content on show is seemingly not worth it.
+/- If you play one character only the game is short, about 3 hours which may be bad for some.
+/- The story is so 'meh' but in all fairness I ignored it early on as it made no sense whatsoever.
+/- Hyper linear corridor walker with some hidden item action.
+/- The voice acting is mediocre like a badly dubbed anime.
+/- Lacklustre background visuals like muddy texture work, pop in and blocky shadows.
+/- Has some performance issues when loading the text name of an area but this maybe due to the version of Unity used, probably 4.5 rather than 5 where this issue was removed.
+/- Menus feel like programmer art, it's ok but could be way better.

I'm not one to normally write game reviews but Loren The Amazon Princess  seemed to spark one in me.
Loren is a very straight forward game when it come down to its gameplay and one I recommend if you enjoy a turn based RPG. The big trick is making sure you take advantage of the Pokemon like element type system since some foes are weaker to say Dark damage then they are to Normal, Wind, Water, Fire or Earth (meaning you might want to stalk up on even slightly weaker weapons if they have a different damage type then that more powerful sword you got off a boss, just s you are not dealing 30 point of damage when you could be dealing 100 points just for doing a mid battle swap out)
I noticed Loren The Amazon Princess has some similar trait to Dragon Age when it comes to uniting the races of the world against the main villain (mainly in getting them to stop trying to kill each other and not making the live of the bad guys that much easier) but unlike DA, you do not need 2 hours wandering through caves, forest or ruins to find your target, the game stream lines this by being much like a book that takes you right to the heart of mission, fight the target an move onto the next plot point.
Since the game is so streamlined, you do not need to grind for levels though it is still an option by doing Tasks that are in most village (which also build up local fame and provide discounts at the local store) the big thing about grinding in Loren is...its not easy as the game was clearly built for you not needing to be level 50 to win. I myself only had mot of my guys at 18 to 21 by the time I faced the final boss.
Now as for the main character, you get two options for him/her: Human Male and Elf Female and both of those have the option of Warrior or Rouge as a base class plus your pre-chosen second class of Hero. At first this might be a let down to those who like Mage style builds (or arcane knight style player like myself) but this is probably for the reason of if the MC could sling a fireball as well as cast the support spells the Hero Class gives him or her well... can see a pure mage just being over powered if that were possible so this was probably good move from the game's creators to take away the mage route for the MC in this case.
Now as for romance (as we all know is common thing in all RPGs to provide non critical but interesting side plots for the game) your chosen starting gender let to romance some characters but not all, though most swing both ways so you have a classic Bioware style romance system in this game. Loran for example can be romanced by both MC genders but Draco can only be romanced by the male MC.
Overall Loren The Amazon Princess is a fun (though short) game I recommend for those enjoy a good turn based RPG.
A surprisingly fun, simple game that's almost completely polished.

The game certainly has unique features, but is still very far from being excellent, although the beginning is promising. For once you do not play as the namesake of the game, but her servant - a "lowly" male by the Amazon's standard, or a female elf (both slaves), accompanying her to go rescue her mother. You make some choices about your past actions and here you go for your stats boost. And the whole thing is very verbose, as promised.
Problem being that for a game mostly a visual novel (the RPG aspect is just there to flesh out a bit the adventure), the story is too standard. After rescuing Loren's mother, you learn that Evil lurks. And yes, once again, it's an Evil that was already vanquished in the past, but as everyone know, there's not a soul in the multiverse able to properly seal any evil being whatsoever. Fost, said Evil is uninteresting and cliché.
Let's be honest, for the game's lenght, the background is detailed enough, but still... Too classic. Elves antagonizing humans, orcs, dwarves, dark elves, demons aplenty, lizardmen, etc., things we have seen a bijillion times before. And if there are some talks about tolerance and all that, do not expect much subtelty from the plot, neither originality. Gather all the nations, go to the Big Bad's lair, insert fights, slay said Big Bad, get the girl, the end.
Now the dialogs are quite decent, and some characters are delightful, like the female dwarf Dora (beg yer pardon, totally not a thief !) or the snarky dark witch Chambara. For what I saw, the romances are pleasant too- up to six possibilities, and yes, you can flirt with characters of the same gender as yours.
Concerning the dialog options, you will have three most of the time : joking, friendly or forceful. Of course other people will react differently depending on your choices, I couldn't estimate if having a majority in one kind really forged a real reputation, but that may very well be.
And where does the gameplay fit in all this ? Well, you'll have a great number of fights, six VS six at maximum, with some scripted ones (like having only two members in your roster). Back row cannot be targeted by melee attacks while there are still at least one unit in the front row, wich make it ideal for missile units (bow/magic). On your right you can see in what order characters and ennemies will act, then plan accordingly. There are three classes (warrior, thief, mage), and each of your characters has a skill tree rendering him unique, like the druid being able to cast a heal spell on all a row.
Thieves can use mana for special arrows (fire, ice...), warriors can force an enemy to switch position with one on the back row, etc. Insert potions when needed.
All in all it plays smoothly, but I really fail to see the claim of the developers : there's nothing hardcore in it. If anything, it's quite casual and simple, not much strategy is involved. Money and equipment are not being scarce, the game is quite easy. Towns have an infinite amount of replayable tasks for money, XP and discount at the local shop ; making the possibility of skipping the odd random encounters sound.
Now, I'm one of those stressing the value of story over gameplay for RPG, a reason why Planescape Torment is one of my eternal favorites. But I must insist : the game's intrigue has been seen too often to really be epic. The lack of artworks is rather grueling in that regard, many scenes would have benefited from a dedicated drawing to better depict them. Decently fleshed out characters (the personal quests help) cannot alone bring all the appeal. This not to say a simple story is something bad, here, it's just lacking in a genre where it should shine.
One great flaw is the DLC. I do not know about you, but 17 buckazoids is already a bit steep a price. 6€ for content which could (and should) have been in the vanilla game is a blatant rip-off. You'll even get a message in the base game stating that you could recruit Chambara and a certain monk, but, hey, show the money first ! Worse, those two characters can have a crucial impact on the game's ending, wich is just wrong.
And as for the replay value ? Yes, you can still change the starting character, romance other people, make a few other choices... But is it really worth going back to the same story without any surprise ? The game itself is not sure of that, as you can skip all the dialogs you want, and have cheat mode enabling you to win all the battles once you have completed the game for the first time.
I was intrigued by the aspect of Loren the Amazon Princess at the start and still enjoyed it. It made me think of a Fighting Fantasy gamebook with actual character development.
But if you are tempted, my advise would be to wait for a special promotion like -50%. 14 hours-ish of a classic plot (DLC accounted for) with marginal gameplay and satisfying protagonists are just not enough to be worthy of such a price. "Two novel's worth of in-game text", by the way, is quite meaningless : are we talking 100-ish pages sized novels, or Stephen King's sized novels ?

I'd say the screenshots don't really do this game justice. They look like a flash game but this is better than any of those that I have played.

If your into old school RPG turn based style combat with some light strategy, you will like this. If you wanted real time action rpg - then this ain't it.

More gameplay than a typical visual novel, and more story/character development than a typical RPG.  Obviously one can easily take a negative view of this approach, as some opinions on the forum point out that the gameplay pales to other classics ranging from Wizardry 8 to Final Fantasy Tactics, and at the same time, more opinions claim that the visual novel aspect simply doesn't match the same kind of brilliant depth as Baldur's Gate II or even the granddaddy of them all - Planescape: Torment.
However, I think for anyone who might be curious about this game, I would like to point out the earnest effort in making and polishing this product.  This isn't something rushed out of the door (coughE*cough) just to catch a sale season, or some "early access" taking donations with promises.  The game plus the DLC have been available outside of Steam for quite some time now, and it has been continuously tweaked in various aspects - story, writing, gameplay, graphics, etc.  It's a well-oiled piece, ready to be enjoyed, and it's definitely not a half baked beta test that expects regular patches and headaches.
Speaking of the gameplay, sure the RPG element isn't as robust as, say, FFT or the Disgaea series, but it's got the standard character attributes, skill trees, affinities/weaknesses, skill combos, and not to mention, more characters than you could field in a single playthrough for some replayability.  Nothing extraordinary, but solid enough to service the game well.
The visual novel part of the game is evidently made with much dedication and care.  The typical "ancient evil and the heroine who saves the world" plot line notwithstanding, I could appreciate when a writer tries to develop each character as much as possible - interactions, background story, and personalities.  Each character also has a personal quest to build more depth (and loot!).  Similar to reading a book, I think it's up to each player to use some of his/her imagination to meld the words and the art together for the game world to take substance, so to speak.
I'm not some kind of educated art critic, so I'll just say that WYSIWYG, the characters, backgrounds, etc, if I recall, were all hand drawn, so it does have a certain style to it.  At least there was no 50 caves that all look the same as infamously seen in some -other- "AAA" RPGs.
Word of advice - if you want some kind of game with heat of battle and adrenaline rush from defeating a boss or encounter, this probably isn't it.  If you, for some reason, are looking for straight up visual novels, well, Steam isn't the best source for that at this time.
But for a relaxing game with some art, some story, and some RPG gameplay?  This game with the DLC should easily last you 10+ hours in one playthrough, longer if you stop and smell/read the roses, and maybe another run for a bit of replayability.

The biggest issue the game has are the dialogue choices.
After the character creation, every dialogue option is: Joking, Friendly, or Forceful. (and sometimes "romance" >_>)  These descriptions are simply not enough to make the choice you want.  It forces you to either pick dialogue options you don't like, or (if you're like me) just save before every single choice and then try all three answers to see which one you like most.
Update: I've learned that you can use the mousewheel to scroll back to the dialogue choices, and choose a different option.  This makes figuring out the dialogue choice less tedious, although it still is annoying to have to select and then back out of each option.
To give you an idea of how bad these dialogue options are, lets do a scenario.  Person A Is arguing with Person B.  They turn to you for your thoughts.  Your options are Joking, Friendly, or Forceful as always, without giving you any indication of who those options side with.  It's only through saving and reloading 3 times that you learn  Joking and Forceful side with Person A, and Friendly sides with Person B.  Very tedious.  Very annoying.
Now imagine the above scenario for Every. Single. Dialogue. Choice.
TL;DR
The dialogue system is an utter failure. (and that's without mentioning my issues with the story or the problems with combat)

You won't find many other games out there quite like Loren -- fantasy RPGs and visual novels with lots of romance options are nothing new, but there aren't many titles combining both.  This is one of my all-time favorite games and the main reasons are:
1) The characters and storyline.
Loren's cast is extremely memorable, likeable, fleshed-out and well-written.  You will really feel for these characters.  Some you'll love, others you'll love to hate. ;)  The story is overall nothing you haven't seen before, but the well-done execution and vibrant characters really make it come alive.
2) The replay value.
There are tons of branching choices to be made, tons of different romances, and several different possible endings (buying the N'Mar DLC adds even more endings!).  I've had this game for about a year and I still haven't seen every ending, branch,  and bit of plot or interesting conversation it has to offer.  There are a variety of places to visit and things to do, and a lot of little secrets and interesting tidbits you can uncover when backtracking to places you've already visited.
3) The art.
The general art style of the game remains as in the screenshots, a sort of blend between manga and Western comic-book style.  Somehow it works surprisingly well, and the artist is very talented at creating gorgeous characters.  You will want to romance these cast members.
I could go on really, but the point is that Loren is a great game and well worth your money!

Play this game if...

+You like looting and levelling
Don't play this game if...
-You don't like to read text
-You don't like linear stories

A review for the other noobs out there.
First time playing Tekken. I've put in 14 hours (which I acknowledge is less than nothing), and I'm pretty sure I'm the single worst Tekken player alive. I have won a couple matches out of a few hundred, but even people with 10 game losing streaks beat me over and over. I get triple perfected pretty regularly (meaning I landed 0 hits in three consecutive rounds). I could put down the controller and fight as well as I do holding it (oh right: get a controller) All of this is to say that if you've never played Tekken before, as I hadn't, prepare to get REKT. Like absolutely annihilated. Every. Single. Time. If you want to get to a point where you can hold your own, you need to study this game harder than you studied calculus. If you jump right into matchmaking, you're gonna get juggled for 20 seconds straight, and you'll feel like punching your monitor. Get out of matchmaking and go watch tutorials online, read combos and practice them a billion times, then another billion. In fact, forget combos, learn how to move - you'll soon start hearing the mythology surrounding the "Korean backdash" and other seemingly obscure crap that actually matters a ton. Then once you take what you've studied into matchmaking, you're still gonna get destroyed because people know how to block and counter everything you just learned - so keep practicing. As frustrating as it is to get pulverized all the time, I have to respect the game for not going easy on people, and rewarding those who really spend time practicing. It takes itself and its players seriously, and newcomers shouldn't expect to waltz in and start winning rounds. You'll get there, but you have to, well, get there.

Okay,
After I read some of the reviews (both pos & neg) I was a bit skeptical and wasn't sure about buying DE:MD.
Most of the reviews on the negative side are ranting about the graphics, the controls or most importantly, the store in which you can appearantly buy stuff for ingame use.
Now, firstly, I've got a GTX960, 2G Ram. I can run the game on 'high' graphics, no problem.
Secondly, I don't see the problem with the controls being "ported from console" as some say. They're nearly the same controls as DE:HR. That's just the way the controls are. Don't Like em? Change em.
Third, and appearantly a huge problem for most people:
The store. I haven't used the store, and quite frankly I don't give a flying **** about the store. If Eidos wants to put a store in it, that doesn't interfere with the game that's perfectly fine. And I'm sure that they figured that if this would actually interfere with gameplay, they would have a serious sh*tstorm on their hands. Like every other developer would get one.
This game is perfectly playable without it. In fact, it's nearly as good as DE:HR.
Now, to business:
The game:
I liked it. I've played on Give me Deus Ex, didn't regret it. Stealthed through, next try is charging trough like a bull. Will try 'I didn't ask for this"(permadeath) difficulty after that.
Anyway, plays nicely, main story is nice, albeit a little short. Probably because of the added Breach mode, and the Jensen storymode. In any case, story starts a little abrupt, or so I feel. It's good from there on out. Combat is good, stealthmodes are good. You have plenty of different approaches to getting your objectives, and I never felt obliged to take a path i didn't want.
Without telling much about the story, I was gratified, but left wanting for more answers. I'm hoping this might come in additions to the game, or another Deus Ex. But i felt kind of left in the middle of something at the end of the game.
The Jensen storymode feels like the perfect place to add the probable DLCs. It's nice, but again short.
Breach feels like the Mass Effect Multiplayer, but then singleplayer version. It has a leveling system like storymode. It's okay, but not the reason I bought Deus Ex. I feel the game could have done without.
In conclusion:
If you're a fan of the Deus ex Franchise, you should really consider purchasing this game. It's obvious that they did put a lot of effort into it, and the tie-ins to the Deus ex universe is well done.
If you're unfamiliar with the Deus Ex Franchise, you might want to consider buying Human Revolution first. It's a better introduction to the Universe, and might make you warm up to this game. Which you really should.
If you're unfamiliar with this style of game and still reading this review, you might want to consider getting familiar with it. It's quite fun. And entertaining.

Pros:
clean, efficient interface - easy to use.
The prevention of overwrites feature is nice/convenient (e.g. x out what has to, then click/swipe to fill whole row)
forgiving to mistakes (e.g. unintentional misclick isn't penalized)
free
Cons:
several ambiguous puzzles (multiple solutions).  This is a nonogram no-no.
Engine doesn't support partial solved lines (e.g. if you get a line '3 1' and you've filled out through the 3 completely, it doesn't grey out the 3)
Could have a timer for self-challenge (or leaderboards)

Based on: one 100% complete SP campaign on Brütal difficulty + MP boosting with a partner and solo grinding
An homage to heavy metal and a peculiar, if mediocre blend of a 3rd person hack-and-slash with a sandbox world and RTS-lite mechanics. Excelling in art direction and soundtrack, but bogged down by the gameplay design choices and console controls, it can make you hum, finger drum and fist pump in a mosh-pit-like excitement or bang your head in gloomy frustration. Fun enough to play on your own, but the MP is pretty much dead without friends. Brutal, perhaps, metal, definitely, but not enough to rock my world.
I received it for free through a Humble Bundle giveaway.
(+) the entertaining main story of Eddie Riggs, a roadie who is transported into the fantastical Age of Metal and joins in the human rebellion against their supernatural oppressors, told in 22 chapters (main missions), with some interesting lore to delve into
(+) dozens of over-the-top characters, both the allies like the sassy groupie and Eddie’s love interest Ophelia, self-obsessed king Lars, stubborn rebel Lita, cowardly engineer Mangus, bassist healer Kill Master, amazon queen Rima, biker gang leader Fire Baron, flippant Guardian of Metal, as well as antagonists: the BDSM-loving Emperor Doviculus or his lap dog, the glamorous Lionwhyte
(+) spawned from the twisted mind of Double Fine’s taskmaster Tim Schafer and assembled by his minions under the watchful eye of their Electronic Arts overlords at a time when EA still gave a hoot about releasing fully-realized products and even went as far as snatching this diamond in the rough from the indecisive clutches of one of their prime rivals in the anti-consumer practices department, Activision Blizzard
(+) Schafer’s brilliant writing cranked up to eleven by a near pitch-perfect voice cast, featuring Jack Black as Eddie, Jennifer Hale as Ophelia and the wickedly diabolical Tim Curry as Doviculus, with many metal legends lending their voices to the characters: Motörhead’s late Lemmy Kilmister to Kill Master, The Runaways’ Lita Ford to Rima, Judas Priest’s Rob Halford to Fire Baron/Lionwhyte and the surprisingly coherent Ozzy Osbourne to The Guardian of Metal (duh…)
(+) the spot-on art direction, inspired by the artwork of heavy metal album covers under Scott Campbell and Lee Petty with an unmistakable flair of Peter Chan, lends itself perfectly to the game’s overall theme and makes up for the inadequacies of the 2009 graphics ported from the consoles in 2013 with some improvements (increased draw distances, better anti-aliasing, etc.)
(+) the rock-fueled soundtrack by Peter McConnell serves as an important, albeit supporting act to the real headliners, the huge collection of no less than 107 licensed tracks from across the heavy metal genre, which serve as both a refreshment course for the fans and an introduction to the genre for the novices
(+) the SP campaign doubles as an extended tutorial for the RTS-lite stage battles, gradually introducing new mechanics or units and upping up the ante with each confrontation
(+) the covert tutorials are interspersed with a variety of palate cleansers in the form of arcade-style boss battles, racing, herding or convoy missions, which are entertaining in their own right
(+) the open world, which evolves as you progress through the SP campaign, is quite fun to explore, full of content (40+ side missions, hundreds of collectibles) and populated by crazy creatures, allies and enemies alike
(+) each of the game’s three main factions comes with its own leader, wildly creative units, special attacks and rock-paper-scissors rules of engagement, requiring different strategies to effectively utilize, manage or counter them in the SP open world or stage battles, and especially in MP
(+) the pretty simplistic, but enjoyable enough hack-and-slash combat utilizing moves and combos with a melee weapon and a guitar to cast basic spells or use more potent powers by performing note-matching solos
(+) by performing a specific solo, Eddie can literally drop The Deuce, i.e. summon his personal hot rod, customizable and upgradable in the metal forges through in-game currency
(+) the metal forges in the SP campaign also offer cosmetics and upgrades to Eddie’s melee weapon, guitar and clothes, as well as unlockable combos and even effigies to carve into Mt. Rockmore
(+) the immense attention to detail: from obscure inside jokes, through more overt references to the ridicule of the more over-the-top heavy metal trappings, hidden gems and missable interactions, the game is the ultimate fan service for the enthusiast of the genre such as myself
(+) the opening live-action intro is ingeniously integrated with the game’s main menu made to look like a heavy metal vinyl record album
(+) the pretty impressive facial animation and lip syncing for a game initially released for consoles in 2009 and re-released for PC in 2013
(+) the extensive concept art gallery unlockable through completing various tasks in-game
(+) full localizations in German, Spanish and French with an option to retain the original English voiceovers, plus a partial localization in Italian (UI and subtitles)
(−) the RTS-lite elements are mediocre at best, which made me wary of the stage battles, especially on Brütal difficulty when you need to be in full command of your environment to succeed and progress through the story
(−) clearly designed for analogue controllers and lazily ported as such to the Windows platform without any concessions for the PC users: neither the radial menus for units’ and solos’ selection nor waypoints, individual orders and other controls work especially well with a mouse and keyboard setup, which makes issuing collective or individual commands in the heat of a hectic stage battle frustratingly ineffective; they should’ve redesigned the controls with e.g. quickbars, hotkeys, drag unit selection and click-to-issue commands while in the air
(−) the driving controls are a bit wonky, too, and the car itself can be a little unwieldy at times
(−) the painful lack of a minimap, both in the open world, which would help drive the car between waypoints GTA-style instead of relying on an arguably more immersive, but less effective turn signals while trying to spot the inconsistent column of light over the destination, and within stage battles to keep track of the units and identify hotspots
(−) no fast travel mechanics: it should have been possible at least between the motor forges, especially since the game autosaves your position every time you leave them anyway; as it is, you’ve no choice but to drive in your car
(−) not enough checkpoints or autosaves in the open world, so you might need to drive between distant spots all over again if you happen to die en route, unless you visit the nearest motor forge
(−) Eddie gets wings every time he enters a stage battle, but is unable to use them in the open world, which would potentially make it easier to travel from place to place, cutting down on backtracking
(−) Eddie cannot jump nor climb up slanted surfaces, which made me stuck in the environment on more than one occasion
(−) it’s impossible to set waypoints on the map to places other than the markers, which are few and far between; there should have been more markers appearing on the map as you unlock viewpoints, tab slabs, legends, etc. should you want to return there later and helping you keep track of the collectibles you’ve discovered as well
(−) the MP sounds like a lot of fun, but the match-made ranked mode is a ghost town now, even though I waited for a full hour, so I had to find a partner to boost me for the MP achievements and grind some on my own against the AI or in solo custom matches
(−) occasional camera problems and clipping issues
