I got this for christmas from a good friend of mine and I have to say that I am very grateful he gifted me the Thief series. And although he forgot Thief: Deadly Shadows, I had more than 20 hours fun with Thief Gold to this date.
So. Let's review it, shall we?
I'll split this into two main points,
and
. I won't touch on the story so much, you should play the game yourself to fully appreciate it.
All set? Cool, let's go.
As you would expect from a game released in the late 90s, it's quite dated. If you start it up for the first time, it is downright horrible. You'll need to change the controls accordingly, and you want to install TFix for the game to work in your favor, so that you can properly play it. I set the movement to wasd, looking around originally was on the Arrow keys, if someone knows the Might&Magic series, that was a popular control sceme back then.
You can cycle all your weapons with the Mouse wheel and you inventory with MOUSE4 and MOUSE5 (that's what I used at least). It is actually quite clunky and confusing if you have collected many items in a mission and you try to find your flash bombs while being chased.
Movement is pretty straight-forward, you can run, crouch and toggle walk (which I never used), look around with the mouse, you can even bhop if you have an even stretch of terrain going in one direction, which helps you getting away from danger. I think they fixed it in the second installment of Thief, there you cannot gain speed with bhopping anymore.
If you stay in the dark, you'll be hidden from eyesight perfectly. That is, if no one is searching for you. Otherwise they will spot you, no matter how dark your light gem at the bottom of the screen is.
Concerning the light gem: it's probably the most useful tool in your arsenal. It tells you how well hidden you are. If the light gem is white and a small, red dot is glowing on the side of it, you're visible to everything that should lay an eye upon you. If the gem is dark and the dot is green, you are perfectly hidden.
As explained, this will not always protect you from enemies. If they are alert enough, they will actively search the dark for you, also looking around doorways and scoping out dark corners and crevices.
Another aspect of the gameplay are footsteps. Maybe you know this from Dishonored. If you run, the enemy will hear you, you can purchase special boots to soften your footsteps, that feature is absent in Thief. Different surfaces will make different sounds, some louder, some not audible for the enemy. If you walk on metal, gravel or marble, you make the loudest noises, carpet or grass are silent. Wood and stone are generally pretty nice, if you run on them up to a guard from behind he will most likely go into stage 1 of "detection mode" before you knock him out, not more.
There are some useful tools to help you get around in a mansion spiked with marble floors or in a tower with too many iron walkways. You can purchase Moss Arrows, which make your steps silent. You can shoot it onto the floor and it will spread out in a circle, allowing you to walk on it silently. Enemies won't notice this change.
There's also a rope arrow which can be shot into wooden surfaces, helping you to get to elevated or hard-to-reach places.
Water arrows can douse torches and fires, helping you not getting spotted that easily.
Combat is clunky and hard, encouraging you to sneak. If you meet a guard directly, you're most likely dead.
However, I found that there's a small window of opportunity with knocking out unsuspecting enemies:
Of course you can walk up behind them with your wooden club (called Blackjack, for non-lethal takedowns) and give them a little strike, rendering them unconscious. Or, you can also hide behind a corner, jumping out at the last moment before the enemy rounds it, giving them a whack with the blackjack.
Most of the time they'll go: "Hey! Who are y... OUF!" meaning that you knocked them out before the AI could grasp you're really there and go into stage 2 alert mode.
You also have fire- and gas arrows, which are quite rare, but your best bet against any enemy. Also, you can use Holy Water on your water arrows to deal with some of the more paranormal enemies.
If you fight and seriously injure a guard, spider, etc. they will run away and call for help, alerting everyone around you, and let me tell you, you don't want that.
Especially the later enemies are quick and very tough to fight, so sneaking is generally your best option. You can always distract them by shooting noise arrows or throwing an object in a certain direction.
If you play the first two hours, you'll notice where Dishonored got its inspiration from. Guards constantly speak to themselves, cough and mutter, whistle or hum a song. Occasionally you can overhear a conversation between two guards, telling you more about a situation or giving you subtle hints where a specific object is located.
Ambient noises are more rare, but they are there, for example dripping water in a cave or running machinery.
The music is gloomy and dark and it changes from area to area, when you walk out of a house into the courtyard, there might be something else playing than two seconds ago. The transition is quite fluent and on-point, immersing you pretty good. Usually, you can hear when you are in an area where you need to go, it is just the subtle change in tone of the tune playing, you'll notice it when you get there.
The game looks dark and moody, with some impressive shadow casting for the time. Also, Thief 1 & 2 still have one of the best sound engines ever made, when you hear sounds from a certain direction, usually, there's also something there that makes these sounds. I found that the engine bugged sometimes, but maybe that's because of the level design.
Speaking of that, the level design is impressive, yet sometimes confusing, with parts branching off and running back towards the main path. it looks very believable and has some special detail for it, although things like debris and small objects lying around are missing. I think the maps are quite innovative and they never get boring, they are nice and rememberable. Also, the lighting is one point most of the time, a cave is rather dark and cold looking, a library is either flooded in warm light or also gloomy, depending on who possesses the house it is built in.
Not all enemies have the same voice lines, and especially the Hammerites impressed me, using old, Shakespearian language to indicate that they are quite sophisticated, yet a bit fanatic. Mages are very calm, but also have a certain majestic undertone. Guards can sound professional or quite dumb.
The voice acting is alse very believeable and shows that the Thief voice team did an outstanding job with recording them.
Special mentions go towards the voice actor of the thief himself: Stephen Russell, who is the perfect fit for master thief Garrett, providing him with just enough character to not be over the top. He often gives remarks (that can be quite snarky) when reaching key locations or targets. Also, before each mission, he tells a bit about the following task, that he has to do. This is combined with some of the most fitting musc for a serious "mission briefing" by the main character himself.
I'd like to mention a very specific thing I looked forward to after each completed mission. There's a segment where the screen shows quotes from books of the Hammerites or other parties, accompanied by music, which is drastically rising in intensity, indicating a climax, which is usually a deep tone switching over to the briefing music. Shortly after the tone, Garrett starts talking, which is the point the intense music was building up to. Absolutely well done and awesome.

It's hard to review a game you picked up so long ago, especially since I just repeat-flashed through the final act to speed things along (Embermage = op).
Torchlight like any game of this type was bound to be a grind, and with 44hrs on record it kept me busy for quite a while, but I'd wager only a fifth of that time was spent in fights worthy of my character. Perhaps it's my guilty pleasure of min-maxing that led to this... and the skill system certainly gives you that option: With abilities and items and set bonuses and socketables and enchantments and pets... the list goes on.
Quests have no voice-over and can be ignored, FMVs are dull and music is nothing to write home about; however gameplay is smooth and enjoyable. After account setup, multiplayer is quick and easy and the game relaxes some of its rules to make it easier to find your team or hop out and shop. The game seems to try its best to remove all the little annoyances.
Finally the boss fights... There's minibosses scattered about, and they seem to have randomly assigned buffs that can lead to some interesting encounters... some can even pose a threat! Final area bosses are built up, and many have scripted mechanics such as area denial, pulls or spawns; but with difficulty the way it is I never found a reason to do anything other than stand still and spam magic missile. There's potential, you can see it, but it's too weak and fragile... too easily crushed under my lvl 51 heel. Muahaha!
As a side note: I've tinkered with the overhaul mod called Synergies and it claims to fix many of the pacing issues and throws in more mobs for you to squelch. A coop permadeath run with this enabled still intrigues me, and for this reason I raised the score a bit. There may be life in the old dog yet.
Recommended... if it's on sale.[6.2]

Got this game for free from Humble Bundle a couple weeks ago and I've gotta say this is a damn good game. Not a fan of RTS games but this made it tolerable and even enjoyable with simple mechanics and non-BS AI. Full of jokes and references and even people from metal and the music industry as a whole, including Lemmy from Motorhead as "Kill Master", Jack Black (the protagonist and playable character) from Tenacious D as "Eddie Riggs" and Ozzy Osbourne as the "Guardian of Metal".
Campaign: About 6-7 hours long and not difficult or challenging by any means on the Normal/"Roadie" difficulty. I'll eventually get around to doing a hard/"Brutal" playthrough and update accordingly. Some of the occurences in the storyline are cliched and overdone but it does have some unique elements in it. The sense of progression the campaign gives you however, as you unlock new powers, an upgradable car, new allies, new songs and character customisation options. There's no branching storyline so replayability isn't really in the cards.
Story - 7/10
Characters - 8.5/10
Locations/Map - 8/10
Multiplayer: Multiplayer in this game is an RTS minigame where you have to capture these glowing green points to gain "fans" which essentially act as resources. You can then use these "fans" to create units or upgrade your "stage" or base of operations. You can set per group or per unit commands and way points and control your units using what amounts to "Kill those things", "Stay Here", "Go There", and "Follow Me". Where this differs from most RTS games is that you yourself are a playable character and can fly over the battlefield using demon wings which greatly assists in setting waypoints and moving units fast. You can also use "Guitar Solos" to buff your units, debuff the enemy units, kill the enemy units or
. You win by destroying the enemies stage. There are 3 options for multiplayer: online matchmaking, vs games with friends and practice vs AI. Online matchmaking is dead, so the only 2 options left are vs friends or vs AI. One person on my friends list owns this game so I have no experience in vs friends at all. Practice vs AI was OK and because I suck at RTS I can't beat anything beyond the middle-tier of difficulty.
What to do after beating the main game: Sadly, not much. There are side quests but there's only 4 variations of them except for a couple one-off missions that are entirely unique, such as clearing a cave for a family of bats or helping one of your headbangers smash by keeping the more attractive dudes away from the girl he's hitting on. Some of these are hilarious but the sidequests add maybe an extra half hour to hour to the game. The variations are:
- Ambush a group of enemies,
- Ride "The Death Rack" which basically is your car sitting on a piece of metal and either using your weapons to shoot incoming waves of enemies or directing your units to defend or attack points around you,
- Race Fletus, a guy with a striking similarity to Slippy Toad from Starfox,
- Kill X amount of animal Y to beat the hunters record.
The facial animations for the side quests (especially the ambush ones) are noticeabley off and bad and feel rushed and with nowhere the same amount of care, effort and polish the rest of the game has.
There's also collectibles in the form of buried metal, bound serpents, legends, motor forges, landmark views and lightning plug jumps. The problem with all of these is that although they are easy to collect, the game doesn't really incentivize you to go search for them nor does it give you any hints when they are near. You'll collect quite a few of the lightning plug jumps, bound serpents and motor forges from exploring between missions, but not all of them.
Pros:
+Humour
+Lots of character
+Character Depth
+Cameos from famous people involved in metal
+Jack Black did FMV for this, no matter how cringey
+FOV slider in a 3rd person game. Neato.
+Managed to hold my attention which is very difficult for single-player campaigns to do nowadays.
+Damn good, fitting soundtrack.
Neutral:
•Controls can be clunky but are rebindable.
•AI varies between idiotic and reasonable outside of RTS battles.
•Doesn't hold your hand or recommend the best ways to counter specific enemies.
Cons:
Turns out Double Fine itself published this game for PC and EA only published the console versions. Hats off to Double Fine.
-60FPS cap
-Some of the textures and models aren't that HQ
Conclusion: If you like metal and/or have an understanding of metal and the people and songs included in it, this is definitely a must play. If you like light-RTS games that don't require you to thing like a Chess Grandmaster, give this a serious look. Overall score: 8.5/10. One of my favorite games to date.

This game has three aspects: The OK, The Meh and The Awful.
The setting, story and characters are quite funny. Cutscenes are cool. Metal references are great. Some gameplay elements feel very fresh and imaginative at first - although they get old pretty fast too.
Action gameplay is quirky, unchallenging and mostly boring. Exploration and side-quests are just like your typical Ubi-style openworld game: lots of collectibles and repetitive activities, all pointless beyond earning "fire tributes" used to purchase some upgrades (which are mostly decorative as well). Except Ubi games at least have AAA visuals. Racing around in your car feels surprisingly good, though. Well, maybe not that good during some trickier chasing / running sequences...
Did you see that RTS tag? Did you wonder what the hell did they mean by it? Well, for a pretty long part of the game, I was wondering too. Then I reached the first "stage battle", died and respawned a lot of times without even understanding what the hell I am supposed to do to win, and still won eventually (somehow). Then I reached the second and things got even worse: I had to lower the difficulty to "gentle" just so I could stop that confusing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t already and move on... Well, from there, it only gets worse and worse. Now it's my fourth "RTS battle", and I'm not even sure I'll find the strength to keep going to see the rest of the story. I just desperately wish for a magic button to skip the damn thing.
Oh, and here I am ranting while people are still wondering what the hell that RTS tag actually means. So, long story short: you build resource towers, destroy resource towers, train troops and tell them to attack in a typical RTS fashion... except your commanding character has to do all this stuff personally, while running or flying back and forth around the battlefield, wasting tons of time on simplest commands and then wondering why is everyone dead after you just took a quick stroll back to your stage to command some fresh reinforcements to join the rest (yes, you have to command them every time - they won't move automatically to your latest rally flag like anyone sane would expect them to). It is also often hard to tell the enemy apart from your own troops. The result is a horrible, anti-fun abomination. Calling it a strategy, real-time or not, is a grave insult to real strategy games. As a major fan of rwby who loves the show to death and pesters my friends relentlessly get into the show, i love the series as a whole. I bought this literally day 1 in early access so i've been there since the start. That being said i was super excited for the full release, so how does the game stack up?
as a 15$ game... its meh, it's decent it's not ungodly awful but i wouldn't say it's "good". as a 25$ game... it's awful and i'd never pay such a price for the content provided, so let's break it down.
-Combat, the core of a hack n slash, in all honesty it feels very lacking in most if not all departments. Most characters just spam 1 combo because it's the best thing they have. a REALLY annoying thing is how every character (friend and foe) has the exact...same...audio lines... for every single combo and attack! you can hear an ursa grunt from being hit like 50 times trying to kill the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (same with other Grimm as well as players doing combos).
-Characters, even though the main cast is present, none of the charm is there. There's little to no true interaction between the cast (they literally never address one another outside of being revived and maybe the occasional team attack) and overall come off as bland and boring.
-Music + sound, the music is pretty good, all songs from the show that usually hit at the right time (wish the songs had lyrics though, i do like to sing along). Sound wise like i said most of the sound assets are massively overused and repeat themselves to an insane degree to the point of irritation/frustration.
-Visuals, game look's decent, doesn't blow my mind but it's not bad by any stretch of the imagination (i did hear of some bugs but never witnessed any)
-Story, to be honest it may as well not exist, has some mystery and adventure at the start but becomes very boring and dull halfway through, the villan is very weak (though to be fair nobody in this game is strong in the character department.)
-Misc information, level design is hyper linear (some levels look good aesthetically, others don't). Enemy variety is very very low, (there's an okay amount of enemies but your normally fighting the same 2-3 types en mass depending on the area). When your not fighting Horde A and moving to fight Horde B (literally 98% of this game is horde wave battles) the world just feels empty and hollow.
-Progression, standard 10 levels get a point as you lvl up and put it into 1 of numerous passives only a handful of which you will see and actively use. You keep levels and such through numerous playthroughs but to get more challenges to grind more you need to reset.... why?
-Conclusion, this is nowhere near worth 25 dollars i'm sorry it's just not enough there to justify it. at 15 it's a hard sell unless your a hardcore fan. I know i'm being hard on this but that's because i want RT to learn and grow from this experience to create bigger and better things. We proved we'd support them however we can (this game got greenlit in 1-2 days). I do realize this isn't a triple A title and i don't judge it as such, i judge it as a 25 dollar game and i don't think it's up to par. Thief Gold is the definitive version of Thief - The Dark Project, released in 1998 and developed by Looking Glass Studios. It was one of the first games of its kind, and practically invented the stealth genre - but should you play it today?
Well, the short answer is yes. Here's the long answer:
Firstly, let's talk about the presentation. Thief Gold runs on the Dark Engine, which isn't exactly brilliant on the graphics front even for its time, but it does allow for some fantastic lighting effects which help make up the core gameplay mechanics. The fact that the game runs on an engine that's basically the software equivalent of masking tape and rubber bands means that the game isn't too demanding for a pc, and therefore allows some gigantic, sprawling levels, which I will talk about later. The voice acting is really quite good. The main character, a likeable Han Solo kind of guy named Garrett, is voiced by the legendary Stephen Russell, who also voiced half of the characters in Skyrim. He does a great job bringing Garrett to life and I think that a Thief game without Stephen Russell is not a Thief game at all. So don't bother with the 2014 reboot. The graphics, as I mentioned before, are not all that great but that can be easily overlooked because the real fun lies in the gameplay.
On that note, the gameplay is really quite fantastic. Thief didn't just invent the stealth genre, it also invented first-person ledge mantling, which makes the platforming seem far more satisfying than it would be otherwise. Stealth revolves around visibility and volume, and is the main part of the gameplay. Crouch-walking will render you silent in movement, and shadows will obscure you from enemy guards' vision. The amount of noise you make also depends on the type of floor you're walking on, which is another of Thief's innovations. If you're on carpet, your movement is rendered silent, but if you're on metal, you can be heard a mile off. Non-lethal takedowns can be achieved by smacking someone from behind  with your Blackjack, and there are so many creative ammo types for the bow that the game becomes your own little stealth sandbox. It's amazing how much more fun a weapon is to use if you give it creative ammo types, and this is one of the game's chief merits.
Not everything is great at all times, though. In most levels, the game is awesome. You navigate through sprawling complexes, stealing massive amounts of gold and being hugely satisfied in the process. The levels where you're just being a master thief are easily the most enjoyable. It's just the levels where the game turns into Resident Evil that the game becomes annoying. I really could have done without the satanic demons, to be perfectly honest. The levels where you have to fight undead spirits are straight-up frustrating, and on my second playthrough I skipped The Lost City level completely. It really is that annoying.
But don't get me wrong, this game is hugely enjoyable for the most part. It offers far more than the 2014 reboot ever could, for a fraction of the price, and the sequel, Thief 2: The Metal Age, improved on every single problem I've mentioned. So do yourself a favour and play this game.

‘Brothers – A Tale of Two Sons’ elegantly combines unique gameplay with stunning visuals to provide an experience that could potentially satisfy anyone.
You take control of two brothers, one older, responsible one and one younger, playful one. Tasked with finding a cure for their father, you take them on their quest, which couldn’t be any more satisfying. The game tells it’s tale through character mumbles (similar to the early Lego games) yet the story is completely coherent through actions and mumble-quality (technical term).
Complemented with a stunning soundtrack, ‘Brothers’ has one of the best stories I’ve seen in an indy game (not that I usually go looking for indy games). In its roughly four hours of playing time, it really has some great moments. Although the start is a little slow, this isn’t an issue because the ending makes it all worth it.
The story is progressed through a series of elegant puzzles. The player needs to control the brothers to solve them. This is satisfying in itself as the player has the option of controlling both brothers simultaneously if they opt to play single-player.
One thing ‘Brothers’ does particularly well is show the dynamic between the older brother and younger brother. Through interactions with other people and objects, I often found myself laughing at how different they were. While one brother may interact with and play a harp beautifully, the other brother interacts with and fumbles over the strings. While one brother tries and fails to fit through the gaps of a fence, the other brother slips through with ease. The subtle differences are pleasing to watch and this added a level of immersion to the game for me.
The picturesque landscape completes the whole experience. In designated seats, the player may choose to take a breath and stare at the background. It’s like climbing up a mountain and stopping to stare at how high up you are. Don’t let the indy-styled, simple graphics fool you. This game has stunning visuals and breath-taking scenery.
To address the question on everyone’s mind “Do we
need a controller?” In short… no. I played through this game on a keyboard by myself and have never had the experience of playing it with a controller. The controls are a bit mind-boggling on keyboard but, that said, I consider myself a bit uncoordinated in games and the keyboard controls (simultaneously controlling big and little brothers on WASD and arrows respectively) didn’t take anything away from the game for me. If you have serious coordination issues, either play co-op or use a controller.
In short, I wish I had played this game when it came out. It is seriously one of the best games I’ve played in a while. Although it is short (approx. four hours), it has something for everyone. Complete with stunning visuals, satisfying puzzles and a great soundtrack, the story is amazing and I would recommend it to anyone.
Verdict: 9.8/10

Brothers is a beautiful game that I would highly recommend to those that enjoy smart gameplay and beautiful stories. If you enjoy games such as ICO and Shadow of the Colossus, then this is a gem that was obviously made with these in mind.
Story:
As the title suggests, you play a pair of brothers. Still in grief about their late mothers, they suddenly are confronted with their father becoming lethally sick, too. Desperate to not lose him as well, they set out on a journey to find the Tree that might hold a cure according to the doctor. What sounds easy enough soon becomes a terrifying, exciting and dangerous venture across mountains and caves to save their father.
Art:
The game is generally low-poly with a touch of cartoony simpleness, yet remains breathtakingly beautiful. The benches that can be found in the game continously allow for a calm look around the scenerey (similar to the benches in Pokemon X & Y). The landscape is detailed, yet always straight forward. The athmosphere is fitting and always seems lively with just enough creatures in and about it to not make it feel deserted, yet keep it from being distracting. Obviously inspired by nordic landscapes and architecture, it feels like taking a trip through a scandinavian fairytale.
Gameplay:
The strongest point of Brothers is definitely the gameplay. You play a multiplayer game as a single player, controlling two characters simultanously with one controller. What sounds easy enough is at times quite challenging, especially as none of the brothers allows the other to run too far off and thus sometimes allows for smart enviromental puzzles. In general are the puzzles mostly natural obstructions that the brothers have to overcome with their combined efforts or smart thinking by the player. Interesting is especially that all interactions run with just one button and that - other than introducing said button - no tutorial helps the player in figuring out how to overcome a obstacle. Yet all areas and puzzles are solvable once the player figures out which brother to do what.
Audio:
The music is amazing with a woman singing lonely in the background, setting the mood for the brothers travel into the wild, unprotected with no one but each other. The sound is sparse and appropiate, the vocalisation simple and - since it is Gibberish - relateable without feeling weird.
Other things I enjoyed:
Special mention should go to the achievements. In contrary to most games that throw out achievements for everything and especially feats that every player does (such as finishing a chapter), Brothers only gives out achievements when the player actually does take his time to explore, to be kind or mean and to enjoy the world that was build. Every achievement received feels like an actual achievement that the player found for their trouble instead of a throw-away gift.
Another special mention should go to the story itself. Unexpected for me was the emotional impact of it, especially concidering the fact that no text or understandable language appears in the game. The developers took extra care to make the animations readable and the speakers understandable so that the player instinctively knows how the characters feel. That plus the amazing music sets the mood and controls especially the later part of the game as the brothers get confronted with dangers that no child should usually encounter.
Summary:
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a adventure with beautiful graphics, great music and a story that simple, yet effective. Especially people who love challenges, interesting gameplay and highly emotional stories will love this little gem.

The only shopkeeping game I can really think of to compare this to is Recettear, but the games play too differently to really recommend one over the other. Recettear is a shop simulator where you sell items and haggle one by one to customers who come in, and you get a dungeon crawler bundled with it. Shoppe Keep is a shop simulator where you watch numbers go up, listen to customers happily hum (or grumble) about your prices, and (if toggled) get pillaged by barbarians for being too successful. Also there are people who try to steal your♥♥♥♥♥♥and try to run, so naturally they pay with their lives.
I got this game in the humble monthly, and frankly, I'm appalled all the hatred piling up against it, I've had a bug-free experience so far, and while there are some missed opportunities and general clunkiness that goes with the game, I think it's a great game to pick up if you want to just relax and waste some time. It definitely has enough content to warrant the price tag assuming you're not a lunatic that expects every game to have the same amount of content as Witcher 3 (or a Bethesda title).
For anyone who's just gotten the game in the humble monthly and reads this, there are only a few things I can recommend/mention.
1. Starting out: Days 1-5 To get your shop up off the ground, buy some health potions and invade everyone's privacy. Run around town like a lunatic selling people health potions directly until you can afford other items (like swords.)
2. Kpoints seem to be earned in two ways, gradually by selling items in your store, or by doing quests. Doing quests might take a more hands-on approach, but it earns them way faster than waiting. Only one quest can be active at a time.
3. Thieves: They steal your♥♥♥♥♥♥ you need to zap or stab them so they don't run off with your goods. Zapping doesn't scare your customers (maybe a bug, maybe not), so it's preferable to do that.
4. Apparently, you can lose by getting 0% appeal. I'm pretty sure that only happens if you haphazardly murder your customers.
5. Barbarians need to be toggled in a 2-step process. You need to enable them in your options, and get the Popularity perk (which makes it so if you have an item someone wants, they will have a much higher chance of visiting the store.)

People will inevitably compare this game to Shiftlings - maybe even call one of them a knockoff. Despite both games having some identical game mechanics, they are very different games. It's similar to Halo versus Doom. Both are FPS games where a green marine blasts through unnatural creatures, but the gameplay is not the same. Having played around 5 hours both shifty games, I'm making a short comparison.
Shiftlings:
- Shiftlings singleplayer/co-op is both the same game, in singleplayer you just switch between characters
- Shiftlings ties  players together with a leash
- Puzzles  focus more around the leash and the bigger character working as a bouncy platform for the little one
- Somewhat cruel: single checkpoint per level. Puzzles easy to screw up with wrong shift move
- High production in graphics and animations
- ...but overproduced and visually crowded
Shift Happens:
- Separate singleplayer and co-op campaigns, though in singleplayer you keep switching between characters
- No leash: the players are more independent
- Puzzles resolve around shifting, bouncy platforms and big character throwing the little one
- Forgiving: death is only punishing if both screw up at the same time
- ...but offers also hard challenges, eg. bonus levels
- Visually simple, but very pleasing to the eye
Biggest problems in Shiftlings are the overcrowded visuals and rope. Rope mechanic works in Red Rope: Don't Fall Behind, but leads to quite frustrating puzzles in Shiftlings. Especially as the gravity pulls bigger player down. Shift at the wrong moment, the hanging bigger player drops down and drags the smaller player with him, starting the puzzle all over again. Shiftlings could have benefited from leaving either shift or rope away, or introducing the second mechanic later in the game. Shift happens has a little more leisure pace still offering a challenge. Tiny bit of the challenge comes from some rough edges: Catching the other player midair can be confusing, since there is a special way to press the button. If you press it even slightly too long, the grab is not performed. The small effective area for grabbing can also lead to mild annoyance when you are trying to position the players correctly.
I do not mind both games existing - they both cater to a niche: co-op focused games. Either one is NOT recommendable for singleplayer only. I'm definitely preferring Shift Happens over Shiftlings due to visuals, less frustrating puzzles and separate campaigns for one and two players. As a co-op puzzle platformer, Shift Happens is not the best I've played, but clearly in the top.

This is the first game I've ever bothered to leave a review on so I'll just leave this here:
Pros:
-Solid story and voice acting

-Great jokes and references

Cons:
-Story is a little on the short side
-It's hard to tell what's going on sometimes in the RTS sections (could just be me, though)
-Battle moves aren't too exciting compared to games like DmC, but it's not too big of a deal
-End of the game feels rushed, probably due to time constraints set by EA. It has a ton of important questions left unanswered and a huge missed opportunity for great and satisfying conclusion to the story.
Overall, Brutal Legend is freaking awesome and it's become one of my favourite games of all-time. I should have picked it up a long time ago. It's not flawless but its shortcomings don't take away from the great journey this game brings you along for. The only major issue I have with it is the ending. Other than that, it's fantastic.
Ignoring my disappointment with the rushed ending, I'd give it a 9.5/10, but considering my overall experience with the game, it gets a well-deserved 8.5. I love it.

As a major fan of rwby who loves the show to death and pesters my friends relentlessly get into the show, i love the series as a whole. I bought this literally day 1 in early access so i've been there since the start. That being said i was super excited for the full release, so how does the game stack up?
as a 15$ game... its meh, it's decent it's not ungodly awful but i wouldn't say it's "good". as a 25$ game... it's awful and i'd never pay such a price for the content provided, so let's break it down.
-Combat, the core of a hack n slash, in all honesty it feels very lacking in most if not all departments. Most characters just spam 1 combo because it's the best thing they have. a REALLY annoying thing is how every character (friend and foe) has the exact...same...audio lines... for every single combo and attack! you can hear an ursa grunt from being hit like 50 times trying to kill the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (same with other Grimm as well as players doing combos).
-Characters, even though the main cast is present, none of the charm is there. There's little to no true interaction between the cast (they literally never address one another outside of being revived and maybe the occasional team attack) and overall come off as bland and boring.
-Music + sound, the music is pretty good, all songs from the show that usually hit at the right time (wish the songs had lyrics though, i do like to sing along). Sound wise like i said most of the sound assets are massively overused and repeat themselves to an insane degree to the point of irritation/frustration.
-Visuals, game look's decent, doesn't blow my mind but it's not bad by any stretch of the imagination (i did hear of some bugs but never witnessed any)
-Story, to be honest it may as well not exist, has some mystery and adventure at the start but becomes very boring and dull halfway through, the villan is very weak (though to be fair nobody in this game is strong in the character department.)
-Misc information, level design is hyper linear (some levels look good aesthetically, others don't). Enemy variety is very very low, (there's an okay amount of enemies but your normally fighting the same 2-3 types en mass depending on the area). When your not fighting Horde A and moving to fight Horde B (literally 98% of this game is horde wave battles) the world just feels empty and hollow.
-Progression, standard 10 levels get a point as you lvl up and put it into 1 of numerous passives only a handful of which you will see and actively use. You keep levels and such through numerous playthroughs but to get more challenges to grind more you need to reset.... why?
-Conclusion, this is nowhere near worth 25 dollars i'm sorry it's just not enough there to justify it. at 15 it's a hard sell unless your a hardcore fan. I know i'm being hard on this but that's because i want RT to learn and grow from this experience to create bigger and better things. We proved we'd support them however we can (this game got greenlit in 1-2 days). I do realize this isn't a triple A title and i don't judge it as such, i judge it as a 25 dollar game and i don't think it's up to par. If i missed anything or you have something to add feel free to drop a comment below and i'll try to answer everyone best i can.

TL;DR Ultimately the game ended up being disappointing, even as a long time fan of the series. The devs rushed the full release out, overcharged for the amount of content, and plan on charging even more money for future additions to the game.
I really hate to say that I am ultimately not satisfied with this game but I have to. I love RWBY and have had a ton of fun following it. I bought this game back when it first released into early access and have run through it with my friend many times now. Back then the game looked really promising. There was still more to add and many things that needed to be worked on but I thought "it's okay, the devs will definitely get there in time". Each time a new update was released we would run through the game again and each time it got better and better. That is until the final release.
So what exactly is the problem?
1. The devs decided to change the player models for some reason. Originally they were using the exact models from the show but claimed they were causing performances issues (they weren't, even on ym friends lower end laptop). The ones that ended up in the game in the full release aren't bad, but they still aren't quite as good as the originals.
2. Ultimately the game feels hollow and rushed. Each time I got a new update it felt as though a lot of new content was added...until I actually completed that content. There are only 10 levels and they pretty much all involve doing the same thing over and over, fighting waves of enemies. This isn't inherntly bad but the game doesn't do anything to make it good.
3. The environments are all basically the same. In pretty much every encounter your move into a slightly differently shaped flat open plain and fight monsters. There is basically zero exploring to do, you are often blocked off by invisble walls for no real reason, and there isn't really anything in the environment to use during battles (save for a few exploding barrels in the later levels which is pretty lame).
4. There are no more than 10 enenmies in the game, and 10 is being generous. You basically have 4 different types of grim and then larger versions of them plus some robots. This wouldn't be so bad if fighting them wasn't the same every time.
5. The full release price is far too much for the amount of content it has. I only paid $15 back in early access and even then I feel kind of cheated because of how most worthwhile future updates are going to work.
6. The devs decided to make most future updates paid DLC. The only free content is horde mode which honestly I don't feel is even difficult for them to add. The original prototype for the game was a horde mode and the entire game is mor eof less just a series of horde mode battles. They basically don't have to do anything besides make an arena and then make wave sinfinite.
7. Future DLC will be massively overpriced, just like the base game. The devs are planning to add other teams to the game which you will have to pay $10 for (only JNPR confirmed). As far as I am aware this is just the characters and nothing else. No new levels, no new enemies, no new modes.
8. The music. This is more of a personally thing but it drives me crazy that the decision was made to use instrumental version of songs from the show that don't even loop properly. It would have been much better if they included the vocals where appropriate.

*************Before getting into this, keep in mind that I have only played 4 player online. I haven't tried any special game modes, never played teams, never played 1v1. So the following is all based on my 4 player online experience*************
[For my short answer/pros n cons list, skip down to the bottom!]
I'm sure 99% of you have already realized/heard this, but i might as well start off by saying that brawlhalla is very similar to smash bros. If you like smash bros, you'll probably like Brawlhalla. The goal is to knock your opponents off the screen, just like in smash bros. Characters have health, which is basically % from smash. Some important differences to note: you gain a point when defeating an opponent, but they also lose one. you lose 3 for suicide. Instead of items there are gadgets, currently there are only 3 (spike balls to do numerous up close hits, or thrown for strategy or to knock someone out. Bouncy bombs to throw and boom. and sticky bombs which are basically mines. they can all be charged up before thrown. finally there's a horn item, but i don't think it counts as a gadget necessarily. this summons some flaming thing from the right side of the screen that travels to and leaves out the left side, damaging all opponents it touches. note: it travels in a straight horizontal line consistent with your position at the time you use the horn. It's important to also note that the flaming thing drops a weapon for you, which brings me to perhaps the most notable difference between this game and ssb: the weapons. Weapons in this game are not like items in ssb; in this game all weapon pick ups can be one of two weapons based on the character you are. The idea is that weapons are a crucial component to achieving victory; going up against a weapon when you're unarmed is almost certainly a death wish. Each weapon has it's own set of unique attacks with different priority, range, and damage. as is with ssb, you can attack in different directions, neutral, or different directions when airborne to perform different moves. And to be clear, weapons spawn in abundance, everyone generally is able to grab one. (A strategy I use sometimes is to deprive others of a weapon by throwing mine away to pick up any new weapons. Even when doing this, it doesn't keep opponents unarmed for very long.)
There's a lot more to the game of course, but those are some key differences between it and ssb.
The controls are simple: You got your jump, dodge, light atk, heavy atk, and throw. You can use either throw or light atk to pick up weapons/gadgets.
This game does have controller support, with which i unfortunately had an issue. With 2 ps3 controllers plugged in, one does not work at all, and the second one controlled 2 characters... So when I play local only one person gets a controller. This issue is not a huge deal because online multiplayer is fun enough to keep me busy. Being able to use multiple controllers in the future however, would be awesome! Other than that the controller support is great, very responsive. Again, this is an unfinished game, and honestly it surprised me with how well put together it is and how smooth everything runs.
This game is good because it doesn't rely on any gimmicks. It doesn't rely on the fun of discovering new things or of getting to any particular place. It's just fun by itself, and that's why it's great. You pretty much get everything the game has to offer after a round or two, keeping gameplay simple like this is great especially for multiplayer versus games such as this one. The character roster is great, I love the variety of not only the characters themselves but also of the different stat and weapon combos each one has. I think they've all been balanced rather well, without making any one character too similar.
TL;DR---> Pros:
-ssb type game but core gameplay mechanics different enough so that it doesn't feel like a clone with different graphics.
-variety in characters is great going from a pirate to a knight to sci-fi and cyber punk looking characters.
-still early access, but already amazing. finished product will likely have a bunch of new content.
-online works perfectly, always able to quickly find and connect to a match
-fighting is really satisfying and smooth
-controller support is tight and responsive
Cons:
-Won't let me use two controllers
I 100% recommend this game.

Holdfast: Nations at War is a fantastic game for being in early access.  At the moment, for a game that's only 2+ months old (in early access), the amount of variety is pretty impressive.
Pros:
- Really fun boats.
- The modes around boats, but especially coastal siege, are super enjoyable.  Although I wish individualized positions were a bit more relevant than just "now you have a different weapon", the roadmap shows some incredibly interesting choices they want to make going forward.
- Line Battles
- Although it requires you some level of coordination, there's already regiments popping up that are fairly detailed and feature line battles.  In general, the line battles are enjoyable and feel somewhat realistic (or as realistic as I imagine them to be).
- Variety
- Maps, weapons, modes: choices.  There's a variety of choice.  Individual characters have their own abilities, with some of the more interesting ones being musicians (who have music they can play), carpenters, surgeons, and others that aren't entirely fleshed out yet but the core is there.  The first time you select say a drummer, and play music while your team marches, it just really entertaining.
CONS:
- Rifleman are just too OP right now.  The accuracy, even if historically accurate, is just too much.  Additionally, because of limited numbers of slots (typically ten per spawn points), it means you're often stuck with something that is not only less accurate but generally not nearly as fun.
- This is a pie in the sky type thing, but I really wish there was an "Arcade Mode" as well as a "Extreme Simulation Mode".  Right now, the gameplay straddles the line and is fun, but it would be cool if in edition to "Standard" it had either or both of those.  Maybe arcade mode doesn't require full reloads at that speed where as extreme limits the amount of materials and makes the necessity to work as a group better.  I don't know, just spitballing, but it would be cool.
Overall, for an early access game, I've had more fun in Holdfast then many full featued, AAA games over the past year or two.  If you're contemplating buying this game, it's worth it.  Even in this early access state, I've had a lot of fun.

Thief 1 is pure interactive poetry. Though the game's insecurity towards being a pure stealth game in 1998 led to some choices that feel right out of place and might leave a bad taste in the player's mouth (zombies), it doesn't keep it from being a superb mesh of flawless emergent gameplay, beautiful writing and brilliant atmosphere.

If you like hearing "What was that?............ must've been the wind" or "What was that?.............. Damn rats" then this could be a game for you.  Otherwise, it's a dated stealth game with questionable mechanics that don't really shine.
I like the general idea of the game, and I think I might've had fun on the first level, but every level after that I found to be mostly obnoxious rather than fun.  I also like that the gold you earn on any level is used to purchase goods for the next level and that you're encouraged to use all your gold and items since you don't keep them from level to level.  I'm not sure that I have a lot of other positive things to say though.
So starting with the game's problems, the cutscenes for the game don't work.  Imagine my surprise when I found out there's actually suppose to be a story to the game.  Apparently you need to go download a patch to actually see them.
The sneaking mechanics are inconsistent.  Sometimes enemies who shouldn't hear me will hear me sneaking about or doing things, other enemies who should hear me somehow don't.  Enemies also seem very suspicious of footsteps in areas where they know their friends patrol.  Likewise, sometimes enemies will see you from far off but other times they won't.  Sometimes they'll think they see you but keep looking forward instead of simply turning sideways to look in your direction.  Especially fun is when they somehow don't see you from 10-15 feet away out in the open and murdering their friends and they continue standing there going “What was that?................. Something something seeing/hearing things”.  Sometimes you'll be 3 feet in front of them out in the open and they'll still be searching around for you with their hands up to their eyes.  I got so tired of the sneaking mechanics by the 4th level that I simply started killing anyone who saw me since it was much quicker than wasting time hiding and trying to sneak by again or hoping to knock them out.
Another problem is that killing enemies can often be annoying since they have a tendency to run off after you've hit them 6 or so times with your sword.  They run faster than you so to catch up you have to put your weapon away, then they pull a 180 and run by you in the 5 seconds it takes to pull your sword back out and actually swing it at them.  So you have to waste time cornering them down or being ready for when they pull the 180.  Also of note is that enemies can hit you with ranged/melee weapons while facing a different direction from you.  Especially fun is when you finally notice that the archer you've been circling and chopping at has been shooting arrows into you while looking and aiming in a direction 80 degrees away from you and now you're almost dead.  Combat overall is fairly clunky, probably to encourage you not engage in it, but when the sneaking mechanics are just as bad, you have to choose one or the other.
The level design for several of the levels is large and convoluted, and they're not particularly fun to explore.  Another big problem is the climb mechanic.  Sometimes it'll work and sometimes it won't.  Especially fun is trying to use your rope arrows.  You're far more likely to fall to your death/take heavy damage trying to use them then you're to actually attach to them while holding the climb key.  I learned very quickly to always save before attempting to climb down one.
The game also suffers from some annoying glitches.  Had an enemy who was stuck on the wall that was able to see/hear and attack me but was completely invincible to any of my attacks.  Had to run around him and hope he didn't hit me.  Later on I came back and he'd managed to get himself unglued from the wall and acted normally.  Sometimes you'll get stuck on bodies on the ground, or get stuck behind objects you just walked around, or be unable to crawl back through some area that you just crawled in from.
I might have put up with all this stuff if not for my largest issue, and that's the Where's Waldo quest objectives you have to complete.  The game often wants you to find quest objects that are placed in obnoxious spots.  If you happen to not find one, it can take a long time to search and re-search every likely area they could be at since the levels are so damn large.  My favorite was the silver fire poker on the 4th level.  Hmmmmm, a silver fire poker, probably near a fireplace right?  Search all fireplaces, hmmmmmm... no poker.  Maybe it's in that room where there are 2 guards hanging out talking for no reason.  Lure the guards out, search the room, hmmmmmm...... not in here.  Maybe it's in one of those other rooms I didn't explore because there're 3+ people in them.  Run through those rooms while being chased, hmmmmm.... not in those rooms, maybe I missed it while exploring, guess I'll recheck all the fireplaces.   Hmmmmmm.... I've rechecked all the fireplaces, I give up, walkthrough time.......... Oh, I was apparently supposed to shoot a water arrow at the fireplace in the main bedroom and then go inside of it, turn around, look up, and see that there's a switch in it that opens a secret door in the fireplace that leads into the walls and the fire poker is hanging out in there for some reason.  How intuitive.  I gave up playing the game on the 5th level after I missed the guy's bracelet and didn't feel like re-exploring every area or even looking it up and running through the obnoxious level again to find it.
Just not sure I get the appeal of this game.  It simply has too many issues and outside of the first level, I was never having fun.

Listen, forget assassin's creed, forget splinter cell, forget metal gear, forget every stealth game you ever played.  The stealth genre would be nothing without Thief.  And unlike the former titles mentioned, Thief is TRUE stealth.  At no point can you decide "Oh to hell with it" and run out of your hiding place guns/daggers/et al blazing, killing everything with a consciousness in your path.  You are a thief - you stay hidden by shadow and silence and steal stuff.  As soon as you leave the shadows you are fair game to be hacked to pieces like the taffer you are.  That being said, stay hidden and walk with shadows and you are a force of nature.  Thief is to this day a one of a kind game with mechanics that are still mostly unique.  The only games I can think of that come close to hardcore stealth like Thief are the Styx games (Master of Shadows/ Shards of Darkness).  I love the story, the world building, the environments, the characters - everything narrative about this game and cannot recommend it enough.  Only drawback is because it is an older game, it has a hard time running on newer operating systems (Windows 7,8, and 10).  There is a workaround for this though and it's super easy: go here
and install the necesarry patch.
TL;DR
+The OG stealth game
+Dope story, characters, and world
+Gameplay that challenges you to be one with the shadows
-It is dated, so graphics aren't up to snuff
+/-Have to download patch to get it to run on present day operating systems (Takes no time, is super easy to do)

Tekken. The only fighting game franchise that has a legacy just a big as street fighter. I remember back in the day when people said "Fighting game" The Tekken vs Street fighter rivalry immediately came to mind. After what seems like an eternity since Tekken Tag 2 release, we finally got another main installment of the tekken series. This is the first tekken game I started to get serious in. So, Is Tekken still a worth rival to SF, or has Harada gotten rusty? Like my UNIEL review I'll be breaking this review down into several parts: Story, presentation, Casual Content, mechanics, accessibility, and netcode.
Story:
For the sake of time, I won't be giving a synopsis of the story because it would take A LONG♥♥♥♥♥TIME for me to type it up. In short, Heihachi and Kazuya still hate each other's guts and Jin gets screwed in various ways because of it. Akuma is there because Heihachi's wife, Kazumi, told him to kill her husband and Akuma for some reason agrees to do so. The story mode is actually pretty good. There are some minigames mixed in to the actual combat to make things really interesting. For example, there's one part where you play as Lars and you have the ability to use an assult rifle and switch between that and your bare fists. Needless to say, I had a blast with that scene. The only thing that ruined story mode is that monotone narrator. There were several points of the story where I questioned if he even had the ability to feel emotions.
Presentation:
If you noticed the spec requirements for this game, you would see that they are pretty high. The graphics are the reason for it and let me tell you, it looks really damn good. Most of the physics are accurate and the characters look awesome all the way down to the minor details. I'm not kidding when I say you can literally see the raindrops roll down their face or skin when they are fighting on a rainy stage. It's THAT DETAILED. Let's move on.
Casual Content:
Good news for casual players! Although you guys don't have a lot of modes to choose from, the quality of them is more than enough to keep you playing. There's still arcade mode with all the characters, treasure battle which is a survival mode and not mention, a whacky minigame true to tekken nature. Tekken bowl. I never get tired of seeing akuma popping off hard when he gets a strike, it's hilarious.
Mechanics:
Tekken is pretty barebones compared to the anime fighters I like to play. However, adding that third axis complicates everything. Sidestepping effectively, maintaining center ring control are key components to being successful. Rage is still a mechanic which activates when you are low on health and it allows the affected player to do more damage. However, rage arts and rage  drives are a first in the series. Rage arts are you super moves that you can get access to while in rage and rage drive effects a certain string and gives it certain properties. However, if you use either one of these, you will not be in rage state anymore so make them count! Other than that, it's pretty barebones, but that doesn't make it any easier to get into.
Acessibility:
While the controls are super simple with each button corresponding to a limb to a certain side of your body, some combos are hard and the neutral is EVEN HARDER. However, there is a fatal flaw for this game and if you read my Uniel review, you can guess what it is.
No tutorial mode.
All the universial mechanics are explained with random tips near the bottom of the screen in between loading screens which is the least likely place for the player to look for that kind of information, or even pay attention to for that matter. Seriously, for a week, I did not even know you can roll into the foreground by pressing  down + 1 and into the background by pressing 1 as soon as you land. It took me another month to figure out how to do a hopspring.
Quite frankly, for a big name fighting game to not have a tutorial mode, is unacceptable. Harada, if you're reading this, this is why  people are dropping the game. Most people are not willing to do outside research to get good at the game. Now I'm not saying that you should be spoon feeding everything to them. Just teach the basics:
- How to move including side stepping
- options you have when you knocked down
- how strings work/how to combo
- how walls work and wall/floor breaks.
Cover those areas and you've got a decent tutorial. Although I reccomend you talk about Korean backdashing but it's understandable if you don't.
However, once you get a feel for how the combo system works, it's not too bad.
Netcode:
Ok, this is the most important thing about fighting games and I'm glad to say the netcode is good. It's not rev 1 or KI levels of good, but it makes online playable. One thing that does help is the native 8F input delay that is in the game. Games are good if the connection is 4 bars are higher but it gets problematic when it is 3 bars. There's really not much else to say about it.
Conclusion:
So Tekken 7 blows Street fighter V out of the water to be honest. The game looks good, quality game modes for casual players, tight balancing of the roster, and good netcode. Although, from what I'm told, it is the best tekken to start with, but even then, it's pretty hard and scary to get serious with. The lack of a tutorial mode does not help. The player base for online is medium sized but it should be bigger. Keeping your veterans playing the game is important, but bringing in new players is just as important if not more important.
This is game is fantastic but it's being held back by a lack of a tutorial mode. If you're a fan of fighting games and you're sick of capcom's ...questionable business practices or don't like SFV, I definately recommend picking this game up. Heck, even you play tekken casually, i still recommend you pick this game up. However, if you're trying get serious, you're gonna have to do your homework.

Welcome to the more recent installation in The Sims franchise.  I'm sure anyone visiting this store page and looking into this game already knows what Sims is all about, so I'll keep it short and sweet.  The Sims is a life simulator basically.  You take control of a household of people and live a virtual life basically.  You make them use the restroom, sleep, eat, go to work/school, play games, watch TV, interact with others and so on.  There is also a fairly average home building/modifying feature in The Sims that allows you to create your own house, or add on to an existing one.  You can work at your leisure, picking the wallpaper/paint, flooring, exterior siding, roofing, grass type, placement of interior and exterior lighting and furniture and so on.
This game is uniquely addictive and fun, with plenty to satiate your simulation needs, however.  Keep in mind that this is made by EA, and as such, comes with a lot of baggage.  Yes, there is a lot of DLC that adds some neat little features and whatnot, but
you do not want to buy it.  The DLC is ridiculously overpriced and never goes on sale.  To add to that, this game itself should honestly only be bought on sale for $15 or less, considering that EA has released The Sims 4  recently.  But, in spite of the financial issues that plague all EA titles, this game is still a solid outlet for entertainment.  8.5/10.

I literally cannot stop playing this game. I tried it late last night and i stayed up for waaaay too long. It's so well balanced, enjoyable, and some moments are downright epic. Makes me want to watch How To Train Your Dragon again. 10/10.
Okay, I GUESS there are a few things wrong in its current state.
There's no AFK auto-kick, so if a guy goes AFK, the teams get super unbalanced because they never spawn in. Speaking of team balance, there is no way as of now to manually switch teams. I'm not too sure of any plot, although there is certainly framework for a cool story. There are currently only two gamemodes, Team Deathmatch and Deathmatch (free-for-all). A gamemode caled Caravan is currently in the making. The individual sounds aren't exactly...awe-inspiring, but they do the trick. New adio files can be added later on if development continues.
On the plus side, there is no buyable currency, and everybody has to grind for their dragons. The way the system works is each time you level up, you unlock a 'DNA point' that you can use towards unlocking another dragon. Each dragon takes 3 DNA points to unlock, as they are all only as effective as the player can make them. There is no 'be-all-end-all' dragon, they all have their strengths and weaknesses, and are overall very balanced. There is no marketplace, although i'm sure one wil be implimented for cosmetics. The soundtrack is very suiting, and I felt like a total bada$$ when a massive orchestra swept up into a chorus as I shot down a giant flying ogre with goddamned lasers.
On the 'meh' side, it's built on the Unity engine, which means it can run on any computer relatively well, but the graphics aren't exactly mesmerizing. In my opinion graphics aren't necessary if the gameplay is good, which it truly is. Controls can take a bit of getting used to, and they cannot be rebound in-game (you can do some limited rebinding through the launcher).
All in all? I find this game to be more fun than most modern AAA multiplayer titles. With certain tweaking and addition of more content, I truly believe this game has E-sports potential. You know what? This isn't '10/10'. This is 'Giant Dragons Shooting Each Other Out Of The Sky While 100 Band Members Simultaneously Make Their Instrument ♥♥♥♥♥♥/10' And it's free.
Mangled out.

Based on 11.6 hours of gameplay.
Pros:
- R.A. Salvatore, a modern writing legend, helped write the story and lore, Grant Kirkhope of Rareware fame composed the soundtrack, and Todd McFarlane worked on the art design. If a dream team for a game existed, it'd be these three.
- Combat is a satisfying hack-and-slash, with a completely broken berserk mode appropriately called "Reckoning Mode".
- The VAs put great work into the characters, with Alyn Shir being noteworthy.
Cons:
- R.A. Salvatore, while famous across fantasy fandom, does tend to rely on tropes a little too much, and it shows in this game.
- Because of Reckoning Mode, bosses are complete pushovers; this would be fine, if they weren't so sparse. I've only encountered one NPC that could've been considered a boss and she went down after a short Reckoning session.
- 38 Studios is no longer in existence, so a sequel is out of the question. Not that the game did well enough to warrant a sequel in the first place.
Summary:
Amalur was described at release as a perfect marriage between God of War and The Elder Scrolls: Oblivion, and considering the team that helped develop the game this should've been true. However, due to some poor marketing on 38 Studios' part and the involvement of EA and its imfamous DLC practices, it became a fun game that never got the chance to shine as brightly as the team had hoped. While Amalur definitely has flaws and the marketing team did little to help its image, I'd urge you to treat as you would any underappreciated game: try it out and make your own opinion. Many people, myself included, have mixed feelings about this game, but only through actually playing it can you truly judge its worth. And considering that it has one of the longest playtimes in my library, I'd say that I rather enjoyed ripping monsters to shreds with my fate-rejecting powers.

I've been watching this game ever since Jordan Scott was the only one working on this (before he was hired by Rooster Teeth)
So now, here it is! The "full" release.
Here's what I think.
- Story is fine, pretty mediocre.
- Voice acting is top notch, since it most of them were already audio used in the show.
- Graphics are quite close to the anime itself, which is good as low usage of memory will let people with lower pc specs be able to play the game.
- The fighting styles are different, BUT their basic skill are very very common having one AoE skill and one that... isn't. (Team RWBY)
- Decent video customization options, there aren't any much advanced options but there are some.
- Full controller support, which is good for hack and slash games. However I heard some people saying that their Logitech controllers do not work. Might need someone to clarify that. (I'm using an Xbox 360 Controller)
- Few updates, but they are working on it. They have a small development team and are trying their best as they are active and listening in the Steam discussions page.
- Very repetitive. Hey team defend the control point! Okay, defend that control point! There's a rock in the way kill some grimm to magically remove it.
- Super super short campaign. It's like one campaign of Left for Dead just about 40 - 60 minutes of the whole campaign.
- Spoiler for the game's ending that I have to mention --->
(It's been changed, its still pretty meh but its better than the last one)
- If you don't know what RWBY is, you will not get the full experience (of course)
- This isn't worth the price, there is little content to get here, only thing you can do is to play the campaign online and single player.
- In my opinion, this isn't worth releasing it out of early access. It doesn't mean that the campaign is finished doesn't mean it should be a full release. It was rushed just to get it out of early access, and you can clearly see that from the ending that I have mentioned before.
I'm a big Rooster Teeth fan, I really loved the RWBY, Red Vs Blue, Camp Camp and other series, but them trying to go for games with a small development team. I can't recommend this as of right now, but they are trying.
TL;DR
The game is not worth of its price right now. Few content.
If you're a fan of RWBY, it might be worth looking at, otherwise I'd recommend against it. I personally do enjoy the game however.

Hard to believe the Tekken franchise is finally on PC.  Even though the game has been out for years in arcades, the home version is so finely tuned that it sets the bar for all future fighting game releases.
If you're new to the series, this game will make you feel a rollercoaster of emotions.  It still gets me even though I've been playing the games since Tekken 5.  The hardest aspect of this game is movement and blocking.  Work on those fundamentals and you'll begin to understand how to play this game.  Just a heads up.  You are going to lose online.  A lot.  To players that are essentially rolling their face across the stick/pad/keyboard.  Endure and you'll find ways to beat these players.
While there is no real tutorial for new players, there are certain aesthetics and hints that Harada-san and his team of made along the way.  Certain attack properties like moves that track sidesteps, or knock down aerial opponents are noted each fighter's move list.  At first glace learning a characters moves can feel like writing a thesis paper for finals.  But I understand Harada's viewpoint on the lack of one.  If you're truly serious about learning the game, you'll seek that knowledge on your own.  There are plenty of resources and people to help you on this path.
The game does feature a story mode, and it's ok.  Making a decent story mode for a fighting game is definitely a challenge.  This was a good attempt and it did conclude the story that started over 20 years ago.
My only other complaint is the lack of some fan favorite characters.  Mine is Lei Wulong.  Again, it's something that Harada has explained.  If no one has really used the character in past games, it wouldn't make sense to bring them into the new game where they rebuilt the entire game with the Unreal engine.  Maybe someday.

The game is for fans of the show. That being said, if you are not a fan and have not watched any season of RWBY, I suggest you do so before even considering purchasing this title. Especially at the price that it's been raised to. With that out of the way, let's begin the actual review.
The game itself is about ten chapters long and can very from 2.6 hours to, maybe, 4.8 depending on your skill level and if your using multiplayer or not. There is no tutorial, the game relies on your knowledge of hack-and-slash in general but there is a control menu in case you absolutely need to use it. Wasn't a problem for me but apparently it-did-erk a few people judging by one of the negative reviews in particular.
Since the last update the game has had a massive incline in both artstyle, combat, organization, as well as music. Combat is smoother then ever and chaining together combos is a cinch, the artstyle as well as the music does a good job making you feel as if you are actually in an episode of the show itself, and since said last update the level cap has been increased to 10 for each of the four playable characters. Along with these upgrades has come to the additon of achievements, much to the pleasure of all those completionists out there who'd love to dig into the game.
Now as I stated above the game is short and the six chapters themselves are, for the most part, repetitive. The game is best played with friends or just in multiplayer in general, unless your just that big of a fan that doing the same missions solo for exp grinding and achievement hunting is enough, and yes, that's just about all you'll be doing when you complete the game the first time.
There's nothing notable about it. After the base game you'll be working to max out each character, to find all the hidden relics in each map and obtain all of the steam achievements. That's about it. The game becomes little more then a time breaker and if not just that, a damn good avertisement for the show itself. After each game I found myself wanting to go back and rewatch the show from season one, though maybe it's just me.
Overall: This game is good for maybe an hour or two of fun a day if not just to pass time. I'd only agree to the full price of this game now if you just really, really loved the show but otherwise I'd suggest buying it on sale or watching one of the seasons to see what you think. Really, those are all that's supporting it. As of now I've put about 47.8 hours into it since its greenlight release and I am enjoying it quite abit.

The game is fun for being a 4 player coop hack and slash, but can and will get boring unless more content is added and the game becomes way more difficult.
As Ruby said, "I'm bored! Entertain me!"
But really, more content, harder difficulty = better RWBY.

Finally the game is out of beta! The glitches are all removed as far as I can see, but unfortunately I can't give this game a positive review. I would love to give it a neutral, or "eh, not bad" for a review, but the bottom line is this: RWBY isn’t worth the pricepoint. Hell, it wasn't exactly worth the $15 I paid for in early access, and I wouldn't pay $25 or recommend you to do so. Then again, its a refreshing game for any RWBY fans out there, and it's always a bonus to support the game devs!

For the current price tag, this VN is totally worth getting: the art style is beautiful, BGM is good and relaxing, and there’s even voice acting (in Chinese). This title is also quite short, so if you want something “quick” to read,
can be a good call. I only have two complains: sometimes the text surpasses the text box, and it can get hard to read the last lines since they get mixed with the menu options. That might be a problem of the English version only, I don’t know.
Speaking of it, the translation feels like it was done by two or three different people. Maybe I’m wrong, but it just feels like that. The game begins with a good and consistent narrative, and it suddenly changes; typos and awkward sentences appear and even tho I’m not a native speaker of English myself, I felt confused sometimes since a few sentences were very awkward and made little sense in English. Even so, I enjoyed this VN. It was short and still, I have this feeling that the devs put effort in it.
6/10. I hope that the developers will fix the English translation soon.

Short version: you like puzzles, especially those that have more than one solution? You'll like this game. Pick it up.
Graphically simple, The Dweller is actually pretty genius at its puzzle design.There's a couple real head scratchers throughout the game, usually placed right when you think you're getting the hang of what's going on. There are new elements to the game introduced all the way up until the end, keeping things fresh and renewing your desire to see the different ways you can use and abuse your monsterous abilities. The introduction of new mechanics is done well too, as there's no direct instruction on how they work but they're given to you in simple levels that force you to figure it out while making it intuitive.
There is lore and backstory introduced as you go, which do a great job of building a narrative. My only complaint is how abruptly the game ends, teasing you with new information and denying you any kind of follow-through on it. I have so many questions, and barring any DLC or a sequel they'll just have to remain questions.
Short and sweet. Definitely worth it for a big of a mind jog, hope to see more games from this producer soon.
