pretty neat game, the review doesn't look smart if it doesn't have alot of text so here's an apple pie recipe
Ingredients
2 1/2 cups King Arthur Unbleached All-Purpose Flour
3/4 teaspoon salt
1/3 cup vegetable shortening
8 tablespoons (1/2 cup) cold unsalted butter
7 to 10 tablespoons ice water
FILLING
8 cups peeled, cored, sliced apples
2 tablespoons lemon juice
3/4 cup sugar
2 tablespoons King Arthur Unbleached All-Purpose Flour
2 tablespoons cornstarch or Instant ClearJel
1/4 teaspoon salt
1 teaspoon cinnamon*
1/4 teaspoon nutmeg*
1/4 teaspoon allspice*
1/4 cup boiled cider or undiluted apple juice concentrate
2 teaspoons vanilla extract, optional
2 tablespoons butter, diced in small pieces
*Substitute 1 1/2 teaspoons apple pie spice, if desired.
Instructions
To make the crust: In a medium bowl, whisk together the flour and salt.
Work in the shortening until the mixture is evenly crumbly. Dice the butter into 1/2" pieces, and cut into the mixture until you have flakes of butter the size of a dime.
Add the water 2 tablespoons at a time, mixing with a fork as you sprinkle the water into the dough. When the dough is moist enough to hold together when you squeeze it, transfer it to a piece of wax or parchment paper. It's OK if there are some dry spots in the pile. Use a spray bottle of water to lightly spritz these places; that way you'll add just enough water to bring the dough together without creating a wet spot.
Fold the dough over on itself three or four times to bring it together, then divide it into two pieces, one about twice as large as the other. The larger piece will be the bottom crust; the smaller piece, the top crust. Pat each piece of dough into a disk about 3/4" thick.
Roll each disk on its edge, like a wheel, to smooth out the edges. This step will ensure your dough will roll out evenly, without a lot of cracks and splits at the edges later. Wrap in plastic and refrigerate for 30 minutes before rolling.
Preheat the oven to 425°F.
Lightly grease a 9" pie pan that's at least 2" deep. This will make serving the pie easier after it's baked.
To make the filling: Combine the sliced apples and lemon juice in a large mixing bowl.
In a small bowl, whisk together the sugar, flour, cornstarch, salt, and spices. Sprinkle the mixture over the apples, and stir to coat them. Stir in the boiled cider (or apple juice concentrate) and the vanilla, if you choose to use it.
Roll the larger piece of pastry into a 13" circle. Transfer it to the prepared pan, and trim the edges so they overlap the rim of the pan by an inch all the way around.
Spoon the apple filling into the pan. Dot the top with the diced butter.
Roll out the remaining pastry to an 11" circle. Carefully place the pastry over the apples. Bring the overhanging bottom crust up and over the top crust, pinching to seal the two and making a decorative crimp. Prick the crust all over with a fork, to allow steam to escape. Or cut decorative vent holes, if desired. Alternatively, you can weave a lattice.
For extra crunch and shine, brush the top crust with milk (or an egg white beaten with 1 tablespoon of water), and sprinkle with coarse sugar.
Crimp the edges of the pie, then place it in the refrigerator for 10 minutes to firm up the crust while the oven finishes heating.
Place the pie on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Bake the pie for 20 minutes, then reduce the oven temperature to 375°F and bake for 40 minutes more, until you see the filling bubbling inside the pie (and perhaps dripping onto the parchment). Check the pie after half an hour of baking time, and cover the edges with foil or a pie shield to keep them from browning too quickly, if necessary.
When the pie is done — you should see the filling bubbling vigorously, either around the edges, or via any decorative vents — remove it from the oven.
Cool the pie completely before slicing — really. Cutting any fruit pie that's still warm is a messy business. The filling continues to thicken as the pie cools, and if you cut it too soon it will run out all over the place. It's better to bake the pie in advance, cool it completely, then warm each slice as needed after it's been cut.
Store any leftover pie, lightly covered, at room temperature for several days. Freeze for longer storage.

"Should you play RWBY: Grimm Eclipse?" is a question entirely relative to one's love for the show this game is based on. RWBY is a shonen anime-inspired American animated series created by the now deceased Monty Oum and produced by Rooster Teeth. It is an exeptional show that started off pretty mediocre and since has become increasingly exceptional. That sets the standard pretty high for this game which is at its base core is a low budget hack and slash.
I should mention I bought this game in early access so I have how the game has evolved in the past and can speak to the ways the game has improved and how it has become worse.
Story and Characters:
The narrative is the least impressive part of this experience. If the writing team from the show actually wrote this then I will be surprised because the writing here is absolute trash. The new character, Dr. Merlot is your typical mustache twirling villain who is probably written so poorly so that they don't accidentally make a good villain that they can't use in the show. I have only played as Ruby Rose in the story so I can only speak to her dialogue but she seems pretty unperturbed by the events at hand and seems to never be concerned by anything. This could speak to her positiveness as a character prior to the end of season 3 of the show, but it still doesn't create much dramatic tension. Although some would argue that the point of this game is the gameplay and that the story shouldn't be that important since it is a hack and slash adventure, but to not even have created cutscenes for the game seems to imply that the developers didn't really try living up the narrative of the show in anyway, and there are certain visual effects at the end of the game that are laughable.
Combat:
Oh boy this next part is a doozy. Prior to the final release people who played the early access version had access to a the first five or so missions before a cliffhanger that wasnt resolved until the final release. This gave the devs enough time to answer feedback and then tweak the features. As so playing through those missions again in the final release was delightful... however after that the problems started surfacing as we got into uncharted territory. But for now lets look at the basic components (Keep in mind that I played with a wired Xbox 360 controller). There are two buttons for attacking. X for light attacks and Y for heavy attacks. Rather than have special attacks accessible only through holding down right trigger and a corresponding button like in early access, the final version implements combos that are pretty entertaining. Don't be expecting Bayonetta or Devil May Cry levels of flexibility, but be prepared for some cool looking and pretty entertaining attacks and a special move for each character used by pressing both shoulder buttons when the ultimate meter is filled up. There is a dodge/sprint button that can be used to avoid attacks and there is a counter function by using the B button, but these two functions are where my chief complaints lie. See in games like Bayonetta, when you press the dodge button... you dodge, but in Grimm Eclipse, the dodge button doesn't always work or at the very least it is unresponsive. As for countering, occasionally a prompt will pop up above an enemy's head and you can stun them by pressing B. There are two issues to this: The first is that the button doesn't always respond that well, much like the dodge, and the second being that some enemies will literally warp to you to complete their attack, even if they are off camera. There is a limited range, but it is a bit too generous to the enemies you are cutting down. To further analyze my issues with the combat I'd like to point out that in most action games of this nature, the developers with usually dedicate themselves to either dodging OR countering, and not always a button press away. Devil May Cry incorporates dodging with its lock on, sure, but Bayonetta's dodge mechanic is a simple button press and it still mangages to be increibly challenging. And if a developer incorporates both dodging and countering (Batman Arkam series or some Assassin's Creed titles) they usually are done much better, or at least tailor the controls better. This leads to another issue I have. The controls cannot be remapped to new buttons, and this is very annoying. While the mechanics I just mentioned definitely need to be worked on, changing the layout of the controller would help me circumvent these issues by being able to make the controls similar to other spectacle fighters like Bayonetta.
Upgrade Mechanics:
The upgrades in Grimm Eclipse consist of general upgrades to health, coop abilites, and the number of ultimate ability uses, as well as upgrades to the ultimate attacks themselves, and other special attacks achievable through combos or the characters' ranged weapons. XP is gained through the slaughter of enemies, XP orbs found in vases and crates, and artifacts shaped like chess pieces. Each character's max level is 10 and so you won't always be able to get every upgrade, but you can redistribute the points at any time which is a nice feature. The upgrade system could be tweaked but it's certainly the least offensive feature of this game.
Miscellaneous (prepare for a lot of nitpicking):
So the worlds are cool and all, but I feel like the proportions are really messed up. Like, You walk up to like a fence and the fence is ♥♥♥♥ing huge! like so huge that the people constructing the fence had to have used a lot of man power or machinery to build it, and yet didn't stop to think that maybe they should have used the obviously existant construction budget to build a fence that wasn't made of large wooden planks made to evoke a standard hand made wooden fence. Plus there are flowers that look huge. There are areas where the size of objects relative to the characters are better but that just makes the moments of misproportions even more crazy because of the inconsistency. Anyway small nitpicking aside, the environments vary from colorful and pretty to just dull.
Final Thoughts:
RWBY Grimm Eclipse is a fun mess of a game, but the fun part of that mess will probably only be apparent if you have watched the show and can appreciate these characters. The combat shows promise but just isn't as polished as other action games of the same ilk. If you like crazy action and want enjoy killing demonic creatures with big weapons and guns, then just play Devil May Cry or any of the Platinum Games archive of great spectacle fighters and only play RWBY if you already enjoy the show. So to conclude...
SHOULD YOU PLAY RWBY: GRIMM ECLIPSE? NO

General information: I am a huge RWBY fan, so this'll be biased no matter how much I try to put into the bad points. Also keep in mind I'm more of a filthy casual when it comes to gaming, so take this review with an entire ocean of salt.
Bad points:
- Countering is a bit sucky. It barely ever works, and when it does it's because I stand still in order to do it and if then it doesn't work, a mutant beowolf messes me up and I have to hope it's next attack is the dust trail one so I have time to recover. I spend all my points on health upgrades so I can tank hits, it's a broken feature and needs looking at.
- No accessibility to reviewers who haven't heard of or seen RWBY. Whether it's a World of Remnant type animation explaining quickly what the universe of RWBY is like (a shortened version of the opening sequence in the pilot) or just Ozpin voicing over shots of the environment, something is needed to give players context so this game can be marketed outside of RT.
- There's no conversation between the RWBY girls. This is what a LOT of fans want to see, there needs to be interaction in order for people to feel more involved in the game.
- Invisible walls. I know the game is linear, but I'd like to see them reduced.
- Yang and Ruby's attacks are bland compared to Weiss and Blake's. Neither Ruby or Yang's semblances are implemented, and it would be nice to see the RWBY girls have more passive abilities that don't need to be bought (Yang getting more damage the lower her aura is, Ruby being able to run faster, Weiss and Blake being able to double-jump using glyphs/clones). Also, I feel like Ruby's ultimate is the most lackluster, especially since she's the protagonist.
- The girls models need major improvements. For me, they're constantly glitching and they're very off-putting.
TWO BIGGEST POINTS: Lack of conversation between RWBY girls and countering.
Good points:
- Mainly, I look for a game which at it's core fun to play. The fact I've (at the time of writing this) put 79 hours into playing GE shows that, at least to me,  it IS a game that's fun to play. This is the reason I'm recommending it, though like I've said before, it would most likely not be to anyone outside of the RT community
- The Professors talking to you is one of my favourite parts, since I have a soft spot for all the teachers (especially Oobleck). Their dialogue is easily the most well-written and genuinely funny in the whole game (again, especially Oobleck's)
- I have my graphics setting on low, but even then the environments are absolutely gorgeous. They really make you seem small, which I really like.
- I like how they've put more variation into the music, it's nice to see them utilizing what's considered to be one of the best things about RWBY
- UI looks a lot better than in the Early Access, the whole game feels more polished.
- I like how some of the girls' lines reveal a tiny bit more about their characters and personalities, such as Yang's "I've always been more of the outdoors-y type!" and Blake's "Who do you think built these?"
TWO BIGGEST POINTS: Professor dialogue, incredible environments/level design.

So, just finished the RWBY campaign with my brother, after several months away from it, patiently waiting for more content to be added. So, now that it's finally out, is it worth the asking price of 23 Eu or regional equivalent? Well you can probably tell by the big red downwards thumb. Let me elaborate as to why.
First off, I'm a sucker for RWBY, and so was my partner through the game, and it is great to see how big the series has become. However, even as a fan of the source material, this game just fails to impress. It walked out of the comfortable safety of online show, and headed boldy towards the world of video games. Only to slip on the first flight of stairs, resulting in broken legs and a less than appealing face.
Story: It's about as bare bones as you can get. You're dropped into a forest as soon as you start, with no tutorial, no explanation as to what you're doing here, no nothing. Let's see if you can fill in the blanks. You're a blank send out to investigate a blank who's evil scientist leader is trying to blank the monsters, using blank with no regards to blank lives. To say it's generic is an understatement, and is far from what I expected when they said "new villain"
...............
gameplay: It's your standard hack and slash, with your light attack, heavy attack, and gun. Then you have your counter attack, which will counter enemies when they're about to attack if the stars align and you sacrifice your first born to the Chaos Gods. To say the counter system is unreliable would be an understatement. Then you have a flash, which works as a dodge, which is pretty much useless, since every enemy that uses an attack that cannot be countered has a second for you to react, who's animations are barely different from standard attacking animations, resulting in your♥♥♥♥♥landing on the ground.
There are currently 4 playable characters, none of which seems to have any practical differences, other than "this character has AOE shots and this one doesn't". In the end the only big difference is your animations and one liners you get, which all get ear grading after your character says it 40 ♥♥♥♥ing times after 1,5 hours YES I GET IT BLONDIE IT WILL LEAVE A MARK NOW SHUT THE ♥♥♥♥ UP!
And now seems like an appropriate time to talk about the Team Attacks. Or, As I call it, how to not encourage team play. Team attacks are, as far as I understand, a role of the dice when you use AOE attacks or counters an enemy. Problem is, this is the only time it happens, so you can whack the same enemy as your partner for a century, and if RNJESUS isn't on your side, that enemy will not be able to get team attacked. Team attacks themselves are medium damaging animations, that results in your partner finishing off an enemy you just stunned, indicated by a set of swords over its head. But, as I already have stated, RNJESUS tends to only give these team attacks to the grunts and cannon fodder, so they are often just a waste of time.
The leveling system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. To get XP, you can 1: destroy crates around the map *these maps are long spans of nothingness with maybe tops 15 crates in them each* which might drop 25 XP, the same as a cannon fodder enemy. 2: you collect artifacts, which are chess pieces placed in pre set locations, meaning that if you know where one of them is, it'll stay there even if you play the maps over and over and over. Or 3: You do certain things like clear waves, kill monsters, and collect dust. Here's the problem. You don't share equal XP when it comes to monsters, and you don't share artifact XP or crate XP at all. So, say you're new to the game, and you end up playing with someone who has already beaten the game before, they know where all the artifacts are, and you'll not get any of the XP. When it comes to monsters, they give about a 1/5 of the original XP as assists, which is only reducing an already laughable amount of XP. So you end up fighting about getting the XP before your partner, which isn't very smart when you're supposed to be playing a 4 player coorperation game.
The enemy's range from small cannon fodder, to wolf cannon fodder, to boar cannon fodder, to bears. There really isn't much difference, other than a bear has more hit points than the worms. All the monsters have a startling lack of animations, so much so that if you hit one of the boars into the air, they will just sit in an idle formation, waiting for your combo to end. The damage on the enemies seem to vary, from big green wolves that barely do any damage, to worms that will kick the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you if you said something about their♥♥♥♥♥♥♥sizes.
Most of the game is played like this: Enter an area, walk for a few minutes until you reach a semi circle or square formation, clear waves, progress. This might sound like an oversimplification, but trust me, it gets really dull killing the same cannon fodder enemies wave after wave, only to find that the boss is a slightly bigger version with some spikes on them and bigger hit bars. By the end of the campaign, me and my partner were making bets as to what enemy they would reuse as the warm up for the final boss, and my partner hit the nail on the head.
..........
Level design:♥♥♥♥♥♥ Huge levels of nothing, with often nothing but crates in them, and some times an artifact. One of the biggest Sinners is the city, which has long paths of nothing, leading to squares and circles where you will fight waves, then continue. I can't think of one time where the Grimm spawned in a pact on a road, they only spawned in semi circles or squares. There's also invisible walls everywhere. Some times, you'll find stuff like roads that lead to no where, and gates that you can walk under with certain characters, giving you the impression they planned for something, then suddenly stopped once the voices started praising Salem again.
...........
music: For those who *like me* loves the RWBY ost's, you will get dissapointed, because there is no original scores in this game, only music taken right out of the show. And these songs are played over and over and over again. Just the main title screen music loops 6 times in the span of 5 minutes.
................
Graphics: Barely passable. Low textures, bad effects, lacks animations, and generally doesn't look very nice. It also has disgustingly low frame rate drops for little to no reason, which is inexcusable for a game that looks like this. It's only saving grace is the art style, which saves it from being complete garbage.
................
Final Thoughts: The game is very disappointing, even for an indie game. The main game mode, the campaign, can be finished with 2 people in 3 hours max. The level design is stretched out to what feels like pointless patting, combat is unsatisfying, enemies lack variety and animations, the music is ear bleedingly repeated over and over, and the graphics are nothing to brag about.
If you want a good hack and slash game that isn't nearly as bad, go buy Metal Gear Rising, it has better mechanics, better music, better bosses, better level variety, and is much more satisfying to play. And it's cheaper to boot.

pretty neat game, the review doesn't look smart if it doesn't have alot of text so here's an apple pie recipe
Ingredients
2 1/2 cups King Arthur Unbleached All-Purpose Flour
3/4 teaspoon salt
1/3 cup vegetable shortening
8 tablespoons (1/2 cup) cold unsalted butter
7 to 10 tablespoons ice water
FILLING
8 cups peeled, cored, sliced apples
2 tablespoons lemon juice
3/4 cup sugar
2 tablespoons King Arthur Unbleached All-Purpose Flour
2 tablespoons cornstarch or Instant ClearJel
1/4 teaspoon salt
1 teaspoon cinnamon*
1/4 teaspoon nutmeg*
1/4 teaspoon allspice*
1/4 cup boiled cider or undiluted apple juice concentrate
2 teaspoons vanilla extract, optional
2 tablespoons butter, diced in small pieces
*Substitute 1 1/2 teaspoons apple pie spice, if desired.
Instructions
To make the crust: In a medium bowl, whisk together the flour and salt.
Work in the shortening until the mixture is evenly crumbly. Dice the butter into 1/2" pieces, and cut into the mixture until you have flakes of butter the size of a dime.
Add the water 2 tablespoons at a time, mixing with a fork as you sprinkle the water into the dough. When the dough is moist enough to hold together when you squeeze it, transfer it to a piece of wax or parchment paper. It's OK if there are some dry spots in the pile. Use a spray bottle of water to lightly spritz these places; that way you'll add just enough water to bring the dough together without creating a wet spot.
Fold the dough over on itself three or four times to bring it together, then divide it into two pieces, one about twice as large as the other. The larger piece will be the bottom crust; the smaller piece, the top crust. Pat each piece of dough into a disk about 3/4" thick.
Roll each disk on its edge, like a wheel, to smooth out the edges. This step will ensure your dough will roll out evenly, without a lot of cracks and splits at the edges later. Wrap in plastic and refrigerate for 30 minutes before rolling.
Preheat the oven to 425°F.
Lightly grease a 9" pie pan that's at least 2" deep. This will make serving the pie easier after it's baked.
To make the filling: Combine the sliced apples and lemon juice in a large mixing bowl.
In a small bowl, whisk together the sugar, flour, cornstarch, salt, and spices. Sprinkle the mixture over the apples, and stir to coat them. Stir in the boiled cider (or apple juice concentrate) and the vanilla, if you choose to use it.
Roll the larger piece of pastry into a 13" circle. Transfer it to the prepared pan, and trim the edges so they overlap the rim of the pan by an inch all the way around.
Spoon the apple filling into the pan. Dot the top with the diced butter.
Roll out the remaining pastry to an 11" circle. Carefully place the pastry over the apples. Bring the overhanging bottom crust up and over the top crust, pinching to seal the two and making a decorative crimp. Prick the crust all over with a fork, to allow steam to escape. Or cut decorative vent holes, if desired. Alternatively, you can weave a lattice.
For extra crunch and shine, brush the top crust with milk (or an egg white beaten with 1 tablespoon of water), and sprinkle with coarse sugar.
Crimp the edges of the pie, then place it in the refrigerator for 10 minutes to firm up the crust while the oven finishes heating.
Place the pie on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Bake the pie for 20 minutes, then reduce the oven temperature to 375°F and bake for 40 minutes more, until you see the filling bubbling inside the pie (and perhaps dripping onto the parchment). Check the pie after half an hour of baking time, and cover the edges with foil or a pie shield to keep them from browning too quickly, if necessary.
When the pie is done — you should see the filling bubbling vigorously, either around the edges, or via any decorative vents — remove it from the oven.
Cool the pie completely before slicing — really. Cutting any fruit pie that's still warm is a messy business. The filling continues to thicken as the pie cools, and if you cut it too soon it will run out all over the place. It's better to bake the pie in advance, cool it completely, then warm each slice as needed after it's been cut.
Store any leftover pie, lightly covered, at room temperature for several days. Freeze for longer storage.

The Dweller is a short, twist of a puzzle game where the player controls a spirit, specifically an Eldritch, to deal with venturing spelunkers as opposed to the alternate paradigm. The ancient earth-bound spirit guards a primeval underground city, and all trespassing intruders have forfeited their lives upon entering.
The spirit is physically controlled by first choosing a spawn point in the ground, then by dragging the mouse – it forces the dweller to follow. The creature can also enter and exit boulders or rock pillars to possess them to move off ledges and crush intrepid excavators. Possessing boulders, choosing a spawn point, or creating some sort of unnatural event near trespassers instill fear sufficient to force them to run off of a cliff and perish.
The game is not too difficult to perfect with regards to achievements; most will be naturally attained from progressing through the levels. The most time consuming achievement to get would be the "beat every level" one, as there is 59 levels. Archaeologist notes are also unlocked after completing certain levels, providing insight into the lives and mental faculty of the archaeologists.
The puzzle aspect lies in the inability of the spirit to cross gaps or wooden structures. The player must first move a boulder or rock pillar to bridge the gap or cross a wooden bridge. The boulder only has to be in proximity (one boulder width) with two opposing walls/floors to make a channel for the spirit to travel through. It is also possible to use a boulder In order to move another boulder.
Teleporters allow the spirit to vanish and choose another teleporter to spawn at. There are also teleporter stations that allow the player to create and place two teleporters in the ground of any two locations; the spirit will must first activate the station, and it will spawn beneath the station after placing the teleporters. A “power-up” station allows the spirit to freely fly throughout the entire level unrestricted.
Agents, special spelunkers, can shoot a projectile beam that will capture the spirit – the player must go behind their line of sight. The agents do not move; however, they can turn around and investigate a noise. Going from above or below generally do not work.
If the player is truly stumped on a level, it is possible to skip it. If the player desires, the skip feature can be used all the way to the end (to encounter a neat “boss fight”). It is also not required to beat every single level. Each stage is individually unlocked upon completion of the previous stage, however, some provide branching paths to the next area.
The Dweller was just recently released last month, so the player base is still understandably small. Even so, the developer has shown active interest in player support, as seen in the Discussions board. Every question has a direct response, and the developer also seems to be willing to give hints to anyone that need it.
There are a couple suggestions that may improve gameplay; these are listed below.

The Dweller is a rather cute and fun puzzle game, despite the oh-so-scary Eldritch monster lurking around. The game’s originality and gameplay mechanics earn it a recommendation for any casual puzzle solver. Although it is rather short, the joy attained from killing that last, isolated spelunker provides a truly unique experience. Happy hunting!

The PC version of Mortal Kombat X is a bad version of a great game. You should play Mortal Kombat X. Don't play it on the PC.
To say the game was rough at launch is an understatement. It was varying degrees of broken for many and it took them a long time to get the game into a reasonably decent shape. Some still aren't so lucky, but it at least runs passably for most now.
Problem is, WB Games is continuing its well-known track record with PC games. Look up the Arkham Knight fiasco if you're not familiar with the respect they've been showing to the platform lately. The short version is that PC players who have loyally stuck with this lousy version of a great game are getting another slap in the face, because WB Games is ending support. The console versions are getting exciting new characters, a new stage, new costumes, and even a netcode patch that should make online play more pleasant.
PC players are getting jack.
PC support has been officially dropped. As a long time Mortal Kombat fan, this is pretty heartbreaking. Mortal Kombat X is a fantastic game and it deserves better than this. Its fans deserve better than this. The people who paid good money for a broken game only to stick with it and get abandoned by a negligent publisher deserve better than this.
If you have the ability, go buy Mortal Kombat X on a console and send an email to WB Games letting them know which version you'd rather be playing. This game deserves to be played and enjoyed, but this version, and frankly any future PC release from WB Games, is impossible to recommend. Shame on WB Games for treating its customers this poorly, and shame on NetherRealm for standing idly by as its fans get trampled on by a publisher who's dragging the good name of its series through the mud.
If the company won't support the game, don't support the company.

This game has seen a lot throughout its lifetime on PC. In the beginning, it was nothing but a glitch fest with optimization errors, crashes and unplayable online. Things have come a long way though. The studio that Nether Realm hired to create the PC port has really changed things from launch day. Optimization is acceptable and a hell a lot better than launch day. Now player have benchmarks in the video options to test out graphical settings. In addition, players have fps meters online. So you can see what fps your oppenent is playing at. Thus you can avoid players with weaker systems and save yourself trouble with lag and such. Speaking of lag, the game is still really hard to play online because of the input delay. I find myself dropping delicate combos with air tight timings frequently online. Its a pain in the a$$ but you get used to it with time. You just have to know your combos very well to input them before they actually play out. But something that you can't really account for with online lag is punishing certain moves. Like Sub Zeros b2, which is normally easily punishable by attacks that are 12 frames or less. But because the attack pushes you back on block, you have to run in and attack. Still easy though. But the input delay, delays your attack ever so slightly that you can't quite punish something that you normally should. If you try and fail, Sub Zero can catch you and full combo you. But after time you will know what attacks are punishable online and what aren't. Its a matter of time. HOWEVER, Nether Realm Studios has addressed this major issue in the Mortal Kombat Community by introducing a netcode system for online called the GG PO. It is a roll back netcode that will be used in the upcoming titles Street Fighter 5, Injustice 2 and Mortal Kombat 11. It will completely DESTROY any input lag problems in online matches. There is currently a closed beta running and so far the results are jaw breaking. The characters in this game are AMAZING. There is so much depth in each and every character avaliable. And even more depth in each varation of the same character. Effectivly tripling the cast. In addition, new mechanics were introduced in mkx that we never saw before. Such as running, run cancels, reversals, FRAME DATA WRITTEN IN THE GAME (Thank you Nether Realm Studios) and interactables. These take some time to get used to for mk9 veterans, but not very time consuming. I find combos harder to pull of on keyboard in mkx appossed to mk9. Especially the jump teleports but again, it comes down to practice in order to perfect. If you have a controller, then less worrying for you. The game was designed for controllers and thus you should have a better time. None the less, keyboard is still do able. I am personally a keyboard player and have no problem DESTROYING controller players.  In the end, if you are into strategy and depth, this is the game for you. The problem is that this might be a bit overwhelming for newer players. So in conclusion, get this game if you are able to put up with the frustration of complexity and online lag... for a short while, after which you, will become a pro and DOMINATE EVERYONE. Plus online lag is getting fixed soon so thats one less thing to worry about.

*contains heavy SPOILERS*
First of all I'm a huge fan of Deus Ex Universe and was waiting for this game with *heavy breathing* expression. When it was delayed by six months I had to pull my pants up and don't let my hype implode.
So now, I've played it through on hardest difficulity and I have such a mixed reaction that I feel kinda obliged to write a review for others and devs.
This game has everything HR didn't have, but loses for not having a single thing HR actually had right.
The game feels like a filler between part 1 and 3, as if it was created only to build up the hype and earn as much money as possible for the next release or DLC. (The microtransaction drama). The feeling of creepy story, immersive narrative and engaging character leveling and customization vanished really fast after the first hours in Prague, hell, even after Dubai. It's all very cleverly covered with brilliant level design, graphics and huge customization options, but if one sees it through, there is not much left in this game, which overall, makes me very sad, and thouroughly disappointed.
- Huge step forward in the game engine. The visuals, the audio, the immersive locations packed with so many details my eyes were hurting (Golem City). The lighting, ambient occlusion, high resolution textures and other graphical enhacements make this game worth a purchase for any enthusiast of graphics-porn in games.
- The soundtrack - Just as good as it was in HR. What I really like is that the tracks are playing all the time in the background, always immersing player into the world. There are no moments of silence, music is subtle, yet has its effect on Player.
- Customization - The number of customization available to the Player is huge. Not to mention new, really cool combat augmentations on Jensen, there are also options to customize every weapon with various bullets and shooting types, attatchements, optics, etc. All accessible via the new on-fly customize interface.
- Interface - Big step forward on that as well. Improved inventory options, augs menu, weapons customization, crafting, etc. Everything was clear and comprehensible to me unlike in other games with complex crafting system.
- Combat - With the new augs, combat is even more flashy and action driven. Nano blades and tesla are great. I saw people complaining about it in other reviews that combat feels clunky and glitchy, but I haven't experienced any of that, apart of the aspect of level design being completely broken after I slaughtered the whole cities / locations. Do as they say - direct combat breaks immersion and gameplay, go stealth instead.
- PC version - I say it's overall very well done. Constant 50-60 FPS on my i5 and 970. However the loading times are a bit too long, for an SSD drive. I saw big applause for how smaller locations on the map don't need to load and are fluently generated on-fly (city-TF29 transision), but still, reloads after death were sometimes upseting me greatly.
- The beginning - I really liked how the story began, with Task Force being attacked by an unkown force in far Dubai, now being an abandoned skeleton metropolis after the incident - it really made an immersive impact on me. + the cutscene with Illuminati making up new sinister plans for humanity. I thought: "holy crap, this game with all my flashy augs and story like this will kick♥♥♥♥♥", until....
- SETTING/STORY ...Until I realized that the game ends where it should start. The story plot is really poor. Unepic, dull, predictable as hell. The characters are okay and believable tough, (I actually didn't suspect the psychologist after I've done quest for her and I felt really sorry for mistrusting Jim), but there are SO many unfinished story threads! The main antagonist is all right, but I thought he was sort of build-up for bigger events and Illuminati freaks. There is only 1 boss in the entire game! What the hell? (Apart from that kitten mad woman in sewers, lol). The setting is all right, I could really immerse myself in Czech location as I'm polish myself and the langauge, as well as architecture design really appealed to me. But why 90% of the game takes place in this little 100m x 100m Prague? Making a game setting solely in one insignificant (for majority of gamers) place like this isn't a good idea. I was really hoping for a foreign mission like Dubai or Hengsha but that never happened. Instead we get a 15 minutes mission in a small Swiss Alps base location and a finale in London. If you wanted to focus on "old continent* you should've present us a bigger picture of its diversity, especially during this mechanical aparthied turmoil. Tutorial in Dubai, first mission in Prague, also a HUB to make sidequests, Golem City, back to Prague, then a long mission somewhere outside (like GARM but WAY longer and deeper), hidden base on Iceland, futuristic setting in 2029 Paris/Berlin/Warsaw, Versalife headquarters infiltration, Hong Kong infiltrtation (we were tracking the singal from there!), this city in Oman (i forgot the name), also had a huge potential!. I feel like the setting, although I enjoyed it, shows how limited the Player is in that sandboxy world and the other missions really didn't help much due to its content. Human Revolution did a great job on that. Many interesting locations, as well as HUBS. Oh, and Golem City is by far the most missed opportunity in game design I've ever seen in RPG game probably. I went there, was amazed by how great it looks - searched for all side quests, accidentally entered the Marchenko cutscene room, so I proceeded with the main story for a while, it pushed me towards ending and escape via VTOL... Goodbye Golem City, never to return here. Kitten all my sidequests, merchants, and interesting locations. You guys make such a great location and don't let Players to return there? Did I miss some option?
- Difficulity - Maybe it's because of the lack of location content but I didn't feel the game progresses in difficulity with how far I am. In HR I had that feeling that every next mission, there are more enemies, more advanced security measures. Guards having eyes on every angle, lots of hacking, lots of secret paths. In MD there are loads of hidden paths, (hence the level design applause), leading to nothing rewarding, as there are not enough enemies/cameras per location. Looking for other routes seemed pointless after a while and I was running through main corridors stunning everyone, without others taking any notice.
- Controls - PC default controls are stupifyingly odd. I know you can go to options and change whatever you want, but default option means the majority of people would pick this button for this action. I don't think that most people would choose holding down "E" for pulling corpse and look into data at the same time. I literally had foam all over my teeth when I was opening a goddam intel menu each time I pulled a fallen guard during the sealth mission in London.
- I have nothing against foreign languages in video games, but at least hire Czech voice actors for Czech lines. Half of them sounded like russians or english. Seemed unprofessional.
- After a while playing this game I've noticed I can't find any Praxis Kits as they were in HR, and I've been gathering as much money as I could for them.... then I've remembered what people said and entered shop menu... Guys,♥♥♥♥♥♥like that breaks leveling design, game economy and game industry ethics. Don't tell me it doesn't, other games in recent years got 10/10 and huge $$$ income and didn't have to deal with such sinister solutions. At least tell me you need that money to make a 3rd game FAR greater than MD, and I'll give you the $ freely. Honesty in gaming pays off for devs too. (see CDPR, lol).
I give a thumb down - not due hate, I enjoyed the game moreless, take it as sort of motivation to make a better 3rd one.

My rig:
I wish I could pick an "in-between" rating instead of just recommended or not recommended. This review may be updated again based on new thoughts as time progresses.
Things I liked:
Things I didn’t like:
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided (MD) builds upon the gameplay and story foundations set by its 2011 predecessor; Human Revolution (HR).
It’s certainly a more competent game with regards to mechanics and technical fidelity, which is definitely due to its new Dawn Engine (based on the Glacier II engine that debuted with Hitman: Absolution (2012)). Conversely, HR used a heavily-modified Tomb Raider engine from 2006, so yeah.
During my 30+ hours, I discovered many tools and solutions to tackling the various objectives compared to HR. I feel that MD is closer to the original Deus Ex (DX) than HR was, which I think is very good, though some may disagree. The game only features one city hub in Prague, so this was a little disappointing after the variety of hubs that could be explored in earlier games.
There’s a lot more vertical exploration compared to HR (hooray!) so I recommend upgrading your jump boost aug to help with your traversal around the city. The Smart Vision aug is also very useful in identifying environments you can interact with, like destructible walls, though it did seem a little cheesy for it to spot hidden areas for you. It reminded me of the obtuse visual indicators for the multiple paths you could use in Crysis 2. It’s not emergent gameplay if the game visually labels everywhere you can go.
I like playing Deus Ex stealthily - hacking past enemy defenses and ensuring I’m never spotted. To play like this in MD, you have to use the third-person cover system. This same gameplay was present in HR; both games require you to use the cover system to efficiently stealth your way through the game. My problem with this is that I feel like I’m “cheating” because of the third-person camera. It dampens the immersion and makes things too easy when you have such a wide field of view over the level. There have been times where enemies have begun spotting me whilst I’m out of cover, yet when I pop in, still in their field of view, their detection level goes away. I don’t like it, and I wish there was a way to play the game stealthily in first-person, just like in the original Deus Ex.
In addition to the above, takedowns return though they definitely seem more fluid compared to HR’s awkward takedown animations. Unfortunately, as fluid as they look, MD’s takedowns still retain HR’s weird effect of freezing the world around you during the animation. It’s jarring and weird, and I don’t like it. That said, takedowns are quite effective in dispatching enemies because you don’t need to worry about aiming or missing shots. Plus, they give you a lot of XP so it’s kind of a no-brainer to use them as much as possible.
Ultimately, my biggest gripe with the game is its story. Specifically, the writing and how expository it is. It’s littered with so much obtuse exposition, I feel as though it’s catering to the lowest common denominator of players who need story and information spoon fed to them instead of working things out themselves. The way the main characters speak during story segments doesn’t feel natural; they state the obvious and ask questions that they should already know the answer to. Where is the subtlety?
The conclusion left me hungry for more. I had spent 30 hours exploring as much as I could during that time. The critical mission path is not very long at all; possibly around the 6 to 8-hour mark if you ignore everything else in the game. I anticipate that the story will be expanded upon in future paid-for DLC, which I personally don’t expect to buy at full price.
Cutscenes. I wasn’t a fan of them in HR, and I certainly don’t like that they’ve returned in MD. Considering that Deus Ex is very much about player agency, it’s baffling that Eidos Montréal still incorporates these immersion-breaking cutscenes where you lose all control and watch your character do or say things you may not have done yourself. The original DX did not incorporate cutscenes during gameplay and it aided greatly in immersing yourself in the world. The silver lining here is that the pre-rendered cutscenes don’t look like an orange mess as they did in HR, although they do look a bit fuzzy, which suggests a low resolution was used when recording them.
As far as the PC port goes, I think it’s competent but not excellent. I’ve been playing the game since it went live, so I experienced the weird sensitivity disparity between the mouse’s X and Y axes. Taking into account Nixxes’ long history in delivering PC ports, I was a little surprised by this oversight. It’s also worth mentioning that, on launch, the FoV slider displayed a percentage value instead of how many degrees it will be. Another odd oversight that has since been addressed, just like the mouse sensitivity issue.
Performance wise, it’s okay. I’m still using hardware I bought in November 2012, so I’m quite chuffed it runs relatively well on medium/high settings at my native resolution. I have tessellation, bloom, subsurface scattering and temporal AA on, and motion blur, sharpening, cloth physics (heavy on the CPU) and chromatic aberration set to off. I’ve left volumetric lighting on because I think it makes scenes look that little bit nicer, though it does come with a performance impact. I encourage people to follow Nixxes and Eidos Montréal’s advice in disabling MSAA and being realistic in your expectations about running the game at 60FPS on Very High and Ultra.

DEUX EX: MANKIND DIVIDED a futuristic world of cybernetic wonders where man and machine have merged for a better way of life all the while there are those who wish to prevent this new era in humanity's progress as a race. The story and plotlines are excellent with many shades of grey where you can empathise with the so called bad guys and where things from any direction could make a turn into a malevolent future even if doing what one thinks is right. The only true good seems to fight for humanity whether it be half technology or completely made of flesh.
Gameplay is fantastic with huge gobs of science fiction eye candy and hardcore sci-fi game mechanics with a very intuitive user interface full onscreen prompts to guide one in using ones cybernetic body adding to the sense of being a enhanced unit. Hacking is just as intense as previous games and combat is incredible with some very nice ideas added to maps making them difficult to survive and pushing the player to use their cyber enhancements. Ammo on weapons is limited so its good idea to loot bodies for ammo and new weapons as well as other things such as credits. Plenty of loot variety all of which is of use.
The game world itself is so fully realised and fleshed out it is a masterpiece of artistic gaming craftsmanship. I feel like am in a actual real world with every fine detail showing. It wouldnt surprise me if i could separate small grains of sand if i tried. Its the type of depth of realism one finds in a Elder Scrolls, Fallout and Dying Light open world game.
Voice acting delivers with Hollywood flair and drama alongside well paced taunt tense music and emotionally stirring cutscenes delivering a zapping coffee jolt to the emotional senses.
Framerates are slipping on ice fast on my i5 3570k 3.40ghz, 8gb ram, Geforce GTX 970 with 4gb vram with all settings on high and MXSAA off. I will probably check things out on max settings in the future to see what results i get.
There are tons of things to tweak in the options menus to make the game perform on many different levels of pc systems. I have been playing as of August 27 2016 with at least two patches having been released before then and i have had no issues at all.
Oh and do yourself a favor and checkout the credits. Cool and funny stuff there.
DEUS EX: MANKIND DIVIDED a stunning masterpiece of a violent science fiction future where as always differences stir up troubles to be manipulated perhaps for the over all good.. perhaps not.

To start the review off, this game has some of the most fun combat in an action RPG i've ever experienced. There's a plethora of weapon types to choose from, and a basic skill tree leveling system with a bit of a unique twist that i'm quite fond of, there's three skill trees, Finesse, Might, and Sorcery. Sorcery is, well sorcery; might is most useful to warriors and finesse is basically for rogues and rangers. You can invest skill points in each of these as you please, you aren't bound to only one. The interesting part is unlocking destinies, you can obtain destinies by investing skill points in specific trees. Say you have six points in Sorcery, and six points in Might. This will unlock you the Guardian destiny, providing you with specific resistances and the ability to regain magic upon enemies hitting you. There's plenty of destinies to unlock, and you can switch between them as you please. Something i found personally interesting, is the lead designer for this game is Ken Rolston, also the lead designer for games such as Morrowind and Oblivion. You can definitely see the influence from those games in this, not in the core gameplay but minor things such as a similar lockpicking system, enchanting, harvesting plants to make potion with the same annoying possibility of failure, pursuasion, sneaking, pickpocketing and smithing, and Michael Gough, a voice actor who was in Skyrim and voiced multiple characters, most notably Jarl Balgruuf.
The graphics in this game hold up well, it's still pretty in my opinion and it can run on medium settings on just about anything. Now, for the things i don't quite like about this game. The world is very linear despite being so large, it feels like a mass of rooms and hallways. The quests for the most part are fetching missions/go here and kill this missions. Don't let those turn you away however, this is still a great game that i'd recommend to any RPG fan.

I have said time and again among my own circle of friends that a game set in the era of muskets would fail, due to a lack of cohesion between players and the slow pace of the game. I said that among the CoDs and Halos and DOOM, there was no fun to be had in a game with 3 rounds fired per minute per player. I was wrong. I was horribly wrong.
Big battles or small, land or sea, drummer or rifleman, there's a gratifying amount of variety for a game that wouldn't be expected to have any. Even a server with few players can turn into an amusing game of small-scale flanks and cat-and-mouse tactics. The classes, though needing a little work, each have their role which is more or less effective.
The players themselves vary as well, from roleplayers, to casual tacticians, to madmen. On one end of a battle, an organized British line fires in vollies at approach French. On the other, the French yell out in cacophonies of "Hon Hon" and "Baguette" and forgo tactics in favor of scattered hit and run. Both teams have their share of either type of player.
Firing, reloading, utilizing support functions, those things work well so far. Movement, however, suffers from occasional failures when navigating the environment. The melee system is, for all intents and purposes, utterly broken. Most melee fights can only be fought by wildly waving one's blade or stabbing randomly with a bayonet, because actually TRYING to hit them yields worse results.
Hold Fast could have been rated well even without naval warfare, but Anvil Games apparently thought such a game was only half finished. Naval warfare feels like a completely different game - as it should. Players spawn in on ships and take up the roles of various crew members. Cannons are loaded, pushed forward, and manually aimed and fired.
While mechanically sketchy, as is to be expected at the moment, naval conflicts are my favorite way to play at the moment. I could play a game that was ONLY this type of naval warfare and be happy with it.
This game is made by a clearly supportive, and highly dedicated dev team. With frequent updates addressing broken gameplay and adding new content, this game has a bright future. Unless the devs get bought by EA (pls no).
Buy it. Play it. The more money they get, the more they improve the game, and with this game being as good as it is right NOW, I can't imagine how good it will get later.

One of my favorite games of all time, Thief is an enduring classic.  Stealth is your path to glory as trying to do the "run and gun" approach will only get you dead, quickly.  Sneaking around, stealing treasure, right from under the guards noses, is fantastic fun.  Throw in zombies, spirits, strange creatures, immersive sound fields, and dark, forboding maps, and you have hours of entertainment.  I love this game and keep coming back to it over and over again.  To think that the original copy I bought came for free with a video card I bought years ago and I almost didn't bother to install it.  Am I ever glad I did.

Thief Gold is probably the best game I have ever played. It has just the right amount of story, mystery, atmosphere and difficulty that make a game really good. The graphics may not be up to scratch by todays standards - but that doesn't take away from the gameplay - which is what really matters in a game.
There is a good contrast of humour and darkness throughout the game, as it's story progresses. The level design is amazing, and the world is wonderfully shaped and described throughout dialogue, cutscenes and gameplay to create an amazing feeling of a steampunk city, still partially trapped in a time before guns, yet with steampower and electricity.
The game has no particular focus on combat, and is about the sneaking rather than the killing. If you get engaged in a sword fight, you're more than likely to die, forcing you to sneakily kill an enemy in one hit, rather than running up and whacking at it - or, if you're a nice person and don't like killing, you can use your blackjack to knock them out. In fact, the game encourages you not to kill people, and on the hardest difficulty even has a goal that always says something along the lines of: "You're a Thief, not a Murderer. Don't kill anyone!"
The main character, Garrett, may be a criminal, but he's not evil, or even bad, giving the player an interesting hero to play. The world is filled with many different types of people to come across. There's bystandards, guard, hammerites (a group of highly religous, hammer wielding fanatics that seem to basically rule the world), pagans and much more. There's even wizards! There are also Zombies, Apparitions, and the truly wonderful Haunts. The creatures of the world have massive variety, ranging from Craymen to Burricks! By far the most intricate levels being the Bone Hoard and the Lost City.
And the Zombies are actually scary! Despite not moving fast, the noises they make, and the fact that you can almost never best them in combat - and can't permenantly kill them without holy water! - makes it truly haunting to have to sneak past a huge horde of them in a crypt, eventually with the eerie sound of a horn in the background when you get close to that level's goal. And that noise they let out when they see you is just terrifying.
Overall: My all time favourite game, that despite being eighteen years old is still better (in my opinion) than massive hits like Skyrim and Portal.

This game is the king of stealth! I played THIEF: THE DARK PROJECT back in 1998 then it was released and was totally shocked! I replayed the THIEF GOLD (same game but with 4 additional missions) back in 2009 and was shocked again! Thief was the pioneer of stealh genre on PC and managed to get most things right. All stealth games I played after Thief was just not sophisticated to that level. DISHONORED is the one that is very close to it but I can't call it better because it is a THIEF's clone.
THIEF offers:
Authentic athmosphere (the mix of steampunk and fantasy).
Charismatic main character thief Garret with very good voice acting.
Freedom of choice (most missions you can complete in different way and path). You can even get more objectives choosing difficulty level.
Great level design with perfect horror and mystery elements. And there is NO LOADING SCREENS!!!
You can fight (not on all difficulty levels) or go complete stealth.
Different inventory items and tools for your style of game which you can purchase before each mission (for the gold you stolen in previous mission).
PUZZLES! Not much but some puzzles are really challenging and rewarding.
You can hear or read (and sometimes need) a lot of background information in books, scrolls etc. which can help you complete your objectives or find secrets.
SECRETS! There are many and most hidden really smart.
This game has to offer so many elements we can find in modern games BUT almost none of the games can manage all of them in a one single game so well that the THIEF does in 1998. For example the ROPE ARROWS! You can't use them where you want to like some kind of grappling hook like in JUST CAUSE neither you must to use them on some highlighted objects like in TOMB RAIDER. They are almost optional but very usefull if you want to.

Think Indiana Jones...  Now, imagine he's incompetent and you're the boulder.  This game in a nutshell.  A few of the puzzles really made me think for a while.  Some of them were easy, others required a few tries.   Overall, pretty well balanced.  There are a number of little things that change up the game as it progresses.  Mechanics are added periodically to spice it up and keep you from getting bored. Also, gotta love the little bits of Lovecraftian inspiration thrown in.  I'd say it's worth your five bucks (or, well, a little less as it is on sale at the moment).
Edit: Just a warning though, it is on the short side if you catch on quickly.  Some people might take longer than myself, and others might breeze through it even faster.  I thought I should throw that in there.
To the developer:
First game, was it?  I think I remember seeing that.  If so, well done.  It was entertaining.  The ending could've been a little more complex, but I won't elaborate to avoid spoilers.  Also, if you do future endeavors such as this one I'd suggest ramping up the difficulty considerably toward the end.  Almost felt like the hardest part was around the half-way to three-quarter mark.  Perhaps it was the final change, or evolution if you want to call it that.  It kind of felt like the last added mechanic was highly overpowered, but it was satisfying in its own right so I personally forgive it.

With a evga gtx 970 ftw I can run it on ludicrous settings now. But the problem is that it randomly crashes on those settings so I have to play it on high settings. So far it has also crashed around 5 times on high settings. As far as performance goes, it runs mostly at 60fps on high settings but sometimes has really odd bad slowdown that is dependent on the weapon you are using and the place you are at. On the first boss when you first start it and a load of guys come out, I killed them all with the 4-way napalm gun and it made my fps drop from 60 to probably 30 permanently so I reloaded the game and killed them all with the machine gun and it didn't happen then. Several other times in the game give bad frame rate as well. Right after the boulder rolls down behind you then blocks the way and you are in a new room, the framerate takes a dive to down around 30 or less. This game is, for sure, one of the most horribly coded and/or optimized games I have ever seen.
The two things that buried this game in the ground and made reviewers like IGN give it a 4.3/10 which is accurate even two years later after all the patch work they have done are the horrible jumping puzzles because of horrible jumping controls, and the awful environment hazards, and sometimes a combination of both making it a double nightmare. In-air navigation is very janky and causes you to miss platforms very easily after jumping. Hitting jump pads in this game during tough jumping puzzles is a nightmare. I constantly overshoot platforms or miss them early or to the sides if they are rotating. Rotating blades are not fun at all. They can sort of lift-glitch you in the air and do dmg to you while you are sort of stuck on them. Fire traps are poorly thought out too. There are even some points where the floor gives out to a spike pit but there is no way to know it is coming, just a trap to get 100% of players the first time playing which is horrible and should never, ever be put in any game. At one point this game did not have quick saving and had horrible checkpointing. After many complaints, they added quick saving. It still has God awful checkpointing, so make sure you are using the quick save option frequently now that it is in the game.
Every level in the game is just a different variation of the color gray or similar dull colors. The levels are not designed good at all, filled with torturously bad jump puzzles and cheap environment trap deaths. The enemies are all gray or some variation of tan/gray and they blend in with the background, meaning I often get pelted by gunfire longer than I should because I have to try to find where the guy is because he blends in with the walls/backgrounds. The graphics are nothing special at all and in fact are just dull, bland and depressingly lifeless. Enemy AI is dumb too. They just stand and fire or barrel roll to the left and right a hundred times until you kill them. Sometimes the dead enemies or flags will glitch out and stretch across the whole level in a crazy weird glitch fest.
It is too bad the problems I mentioned overshadow the rest of the game because the combat is great. Firing bazookas into dudes faces never gets old, that is until it is ruined by crashes or horrible jumping puzzles or awful horrible environment traps/deaths that rip you out of the action entirely. The boss fights in the game are not good either. The first one is fine, but the rest are bad.
This could have been a great reboot but it just isn't. If you want to see how a reboot should be done, play the newest Shadow Warrior game. And play the original ROTT, not this one.

Got a free beta key from an Alienware Arena mass key giveaway.
Pretty good from what I've seen.  Similar to SSB in style, but has it's own unique take with the weapons system and some of the mechanics.
Overall rating: 7 or 8 out of 10.
Things I like:
-Already have most of the staples for a good ssb style game:
--Variety of characters, none of whom seem especially unbalanced (haven't really seem much yet, so I can't say) and all of whom seem interesting
--Gamemode options like stages, game types (stock or time, etc.)
--Lack of gimmicky stages/items/characters.  Stages are simple without much movement (if any), only a few items none of which are massively gameplay changing (cough cough, hammer) beyond the weapon pickup, which is a core mechanic.
--Built in ranked 1v1 system, still needs work, but good for giving a game some draw.
--Good for pick-up-and-play.  Matches are only a few minutes.
-Weapons system is unique and gives each character a lot more variety (every character has two different weapons which change specials and can be used by picking up a certain item), but still retains similarities across the board (aerial and quick attacks, usually) that allow some skill crossover between characters.
-It looks good, has no glitches that I've seen, and plays well.  I assume the beta tag is mostly for balancing and adding more content.
Things I'd personally be interested in seeing:
-More character sounds, rather than just weapons sound effects. (mostly wishful thinking)
-Smoothing the dodge system to be a bit more responsive.  Might just be from playing too much ssb, but it often feels a bit sluggish, and the cooldown is annoying.  I guess this is more personal preference than actual balance concerns.  It's just annoying how some characters can spam certain moves but you can only dodge once at a time.  There's also no shield/guard, but I feel like that's part of the games concept rather than something missing.
-Ability to select/vote on a stage for ranked/random online matches.  Or, even better, a stage made specifically for ranked, like how competitive smash is just final dest.  Just something to make it more reliable.  More info about how ranked works too.
-SImilar to the above, a way to choose which weapon you get when you pick up a weapon item.  If there is one, I haven't found it.  If there isn't, well, no one likes RNG in something that has a competitive mode.
-Some non-paid cosmetics options other than just recolors for characters (and none for items).  Could be ranked rewards, unlocks for playing/winning with a character X number of times, etc.  (again, more of wishful thinking, doesn't affect gameplay at all)
Anyways, I do recommend this game if you in anyway enjoy smash and it's type.  It supports both controllers and keyboards, so you can use whatever you like to control, it's got a variety of online and offline modes, and it's fast fun.

To start the review off, this game has some of the most fun combat in an action RPG i've ever experienced. There's a plethora of weapon types to choose from, and a basic skill tree leveling system with a bit of a unique twist that i'm quite fond of, there's three skill trees, Finesse, Might, and Sorcery. Sorcery is, well sorcery; might is most useful to warriors and finesse is basically for rogues and rangers. You can invest skill points in each of these as you please, you aren't bound to only one. The interesting part is unlocking destinies, you can obtain destinies by investing skill points in specific trees. Say you have six points in Sorcery, and six points in Might. This will unlock you the Guardian destiny, providing you with specific resistances and the ability to regain magic upon enemies hitting you. There's plenty of destinies to unlock, and you can switch between them as you please. Something i found personally interesting, is the lead designer for this game is Ken Rolston, also the lead designer for games such as Morrowind and Oblivion. You can definitely see the influence from those games in this, not in the core gameplay but minor things such as a similar lockpicking system, enchanting, harvesting plants to make potion with the same annoying possibility of failure, pursuasion, sneaking, pickpocketing and smithing, and Michael Gough, a voice actor who was in Skyrim and voiced multiple characters, most notably Jarl Balgruuf.
The graphics in this game hold up well, it's still pretty in my opinion and it can run on medium settings on just about anything. Now, for the things i don't quite like about this game. The world is very linear despite being so large, it feels like a mass of rooms and hallways. The quests for the most part are fetching missions/go here and kill this missions. Don't let those turn you away however, this is still a great game that i'd recommend to any RPG fan.

From the perspective of an RPG fan, I regret buying into this game's surprisingly positive reviews. I assume many people review it before they realize how monotonous it eventually becomes.
It's not a bad game per se, but if you're looking for depth or immersion, look somewhere else. It's about as deep as you'd expect an MMO to be, with a very generic story. At times it feels like you're on rails, with little challenge, until a high level mob one-shots you, just like in an MMO. The landscape is very claustrophobic and constraining and feels more like a series of rooms that you're being ushered through as you level up. The world doesn't seem alive in the same way that something like Skyrim or really any other true RPG does. There is no charm or actual roleplaying here, only fetch quests and loneliness.
The game is long enough that the combat, which is definitely serviceable, gets repetitive after a while. By the time I realized what a mistake I'd made, I had passed the point of being able to refund it. If you just want to pummel some monsters, maybe you'd like this, but in that case there are a multitude of more recent ARPGs on Steam that probably do the same thing better.
If I was locked in a room with nothing else to play but this game I wouldn't complain, but there are so many great RPG titles available these days that there's no reason not to look elsewhere. If you value roleplaying, story, or immersion, please skip this.

I got this game as a gift from my BF, and I was quite happy to have gotten it since he knows I am a huge RWBY Fan, and it saddens me to death that I was excited for the 5th for the "Full release" only to be pretty much done with the game in one day. It doesn't feel like a full release at all, not for the scale RWBY fans know and love.
Story:
The story itself feels extremely rushed, basic and downright insulting for what the main show has to offer. There's no opening cinematics, no introduction as to why team RWBY's out in the Emerald Forest, it's all told through Professor Port and the team's "phone". If it wasn't from a series like RWBY that's known for its animations, I'd give it a pass, but there's no intermissions inbetween the chapters, Ruby and the gang are literally picked up and moved to the next area when they're done with one chapter.
(SPOILERS) The story is essentially team RWBY goes to this place, to check out this place, to check out this other place that has Grimm activity, soon follow a (dreadfully linear) trail that leads to the big bad, big bad has evil plans, evil plan gets foiled, heroes escape, game's over.
Gameplay:
It is a hack and slash, and that style works for a game based off RWBY, but what doesn't work is how poorly it was executed. The first level gives you no indication of what kinds of combos you're capable of, nor which buttons to press to attack, it's all supposedly intuitive. You're also supposedly rewarded for a big combo, but it's impossible to rack one up when a larger grimm just blocks your attack and you're forced to use heavy attacks. Heavy attacks are also too effective, they usually one-shot smaller grimm and the game can be shortened even further when your entire team just uses heavy attacks to set up a team attack to finish off even larger grimm.
The levels in the game consist of no puzzles except for one obvious one that's called out by Yang when you pass by it, and it's usually just a hold off waves of Grimm in one spot until you finish them off and move on. Even the end of the level is just a 4 wave survival round.
The skills you can use in the game are all hidden behind a small amount of leveling up, or "challenges" for better abilities, but they're all a complete chore to go through. Even worse is the skills that stun large amounts of enemies from a simple R combo from Yang and Blake's ranged combo, makes a lot of the combat far too easy.
Even the end-game boss, while at first you have to figure out how to attack it (Unless you've seen the show and know exactly what you're aiming for) is pathetically easy to bait out and get its only weak spot, even more easy to dodge since its so slow is many of its attacks, and then when you're done with that, you might expect an escape sequence when you hear you have to escape the place your in exploding, but as soon as you reach the next room, the game's over, you're immediately rescued, any sense of tension that could have been applied is immediately thrown against the wall for an airship to come pick you up.
In short, it doesn't feel worth the 25 dollar price tag at all, I'm thankful for the gift of it, but... it feels so lacking in content you feel like you're missing a download somewhere, or you have to insert the next disc, when you've literally reached the end, and the only option is to just play again. There is a "horde mode" option coming soon, which in itself is a sin since the 5th was supposed to be a "full release"  but there's still content missing.
Not worth the money, worth maybe one playthrough, but I hope Rooster Teeth truly finalizes the game and doesn't hide everything behind DLC. *Shudder*

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse - An unpolished gem yet to shine.
The game promises a lot of what you'd expect from a hack & slash type of game, but unfortunately has its drawbacks -  a fast paced, flashy, fluid yet restrictive combat system, a skill tree to beef up and customize your characters with limitations and a linear storymode which you can experience solo or in multiplayer (the latter being recommended for this type of game).
Comboing, which this game basically encourages, is clean and simple - though a bit /too/ simple for my taste. A lot of it relying on mashing a single button with no rhythm, timing or abbreviation - occasionally pressing another button to change the finisher. Combine this with the fact that a lot of enemies counterattack you, which for the most part you can interrupt yourself,  but it seems like some enemies break away too easily from combos leaving you to pick more desirable "small combo-chains" or staying in range to deal with this mess from afar and be safe.
Speaking of safe; Enemies hit hard. Very hard. Don't be surprised if you fall to your knees within 2 or 3 hits regardless of playing solo or in multiplayer, well, multiplayer having the advantage that friends and people can revive you if they stay close, but that is not the point. Difficulty cannot be changed, so be prepared for  a great challenge on top, which can be fun or frustrating - depending on what kind of person you are.
Bosses are very few and inbetween and mostly not that obvious; Actually there's only one true boss which you fight at the very end of the story arc while the rest I'd more or less consider mini bosses. They're not that tough, but rather have a sluggish feeling to them and rather uninspired. Not the forte of this game for sure unfortunately.
Story is weak and almost non-existant, which is alright if you have prior knowledge through the RWBY series on Roosterteeth, but other than that you won't find much, however - characters, dialogue and voice acting are great and stay true to the animated series. So, you'll probably find just as much pleasure from this granted quite a lot of characters are missing or simply won't show up because of the focus on RWBY's team. Maybe in the future?
These are just my peronal qualms about the game. Every character feels different from another which is great and I personally appreciate that aspect - even further if you consider the fact that you can tweak your character a little with their own personal skill tree, but I had hoped for more customization. Maybe costumes and more emotes/taunts as a bonus? More modes? More characters in general?
Who knows what the future may bring, but as of right now I think the game is worth the purchase if the price is right and if you follow the RWBY series closely and consider yourself a fan.
Bought the game during the summer sale and I don't regret it, but as of now - you'll probably end up a bit disappointed.
Multiplayer is a ton of fun, but I don't think the game should solely get credit for what your friends have done.
One last note: OH YEAAAH.

Got the game for free during Humble Bundle store promotion. However, I do think that this game is worth it full price of $15.
The world and its "creation myths" are amazingly build by both embracing and making slight fun of Metal/Rock genres. The characters are also pretty great and fun. Ozzy Osbourne as the "vendor" is plain hilarious, and Jack Black as the main character is, well, pretty much Jack Black (
Art style is also pretty decent, even 8 years after the release.
Gameplay is a combination of third-person action adventure like Psychonauts or Legend of Zelda and RTS, where you need to build gathering structures and summon units. You then have the option to just sit away and command from afar, you join you forces in battle (on harder difficulties, this is pretty much a must, especially later on). The command system is pretty good as well, although takes time getting used to it to fully grasp it. Some enemy unit are brütally overpowered, which is where you need to come in with Eddie, as your regular unit can get easily overwhelmed.
Then there is obviously the main draw of the game, the soundtrack, which is again excellent, featuring many legendary bands of the Metal/Rock genres and even few less known. The ability to manage the playlist is very nice, in case you dislike specific subgenre like say trash metal.
------
There are few nitpicks to be had with the game though.
First, the driving minigame is ludicrously hard, given how difficult the vehicle controls are (at least on KB/M), and how easy it is to get completely knocked around by hitting the smallest obstacle. Single hit from your opponent mean you can reset the race (and you cannot do the same to him)
Second, the game is somewhat lacking in few Quality of Life things that are common in games, although that is probably because a lot of thing have evolved or got dumbed down in the years since the game came out.
For one, there is no option to quick travel between points on the map, despite there being a perfect way it could work (on the other hand, having this option would mean less time to listen to the awesome music while driving).
Second, and my biggest "complaint" is lack of recording collectibles on the map. While you can collect them as soon as you encounter them, it is not really clear what you should do to get them, as the game does not explain it at all (I assumed I needed to unlock something or progress the story first), leading you to forget where they were, and it is really hard to find them later on.
-------
Still, I fully recommend the game, unless you absolutely hate Rock and Metal (in which case, I wonder why are you even looking at reviews for this game)
