This game is a super smash bros clone, which has many different aspects and differences between the main series.
I.Gameplay
The gameplay is similar to a smash bros game. You have one button for weak attacks/combos, and another for special/heavy attacks/combos. You can control the direction of your shield, however there is no "wavedashing" in this game sadly. In order to max out your character's potential, you need to pick up the glowing swords in the battlefield. They give you weapons which are unique, but do overlap between the characters. Each character wields a weapon a different way, even if some characters use the same weapons. The characters are mainly balanced, although some are much more used than others. The options for the gameplay are decent, and offer some sort of a unique and fun time. However, this game can get a bit boring after a few hours, but this game updates every week or two, which is always good.
II. Graphics
This game has toony graphics. They do look cheap, but they do fit the game well. Due to the lower end graphics, this game can run smoothly on any computer, and near no lag. Even the online modes have no lag, no matter where you are, which definitly is due to the graphics. The models can be a bit ugly at times for the characters, but it really doesn't matter since there are plentiful characters and options you can pick.
III.Logic
This game does not really have too much logic due to being a fighting game, but I will use this segment to describe anything out of place. The menus seem good, and the options for the menus are not bad either. The idea of not having too much logic is exactly what this game needs. It is a fighting game and fighing games are full of anarchy and destruction. That is exactly what brawlhalla is.
IV Replayability/Multiplayer
In order to get good for the multiplayer, you do need to practice. Therefore, this adds hours of gameplay in order to get good at brawlhalla. There is a decent sized roster of characters you can choose from in order to have a smashing good time. The multiplayer consists of a group(4 man free for all) to a 1v1(Similar to 'For Glory' on SSB4 for 3DS and WiiU), which is very fun, and little to no lag. You are near instantly put into a match to play in, and while you are waiting for a match, you are pit up against CPUs for practice to hone your skills before a match. This game has a ranking system for the 1v1 matches. After your first 5 matches, you are put into a league based on how many you won/lost. I hit bronze, and pvp is very exhilerating.
This game gets an 8/10. This game has some work to do, but remember this is still a beta. One of the best betas I have played. I hope this game goes free for beta testers or becomes f2p. The item shop is only currently visual effects, which means it hopefully will not become pay2win. Great game and I recommend you enter every givewaway and signup you can in order to play this one helluva game.

This game has seen a lot throughout its lifetime on PC. In the beginning, it was nothing but a glitch fest with optimization errors, crashes and unplayable online. Things have come a long way though. The studio that Nether Realm hired to create the PC port has really changed things from launch day. Optimization is acceptable and a hell a lot better than launch day. Now player have benchmarks in the video options to test out graphical settings. In addition, players have fps meters online. So you can see what fps your oppenent is playing at. Thus you can avoid players with weaker systems and save yourself trouble with lag and such. Speaking of lag, the game is still really hard to play online because of the input delay. I find myself dropping delicate combos with air tight timings frequently online. Its a pain in the a$$ but you get used to it with time. You just have to know your combos very well to input them before they actually play out. But something that you can't really account for with online lag is punishing certain moves. Like Sub Zeros b2, which is normally easily punishable by attacks that are 12 frames or less. But because the attack pushes you back on block, you have to run in and attack. Still easy though. But the input delay, delays your attack ever so slightly that you can't quite punish something that you normally should. If you try and fail, Sub Zero can catch you and full combo you. But after time you will know what attacks are punishable online and what aren't. Its a matter of time. HOWEVER, Nether Realm Studios has addressed this major issue in the Mortal Kombat Community by introducing a netcode system for online called the GG PO. It is a roll back netcode that will be used in the upcoming titles Street Fighter 5, Injustice 2 and Mortal Kombat 11. It will completely DESTROY any input lag problems in online matches. There is currently a closed beta running and so far the results are jaw breaking. The characters in this game are AMAZING. There is so much depth in each and every character avaliable. And even more depth in each varation of the same character. Effectivly tripling the cast. In addition, new mechanics were introduced in mkx that we never saw before. Such as running, run cancels, reversals, FRAME DATA WRITTEN IN THE GAME (Thank you Nether Realm Studios) and interactables. These take some time to get used to for mk9 veterans, but not very time consuming. I find combos harder to pull of on keyboard in mkx appossed to mk9. Especially the jump teleports but again, it comes down to practice in order to perfect. If you have a controller, then less worrying for you. The game was designed for controllers and thus you should have a better time. None the less, keyboard is still do able. I am personally a keyboard player and have no problem DESTROYING controller players.  In the end, if you are into strategy and depth, this is the game for you. The problem is that this might be a bit overwhelming for newer players. So in conclusion, get this game if you are able to put up with the frustration of complexity and online lag... for a short while, after which you, will become a pro and DOMINATE EVERYONE. Plus online lag is getting fixed soon so thats one less thing to worry about.

It's fun while you're shooting at dudes, running around, jumping around and shooting rocket launchers. That is the apex of the game, and it's what the game does REALLY well. If the game was ALL running, jumping and shooting at dudes... it'd be an effortless 10/10.
Unfortunately they also decided the needed other things. Like traps. Like instakill traps and jumping/platforming sections. In a first-person game. I thought we all realized long ago that if you're gonna have any sort of platforming stuff in a game, make it a side-on platformer or make it third-person. It doesn't help that the jumping mechanics/air control parts are pretty predictable when you're the one running and gunning, but the instant you get near a jump pad, which some of these sections rely heavily on... it all goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥
The boss battles are also... not fun. Multi-stage battles with instakill attacks, where you cannot save during and where the checkpoint takes you back to the start again every time. I sure do love redoing the same trivial part over and over just to get to the part that's actually giving me grief. Not a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥at all. PS: The post-boss animations? You are not Duke Nukem: Forever, please don't TRY to be Duke Nukem: Forever, you can be better than that.
Also for some reason it resets all my controls and graphics settings every time I quit the game. It's not a huge bother, but it's the sort of bother that makes you wonder if they ever playtested the game, along with the fact that once or twice I've had sections of a level fail to load, forcing me to reset to a checkpoint to progress. I also wish there was an option to disable the chewing-and-burping effect every time I pick up a food item, which is pretty often, considering that they're the only health items in the game, and it gets INCREDIBLY old after the 500th time.

You'll be wanting to play on the highest difficulty, and you won't rest until you're done with it.
If you're new, this franchise has the most outrageous weapons ever seen in a first person shooter, elegant map design that reminds of Quake or Wolfenstein, and some of the most satisfying blood-letting you can find. All wrapped up in refreshing UnrealEngine HD.
This game did okay on release, but it's criminally underplayed by shooter fans, probably as many younger gamers won't have much idea what the original was, and older gamers will suspect it of being another bland modern reboot. Give this one a chance.

I said in my last review the characters are only cosmetically different, but I was mistaken.  Thanks to fellow Steamer Gijz for the correction.  The characters do play differently from each other.  For example, Doug can take te most hits before dying.  Meanwhile, Lorelei is the fastest but packs the weakest punch out of all five characters.  Play with all five to see who fits you best.
The game also has cheats, but if you don't like those, you can ignore them.  The game has plenty of charm and is lighthearted despite its violent nature.  There's not quite as wide an array of guns as other shooters, but the loadout is nice.  Quality over Quantity.

I could just play with another charcter but that would mean starting over, so I think I'll put up with it.  It's not even a major issue, just a minor gripe that I don't hate enough to deal with.

Despite my gripes, the game is worthy of the following it has and all the praise it's gotten and will continue to get.  IF you're a fan of shooters, you need to add this to your collection.  As stated before, it's worth the full price tag, but if you can get it on sale, so much the better.

Its weird to see what kind of arbitrary standards people have for games and performance in general.
I suppose for $60 you aught to expect a lot in terms of quality, which is definitely true; though the recommended system specs are pretty accurate. My rig is better than the recommended and my performance is flawless, no crashes, no bugs, no random framerate dips, just a smooth 60 all the way through the game.
Chances are the minimum required recommendations are for people who are OK with 30 FPS, because I imagine that's how they determine that; with that in mind, the game doesn't lie about performance. You should know what to expect if you pay attention, and anyone who didn't shouldn't complain that they got burned.
The FOV was a little too low for me but you can just hex edit that; which is better than a lot of games in recent memory I was really excited for. Again, not a concern.
I'm actually one of the few people who likes having mouse acceleration on for his FPS experiences; so that didn't bug me too much. Though there's a steam guide for fixing it too, so I imagine that's not somethign to be concerned about either.
The game ironically pushes the anti-corperatism message while putting in some hilariosuly pathetic microtransaction system into the game; making it pretty clear that the marketing of the game was done at a corperate level, rather than the development studio. The microtransactions are basically paying for power; the hilarious thing here being that this is a singleplayer game, you can just pull up cheat engine and give yourself more power that way; no need to even look at the "shop". It shouldn't be a concern.

Aright, I addressed the negitivity, now lets talk about the actual game parts lol.
Gameplay is an upgraded version of human revolution. Its quite fun and quite challenging, even if you do max out on power early on. I played the game batman style and spooked the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of ppl more than anything else.
Plot wise, I would describe it as about as good the mass effect series; Nothing amazing or mindblowing in terms of storytelling but it hits all the right notes for me to be totally engaged. Characters (at least the main ones) are developed well enough (except jenson oddly, he probably could have gone the gordon freeman route and just not said anything and he'd be at the same point). This of course excludes Janus; who is basically just some dude.
The plot progresses in a really weird way though. The first 2/3rds of the game feel like a lot of solid storytelling and character building; while also creating some dramatic buildup as you complete missions and interact with the world around you. You start to learn more and more things about waht's going on adn what kind of conspiracies are happening. Then at the last third of the game that structure takes a total nose dive, and you suddenly wind up getting a bunch of random unanswerable questions, as though the game were suddenly setting up a sequal rather than building on anything; and then the game just kinda ends abruptly.
Sidequests don't really impact the game too much, you get a news article about them and that's it; but the choices you make in the main plot do affect stuff; nothing crazy dynamic, but they tweak the way some missions go later on.
The game also puts in this really neat thing called "breach mode" which is basically a fun progressional sandbox of sorts where you're given randomized loot as you go through a huge series of data servers trying to gather intel; being stealthy or guns blazing. Something that I never asked for; but appreciated none the less, definitely injects more game into the game; even if there's still some weird micropay things going on x3.
If that last half of the game didn't go the way of so many other triple A releases; this would probably be my favorite singleplayer game of the year. As it is though, the gameplay is definitely tight, and the story is tight enough to keep you moderately engaged in the world; at least until the end.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is my all-time favorite game, hands down. So how does Mankind Divided stack up?
The Good:
-	Gameplay is better than Human Revolution’s was. I played non-lethal so I didn’t get to play with the bigger guns like the sniper and grenade launcher, but the tranq rifle and stun gun were better than HR’s.
-	The game looks great and runs great. I know people are complaining of crashes and are calling this a bad port but I never once had a crash or any bug that I noticed. (Keep in mind I’m running a 1070 and an i7 in my system).
-	The level design was great and I had a ton of fun exploring every pathway in the levels. As someone that likes to play the Ghost route MD had excellent level design for sneaking around.
-	The old augs from HR have been upgraded and they feel better and fit more into the gameplay that they did in HR.
The Decent:
-	Jensen’s new augs were cool, but I only used the remote hack and the taser fist (I used the latter like 4 times total.) in my play through, the rest were geared towards a lethal playstyle.
-	Jensen himself felt weird. As much as I love him (Still do) Jensen seemed off compared to HR. (I’m chalking it up to bad writing).
-	The story (until the final level) was good enough to keep me entertained, but not enough to enthrall me like HR. Fortunately the gameplay picks up where the story doesn’t.
The Ugly:
-	The final part of the story was a major letdown. They built to an obvious sequel way too quickly and left me wanting more. (DLC hopefully, if I have to wait for another DE game to clean up this one’s story I’ll be surprised) The game feels like it ended on the climax rather than the resolution, like I finished HR’s first arc rather than a full game.
-	The final (and arguably only) “boss” was sad honestly. Not in a “I feel bad for you” way, but a gameplay way. I explored the entire area and unlocked almost everything only to realize I just had to hit them with a stun gun shot and a melee attack.
-	The CASIE aug felt way too overpowered.
-	The game felt too easy for me. Now you can probably ignore this because I didn’t play on the hardest difficulty and I’ve gotten better at stealth games since Human Revolution.
Overall I believe this is a solid game that suffers from a story cut short. Personally I think that the writers or someone was ordered to cut the game short so DLC could be added. I’d suggest getting the game in a few months when the Winter sale rolls around. Even with a 10% markdown Mankind Divided is still worth your money, just maybe not all $60. People are complaining about microtansactions in a singleplayer game, but I think they fail to realize that it:
A.	Doesn’t affect you if you don’t buy them.
B.	You don’t know that they are there unless you go and look at them. The game never advertises them to you.

I've spent around 3 hours in the "Give Me Deus Ex" mode and here are my thoughts:
:
It's Human Revolution 2.0, which is exactly what I was hoping for. Human Revolution did an excellent job at taking what made Deus Ex fun and brought it up to a modern shooter style. So instead of completely ♥♥♥♥ing with it like Invisible War, they took what worked, improved the gunplay, changed some grievences with the old system like completely overstuffed inventories, and overall made it better.
The new augments are awesome too, although are pretty much completely optional.
I knew that they were going to reset Adam's augmentations at some point (because how else would the game work if you were already completely decked out?), but i'm glad they found a plot point that made it work without looking stupid. I thought it was going to be something really stupid, or even a close repeat of HR, but for the most part it leaves questions in a good way.
:
I can't say much about the story, but from what i've seen, it's really not as bad as RPS and the like make it out to be. Human Revolution was all about Jensen and what he has caused and done for the world and his motivations. If HR is about the character, then MD is about the world behind him. Jensen plays a bystander to the action by large in this game, only engaging deep in the thick of it when he feels he needs to, and that's fine.
I don't want another "love interest, so therefore go through enemy compounds to get girlfriend, find out she's using you, wonder why you did it" story, because that's all HR was besides the Panchea incident.
Overall, Deus Ex was never really about the story, so if you're looking for a deep engagement, just know that this game is more about Illumunati influence than Adam Jensen questioning his humanity, which he has already done in HR.
I will rewrite this some more or leave it by the time I finish the entire game.

This game is a super smash bros clone, which has many different aspects and differences between the main series.
I.Gameplay
The gameplay is similar to a smash bros game. You have one button for weak attacks/combos, and another for special/heavy attacks/combos. You can control the direction of your shield, however there is no "wavedashing" in this game sadly. In order to max out your character's potential, you need to pick up the glowing swords in the battlefield. They give you weapons which are unique, but do overlap between the characters. Each character wields a weapon a different way, even if some characters use the same weapons. The characters are mainly balanced, although some are much more used than others. The options for the gameplay are decent, and offer some sort of a unique and fun time. However, this game can get a bit boring after a few hours, but this game updates every week or two, which is always good.
II. Graphics
This game has toony graphics. They do look cheap, but they do fit the game well. Due to the lower end graphics, this game can run smoothly on any computer, and near no lag. Even the online modes have no lag, no matter where you are, which definitly is due to the graphics. The models can be a bit ugly at times for the characters, but it really doesn't matter since there are plentiful characters and options you can pick.
III.Logic
This game does not really have too much logic due to being a fighting game, but I will use this segment to describe anything out of place. The menus seem good, and the options for the menus are not bad either. The idea of not having too much logic is exactly what this game needs. It is a fighting game and fighing games are full of anarchy and destruction. That is exactly what brawlhalla is.
IV Replayability/Multiplayer
In order to get good for the multiplayer, you do need to practice. Therefore, this adds hours of gameplay in order to get good at brawlhalla. There is a decent sized roster of characters you can choose from in order to have a smashing good time. The multiplayer consists of a group(4 man free for all) to a 1v1(Similar to 'For Glory' on SSB4 for 3DS and WiiU), which is very fun, and little to no lag. You are near instantly put into a match to play in, and while you are waiting for a match, you are pit up against CPUs for practice to hone your skills before a match. Ergh. Bahk! Ermahgerd. Between the mixed emotions of unrivaled superiority and fit-inducing rage I am feeling towards my roommates as a result of this game, I've managed a few breaths to write this review.
As a seeming homage to SSB, this platform brawler delivers lots of wonderful couch-seated gamepad-smashing fun. There are functional online modes with free-for-all 4-player and a ranked 1v1. I never experienced any lag being in New England (close enough to Atlanta, GA I guess). Certainly more servers will arise as people get their hands on this one.
Many mechanics are similar to your favorite brawler, SSB, but with some tweaks. The weapons system gives each character their specific weapons and there are fewer items overall. The simplified approach makes weapons worth having in the game and actually worth picking up. It also makes the game much cleaner and quicker with more overall focus towards play style.
The brawlball and bombsketball game modes offer an excellent change of pace if you (for some alien reason) get tired of  beating on your friends all day.
Get some friends, get some gamepads, a big TV, your favorite chips and soda and go to town. Even laptop to TV is fine, I'm running no problems on my 2010 macbook pro.
Brawhalla is FTP, which is completely ridiculous to me. I would have paid $5 for this. Probably $10 or $15. The in-game purchases are entirely superficial as only skins for your favorite characters or weapons. So, w/e. ignore them if you must. but once you realize how great this game is, spend some money on something and tip your hat to the Devs. After I get some  more practce in, you may find me as Ada or Hattori, probably with an added skin.
Now stop reading and start brawling!

But let me say what made me to give this game a positive review. I played it only for few hours, as I got it on Black Friday sale (an excellent opportunity, use it). Yes.

2,5 hour approximetly.

Depends on.

Meh.

Great

Yes

Here is a quick, postive review of Thief - pardon the spelling errors - I don't have any spell check program.
In my eyes, Thief is a classic game - an ancestor to many stealth games of today. Thief is one of my favorite games to date, as it is a gem in unique gameplay and yet contains a high degree of depthful and artistic elements to it, especially for it's time of release in 1998.
In regards to it's gameplay, this is a game that prefers peaceful completion of missions rather than violence, though still allows combat should the player wish to play that way. The player must move silently, extinguish torches to move in darkness, and evade guards and various monsters. There are different objectives in each level, but they often revolve around having to search for certain items in a large non-linear level. For combat when the need arises, the player has a sword, bow, mines, flash grenades, and a club to silently knock enemies uncounsious from behind. With the bow, there are many different arrow types ranging from the standard broadhead, to gas arrows, or explosive fire arrows, to moss arrows used to cover a hard, loud surface with moss to traverse quietly upon. The game levels are quite varied as well, initally starting with standard castles then changing more into a fantasty setting with monsters as the enemies rather than human guards. My personal favorite level was Constintine's mansion, as the entire level had a surreal Alice-in-Wonderland feel to it.
I would go so far to say that Thief could be considered an art game. The setting of the game is very intriguing, set in a strange steampunk world mixed in the middle ages yet merged with both magic and advanced technology. The characters, especially the protagonist, Garrett, have well-crafted personalities and superb dialogue. The storyline is also well-written with plot twists and a satisfying conclusion that leaves the player wanting more. The storyline is not shallow by any means, with an overarching theme of the nessesity of both personal and civilization-wide balance in life. Last but not least, is the games cinematics. In my years of gaming I have not encountered such distinctive and bizare cinematics. They are done in a very artsy manor that is hard to describe, perhaps the easiest anology would somewhat be like South Park's paper cut-and-paste style, though with darker colors, greater attention to detail, and a more realistic drawing method. It really looks good and fits the game's dark, and mysterious atmosphere.
Now praise aside, the game of course does have its flaws. Regrettably, it has not aged too well with modern technology. First, the game can be buggy. Sometimes, the game might not run without disabling extra processors until only one processor is running. Second, the default controls are just atrocious and it can be a bit of a battle to get them to function in an ideal way. Third, as expected, the graphics are no longer pretty. The models are all triangular and textures are blurry. Despite the expected issues of old games, it does not take long for one to get absorbed into Thief if it's given a chance.
I completely recommend Thief.

To start off, this game is huge. Five large areas divided into several subareas, each with their own distinguishing features and distinguishing features; three large, multisectioned cities, as well as dozens of smaller population centers, each filled with unique characters with lots and lots to talk about, and of course quests to give -- and that's not even counting the DLC content. The game is rich with lore, and even minor NPCs have many things to say that doesn't in any way relate to guests, but is simply there to give you more information about them and the gameworld. If your idea of a good time is walking around and just talking for characters for hours at a time, this is a game for you. There are hundreds if not thousands of named NPCs.
The game is also not lacking for things to do. From simple fetch guests to long faction questlines which takes you across the map, completionists are looking at well over hundred hours of gameplay. The critical path alone should keep you busy for dozens of hours, even if you decide to forego all optional content. So if your idea of a good time is running around fantastic landscapes killing monsters and sneaking around ruins for loot, this is still the game for you.
So those are the pros; now for the cons. The game was developed concurrently with a MMORPG that was never released due to the company going under (due to some very shortsighted decisions by their financial backers, as the online game would've almost certainly recouped their losses and then some, but that's another story), with the two games pooling resources. As a result, the game very much feels and looks like a MMORPG, which initially put me off enough that I stopped playing entirely before making it out of the first area, and wouldn't pick up the game again until much later.
The MMORPG relations shows unfavourably in many regards: The game does NOT look even considering its age, as although much thought has gone into making each area unique, everything seems very flat and low-resolution. There is no proper dialogue system, but instead a topic system similar to e.g. the older Elder Scroll games, with the player character only occasionally getting to form full sentences. Quests are by and large very linear, it being a rare event that the player can actually affect the outcome or even the method of accomplishing the objective in any way. Even then, the choices are pure flavour, having little to no actual effect on the gameworld.
Combat is varied, but not varied enough to not start feeling boring by the end of the game, by which time you'll likely have long since reached max level and pooled enough gold to buy yourself a city, making quest rewards irrelevant. Despite this, you can't buy yourself a storage space that holds more than 155 items, which is a crying shame in a game which features hundreds of books, notes and scrolls, and a truly mind-boggling amount of unique weapons, armour and other items, each with some story attached to them. All of which you have no choice but to sell or destroy.
There is a robust crafting system I ended up barely ever using, as there is nothing you can craft that would be more powerful than the unique equipment you find lying around all over the place. Potions, meanwhile, are rendered very cumbersome to use by the lack of a proper hotkey system – it's painfully clear the game was developed on the demands of gamepads, and even on the highest difficulty it was a rare event I even needed the errant healing or mana potion, anyhow. There is little point in crafting things for sale, either, as the merchants in the game have very little of worth for sale -- mostly just the same randomly generated equipment you find in loot, anyhow.
Despite all these grievances, I still find the game very worthwhile for the sheer amount of story. While an action-RPG in form, it's very much a game for people who like to read, and the gameworld, while not exactly living in vibrant, feels coherent, lovingly crafted, and steeped in lore.

Rise of the Triad is a remake of the off-beat 1994 Apogee FPS of the same name. ROTT's history reads like a "True Hollywood Story" of game development, with origins as a sequel to Wolfenstein 3D, and reusing of elements that were cut from the final version of the first Doom, itself originally conceived as a fantasy RPG. You play as one of five members of HUNT, black-shirted, trash-talking secret agents, against the forces of the Triad: a gaggle of demon-worshiping nazi lookalikes with a penchant for leaving rocket launchers lying around- to their detriment and your amusement. They've taken over an island off the coast of Los Angeles and have nukes or something. That's about the extent of the premise. Thankfully, ROTT isn't the sort of game, or even the sort of FPS, that needs a plot.
We seem to be experiencing a resurgence of the old-school FPS, what with the amazing Wolfenstein: The New Order (which, I might add, has an excellent plot) and the forthcoming, long-awaited Doom 4. If Quake 5 isn't announced relatively soon, I'm going to be profoundly disappointed. With that in mind, this version of ROTT is about as old-school as you could possibly get. There is no regenerating health, no cover, no map, and no voice in your ear telling you what to do and where to go (not that I ever minded maps and mission control). You sprint at top speed all the time, enemies come at you from all sides and there are big, garish collectible coins and health pickups scattered about. There are a large number of jumping puzzles as well, thanks to ROTT's trademark floating platforms and jump pads, a holdover from the original game's engine limitations preventing things like solid bridges from being made. Pounding buttrock accompanies almost every level, enemies explode into ludicrous clouds of red mist and gibs, and the game even tracks your score and percentage of level completion. Your arsenal is limited, but potent: you can carry two pistols, a submachine gun, a special melee weapon and one launcher, of which there are many: regular rockets, ones that explode in a cross-shaped napalm spread, double rockets, horizontal fire waves that travel forward along the ground, seeking missiles and even a rotary automatic minirocket gun are all to be found, as well as the Doomstick: a triple-barreled, pump-action shotgun with alternate explosive fire. If you pick up a new launcher you drop the one you were holding and can return for it later, if you haven't passed any points of no return. The game is split up into distinct levels with checkpoints, across five episodes, each culminating in an explosive, shoot-at-it-until-it-dies boss fight, just like the good old days.
Except not everything about the old days was good. In its anal-retentive effort to mimic the early 90s style of FPS, it also retains the elements that annoyed me about those games. Some of the levels can be a bit maze-like, though not to the extent of Doom, and mission-critical switches and levers can often blend into the background. It's also relentlessly difficult, even on normal: Enemies hit hard and health pickups aren't as plentiful as they could be, and if you take more then one or two bad hits from a boss, you might as well reload your quicksave. There's also the dead horse of color-coded keys and doors, and some of the secret areas are so inane that you'd have better luck nocliping to find them. Many of them all but require you to rocket jump to get them as well, and while I wouldn't call that a drawback per se, shooting yourself in the foot with one of this game's launchers is really not a good idea. The game also has a few glaring technical problems: The lighting is either oppresively dark or so bright as to hurt my eyes, and the game is subject to semifrequent crashes, typically on loading a quicksave.
There's a multiplayer mode I haven't tried, but I would hope it's a faithful recreation of the sort of deathmatch play you'd find in Doom or the first ROTT.
If you grew up playing these sorts of games then ROTT will be a rare treat for you in this day and age, but less hardcore players may want to pass this one up, and I mean that in the nicest way possible: ROTT is not for the casual shooter fan, and it was never intended to be.

Rise of the Triad is a first person shooter that trades in dull brown modern environments for stone gray with stone gray matching enemies that have hitscan weapons. Its one of those tough as nails games that tries to emulate the old school feel of a mid 90s shooter, but I account its difficulty for how cheap it is. Enemies can hit you from anywhere and they blend in with the background as any true soldier should. Its also a vertical game so rather than walking through a shooting gallery of hallways, you get put into large, tall rooms where standard soldiers can sniper you from high above your head. No matter what they distance, if they can see you, they can shoot you even before you ever see them.
This is a modern is a resurrection of a sequel to Wolfestien 3D that was never a sequel. You select from one of five characters and fight Nazis with guns, making their eyeballs launch at your screen when they explode. I can recommend going with the character that you're least tired of their voice over. Each of the characters has their own speed and power, but they are all quick and nimble. Despite how fast you are the hitscan weapons will hit you if an enemy sees you. Foes never even wait to turn around to face you. Their guns go blazing as they turn around.
So how are the weapons? You start with a pistol or two and you will find a standard machine guns that lets you have iron sights. These weapons both have unlimited ammunition with no need to reload, because its just so old school like that. Oh there are still reload animations, but they're unnecessary.
Beyond those two standard weapons, there's room for one larger weapon. These larger weapons are fun for the most part. Several of the larger weapons are too similar such as a homing missile launcher and a straight forward rocket launcher. It feels like a waste. The shotgun is a meaty, short range weapon. The large weapons are quite frequent and other than the secret room behind you when the first level starts, the next weapon you get is a rocket launcher in an enclosed space.
While the enemy intelligence seems dumb as they line up right in front of you rather than fanning out, they do have interesting facets. Such as they will drop to their knees and beg for their lives. Then sometimes they can pop up and shoot you once you turn around. I melee them, which would save on bullets, but the problem is there is no ammunition for standard weapons. Of course this is to compensate for those hit scan weapons. Its tough to imagine bludgeoning an enemy to death that can sniper you with a pistol. Some enemies will roll into you and take your weapon which is always interesting.
With levels so vertical, you'll be rising on floating platforms as lifts and using jump plates to hop from area-to-area. These trampolines and hovering platforms are what Rise of the Triad can hang its hat on to make it different than other modern first person shooters that try to be mid 90s. Nazis sure had some pretty interesting technology back then! Perhaps they should have focused more on space age weapons rather than futuristic trampolines!
Its all dull, dark gray with shades of blue with no sort of flavor to call its own. Its just generic flavor #9 with a darker shade. You go through different areas, finding keys to open doors marked "gold" or "silver." You also flip switches that further your progress. It all just makes the game feel that much closer to the bare minimum of what mid 90s shooters had with none of the fun. Where are the different enemies? Where are the different looking enemies? Even if the enemies are different by a slight degree, the only difference is their color, which is realistic, but its just all so boring.
Along the way there are plenty of environmental traps. Flames that come out of walls, spike traps that pop out of floors and crushing walls. Most of the traps you can time such as the flames and the crushing walls even if the walls are hidden in darkness and it took me a while to figure out what was crushing me. The spike traps cumming out of the floor feel like more of luck than timing.
If you get lost, there is no map; instead, the game has gigantic hovering coins to tell you that you're in a new area. Its like playing a first person Sonic game with guns without the loops!
There are a lot of flaws with the game such as you can see enemies spawn in from thin air. In fact let's say you've played the same level dozens of times, so you know someone is around that corner to the right. So you're prepared and ready for them. You peak around the corner to see thin air, but to your amazement he spawns in before your eyes! Torsos and limbs get stuck in mid air. Debris from smashing wooden barricades will hover every so often rather than falling to the ground.
I've managed to find game breaking bugs such as shutter doors that open when you kill the enemies manage to stay shut. I have also seen enemies shoot through walls several times and even spawn in walls on a consistent basis. These problems are all consistent, but lucky for me there is a reload last save, reload the last distant check point or restart the entire level. Its a bit frustrating to restart a level because the game has messed up and restarting the last checkpoint is unable to help.
Rise of the Triad is also one of the only games that manages to be worse with a 360 controller and still use the Unreal engine. Every other game with Unreal plays great with a controller and that's perhaps because there's aim assistance, but Rise of the Triad becomes that much more difficult to play. Who dares plays a modern first person shooter with a controller though?
The health consists of pudding bowls or white pies; one of those two. As generic as the game is, its a step in the wrong direction from standard white boxes. It turns any health hunt into something you need to put some effort into because its a black bowl on dark terrain. Is that health? No. Is that health? Maybe. You never know until you run into it. On the plus side, you can rocket the rice bowls to light them on fire and give you extra health at the cost of ammunition.
The catch with everything negative is there are positives that I never managed to find in my short time spent with the game. There are mushrooms that make everything look wavy. There's a dog mode of some sort. You fight through a medieval castle with magical weaponry. All that stuff sounds cool, its just that I never enjoyed the game long enough to get any deeper into it. Should anyone endure a bad game for what lies beyond further in the game? It failed to capture me and seeing the positive reviews when I know how flawed the game is makes me feel like people are desperate to like something.
Like most first person shooters, there are online multiplayer modes and that seems to be the sanest way to play the game. Other players have to aim at you to shoot so the game becomes a lot more forgiving. Then you become reliant on other people to have fun.
There's a reason why this game was so cheap when it was released and that's because the game itself is cheap. Its uninteresting, dull and frustrating.

Alright, so I reinstalled the game to fix the crashing, so I can give it a slightly more in-depth review now:
Game is still♥♥♥♥♥ It's got several issues, the primary of which is hitscan enemies. Around 80% of all enemies are hitscan. Which isn't AS big an issue in the first few levels because you're outside and the enemies aren't miles away from you blending into the background. But the later levels take place in-doors, with gray and black uniforms blending into gray and black backgrounds.
Often times you'll walk into a room wondering where the bullets are coming from, which leads into playing the game as a cover shooter. You better enjoy hiding behind walls and taking potshots, cause you're gonna be doing this for the majority of the game. See, when you enter a room and there are 5 people, it's stupid to run in and start shooting since none of their shots will miss. And I have a strong suspicion that part of the goal here WAS to hide enemies in the rooms, since a few of them are up on rafters where you wouldn't spot them easily. So you hide behind walls when entering a room trying to find them, and if they're all in front of you then you take them out one by one.
The mid-game bossfight shows just how fun this system can be. A boss that is all hitscan all the time. Luckily there are doorways for you to hide behind, so the bossfight goes like this: throw two rockets, hide until his 7 second barrage ends, repeat. And no, you can't tank his shots since you'll die in 2 seconds to them. Exciting.
Hitscan and enemies that blend into the background destroy any enjoyability this game might give you. But the enemies themselves are sort of...I mean, they just stand there shooting. Some are a little craftier and roll when being shot. Otherwise, god damn you might as well be shooting target dummies. Target dummies with hitscan weapons. So the task is hiding behind walls, spotting them, and going to target practice.
Then there's the precision platforming. To it's credit, the game's level design is such that there are traps throughout the levels, and for the most part it keeps the game fun and has you weaving and dodging throughout the level. But one level in particular, the castle level in episode 2, is awful. They expect you to jump from jumppad to jumppad in a vertical fashion and make every landing with the floatiest, shi*tiest aerial control around. Now you CAN quick save...
..but the game kept crashing, and when I reinstalled I didn't wanna risk constant crashes again so I just used a flying cheat. Thank God for cheat codes. Fire the guy that designed that level. That room in particular.
Then there's strange design decisions. You have a gun, double guns, and an automatic rifle. All have infinite ammo and stay with you. Why you would have a gun and dual weild guns in the game when you'll just default on the rifle is beyond me. It's unnecessary, a better option would be to be able to carry more of the weapons with limited ammo laying around the level. Often times you're backtracking after using a weapon to pick up another that was left behind.
The game also has special pick ups throughout the levels. You use them, like, 6 times in the whole game.
Game has nice music though. But god damn is everything else a let down. The first level is cool and sh*t and you're getting pumped up. But then you play the rest of the game. I didn't think one issue: hitscan enemies, could ruin so much of the game. But Jesus it leads into several other issues and it all just crumbles from there. Game has a 'mostly' positive rating atm, which means a sizable portion of them are negative. It's roughly a third of the reviews that are negative; avoid this title.

ONE SENTENCE EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
Brawlhalla is a fast paced 2D side scrolling brawler in the style of Super Smash Bros that offers 2D Cartoonish Graphics, Smooth Animations, Fast Paced Gameplay, and a Variety of Characters to play and master with.
LONG EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
Brawlhalla at first glance looks like an easy cash grab for those only looking for a Smash Bros-like experience on their PC's. But once you take a good look at it, Brawlhalla not only does justice to its genre but also does F2P right. Let me start here that the only reason you would spend money on this game (aside from being a Founder to get into Early Access) is to get more skins for both your character and weapon. (At the moment of this Early Access Review...) Everything is unlocked for you from the moment you click "play". This is a game that knows how to handle the free to play model, so for those thinking this is nothing more than a cheap cash grab riding on the success of Nintendo's Super Smash Bros. than you are completely wrong.
Aside from its fair use of its Free to Play business model, Brawlhalla also features great and fluid controls offering fun and challenging multiplayer. At the moment of this review the game has currently only one mode and it's deathmatch. And for what it has, the game does it well by offering Fun and Fast matches with well done maps, and almost Lag-Free matches. Though if there is one problem I notice (at the time of this review) would be disconnections. I may not experience and lag, yet sometimes I just get disconnected from the server, and this isn't just a rare thing because I notice even my opponents keep getting disconnected. Worst case scenario would be what happened to my opponent at the start of the game, my opponent kept disconnecting and reconnecting which painfully affected his/her overall score (which was -12). Now aside from the multiplayer experience the game does include a Training Mode and an Arcade Mode for Single Player fixes. Sadly though, there's nothing really noteworthy about the Arcade Mode and feels like its added there for the sake of having one.
At its current state, Brawlhalla offers a fun, fast paced, Smash Bros-like experience that will please any fan of the Nintendo hit or brawlers in general.

This looks and runs like it was made a decade ago, but that is the least of the games problems. It commits the deadly sin of video games; it's boring. You quickly realise there is just no reason to play this game. There's no plot driving you onwards, and what quests exists are mundane and simple.

The early selling was fun to try and get to a point where you could get the k points and progress further.
Cons-

The main issue I have is that after a while I started asking myself why I was still playing and not playing recettear, Shop heroes, Holy Potatoes a weapon shop or even steam trading. I mean hell if I spent the same hours steam trading which is a similar task I would have probably netted actual money vs a hallow feeling.
Where Recettear has dungeoning, holy potatoes just has lots of tasks, and shop heroes has actual trading with players Shoppe Keep has nothing that hooks you.
It's not a horrible game and if you really wanted to play it you could probably get 5-10 hrs of play before getting bored but the other games I suggested are much more likely to be better.

The Deus Ex magic is lost. What happened? How does a game that looks and feels like it could have been developed 7 years ago get released as a sequel in an amazing franchise? It just beggars belief.
First off, the maps. Prague by day, Prague by night, Prague by (spoiler) gets old fast, particularly as it doesn't look particularly good or exciting (Golem City was cool though). And no player waypoints on the (badly designed) map. And the long loading times between the small maps in the days of sprawling open world à la Witcher 3 or Fallout 4 just made me feel like I was back in 2005... I am aware Deus was never intended to be open-world nor do I want it to be, but come on, spending 20+ hours on the same map in Prague is selling the franchise short.
The character animations: odd running animation on Adam, over-the-top gestures in conversations, basic lip-syncing - really expected more from a AAA title.
Story was always Deus Ex's strength, but this one is miles behind Human Revolution. Nothing particularly memorable. And it did feel short.
1 boss. That's it.
And my personal pet hate: quicksaving while in cover has you sprinting out of cover when you reload.
On the positive side, it was great to play a non-lethal playthrough again, and the level design in the missions was solid, with the different paths to a same goal.
I really hope the DLC raises the bar again. I'd rather see it delayed by a year that leaving a great franchise on such a disappointing note.

Let me start by saying that I enjoyed every minute playing this game.
Having played Human Revolution, I must say that my expectations were quite high but really in the end I was more than happy with what I had.
What makes it so good then?
As usual, the environnement is top notch, it's a real pleasure to wander around the city talking to everyone, helping everybody, visiting the usual places (Red Queen! ;) )
Since the plot doesn't take place in Detroit anymore but in Prague, the scenery looses a lot of its dark atmosphere in the first half of the game, but quickly catches up as the story progresses.
What is even more refreshing is that as in the previous games, your actions do matter and killing everyone might anger some people, meaning you will need to kill even more, while trying to help everyone might save you from having to fight in the first place.
Now I have to be honest, while it's true that there is a lot to discover, meaning that every minute spent playing and every new place discovered feel fully fleshed out and enjoyable, the experience falls a bit short and the main questline ends where it really starts to get intense.
But in the end, it doesn't really matter that much. Because for what it offers, if you take the time to explore it, Deus Ex Mankind Divided is good, like, really freakin' good.
Sure, it feels like it should have been twice as long, and we still have plenty of questions left unanswered, but then what we really should be asking is : When is the next game?
And just hope that it won't be in another 5 years.

While the pros outweigh the cons for this game, there are more cons than pros (which means the pros are really good pros).
Let's start with the cons:
-No tutorial; Yes, the first mission is very easy and set up like a tutorial, but there is no actual learn-to-play guide for this game; you have to look up the controls while in-game and learn that way (and that doesn't teach you how to combo, I might add).
-Linear and simplistic level design; Very little to explore, artifacts are easy to find.
-Too many invisible walls; While I undertsand that this is a coop game and you don't want it to be ruined by someone jumping off a cliff (by accident or on purpose), I like being able to explore and parkour a bit. There's even invisible walls on top of tree stumps to prevent you from standing on them.
-Level to Asset scale seems a bit off; Characters, enemies, breakables, shipping containters, trees, etc. are all sized fairly apropriately when compared to eachother, but when Blake's head doesn't reach above a computer terminal, then the level to asset scale is off.
-Rinse-and-repeat combat; Each enemy has only 1 or 2 moves [other than the last boss] and often follow a simple pattern, making them pretty lack-luster by the end of the game.
-THE BLOODY CAMERA; The camera often changes angle for no reason, making controlling your character intensly frustrating. You'll often miss attacks and sometimes die just because the camera wasn't working properly.
-Not enough game; There isn't a whole lot to the game. The levels are small and there's only 10 of them, and you can only play as team RWBY (so, 4 characters only). This is more of a here-and-now point, as it may change with future expansions.
-Price; This is the biggest con. After the previous point, I don't feel like I'm getting 25$ US (~33$ Can or Au) worth of game. And if they release expansions I don't know how much more I'd be willing to spend. RT may want to consider lowering the price to 20$ US (~26$ Can or Au) for what we're actually getting at the moment.
Pros:
-Visually pleasing; The game looks good. Models, textures, lighting, and particle effects all look really good (I don't understand why some people are complaining about the textures... there's nothing wrong with them, they look like they're right out of the show)
-Feeling like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ While the enemies might not be overwhelming or even challenging in some parts, doing flips and twirls around the arenas while slashing and blasting your opponents into oblivion feels pretty cool to say the least.
-"Lost episode" story; The story feels like it could have happened anywhere during the first or second season of the show, giving it a kind of "lost episode" vibe thats close enough to the show to make it feel like it belongs, but not too close that it interferes with or contradicts the shows plotline.
-Fun as heck; Despite dying to the camera half a dozen times, and despite the enemies being rather easy, playing this game with my friends (or alone) is a lot of fun. Everything bad about this game is more like minor annoyances that crop up here and there; they all get forgotten by the time you and your frineds have kicked butt through the whole level.
All-in-all, pretty good for their first full release game.
6.5/10
(would be 7.5/10 if it weren't for that last con)

If I had to recommend this game I would say no.
It's not that I didn't enjoy it but that it was too short, feels incomplete, the ending unfulfilling.
Don't get me wrong, I did like the game. But at the same time I didn't.
My explanation:
RWBY the game was meant to be like the anime. But as a game.
The anime was amazing, particularly at the end when there is so much fighting and all of it does not feel the same, each fight had something special. This on the other hand not so much. Fights where repetitive. All the fights were mostly the same. You couldn't reach higher levels than 10 so having placements of xp in levels such as the lab was pointless as by then we had already reach 10.
I think I even prefered it when we use to click to use an ability rather than having to use combos. That's how I feel personally, I know lots of people would disagree with that one. But I mean for people like me who don't enjoy combo moves unless it's really cool and exciting and adds something special.
The story felt detached to the gameplay. The story was quite boring and felt like we didn't have any interaction with it, we just did waves of enemies, that was it. We did things as we were ordered (that being the same repetitive fighting) but it felt like the characters didn't have anything special to the story. All we did was do some fights and walk forward most of the time.
The story itself was somewhat interesting and funny from time to time. The concept was also pretty good.
The game itself was short. If your english like me and payed £15 when it was in early access you too had hopes the game would be longer and developed more. But it was not developed much. When I saw the ending, I thought there would be more parts since it was so short. I was wrong. That this is literally it. The game gave no sense of accomplishment. The last fight is too easy, too boring and too repetitive. I would of liked to see that the boss had more attacks as you were fighting it. It was too easy to avoid its attacks and all of its attacks where the same.
When the game first came out it was fun and exciting because we were all waiting and wondering what else will be added to the game. That the collecting of dust and driving a bomb off a mountain was fun and cool, There were also some other good and fun moments. But not enough. To the point where after you finished it, you don't really want to do it again.
Overall the game was fun in some areas but I do not recommend it. It's not worth the price it is currently being sold at. It's a shame too because I really liked the anime and it had so much potential.

However I do hope Rooster Teeth keep adding things and making changes. But since the anime I think people might have had too high of expectations of the game hence why some people may not like it. But I hope they keep tweeking combat inorder to make the game more fun.

Trine 2 is absolutely gorgeous and heaploads of fun. It may be a sidescroller but thanks to it's detailed '3D' environment it doesn't really feel like one. The game features both a single player and a coop section; I have yet to try the latter so I can't say anything about it but the singleplayer is great. You switch between 3 characters with different abilities and use them to solve puzzles, fight goblins and explore the colourful envirnoment. New abilities can be unlocked by collecting 50 orbs; these are found scattered around the levels and whilst you can aquire a few for 'free' most of them require you to reach pretty inacesible spots. The gameplay is mostly focused on puzzle solving in order to advance the level and the difficulty feels just right; most of them take a bit of time to solve but aren't really frustrating and it's satisfying to complete them. Combat is shallow but quick and infrequent and for the most part consists of goblin ambushes. It's certainly not the focus of the game, but injects a bit of fun and bombast on occasion. The game certainly doesn't take itself too seriously and has a fun atmoshpere - it's a cheerful fantasy adventure which is worth playing if you even slightly enjoy puzzle adventure type games. Recommended.

This is an adventure sidescroller with graphics worth a best photography academy award, add this to a very fun gameplay with a constant change of roles between a Warrior, a Thief and a Wizard. The Trine show itself again and it's those three heroe's duty to discover why it is back and save the kingdom again.
Choose Pontius, the warrior when you need an invencible wall and a mighty hammer throw to resist any harm and bring down any obstacle or threat on your path.
Choose Zoya, the thief when you want to sneak past your enemies, swing through death pits, or kill anything with her explosive/frozen arrows.
Choose Amadeus, the wizard when you need to solve puzzles that only his magic can help, create and build bridges and stairways to get to the next level or just imprisonate anyone who try to hit you.
Every level is full of ferocious enemies and mindbreaking puzzles that makes you want to continue evolving your player skill to get to the end of this magical history. This is a must have for any fan of art, magic, challenge, and a good adventure.

Enormously entertaining, creative, fun and engaging! What a fantastical, beautiful and oddly gorgeous world they've built here. Everything about it is so on-point and so fitting to the story and gameplay.
I especially appreciate how they embraced the open-world approach as much as they possibly could. You definitely want to run around, or drive around, and explore everywhere and view it from every hill, cliff, valley and top of every monument. And just tooling around doesn't get old, because there's always something to run down or pick a fight with. I've spent entire nights having a blast just driving around like a mad man, radio blaring, acting like a jerk towards everyone and every thing I come across, laughing so much my stomach muscles and the "big grin" muscles in my face start to hurt. Yes, even when you're not working on progressing the game story, there is still hours and hours of fun to be had.
Soundtrack is
Oh, what's that? You keep reading tons of reviews and they all give ludicrous amounts of praise to how great the track listing is and you're still thinking to yourself "Oh come on, they must be exagerating!???" Well, they're not. It's all true. Even though there is a small handful of tracks that aren't considered prime metal, they still fit into the game well and add to the huge fun. The game even gives you the ability to disable individual songs.

It's a damn shame this game doesn't work properly on modern hardware, with cutscenes etc being glitchy or not working at all. It's also a shame that even with the unnofficial patches, this game is able to blackscreen my machine and force me to manually restart.....
Nevertheless, there is a reason I put myself through hell to get this game to run, and this is why:
Thief Gold is a classic, it's a game that doesn't patronise the player. You play a thief (duh) named Garrett. Garrett is a regular mortal, with the gear to do the job. He makes more noise walking on marble, than on carpet. He doesn't have superhuman climbing abilities. He's got a bow, a sword (but no superhuman strength), water arrows to put out torches, lockpicks, and an affinity for not getting involved in direct combat. He doesn't have an automap, his map directly reflects the method used to acquire it. Treasure isn't located anywhere it shouldn't be located either....... Basically, this game puts YOU in control. Be smart, be patient, the sound design is amazing and the story is told through the gameplay.
I say all of this, because I believe that Thief was an innovative game that has been overlooked for years. The remake didn't do it justice in any way, as it suffered from the same cancer that has infested many other games of the AAA variety. This game tells you the story through gameplay and if you can fight to get it running, you won't be disappointed.

I've forever gone back and forth on this title for various reasons.
I think now that the game is at version 1.5.5 and I've played it numerous times I can properly express my opinion.
ROTT '13 is a mess, a bag of mixed ideas and designs that mold into a product of varying quality.
Like the games very performance it can be fine and drop in a moments notice.
That is because ROTT '13 doesn't use Unreal 3 very well, in fact its the poorest performing Unreal 3 game I've seen (and not exactly the best looking either).
It's not unplayable but for a team that boasts an attempt of appealing to the PC demographic, it's a shame it couldn't cater to performance.
On that note of appealing to PC players, another oddity of ROTT '13 is it's implementation of a checkpoint system.
Something that always came along with old school shooters was the ability to save whenever.
So it's bizzare that the game had to later implement a quicksave function. Sadly this doesn't work well either as it causes more bugs to an already buggy game and for some reason decreases your score.
I have to also make sure to point out the game is extremely buggy. Enemies will often get stuck frozen as well as weapons.
I was also disappointed that an amount of the games level design went against ROTTs unique arsenal.
For instance, there are very few ideal moments to use the flamewall as all the 3D geometry and detail clutter many areas.
The new muliplayer seems to try and be more like Quake than the original ROTTs multiplayer, which was goofy and over the top.
After all this negativity I stated, you must think I have a large amount of dislike for this game.
Well it may surprise you that I find it very enjoyable.
It's nice to have speed and be able to take damage, it's nice to find actual secrets, and it's really nice to see gibs.
I think that I've learned to enjoy it and the mess it is over all this time.
When I see it for 3.75 dollars during sales, it's hard to say the money is wasted.
Not a penny more though.

Edited to add after 34 hours in:
I have mixed feelings overall and am just about to finish the first play through. I would still recommend the game, however, the story seems all over the place, it could be my attention to detail perhaps, but I find it very confusing to keep track of, as it switches around between characters, then you do a side quest and get driven off the main story arc, only to return and lose track of where you were and which events were unfolding etc. & who is who & what is what.
I don't find the characters particularly memorable in general, with one or two exceptions.
So the exposition side, isn't my cup of tea at all.
You do of course have a journal of events and records of Emails etc. to go back and read. I would estimate I bothered to read about 70% of all available documents I discovered and this became another issue, as I lost focus when wading through a lot of inconsequential data. It would be like out here in the real world, rattling through dozens of Emails in a few short hours and attempting to catalogue them in a coherent manner to make sense of what was being projected. They eventually turned into an annoying background noise and I found myself skipping through looking for codes to open doors etc.
So although creating a dense tapestry of data seems like a key layer to help flesh out the world, one wonders how many players actually bother to read everything the developers provide... hmm
It could be me though, I'm getting old and losing patience, or is it an expositional failure?
I'm not sure.
The AI at times is really bad and this follows on from the previous game. If you have a really good hidey hole when the alarm is triggered, wait in the hole with your favourite scoped weapon and you can pretty much guarantee wiping about around 80-90% of hostile entities. How hard would it be to have an enemy "accurately" roll a grenade around the corner or into a vent or pipe? Often the grenades bounce away and at times, take out other triggered enemies. This was disappointing.
Another gripe - the NPC chatter in the city, Some of the dialogue pretty much loops, like you walk past a tramp and he'll say "grrr, the way they treat us now is blah blah blah" and then he'll say the same thing, time and time again ... and if you are in the area investigating / hunting something out, it gets ridiculous. I don't know why they have these triggered scripts. When we travel around a real city, often you just hear a background murmer and most people are quiet up close, unless they have company or are directly prompted to converse.
Other complaint - robbing items and no reaction or occasional extreme reaction (ie. all police alerted for minor infraction) ... this follows over from the previous game and should have been sorted out. You shouldn't be able to walk into a persons home and start rifling through the drawers while they are watching... what about consequences for being a theif? This needs addressing, as the game is supposed to be immersive and these sorts of factors break the immersion.
Anyway - I'll leave it there.
It still gets a thumb up & is a decent game, but far from the idealised Deus Ex experience many of us desire and I have a feeling this will emerge through a different developer under a different title .... Rockstar could make a fantastic Cyberpunk epic in an open world. Here's hoping!

As a returning tekken fan i picked up this game on the basis of nostalgia. I was very pleased with the game. The music was fitting, that it gets you pumped up before a match and the story was stitched together fairly well, although, a bit generic but still enjoyable. The gameplay and it's many variety fighting moves and styles, is what makes this game excel. It's fun playing versus, and it's fun playing against AI. I also loved the fact that this fighting game was very friendly toward new arrivals to the fighting game genre. But, there is one thing that ruined all of that for me. I cannot describe my frustration and disdain enough with the story mode- akuma fight. The game was fun up until the part where you have to fight that guy. Two hours in, i finally get to the point where akuma is 0 hp and to the point where we are both are supposed to unleash our rage arts. All that work, getting k'oed constantly 1000 times, getting 1000 game over screens. All my work of having akuma one shot me when he reaches half health (//sidenote// He will automatically K'O you at half health if he hits you with his focus punch, even if you are full. So you have to play without getting touched after he has half a health bar) has come to this point of my promising victory, what could go wrong? I try to unleash my rage arts when he does with "RB" and nothing happens and to my dismay i lose the game (RB is buggy for rage arts but it's a quick reccomended input).
I uninstalled Tekken, well knowing i was unable to complete story mode. I was looking forward to trying out treasure battle and other game modes right after story mode, but that reocurring cheap, sour boss battle that i lost, and the fact i couldn't complete the story, will keep me away from that game forever. I don't know what the dev(s) were thinking but whomever made that part of the game should be fired immediately for their lack of creativity and lack of consideration to the people, new and old, playing this game. If any readers are reading this, if you are okay with an incomplete story, than buy this game. Otherwise, look forward in trying to exploit this final story mode fight to get through the story. You're going to need it.

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a really good RPG with fun combat mechanics.
You have a lot of options in terms of different and unique weapons and armor and a few classes.There are a lot of useful skils, perks and talents for each class. And the best part is that you do not have to stick with one particluar class and only improve that.
As i stated before the combat is what keeps this game going as it provides a good challenge at times and sometimes you would have to make use of weapons with different elemental effects to make the fight a little bit easier.
The graphics have that slight mix cartoonistic and animated feel which looks very good and polished . One of the best things about this game is the diverse environments which look absolutely spectacular (Check out my screenshots of the game).
The lore and base story missions are aslo fun and great boss battles although rather easy.YOu can also find numerous lore stones with well written poems and small rewards for finding it.
The game also runs really well with high settings at 1080p on a decent setup.
My only complaint with this game would be the slight repititive nature of the missions especially the side missions and tasks. Most of these side quests are "Fetch this", "Find this", "kill this" etc. It seriosuly could have been done a little better with more variety. Oh and you would never run out of things to do since there are numerous quests in this game. The main reason to do this would be for the good weapons that occur during the missions and a decent amount of gold and experience.
Highly suggest you get this game if youre a fan of rpg's with a lot of content and this comes for a very cheap price during sales and it is truly worth it.

At the time of writing, I'm playing a lot of games that are quite heavy on the game-mechanics side of things (HeXen, Unreal, Prince of Persia, STALKER) or story (KoTOR II, Mafia).
For me, this is the perfect cooldown from endless dialog trees, droves of enemy types and labyrinths upon labyrinths of levels. Just shoot the on-rails moving balls with your static frog turret so the ball colours match and clear the level before the time runs out. You have some fairly straightforward powerups like slow moving balls and reverse movement direction, then there's accuracy and explosion. Nothing too fancy, but it's so effective as a time killer.
The music is also very fitting, just hype enough to keep your brain firing but still inocuous enough to not make you nervous (unless you're near death, then the music changes and it's meant to make you nervous).
There's an "adventure" mode, where you complete levels by hitting a certain points threshold, and survival mode with four difficulty levels where the balls just keep coming until you lose.
Don't let this fool you into thinking the game is easy, however. It has that patented PopCap balance of challenging, addictive and still enjoyable. Like I said, I love to play it when I don't feel like watching a movie or series but I don't feel like playing some hardcore 90s FPS either.
The only downside is that the levels in this game are saved as 640x480 JPEG files, so there is absolutely no way to change the resolution, let alone aspect ratio. On my 1366x768 laptop screen, it's not as bad, but I imagine it would be pretty jarring on a 1080 or even 1440 screen.
All in all, it's a shame they didn't update the visuals or even just upscale the whole thing, otherwise this game would be perfect - it's a steal during sales anyway, so even with the dated visuals, I recommend it wholeheartedly.

As one of the PopCap classics from the mid 2000s, Zuma brought me and my family counless fun hours for over a decade.
The gameplay is simple, match three balls of the same color together and get combos, chains or collect randomly appearing coins to increase the yielded score.
There's also a couple of power-ups which appear occasionally which can help you, such as reversing the balls movement, stopping their movement entirely, causing a big explosion which destroys its surrounding balls and an aim help which lets you shoot your balls quicker.
This game is brought down in two modes, the Adventure and a Gauntlet mode (which is pretty much a survival mode).
-The Adventure Mode is a stage-to-stage Level Rush where you have to score a specific amount of points to stop more balls from spawning and then clear the screen to get to the next stage.
All this is split into multiple different worlds with more colors to appear the deeper you get.
-The Gauntlet Mode allows you to play any stage you beat in the Adventure Mode and attempt to survive as long as you can, while attempting to score as much points as possible.
One thing I'd like to mention is the games modability, yes I'm serious!
If you look into the local files, you notice that most image and audio files (except of the background-music unfortunately) use default file extensions and formatting.
This means you can easily replace game files and inplement your own files if you want an entirely new Zuma experience!
I cannot tell you if any format works, but as long as you covert your files into the same extension as they were in Zuma (most of them are .jpg, .gif and .ogg), it should work just fine. (atleast it did for me and a friend of mine)
You might want to backup your save file though prior to the modding, just in case something goes majorly wrong which forces you to re-install the game, thus as always mod at your own risk!
The only problems I have are:
-Maximum resolution of 640x480, which you can get used to in fullscreen, but can cause trouble when playing in windowed mode. (see next point)
-The game does not force the cursor inside the games window when you don't use fullscreen, hence you can click outside the window accidentaly and not shoot while playing. Trust me, this happens more than you'd wish!
-I honestly believe it's not worth the full price of €5 any more. This game came out 14 years ago and its successor is avaiable for the same price, offering way more.
BUT:
If this game IS on sale, I can only recommend this to anyone as it's a very addictive experience which first up seems very simple, but gets more complex when you get to later stages, both in Adventure and in Gauntlet.
The graphics are ok for its time while the music fits the atmosphere perfectly.
Even if my playtime on Steam isn't that high yet, I can promise you my (and also my parents) time spent into this game would exceed your expectations.
