Thief gold is the remaster of the original thief game. It is a first person stealth game with minor puzzle solving elements.
The game takes place in "the city", for it has no other name. A place built on steam and new technology that is slowly being developed, bringing it out from the dark age and into the metal age (the title of the second game). Poverty and crime are rampent, with a small section of the city holding most of its wealth. You, are garrett, a thief trained by a mysterious order in the art of stealth before fleeing and going freelance with your skills. The plot of the game? Steal from rich targets and slowly uncover the mysteries of the city, along with the cruel plots woven by one of its many inhabitants.
The gameplay is easy to understand, but difficult to master. You are stuck in first person and have to sneak around, completing objectives and stealing swag to pawn off. You need to keep two things in mind when sneaking, the first is sound, whenever you move you make sound, this is different depending on the surface you are on. You make less noise when crouched, but move slower. The second thing to watch is light. There is a small indicator on the screen that tells you how visible you are to everything around you, if the light is on, its easier to see you than when its off. Simple stealthing 101. But, you are also equipped with a small selection of items, mostly arrows with different effects, like the moss arrow, which allows you to make a carpet to walk across silently, or the rope arrow, which allows you to reach high places provided you hit wood with it. There is also the trusty blackjack, perfect for knocking out enemies, and your sword, which you use to shank.
Combat in this game is pretty janky, and its very easy to die, but then again, that is the point considering you aren't conan the barbarian. You can go crazy and run in with your sword, cutting everyone to pieces, but you are very weak and it only takes about two or three hits to kill you, even on the normal difficulty setting. While it doesn't force you to stealth, its highly recommended to at least try not to mad dash. As the game progresses, the levels really do change up, at first your breaking into a simple manor house, but by the end you are running through cursed churches and hellish fae domains. Most are designed in a realistic way, which really does allow you to think about the building you are in as an actual building, rather than just another level. The AI in this, for the time, is pretty impressive to, the guards will search for noises and use tactics and they have pretty good pathing for the most part.
This does bring me to some of the faults of the game. Its old, really old, it runs wonderfuly on modern PC's, but the character models are so low poly that they had brick hands and plank arms. The textures for most of the world vary in quality, some look like they hold up really nicely, while others are cringe worthy. Then there are the enemy types, not all of them are terrible, but whenever zombies or ghosts are brought into the game, it really does feel annoying, considering that you can't kill either of them without special arrows, and the moment they spot you, they will hunt you down, even if it takes years to do it. Thankfully they only appear in a handful of levels at most. There are also a few cheap moments here and there that can ♥♥♥♥ you over with traps that come out of nowhere.
But, despite all this, Thief is a masterful game, and earns its place as a classic for being a truly great game. Even by todays standards, its hard to find a game as good as this. This game is one of the grandfathers of stealth games, and is worth your time if you enjoy difficult stealth games, or just worth checking out to see the influences it has had on modern gaming.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is fairly lackluster and doesn't offer much in gameplay other than a service to the brand.
The game is a multiplayer beat 'em up takes place in the webseries world. The four heronies, Ruby, Weiss, Blake and Yang are playable characters that share the same voices as the show's counter parts. You can team up with three friends or play alone and beat up monsters. I can say for sure, this game defintely had multiplayer in mind for two reasons: the maps are large and the waves of enemies are fustrating to fight alone. Those two reasons are some of the games flaws.
The game's developers did a pretty good job depicting the world of RWBY and fans of the show will feel like they are in Remnant, where the series takes place. However, it is fairly empty and lifeless at times. The maps are fairly nice to look at when you are traveling through them but there isn't much in the way of exploration. Other than looking for artifacts that rewards you with experience points, there isn't much incentive to go out and look for them. The game keeps you lock on a set path for the most of the game and just removes any sense of adventure because you are on a set path.
Enemies don't appear on the map as often as they should and only appears mostly at the start and end of the stage with a few random encouters in between. There isn't much variation in the types of enemies and gets pretty dull using the same strategy to beat them over and over again. You can almost always count on needing to clear out a wave of grimm before finishing the stage, its a cheap way of putting excitement in the game and gets boring very fast.
In the show, each of the heroines are unique in their own way and it did meet that expectation. Each of the characters fuctions fairly differently, for example, Yang is a close up one on one fighter while her sister, Ruby, is armed with a scythe is able to do large sweeping attacks that hit multiple enemies. However, when you are leveling up your characters and buying new skills, they all share the same power ups. They all get a damage buff and get an area of effect attack to prevent them being surrounded. I was hoping for some more variety with their power ups.
Another thing that was missing from the game is the show's amazing rock soundtrack. While there is a decent rock soundtrack playing while fighting the horde of grimm, it just doesn't match up with what they have in the show. I was hoping that I could count on the music to bring some life to the game...but sadly that isn't the case.
Overall, ifs a pretty underwhelming game and fans of RWBY like myself thinks the game could use a lot more polish and content. And with the final price set at $24.99, I suggest waiting buying the game during a sale if you are really a die hard RWBY fan. If you want a beat 'em up game based on a popular show, I suggest Legend of Korra. Its 10 dollars cheaper and played much better than RWBY.

This is the most refreshing shooter I've played since the original Halo. Halo was legendary for its recharging hp mechanic, which sped up fights and made decisive actions more necessary because you had to quickly kill powerful enemies or they would be back at full health in a few seconds. The same was true for yourself. This added a lot more dynamism to gameplay than was present before.
Imagine a modern shooter where cover was useful for more than hiding. Imagine you're 80% behind cover and someone can't just mouse 3 pixels over and shoot you in the tip of your nose reliably enough so that fighting stationary from behind cover like in real life was a thing. Instead of fire fights being 2 seconds of running back and forth and jumping to avoid bullets, they were a gradual process of fire and maneuver typically ending in a bayonet charge once enough of an advantage was attained. Just like in real life during the Napoleonic period. Surprisingly, the slow reload of the period weapons adds a sense of tension very different than most shooters and a welcome change of pace.
There is loads of fun to be had already and it’s priced modestly.

Where to even start with this game? This game is the crown jewel of stealth games. Never has any stealth game in my opinion ever put a torch to Thief: TDP. Imagine this game as a fine aged wine if you will. Sip it slowly and really "taste" the game as you play it. The main character is one you will quickly fall in love with and the voice acting and dialog is incredibley well written and acted. The art is unique and creates a immersive and original world that is shrouded in mystery. Often you will wish that you only knew more about the setting and characters as the game often teases you with just enough to make you play the next level. The plot develops at a reasonable and sensible pace making you feel that the developers really thought this game out. The gameplay is suspensful and it does not pander to the inexpierenced player like most AAA games do today. The AI is still rather sophisticated given the games age and the levels are well designed, pushing the player in the right direction without holding the players hand. Unfortunately the modern interpretation of the game by Square Enix simply is utter garbage compared to this original. If you are a true a computer gaming fan, do yourself a favor and add this game to your collection. Almost anyone with good taste will agree that Thief: TDP and its sequel, Thief: TMA are timeless classics from a golden age of gaming history.

This game has proven to be more enjoyable and provide a better experance then modern AAA games, and I do not consider myself a retro gamer, this is the first and only game I've played that I do not consider a modern title, and I plan to finish all Thief games.

I'm going to look at 4 aspects of this game. No spoilers.
1) Graphics:
The visual style of the game is gorgeous: It doesn't aim for realism; it's simplistic yet every scene is like an oil painting. The bright, vivid and sometimes sombre colors and the beautiful lighting are really wonderful to look at. It was a feast to my eyes.
2) Sound:
The game had beautiful ambient music throughout. It was uplifting at times and heart-wrenching at others. Makes you feel like you are living in fantasy world from an ancient tale. The voices of the characters were kind of annoying to me but it's really not a problem at all. Sound effects added a sense of realism.
3) Gameplay:
You play with two analog sticks of one gamepad; left analog controls the older brother, right analog controls the younger one. This was refreshing, nice and challenging at times. At one point I thought: "Well, this might have been better if it had an option for two players where you play with two gamepads." but as the story progresses, you understand why the developers didn't go down that road and why it would actually be worse if they did: I think there are certain emotions that the developers wanted to evoke that wouldn't work if the brothers were controlled separetly.
4) Story:
My goodness, the story... It was so, so heartbreaking. I particulary liked one thing about it: The game has a made-up language so all of the story is conveyed just through visuals and sound and not through dialog. This stylistic choice was really unique to me and it is one of the things that really make this game what it is. You feel a certain connection to the characters but it could have been better with more flashbacks and a much longer story.
In conclusion, I think Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons can be described with only one word: ART. (8.5/10)

Rise of the Triad is a 2013 remake by Interceptor Software of the old ROTT from 1993 which was made by Apogee and Team Of Incredible Power. Well, I would rather call it a reboot. I mean, 20 years is such a huge gap. It's still fast-paced FPS with competetive multiplayer that think that it's very hip due to old-school elements.
They also kept updated since then. Gameplay-wise most important change was inclusion of quicksaves and shotgun-bazooka thing that is placed in almost every level now.
Technical-wise, this game was a complete mess at the launch. It had one thousands and one glitch and had awful performance for many people. If it was some AAA company, people sure would have spent all their time whining, yea. Something something EA access something beta testing something.
But not to worry, developers even today keep updating the game, killing bugs and trying to improve performance, so it's not bad as it was. It still didn't stop me from getting stuck once because of failed trapdoor on Episode 4. Or even to have a level to fail to load next part of itself in that one map where I tried to use quicksaves for first time. Something about getting to checkpoint, then quickloading to pre-checkpoint save and trying to progress from there.
Multiplayer community is kinda there. Usually there is nobody playing, but game's steam group actually runs events where it invites players to multiplayer every saturday. I know that there were few people this winter, but because my game (or Steam) glitched and wouldn't see Steam Workshop maps that I subscriped to at all, I had to miss the fray.
Plotwise it's a same wacky story. Something about HUNT team that is you going to kick butt of nazi-like people and monks of Triad cult, while turning into doges and blowing up everybody with barks. In other words, no plot outside of intro and ending. It's just wackyness, coolness and trolling. Yea, trolling and memes, yay. Over 20 levels that are put into 4 episodes.
And look, there is Escape from Vomitorium level.
Well, actually settings looks awesome and enviroment is often fashinating, like first level of Episode 4 which introduces evil magic monks combines cathedrals and beds of flowers with snake-mouth gates and rivers of blood. That one was awesome.
Gameplay is simple in that it keeps many stuff from the original ROTT. Interesting, even. Like, you still get to pick 5 characters, which are more sanely balanced in stats. Actually, there are only two stats: speed and endurance (health). Sadly, due to this game being a hitscan abuse game, speed matters very little and only will get you into trouble faster, so character with highest endurance is the best, no thinking about this.
Another interesting thing is how weapons work now. You can hold only 5 weapons. But in reality the first 3 weapons are taken by bullet weapons that are direct upgrades over each other so it's silly that they take individual slots. They also have reloading and iron sight for those, but they are just developers being busy with trolling instead of bugfixing. Ammo is infinite and all weapons are always 100% accurate, pretty much. So you spent your time by sniping people and never releasing fire button while waiting around corner.
4 and 5th slots are taken by special weapons. 4th is for bazookas and other such weapons, which have limited ammo. You can pick only one type, if you run over another one then you will swap them. And they say that Halo was newschool. Very explosive. 5th is magic weapon. There are only two of them and you will rarely get them. They aren't really different from bazookas.
You now now use knife anybody as well and it's a pretty sweet addition. You actually don't have to aim as much with this, just press a button and your character will lunge toward the enemy who is close, stabbing with two knives. There are plenty of placed to use this. And there are plenty of places where you will get stuck in geometry and control of your character will be disabled for 5-10 seconds. Yay.
Also you can heat up most health items to double up the amount of health that they give. It's pretty great idea from original, to sacrifice rocket ammo to put porridge on fire. Though ammo was more valuable in original.
Powerups are also fun, having both good and bad wacky ones. The most awesome one is a doge one, where you are invincible, can pounce and bite people to death and can also do an explosive bark/howl, though in this game it will immeditly end the dog mode because it was way too good in original.
But yes, sadly, this game isn't exactly a comeback of 90s or arcade style of FPS. The thing is, almost every enemy that you fight are hitscan attacking ones. So instead of rushing in and circle-strafing around room like a pro like you did in classic shooters, it playes out more like one of those bad shooters from early 2000s, waiting around corner, peeking out slowly while holding down fire button due to infinite ammo and no recoil. Trying to play it in fast-paced way just means you get murdered more.
Heck, when I replayed all my favourite 90s shooters I realize that the thing that I also liked about them is that they weren't focused on precisions there, instead being about movement. Most of them had autoaim or big collision. Now here it's hard to hit anything with bullets when running.
Yea, original has same hitscan stuff, but combination of reliable autoaim and hit stunlock on enemies made it a bit better.
Though at least it uses special enemies with more taste than '93. Enforcers are more rare and then don't take as long to die from bullets. Monks are also more fun, with melee ones being weaker, but having extended range. Also helps that Episode 4 isn't just tiny rooms.
Another thing is how amazingly little of game sense I was getting when playing this game. I mean, I count FPS genre as my favourite, but here I felt like I was a blind kitty, especially when playing for first time. Most of time I spent looking for enemy who kept shooting me.
There actually are few things to contribute that. Damage indicator actually points at the spot where you got hit instead of where this shot came from. And I don't know what player's character collision is, but I doubt that it's a classic collision cube, since there were too many times where indicator pointed in another direction from enemy. Not only that, but the colors style between enemies and background is so similar, it's hard to notice them at all. Also I had hard time being aware about traps and doors opening up. Or even what switches do.
Bosses are fancy, albeit lacking proper boss music. Some are good, but most often, you have to do usual things, like spamming homing rocket out of side room where you are hiding. Yea, phase 2 of the first boss was the hardest thing here. The most cheap at least. And then there are things like Boss 2 spamming hitscan at you. Did they ever play good arcade games?
It also has traps and platforming. Not sure about traps, maybe they are cheap, but that was refreshing to try to handle real traps for myself.  I may have not managed to get out in time, but I felt awesome because I would figure out what to do at the very last second. And die. Now, platforming. A precise platforming in a game with weak air control? I mean, at least I spent my time playing the awesome Jumpmaze mod for Doom Skulltag back in time and I personally still love that. And I like this, when it made my heart beat that I might miss platform. But I shudder to think what kind of experience others are getting.
E2L1 silver key puzzle still sucks.
There is also multiplayer. Didn't get to try. It's competetive, no coop. Just DM, TDM, CTF. Same rules as main game. Probably chaotic too.
I would rather give it a "can't decide" recommendation if I could. Otherwise I was quite dissapointed that instead of playing like FPS from my favourite era, instead playing like one from era that I dislike. Plus bugs and performance.

The concept of the game is pleasing, though at the core it's riddled with problems; be it bugs or optimization issues. To the point where it frequently hampers my enjoyment. I can handle buggy games, though when it comes to a cloud of locus it becomes difficult to ignore.
Mainly dealing with AI, enemies, and their models being utterly janky, often you will see a model in its standard stiff pose as if it's ready to be animated. This is not the rare happening, every single level I have encountered this issue. The shill will say simply agro them, instead of picking them off while they're in this state, I could do this, but it is still a glaring design flaw and bug that any game designer not matter the team, would eventually want to root out.
And then there's the down right poor design flaws, with the hit scan approach to enemies, be it a boss fight or common fodder, every ecounter will leave you with you feeling pain, often in droves. A shooter certainly can use the hit scan enemy, though it requires the designer(s) to be smart about their placement, instead enemies are carelessly placed with no way to avoid the hail of bullets. The most eregious aspect of this, encompasses enemies shooting you from unknow places, and behind gates that rocket's blast radius is prone to miss even when the explosion lies an inch before the enemy. Perhaps not a bug, but it's an awful over sight, that not even many of the classics fell victim too, as much of a carnival ride the Build engine was, it didn't skimp on the explosions.
There's seldom a post, beam, or anything to cover behind, something even a shooter as old as Wolfenstein 3D allows. Even the classics understood it was cheap to be killed by a bullet from someone not readily visible on the screen, often they will design the levels in a certain way to allow the player a means of  playing it smart, or a way for those low on ammo while against a fearsome foe to trudge foward. Instead with RoTT you are left a linear way of dealing with enemies, using you rockets in sellect ways, which with the average shooter would be fine, though may I remind your main weapon in this game is a series of rocket launchers.
On top of that there's platforming which is often used to kill you, and used in the most idiosyncratic of places, as a means of prolonging the length of the game, in a very diabolical way. Even going as far as to negate a star for quick saving for said areas, it's truly silly. Not to say I dislike the platforming, as it stands, if it was used in more opportune situations, and you possibly had more body awareness it'd be more than competent.
There's a good game under all of this jank, despite all of the listed issues, I have enjoyed certain things this game has to offer. Often creative level design, that require one to play like a speed demon, even if its pulled down by those certain moments of linearity, and tight rooms of hit scans, there's some serious fun to be had. That is, if you are able to circumvent the aforementioned problems plaguing this game.
6/10
My framerate is also very sporadic, despite having a fairly good build, ain't no I7, but there's no reason an I5 shouldn't be able to consistently run this game. In certain areas I'll have 150-200 fps, more intense ones 60-100 fps, then randomly in what by all means should be rather low demanding areas, it'll be 30-60 fps. Indie game or not, there is no clear reason why the optimization should be this horrible, it's ♥♥♥♥ing Unreal Engine 3 and an ugly game at that.

I don't normally write steam reviews, but as a massive fan of the show I feel like I owe it to the RWBY community to warn people like myself who blindly bought this because of its relation to RWBY.
The game itself has changed very little since early access, a new UI and a couple new levels is all that has actually changed between alpha and release. The main complaint being the extremely shallow combat system. The few combos that that game has are mostly uninteresting or plain useless, leaving you to just spam one or two buttons the entire game.
My second major complaint the lack of dialog from pretty much any of the characters. This game was produced by RT, they had the voice actors, so why didn't they use them!? The result of having nearly no character dialog besides the occasional out of place "Yeah!" from Ruby is that the game just ends up feeling rushed and unfinished as you walk long stretches with nothing happening.
The iceing on the cake though is how they tried to pad out the game. As boring and uninspired as the game is, maybe it wouldnt be so bad if it wasn't so heavily padded out. RT makes the mistake that many video game developers make, and thats artifical length. Every once in a while they stop you and pit you against multiple waves of enemies in an attempt to make the game a little bit longer. Not only is this extremely boring its also amplified by the games horrible combat system, making the game a huge chore to get through
As for some positives of the game, decent UI, music from the show (only instrumentals, and sometimes the song cuts out for no clear reason) real models from the show, and thats about it. There is hope that they overhaul the combat sytem in the future, but it seems there currently planning paid character DLC so it seems like the combat rework was possible pushed aside.
Honestly, even if you're a die hard fan of the series like myself, I think its best if you just stay away from this game. Theres really not much here for fans or casual players.

Okay so I have watched all episodes of RWBY and I bought this whilst it was in Early Access at a discount price. However, I waited for the full release before playing it. This was because the content shown and promised sounded quite limited, so I wanted to enjoy it as a finished product. I think this was a wise decision.
So I have made one complete playthrough as Blake (clearly the sexiest character), a few random multiplayer levels with Weiss and a bit of Ruby experimentation. No Yang yet though, as she is a bit scary...
You will fight waves of enemies (The Grim) and they are quite varied to be fair, something I was worried about in Early Access. Later on there are a few robotic enemies to spice things up and of course a big bad, that doesn't dissapoint. I played through with one regular co-op partner and a few leavers for about 2 1/2 hours. This was in one sitting but you can break up the chapters, By the end I had hit the level 10 cap with one of the characters. So even if you limit yourself to one playthrough with each character that is 10 hours worth of fun to be had. You do also have challenges that will unlock seperate perks, such as killing so many enemies or reviving chracters, which you can work towards even after hitting the level cap. I did try solo mode once and it wasn't too bad as the difficulty scales down, but it is a lot more fun with others. Especially if you get a full team of unique characters.
If you want more you can trade in all four hard earned 10 levels for 1 rank. This is where I think the game dissapoints. As a rank gain is just cosmetic and doesn't incentivise you in anyway. As someone commented on the discussions it is clearly added as artifical replayability, which is a shame. If each rank rewarded you with perks, outfits or taunts then it would seem worthwile. Something very similar was done in the Dawn of War 2 last stand mode but at least you got a score booster as well as bragging rights.
The story isn't a masterpiece, but it fits well in the Rwby universe and you get to hear a few of the popular characters and a new villain via your phone along the way. This helps immerse you and you will be singing the them tune (badly) whilst pwning the Grim.
As a fan of the series I really enjoyed this game and will definately try and level all the characters up to 10. I am just hoping that more features will be added even if it is in the form of fairly priced DLC. New characters from the show and more missions. Also an arena mode against other teams would be a great addition, but that is probably a seperate game alltogether...

This has been quite the ride from Early Access six months ago to now.

Bigger teams with smaller goals have accomplished less than these guys have. Brawlers like Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance and Transformers: Devastation tend toward being shorter games anyway, and what's here is fairly solid and impressive for the time they had.

All in all, get it now if a stylized co-op brawler is 100% your jam. Otherwise, wait for it to go on sale a bit, but it'll still be a solid indie entry in your library.

Hoo boy, where do I begin.
The combat is shallow, every enemy is just HIT IT UNTIL IT DIES with very little strategy required for any of them. Its also dreadfully easy. Anyone taking this game seriously could beat it without a single death.
The levels look like a bunch of individual assets slapped together, very noticable and poorly made.
The plot is nearly nonexistent; no introduction, no cutscenes, just random dialogue throughout each mission telling you where to go and what to destroy.
The girls are not the main characters of this game. What do I mean by this? The only dialogue they provide in the game is repeated remarks about the battle ("Taste my fist!", etc.), or "Hey lets go through THIS door!" or "Wow, look at that thing!" and stuff like that. They don't talk to eachother, they don't talk to anyone. Just random remarks. And Yang makes lame puns sometimes.
The only characters with meaningful dialogue (and I use 'meaningful' generously) are Prof. Port, Oobleck, and Ozpin as they yell at you to go here and do that.
Not to mention they are the ONLY characters (barring the antagonist) in this game. Hoping to see Glynda or Ironwood? Too bad. What about Cinder and her merry band of misfits? Nope.
Anyone at all from any other team? Jaune? Pyrrha? Nora? Rin? ...anyone? ... no? Welp.
EDIT: Team JNPR has since been added as a payed DLC.
There is no sort of tutorial or even a combo list. You learn the controls by clicking HELP on the pause menu, but you're given no direction as to how to perform combos or what the various attacks you can do are called.
While playing as Yang I could purchase an upgrade to a skill called Blast Wave. What the heck is Blast Wave? The upgrade menu doesn't say how to perform it, neither does the control screen.
The only reason I was able to find out what Blast Wave was, was because there was a counter for Blast Wave kills on the upgrade menu, and I checked it every time I killed an enemy using a different method. THAT is how I had to figure out what the heck Blast Wave was, by running down each way to kill something until the counter went up.
To top it all off, you can finish the game in less than 4 hours. Whats your reward for finishing the game?
Nothing. No harder difficulty, no alternate outfits, just a steam achievement so everyone knows how cooool you are.
If I had to say one good thing about this game, it would be that its mindless.
If you just want to sit down and mindlessly beat the crap out of waves of enemies with no real challenge or substance, and you happen to be a fan of RWBY, then this may be the game for you.
I had high hopes for this game, and I'm relieved I only had to pay $10 for it.
$25 for this "finished" game is an absolute outrage.
EDIT: Price dropped to $20 several months later. Still too much.
You'd be challenged to call this a good game even if you were the biggest RWBY fan on the planet.
This game honestly feels like a beta. Do NOT pay full price for this. For the love of Beacon, wait for a sale. A BIG sale. Like a 75% off sale.

As someone who still enjoys Arcade Fighting Games, but is finding it harder and harder to enjoy some of the more mainstream ones thanks to all the Corporate Malpractice and the online population of them dropping so fast, due to how bad the netcode is usually... I must say that Tekken 7 truly surprised me and has quite possibly been one of the best Fighting game experiences I've had to date, with the last one being Killer Instinct way back when (don't let the playtime Deceive you as I've been playing this game since it came out over at a friend's house and finally decided to pick up the deluxe edition on Sale to support devs)... I will list some pros and cons and will then put some of my final thoughts in the end, so here we go!
+Large Roster with Diverse and Interesting/Unique Characters and Guest Characters as well, with more well on the way!
+Amazing Initial Accessibility, Meaning Easy as hell to pick up and play with 4 buttons and an easy Rage Art button (comeback mechanic), but has enough Mechanical Depth to put even the most Complex Fighting game you can think of to shame.
+Great Story mode with multiple difficulties as well as individual Character stories to play through after you finish the Mishima Story Arc.
+Loads of Content for both core and casual alike such as Treasure Battle (Endless mode with lots of unlockables), Arcade mode, Tekken Bowling (which was legit more fun than I though it'd be), online and offline vs mode (as well as online and offline individual character ranks), Art Galleries to complete, etc...
+The largest retention rate for any fighter by far on PC, with it currently having nearly triple the amount of players online when compared to SF5 and even the finally released on Steam Injustice 2, meaning you will always find someone to play with online, and for the price of admission it's definitely worth it!
+The best netcode of any fighting game, PC or console, by far, which may explain why the retention rate is so high as well...
-No tutorials for even the most basic functions, so even crucial universal character moves (such as low parry or the ultimate tackle break) as well as hidden moves are rarely explained in loading text (which dissapears too fast to be useful anyway), and very VERY limited help outside of user made guides (which you may still have trouble finding if you don't know exactly what to look for)
-Fairly Barebones Training mode with no ability to enable hitbox/hurtbox models on characters and requires a lot of digging to enable certain features crucial to understanding frame data on moves, throws and the like (there's doesn't seem to be an option to enable numerical frame data on all attacks either, just a blue hue and your own perception).
-No Challenge mode which means you have to learn combos either through trial and error or by watching vids of better players (which still means you have to know what you're doing)...
-Rather intimidating command lists PER Character (up to 89 or possibly more per character including the grabs and such) that can throw a newcomer to the game for a serious loop, especially when a large portion of those moves you'd rarely if ever use anyway, not to mention the character 10 hits are still not true combos and are useless overall and are there only to waste your time so don't even bother with them.
-A very high Learning curve (the highest I've experienced by far in fact), with certain moves and grab chains having very strict timing and there being small windows of error when launching and juggling, not to mention that the punish game here is so nasty that more nooby players may feel discouraged to contiue when they get 100 to 20 juggled and then reset into a perfect for 3 matches in a row becase of a single mistake they did.
-No individual endings for Arcade mode (which only has 5 fights anyway) and final bosses (including most of the AI on Ultra Hard), read your inputs, have high priority frame attacks and even super armor attacks which can make them feel dirty, cheap and hair pullingly unfair (you ever heard of SNK Boss Syndrome, well it's turned up to 11 here...)
-Tekken Bowling cannot be played online...
-No PC to Console crossplay yet...
-very few legacy characters (no idea if more will ever be added)
Tekken 7 is not only the most feature complete fighter I've played in recent years that also feels relatively affordable compared to it's competition, it's also one of the most rewarding to learn and play. On a sale (like right now) I highly recommend this fighter as I cannot remember the last time I've had this much fun playing a fighting game since back when I used to play Tekken 5 and Soul Calibur II in my local arcade. You will defs not be dissapointed, and if you are, you can always refund it, but this one is a fighter I will definitely be sinking a lot of time into and I hope it only gets better from here on out. To any of the Tekken Lords out there that I may eventually run into, Go Easy on Me :x , as I still have so much to learn about this game...

I play a lot of smash bros so I thought I'd like this game, but the developers just don't quite understand tradeoffs with balance. Things like weapon throw are completely absurd and some weapons are just badly designed like the spear.
They developed a gun weapon that has great range and quick attacks but is balanced by seemingly weaker attacks and the inability to shoot those directly on top of you. This was a well designed weapon.
Then they went and made things like the lance that has excellent range and great speed, but has none of the previously mentioned weaknesses.
There are things like the amazonian spear woman with smash/heavy attacks with insane range, but it's recovery is the same if not better than other heavy attacks with not even half of the range. Things like this instantly highlighted they didn't really understand balance. Even if it's recovery was just as bad as other heavy attacks, the opponent has to stay at such a far range to avoid it, there's no room for punishment.
Throw weapon is a joke, it's near instant and can be repicked up and spears and lances hitboxes on the throw are completely absurd.
I tried to just have fun with the game but I can't help but get competitive. Unfortunately, you either abuse the bad design or have a bad time.

MD is a lot of fun however it also has a lot of issues.
Pros:
+ Exploring the main (Prague) hub is enjoyable with lots of apartments to break into and side quests to run into.
+ Mechanically the game is a significant step up from HR.
+ The amount of ways you can approach a situation (and resolve it) is incredibly refreshing.
+ New Game+ is a great addition from HR and they've allowed you to keep your credits/inventory (not just your praxis points) this time.
Cons :
- Main story is short and feels like a set up for the next game. Not much really happens or gets resolved.
- PC port has issues. Very long load times (usually 5-10 min on my 7200 RPM HDD), the game frequently freezes for 30-60 seconds (which borders on torture when you're in the middle of sneaking around or you just waited through a 10 min loading screen), the game sometimes drops down to a single digit framerate and the game crashes occasionally. [Ed. Note: I meet the minimum requirements and have been playing the game with all settings on Low/Off except texture quality which I've kept at Medium.]
- The game only features 6 new augmentations. All the other ones are from HR. There's also a few augmentations (like sprinting speed) that they didn't bring back for some reason.
- Very few returning characters from HR (while we at least get to inquire about Pritchard and Megan at the beginning of the game Malik is never mentioned anywhere outside of the optional recap).
- Some ingame menus don't have mouse support (you can only look at markers on your map by dragging the portion of map that is of interest into the middle of the screen where there's a static reticule. Some menus after a hack require you to press down on your keyboard and then select rather than just being able to click on the option you want).
- Most story characters (even non integral to the main story) can only be found when there's a mission/side mission that wants/requires you to visit them.
Conclusions :
MD is a very enjoyable, very flawed game. The fact that I've played the game 40+ hours (on new game+ at the moment) even through the torturously bad technical issues show how much I have and am enjoying this game. However I cannot recommend any port that is in the shape that this one is currently so when/if this port is fixed I'll update this review. Judging the response from the developer I have a feeling that the issues I'm experiencing may not be fixed (the devs still have not made any comment on the games performance other than that if the game is running badly you either need to turn down the settings or you're under the minimum requirements). I'd love to be pleasantly surprised though.

TLDR: Updating after a year since release.  Game’s promise from EA didn’t make it to release and lack of bug fixes and content (even with Horde Mode) I can’t suggest this for anyone except huge RWBY fans that want a quick easy game to waste some time in.
----------------New review-------------
The game’s promise died when it left early release.  The story felt rushed.  Content seemed lacking probably to rush the game out in time such as no cut scenes or Grimm introductions except for in the original EA levels.  Many bugs still exist in the game that probably will not be touched.
Combat for RWBY is especially limiting where there is little difference between each of the main characters in how you react to Grimm between them and each one has a set attack combo that is by far the best which leaves little point to do anything else in the game except spamming one move over and over.  To make it worse is JNPR has decent combat to it.  Unlike RWBY, JNPR combat is unique between each character and no one combo is a stand out best for dealing with all enemies.  The reason I say this is worse though is because you can’t even access JNPR except through paying extra.  Why have the main cast stuck with bland combat and then make the secondary team actually unique?  Either way, we’re stuck with it this way as the Devs had claimed even while still in EA that there is no point in going back to work on RWBY combat.
To go along with combat of course is enemy AI which is just pathetic.  While originally they would all attack you at once meaning you HAD to constantly dodge, attack, and change things up… well the final AI just circles around you and take their precious turns attacking you.  You can go make a sandwich and come back in Eclipse mode and probably still be alive.  The main way you can die is if you keep mistiming a counter which will cause a Grimm to get a free hit on you.
Levels look nice for the most part, but contain lots of features you just clip into partly or fully.  The game is also littered with bugs that often will cause your FPS to take a huge hit, and if you aren’t on a higher end gaming PC to potentially crash your PC.  One area in particular (the end of Mountain Glenn pt 2) is especially prone to this due to the vast amount of Grimm that get spawned in it.  Trying to change the graphics settings to help alleviate this does not help.  There is little difference between  Potato and Ultra settings in the base game.
Another area of lack is the lack of controls you have over the game itself.  As noted there never was much of an effort to change up minimum and maximum graphic settings.  Key bindings is also not an option from them.  So if you want to be able to make these changes you have to download mods created by the community.  Some even exist to try to help alleviate those who get constant crashes from the game.  Sad the Devs never bothered to do some basic game features and that modders had to come in and fix this.  Which means btw if you play on PS4 or Console you are out of luck.
------------------------------
(Original review below.  My new one I focus more on the game itself, while the original one looks at both the game and it's journey from EA to full release and the Devs behind it)
This was a fairly enjoyable game when I first started in early access.  But for me (and many others) enjoyment of it dropped as more patches and information came out that drastically changed combat (for me and some others), or models and looks (for others).  But at least for myself, I tried to stay positive since it was still "early access" and the devs at least when I first joined seemed to be listening to us.
As early access continued though dev responses to complaints became more snarky or seem to ignore them.  Models (which were changed suddenly) that much of the community disliked were first said to be done with and threatened other content would be dropped if the devs had to work on them some more. The thing irking me is they really try to cram in the fact that Horde is "FREE"! and they are doing a grand thing doing such a thing.  Yeah, sure they are. Kingdoms of Amalur is a mixed bag.  A very, very mixed bag.  Outside all the repetition, a lot of it is great.  But there are flubs that make you wonder how they made it into an otherwise polished game.
As the game's strongest element, much of the setting is scenery porn to this day, thanks to its gorgeous use of colors.  The rays of light and vibrant flora give some spots in the game the warmth of a Kinkaid painting, while dark caves and ruins covered in moss weigh in with a sense of scale and age.  Though certain parts, namely most of the houses, look poofy and cheesy by comparison; the comicbook green highlights turning things overly cartoony.  Same deal with the armor, where some sets look dignified enough, but in between you're stuck wearing some goofy looking nonsense off a Saturday morning kids' show.
Gameplay-wise, Reckoning is a Frankenstein mix of pieces taken from several popular titles of its time, including Oblivion and Mass Effect, not all of them meshing.  Most noticeable being the combat blatantly aping God of War, down to its Rage of the Gods mode and brutal QTE executions.  Which is fine, since it is an enjoyably mindless murder spree, especially with other ways to approach combat.  Though the camera isn't especially friendly, letting enemies take potshots at you from off screen, and I'm not sure the dodge roll works very well with a keyboard.  What really gets annoying are the accompanying fight tracks with their repetitive drum beats.  Not wanting to trigger the music in constant short bursts might be the biggest reason to find alternative approaches to offing your targets.
And then there are the blatant missteps in the interface and mechanics that have no excuse to exist.  Some are subtly annoying, like gemcrafting making you uselessly scroll past screens of every maxed out shard repeatedly for no reason, or inconsistent inventory orders where cash items are buried in the middle of hundreds of crafting items.  Others are more obnoxious, like the game pointlessly hiding the stats of equipment in some screens to add annoying extra clicks, or trying to swap the order of spells deleting them from your list instead.  But there is one awful, awful decision in particular that snowballs out of control.
The game has trainer NPCs who can give you extra skill levels in exchange for buttloads of cash, but have an arbitrary, narrow window of said skill levels you must be at.  That doesn't sound like much, but bear with me... it's at the center of a sh*tstorm of terrible ideas.  There are nearly 40 trainers, and even the lowest level ones are sprinkled across every corner of the world.  They are not consistently displayed on some maps, and while you can only use their service once, their icons stay just to make others harder to find in the clutter.  Even stationary treasure and lorestones disappear from the map when you're done with them, and these trainers shuffle around through crowds, sometimes not even revealing they can train or just making themselves unavailable until you complete certain events.  Their "training" option when you talk to them doesn't go away, either, like they are designed to make you paranoidly double check every last one of them everywhere. It is a batsh*t impossible clusterf*ck trying to find, then keep track of them until you earn enough money to actually apply them.
The way the game works, you also have to buy costly skill resets to get in their upgradable range.  Except you cannot see your own base stats and whatever permanent upgrades they've racked up until you reset, so frustrating mistakes are bound to happen.  Especially since every reset is an exponentially expensive investment in an already grind-heavy game to take away any room to experiment.  If you inevitably buy the services of a higher level trainer, you screw yourself out of the much cheaper but completely equal upgrade from any lower level ones you missed.  Then realize your mistake hours and tens of thousands of coins in when there is no going back.  It is a continent-spanning, obsessive compulsive Where's Waldo with math that kicks you in your balls and steals your wallet for your hours of trouble.
Some points you couldn't min-max shouldn't hurt so bad, but there are so many more layers to make the rest of the game sting and fester, I can't even list them all. As just one, there are books that simply and permanently upgrade your skill levels with no prerequisites, as if to show the programmers know how sane upgrades work but felt like sh*tting all over the game's own in-universe logic just to screw over players.  There are only 9 such books, and you will not find them all, because they were put in mostly to mock you.  Within this broken system, they are also traps.  If you accidentally upgrade your skill too soon, you can highten them past training range, permanently losing the ability to upgrade that skill. Each and every factor in what should be pleasant exploration adds a triple layer of bullsh*tception as you accidentally cripple yourself.
Since you otherwise only recieve one skill level per level gain in a long, grind-heavy, repetitive game, each point you miss will haunt you.  And these aren't penalties like doing slightly worse in battle.  Not having the highest alchemy or detect hidden level means all your scrounging for ingredients and cash can often result in no rewards as you work yourself like a dog.  Every point the game screws you out of just keeps compounding into a soulless waste of time and nervous breakdown waiting to happen.  So just cheat.  It's a single player game; for the love of god, just cheat.  If I didn't know any better, the grame is trying to prove that turning to a trainer program isn't anywhere near as petty or embarrassing as its own trainers.  Give yourself a load of extra skillpoints and never bother with that mechanic.  The worst that can happen is you alleviate the repetitive grind while you're at it.
If you pay money for Reckoning, stick to enjoying the good parts and sidestep the idiocy they inexplicably left in.  For all the game's well made pieces, there are some obscene f*ck-ups and the training mechanic is a dominoing dumpster fire that will suck away your life and joy.  It would be so easy to fix, I'm still not sure how it's in there 5 years later, like an eternal sh*t-geyser blanketing all of Kingdoms of Amalur in its wretched stench.  Along with the lack of promotion, the game has done its fair share to bury itself.  There's a lot of good in here, but Cheat Engine is the main reason I'm not thumbing it down.

Torchlight II is a dungeon crawler game that lets you chose to play as a few different classes. The basic concept is the same as nearly all dungeon crawlers:  Explore, level up, find gear, beat the boss, rinse and repeat.

Oh no! the alchemist is going to bring about the end of the world! You there, unnamed random hero, it's your job to warn everyone, and be just a few steps behind the alchemists defiling touch.
As I implied, you're obviously the hero, the villain you will be trying to catch is known as "the alchemist", whom has been corrupted and destroys all that is in his way.
I sense that most dungeon crawlers are time consuming on purpose, I spent a good 30-40 hours before I beat the game, then I kept playing for another 30 hours to get to max level, and at that point I stopped playing.
The whole dungeon crawler genre is criticized for giving us "carpool tunnel", you click, a lot. you do use keys to cast different spells, attacks, and abilities. So for fair warning, you will spend a lot of time in this game clicking.
There is a feature in the game that lets you load up your pet with tons of gear, and send 'em back to town to sell them for you, or buy health potions, basically you never need to go to town to sell gear or buy potions, you're servant pet will do it for you. What does this mean for you, brave adventurer? More dungeon crawling, less vendering trash items! Yay!  (Hopefully!)

So I hit 76% completion on this game, I've given up trying to actively get 100% completed for achievements, mostly because RNG (Random Number Generator) hates me. I decided getting above 75% was pretty good for a game with 123 achievements, many requiring grinding.
Achievement categories: Beat the game/boss, try doing this, kill this many enemies, open this many of these, do this ____ amount of times, get lucky, play long enough to do this 100,000,000 times. Again, basically I assume that I'll eventually make more progress on this game as I find people who are like "hey, play this with me!" and I'm like "okay, I only need to 3,000 more potions! let's do it!"
Half of these achievements are from just playing the game, so you can enjoy that, but getting 100% will require a lot of play time. Just a warning :)
Torchlight II costs $19.99, I've spent 70 hours playing it. That's definitely worth it. Most people will at least get over 20 hours in the game, even if they're not trying to beat it.
As always, I suggest getting the game on sale or in a humble bundle, but the stand alone price is very much worth it, based on the amount of game time I squeezed out of it.

Why did I discover this game so late? When I was meddling with the Total War series I could have played this game!
At first I was shocked by the awful graphics. If you can put that aside, there is a ton of fun to be had with both the single player campaign as well as the Napoleonic wars expansion.
The single player campaign is sandbox with some RPG elements. What I liked the most was the diversity of kingdoms you can join. One nation excells in foot troops, while the other focus on knights or crossbows. Also fighting as part of your army is thrilling. Usually on horseback I crashed through the enemy lines, firing arrows or trying to stick a lance in someones gut. Usually battles start with neatly aligned troops slowly advancing to the front. Once the battle begins, all chaos breaks loose and you just try to kill while keeping an eye on your troops.
Companions join you with a set of skills, you can even marry maidens, aid kings or even start your own kingdom. The learning curve is a bit high. There is no real ending, which is not really a bad thing.
Multiplayer is dead in this game. However, the Napoleonic wars community is still active every night. I must warn that the chat is full of misplaced dictator loving rubbish. Nevertheless, its a very fun experience. (Try the RP server!)
On a side note, hurry up with MB Bannerlord already!

Okay so I thought about to recommend this game or not for a bit and honestly, I can't say I recommend it.
Originally, I got this game in Early Access quite awhile ago. I thought it was solid, it was what I wanted in a shop keeper game. However, playing it now during full release I've realized something. This game lacks a lot of substance. I gave it lee way before because it was Early Access but now, it doesn't have that excuse anymore.
I sunk 21 hours into this game and I was struggling through most of it. I barely paid attention to the game and did other things on the side like watch videos or playing phone games. Yes, I was progressing, buying upgrades, making my shop look nicer, but it felt kind of empty. Progression didn't feel like an accomplishment but just another hassle to deal with. New unlocked items are just the same thing except called something different and remodeled.
The only real thing kept me going through the game was the possibility of an inn since I prefer to buy upgrades in order. I finally caved in after going a few more hours and bought the inn, only to find disappointment. I had seen the tiny inn on the side of the shop and had hoped that I could either run it or had tables in my shop to wait. The inn was automated and added no extra game play at all. It was just another way to do what you could already did, make money.
As for Barbarians, they just felt annoying. I had considered turning them off several times, but I'm a sucker for achievements and I left them on. Since they spawn from two different sides of the town, what I ended up doing was running back and forth while cleaning bodies trying to end the barbarian raid as quickly as possible so I could get back to making money. They don't feel threatening at all. The giant barbarian is really cool the first time you fight her, but that's all she was, novelty. Also, when there's 5 of them coming out one at a time, you have question their tactics.
...also I really dislike there's no small table for the minor armor items or something like that.
TL;DR
The game is really neat in concept, but the actual gameplay is just an overly padded husk.

If I could give this a neutral review I would, but I'll give it a positive for now. If you like story driven games, you'll like this. If you prefer games that focus on gameplay, don't get this. Not work $15, but worth $7.50 or less.
The story isn't the most gripping story, as the story and music are serious while the visuals and gameplay are simplistic. Gameplay consists of walking down the corridor until something happens. The puzzles are incredibly simple and you should never hit a point where you get stuck for more than one minute. It's also pretty short considering I beat it in one sitting, but that's expected with a game like this. It isn't a walking simulator, but it doesn't prioritize gameplay over story.
The story is pretty good, though it isn't the kind that I wanted to see repeatedly; I found the one playthrough to be satisfactory. There are achievements that add replayability, but unless you really care for achievements, the actions performed to get the achievements don't affect the story in any way.
Warning: This game will send you on an emotional rollercoaster, but the fact that it manages to do so alone is worth this amazing experience.

Trine 2 improves on the formula from Trine. It is still a puzzle-based side-scrolling platformer. The sequel has more innovative and complex puzzles, more refined graphics and textures, and tighter gameplay. In Trine 2 you can also play co-op locally, or over the internet! Up to three players can play at the same time, adding more depth and complexity to the game as you have to find ways to get everyone through the obstacles instead of switching from character-to-character as needed.
If you enjoyed Trine, or games like Portal and Mario, then this is a must-buy!

Brawlhalla is a fighting game centered around similar mechanics to Nintendo hit "Super Smash Brothers". Players (up to four local/online) choose a fighter with a weapon set they favor, and go against one another in a 2d platform-based arena. Hitting feels incredibly good, and charging up an attack and unleashing it is extremely satisfying. Each character has their own strenghts and weaknesses, such as attack speed, defense, overall speed, and attack power. The balance is very well done, with fast characters feeling like speedy assassins, tanks feeling like lumbering powerhouses, and gunplay with extremely cool attack patterns and animations.
If you like Smash or Playstation All-Stars, you'll LOVE Brawlhalla. Fighting games allowing for four players are few and far in between, and this one has a well deserved place among the rest.

Brawlhalla is a fighting game centered around similar mechanics to Nintendo hit "Super Smash Brothers". Players (up to four local/online) choose a fighter with a weapon set they favor, and go against one another in a 2d platform-based arena. Hitting feels incredibly good, and charging up an attack and unleashing it is extremely satisfying. Each character has their own strenghts and weaknesses, such as attack speed, defense, overall speed, and attack power. The balance is very well done, with fast characters feeling like speedy assassins, tanks feeling like lumbering powerhouses, and gunplay with extremely cool attack patterns and animations.
If you like Smash or Playstation All-Stars, you'll LOVE Brawlhalla. Fighting games allowing for four players are few and far in between, and this one has a well deserved place among the rest.

The title above was the briefest and most to the point I was able to think of when trying to describe this game.
The world of DX: MD is made of corporations (evil and racist -- yes, they explicitly use the term racism, although the conflict is not about race but about augmented vs. non-augmented humans) on the one side, and governments / government agencies (good, unless bought and paid or otherwise compromised by corporations, then they are obviously evil) on the other side.
Then there's various resistance oragnizations (who are also the good guys) that are basically all marxist in nature (the rich are only rich beacuase they steal from the poor yaddi yadda); one of them even uses sovjet symbolism in their pamphlets.
There's one corporation that is trying to make life better for the augmented - needless to say they are targeted by all the other corporations who are hell bent on making life miserable for the augmented and use every dirty trick to do so.
One can clearly see where the developers are coming from and how they try to maintain the mainstream narrative.
The game doesn't bother to examine the implications and ramifications that a technology like augmentations can come with, instead it shoves exposition down your throat and says "Look! There's people hating and hurting other people because they are different! That's racism! *wink wink*". It's every bit a s cringeworthy as the slogan they used to market this game "Aug lives matter" - Yes, they went there.
I won't go into detail about the plot, others can do that much better, besides addressing some issues that really bugged me.
In regards to gameplay I have nothing noteweorthy to say; it's serviceable, although the game suffers from the console typical 'one button to rule them all'-syndrome. Want to grab a body to drag into hiding while at the same time your mission objective gets updated? Bad luck, pressing and holding E grabs the body ..... and opens the mission log under these circumstances.
Loading a savegame that has Adam hiding in cover? You're dead. To finalze the loading procedure you have to press SPACE .... which has Adam jumping out of cover in the most suicidal way possible as soon as loading is finished.
If you can stomach the leftist agenda as well as the incoherent story and plot, by all means, go ahead and buy this, the gameplay is fine enough, although you might want to wait for a discount ... a heavy discount. Should you seek a Deus Ex experience that at least touches on the philosophical aspects of the matters it discusses, don't bother.
For me it's the new low point of the series -  worse than Invisivle War. This is the only really positive thing I can say about the game, it makes me IW appreciate more. How sad is that?

Going into this game with low expectations due to the reviews, I was rather pleasantly surprised. Sure, the ending is a bit weak, but you've fulfilled your primary goal. I don't get the claims that it's abrupt either - you could see the endgame coming for hours before you reached it. The plot threads that were left danging can be easily pieced together as long as you explore the game's world, do sidequests and read e-mails/pocket secretaries.
And since we're on the topic of exploration, it's the game's strong point, just as in Human Revolution. The amount of secret paths, easter eggs and optional areas is simply staggering. I haven't even explored the Palisade bank in full because I didn't want to use guides during my first playthrough. Some shortcuts/access paths I've only found in the final hours of the game.
I can't really comment on the supposedly improved gunplay, since I went with a silent, non-lethal approach, but the wider gun customization and the improved cover system seem pretty good. Hacking was also built upon a bit, now you have more options than in Human Revolution. The more liberal aug use allowed by the revamped energy system is also welcome. The experimental augs aren't too useful though. Icarus Dash is unreliable, Remote Hacking is very situational, and the others are pretty much only suited for a loud approach.
As for the widely hated singleplayer microtransactions? Frankly, I don't get the hate for them. I mean, it's not like the fact that somebody else makes the game easier for themselves with money hurts you in any way. Now, if there was a shortage of praxis/credits/parts in the game I'd get the rage, but the game simply drowns you with them as long as you're not just rushing the main quest, so I wonder who would even need to buy them.
I'd say, wait until it's a bit cheaper and some issues get patched. But I definitely recommend it as a worthy successor to Human Revolution.

A summary of what I wrote below: this is a great game, I love it as much as previous Deus Ex games (which is a lot). Buy it when you can afford it (Steam Sale & decent hardware), and you'll love it too!
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Visually, this is one of the best looking games I’ve played – from overall aesthetics to minute details, the developers really ensured this was a beautiful game.
Combined with excellent audio, the sounds and voices in the game really capture the tense atmosphere portrayed in the story.
Gameplay-wise, it’s as awesome as prior Deus Ex games: choosing the augmentations that complement your play style – from hacking and sneaking around, to being a one-man army. I play with a mouse and keyboard, and find the controls really smooth now (a bit of a learning curve); ensure your mouse sensitivity is set very low.
I won’t comment on the story, since I haven’t completed the main story line; yet, the side quests alone are keeping me engaged. At the time of writing this review, I had played around a dozen hours: and loved every minute of it. Rarely does a game make me lose track of time and responsibilities in the real-world, and this game does that so well, every time I sit down to play.
[Update: Finished the story; I loved it, and find all the negativity I read to be strange, when other games have been♥♥♥♥♥♥poor in comparison to Deus Ex games. I know I'll enjoy this game for years to come.
RE: Hardware Requirements
I have an older graphic card (NVidia 770 GTX), and I ran this game on high, with no other tweaks, at a respectable framerate (it's an otherwise modern desktop). I would highly recommend installing this on an SSD instead of a hard drive - or the load times will likely drive you crazy (as in some reviews I've read). If your computer isn't modern, wait until you have better hardware before buying, simply-put.]
So, in short: if you love Deus Ex, buy this game - it's an excellent continuation of the series. I’d say it’s worth the full price, if only to support developers that produce excellent games like this one.

MINI REVIEW FOR GAME OF THRONES A WORLD OF ICE AND FIRE MOD
I don't really play standard Warband so go else where for a review or info on that. Please bear in mind this mod is built on a direct x 9 game that's a few years old so it looks a bit like Elder Scroll Oblivion in terms of textures and level of detail.... still the dev(s) have done a good job. The reason I mentioned this is some people have high expectations. The combat isn't as polished as something like Chivalry Medieval Warfare as I know this game looks and play the same.
To sum up this plays a bit like a 4x strategy game but with 3D combat instead of turned based with up to 750 units in a battle and I assume all the standard workings and play from normal Warband.
Being a good Warband combat/pvp person WILL help you influence battles... but at the sametime bad tactics like getting your archers running at horseback knights will end in defeat.
This mod has you starting as a nobody with a bit of back story. It lets you choose a few skills and where you want to come from. I went for a Northerner who learned basic skills off a rich Lord until I came of age. Once you are thrust into the game you then start climbing the ladder by managing your character and your party. Doing things like quests, trading between settlements, taking part in battles all help you become rich and level up. If you earn enough rep and affilate with a great House you have the option to become Lord of a settlement. You'll be building up your towns and settlements until you can use them to raise armies or become a trade hub, but this is optional.
So there is micro management and resource management involved as well as combat and diplomacy if you want.
Everything comes at a cost so you need to get your economy and resources like food and gold working quickly to progress. Keeping your party happy requires food, unit upgrades, entrainment and money. The story kind of follows the story line of Ice and Fire/GOT but any of the main characters or Houses can be defeated, killed, taken over or if they win they control the whole map.
It starts off around the time of Ned Starks death, you can then go and do your own thing or work for the main characters and Houses. For example at the start of the game I had the option to go and tell Robb Stark of his fathers death and visit Stannis to tell him he was the main heir.
In my first 10 hours I've afilliated myself with Robb Stark and the North and have been battling the Iron Islands and Westerlands whilst managing a small village I was given. I have a small army of 25 troops and my village will soon become and town after recapturing it back from Yara Greyjoy with the help of Roose Bolton... well Bolton did all the hard work I just joined him in battle and took the rewards.
It's fairly polished but do expect bugs and some quests don't give you enough info to find the objective so you will lose rep frustratingly. You move around the main Risk style world map by pointing and click and when you go into towns or battle the game changes to first person mode.
The dev(s) are working hard and this shows a lot of promise in terms of where it can go. There are cool things like White Walker invasions and of course the Mother of Dragons can invade if she gets strong enough. I find the difficulty quite hard as I'm not an experience Warband player so the money making mechanics like trading between towns and selling prisoners took a bit of Googling.
If I paid £10-£15 I wouldn't be disappointed if this was a retail game it's about 7 out of 10 at the moment... not perfect but probabley the best Game of Thrones PC game out there at the moment.

Thief is a series that I played very little when I was young, mostly for the fact that I was a child and I only played the shareware version of the game. I remember enjoying it but then again when I was a child I enjoyed playing pretty much any game as long as I liked the art. Going into this game I was afraid that it would be crap compared to what I experienced. I soon realized after the first two levels that the game had way more to discover than I remembered. Now, keep in mind that I like complex and confusing things and Thief can be like this for most of the experience and the game does have a slow pace, at the beginning...
Gameplay:
The first thing I noticed is I had to reconfigure all the controls, I wasn't bothered by this like many other since it kind of felt like I was preparing for the game and the sounds based on a steampunk reality in the main menu was something I rather enjoyed. It wasn't difficult, it's the same as every other classic out there. Upon starting my game I started on normal to get a feel for the game and the first level was difficult. Not because it was actually difficult but for the fact that I had absolutely no idea as to what made too much noise, what would alert the guards. It freaked me out the first time a guard heard me since I accidentally stepped on a metal square on the ground and I froze. Once I got the hang of the game I started playing on expert and that's when I really understood how awesome the game is. The difficulty increases amount of objectives, guard locations, and damage to your health. There isn't any unfairness like in other stealth games where enemies spot you through walls and just know your there. I can say that the AI in this game is much superior to various games today which is kind of sad since the game is (almost) 20 years old at the time of this review.
Sound:
I love the sounds in this game, it's extremely retro while pulling off the whole surround sound effect. You know when you step on grass and you know when you step on metal. I remember of times when I was walking home in the city and I would accidentally step on a maintenance entrance on the floor and the sound would surprise me from how loud it was. I get the same result in thief. When a guard hears you, they hear you, they will taunt you and search for you. The environmental sounds are excellent but sadly I cannot say the same for the voice acting. The voice acting is okay for its time but what really bothers me is how loud and clanky some of the conversations can be. Other than that the conversations are very emersive with a bit of humor at times and I like that. Nothing better than two drunk guards on duty trying to have a conversation while a thief passes right on by.
Overall:
The gameplay is rather superb for a game this old (Although I did have to download some unofficial patches). I honestly love how much freedom they give you in each level but I do have to say that some of the final levels will either be really wierd or really hard. near the end of the game I felt I was rushing just to finish the game since the final levels can be seriously frustrating even when they do start to pick up the pace. This is also partly due to the fact that I wanted to get to the sequel knowing full well that Thief II will be focused more on heists which as in the case of Thief Gold, is more focused on the super natual. I recommend the game only if you have patience and you're prepared to get irritated because you forgot to save.

I haven't finished the game yet, I'm trying to make it last. A "pros and cons" breakdown isn't working for me for this, so let's call this "Observations on Thief Gold Thus Far":
Thief Gold got stealth right. The invisibility that some games call "stealth" for thieves, rogues and what have you, the standing in broad daylight directly in an enemy's eyeline and practically under their nose, without cover, and going unseen because a skill score is high enough, just doesn't do it for me. Actual invisibililty doing that is fine, that's a separate beast, but it doesn't feel like "skill" when it works that way. In Thief, there's an element of logic to stealth; the character Garrett has some training that's meant to make him better at it than the average Joe, and there's some limited tools (including improvised ones) to help, but stealth's otherwise based on player skill and common sense, not on a stat score. If you decide to waltz Garrett right in front of a guard in a well-lit room, better get those track shoes laced up tight!
Thief is a game that uses sound well. Not just for ambience and effect, but for clues, and also as a warning that you're walking into trouble -- or that trouble's about to walk into you. Normally I have videos or music or maybe an audiobook going in the background when playing a game solo, but Thief plays best horror-game style: with the sound turned up and no distractions.
If you hate mazelike levels and "maps" that are a few next to useless scribbles, this might not be the game for you. The thing is... I've never been a fan myself of bumbling around trying to find my way from X to Y in games where a single level goes well over the one-hour mark of wondering what I'm missing. (Or two hours; I admit it, I could get lost in my own backyard.)  But in Thief Gold, wandering around trying to get to my next goal has yet to make me want to stop playing -- take a break and come back fresh, yes, that's helped, but not quit for good -- or resort to looking up walkthroughs. With one exception, where I looked up just enough to be sure I wasn't up against a game glitch rather than a challenge (I wasn't), and then hastily closed the page.
I'm not afraid to use game walkthroughs to get past a portion of a game that just isn't fun, or to drop a game that's become mostly the "not fun" bits, so it says something in Thief's favor that even with help at my fingertips, I didn't want to use it and I'm still playing the game.
I think it's that there's stuff besides the way to the next main goal to find that makes the difference, be it shiny loot, a bit of overheard NPC dialogue, or a scene or a document that tells a piece of a story. (Documents aren't overdone in Thief by the way, and cutscenes are mostly a thing relegated to the beginnings and ends of levels where I'd say they belong. Instead, there are places where things can be heard as Garrett approaches, be it a conversation between NPCs, or... other things I'm not going to spoil...) It feels like there's actually stuff to find besides that which checks off the little boxes on the Objectives page, and that's nice. This is the other aspect of Thief that made a high-def mod nice to have.
So for the price, even if mazelike layouts aren't your favorite thing, I'd say it's still worth giving it a try.
On looting the place:  Oh, how proud I was upon finishing a level, thinking I'd patiently and persistently gotten ALL the loot in that level! That lasted until I checked the Stats at the level-complete screen and learned I'd gotten three-fifths of the loot at best. *Bwaahh-bwaahh*... It was refreshing, after a number of more recent games left me feeling like the designers had forgotten how to challenge the player in ways besides beefing enemy health and damage, or allowing AI opponents to "cheat the system" for an advantage. (Or the ultimate challenge-designing cop-out in my eyes, counting on online PVP modes to provide the bulk of challenge in a game -- in which opponents cheating the system, because it's the lazy way to win, is often even more of an issue than with AI.) Thief is a solo game that doesn't feel like it has to cheat to challenge me, and I admire that about it.
I also like that looting every last shiny object is optional, and that the nature of the character -- a thief -- encourages weighing pragmatic survival considerations against the fact he's, well, a thief, which makes looting the place a survival consideration too. After spending awhile huddled in a tiny cupboard while a guard stomped about just inches away, growling about what happens to thieves when they're caught, and having taken so many risks already, would Garrett leave with what he's got? Or look for more? Or stalk that guard, cosh him, stuff him in that very same cupboard, and then look for more?
I had surprisingly little trouble getting the game running on a recent computer despite its age, so props to whoever may have had a hand in that. I'm having a lot of fun finally playing Thief Gold, if that's not already evident; it's a game I missed out on when it was new, and it's proving worth the wait.
