Thief Gold is an excellent stealth game. That being said, it's not as consistent with its design as it wants to be.
Level design is pure 90's. Big, open-ended levels with lots of alternate paths and rewards for the attentive player. A big part of it is the verticality in a lot of them, with many of them going all the way down or all the way up, occasionally doing both on the same levels. The rope arrows, one of the coolest '' weapons'' in the game, being the best way to explore them. Since I've brought them up, the weapons are mostly tailored to the stealth and are as creative as the uses a player can give for them: moss arrows lowers noise on surfaces, regular arrows can be used to create distractions and hurt enemies and water arrows are used to lower create dark areas for the player to sneak on. Weapons such as your Blackjack are used to knock out enemies and the sword can be used for fighting the non-human enemies.
Story's perhaps this game's biggest achievement (other than the stealth gameplay). With an immersive, complex, multilayered plot that develops in a very unique way. Staying mostly in the background, gradually increasing in reach, before finally grabbing and enveloping the player character. The world of the game is also very unique, mixing medieval architecture and Tesla-like machinery, creating sections which feel very in-line with the story's themes of Science vs Nature.
Unfortunately, not all levels are all about showing the best qualities of the game. For a game called ''Thief'', a lot of levels feel like the developers were in some sort of insecure identity crisis over the direction the game should take, which leads to combat being a major part of them.
Don't get me wrong, I love variety in games. But in the case of Thief 1, many of the cumbersome levels seem to pile up on top of the levels everyone enjoys (the''steal stuff'' levels) and almost force you to engage in really slow, stiff sword fighting. Some might say this adds a layer of survival horror to the game, which somewhat works in that sense, I guess. Unfortunately, it's in most of these levels where the design takes a dive and many of them feel like it's impossible to avoid enemies, which leads to the complaints I've raised above.
Another issue I have with this game is some of the levels added by the ''Gold'' edition (such as Thieves' Guild) feel a lot more rushed and not as polished as they should be and can bog down the flow of the game. Making it feel a little too lengthy and sometimes overblown.
No matter my criticisms, make no mistake. This still is pretty much one of the most advanced stealth games of all time and if you enjoy stealth games, this and The Metal Age are pretty much essential if you really want to experience how deep a game like this can go. I'd still recommend it to people looking for a game with a great story and immersive world, looking for something more ''unique'' than the standard fare of modern gaming.

I may have only played this for three hours, and only got this game yesterday at the time of writing this, but I can frankly say that this game is great! Well, okay, not "GREAT", but sort of in the limbo between "good" and "great", so... "Grood", I guess. The mechanics of this game is rather simple. You are you(not that there's anything wrong with that), the customers are walking wallets, and they are filled with gold. Your job is to get the gold in the wallets by putting various items up for sale, from the cheapest Healing potion, to the most expensive(at the start, anyway) generic sword.The graphics are kind of like The Elder Scrolls 4 Oblivion, but imagine that Bethesda was less experienced with making graphics. It is easy to tell who is who, in this town swarming with males and females with funny names and a bunch of look-a-likes.(I'm pretty certain I've seen four females wearing a red shirt and brown trousers.) Now, as much as I feel like a dirtbag saying this, you do need to be the type of person who likes waiting about, hoping people buy your♥♥♥♥♥♥so you can buy more crap to hopefully earn enough to keep a constant stream of items coming through the magic order chest. The controls are a little confounding. The default controls state that "Plus" or "+" is supposed to increase your price on the items, and that "Minus" or "-" will decrease the price. However, on my spiffy wireless keyboard, which functions with a FN key that lets me actually press F1 or F2 without accidentally booting me to desktop, that doesn't seem to work. Now, this can be fixed by actually remapping the controls. The other controls are easily figured out. The game has several skills to work with, such as increasing haggling, meaning you get more gold from each transaction, increasing delivery speed for orders, and various ways of dealing with thievery. Yes, dear reader, some idiots think it would be a good idea to swipe your goods. You can handle this though, usually through attacks, or spells, the shock varient of which LEAVES A SKELETON AS A WARNING TO OTHERS. Until you sweep it up, anyways. CONCLUSION: I do reccomend this game, despite it's flaws. It is a charming little romp through an unseen side of Roleplaying Games: Being a shopkeep. Now, buy this game. Do it now.

Finally got around to this game, years late. I have to say that I honestly wish I had picked it up sooner. There's a significant amount of content, no 20 hour blow through for this one... not even counting the DLC. Character development is present and relevant, and being able to respec for a cost is awesome because you can try the variety of combat styles and mechanics in a single playthrough without having to go through the tedium of leveling another character. Crafting at the high end is worth the time and effort.
The open world is set-level, stuff gets ridiculously easy to fight, but all of the "instanced" areas such as dungeons, castles, etc, have enemies set to your level, so there's still some challenge, but once you start crafting the highest end gear you can really ROFLstomp the game... it's fine, because after a certain point you're really doing stuff to see what happens with the various storylines rather than the combat.

If you like action RPGs and have not played this one, stop reading now and buy it.

So new Deus Ex has been released this week and alot of controversy surrounds this game right now. Steam reviews are currently "Mixed" because people can find many things to call it a bad game. But is it really that bad? Despite all I'll try to give my honest opinion with pros and cons.
Lets start with positives.
Mankind Divided is very close to Human Revolution gameplay wise. You're still playing as Adam Jensen who's still infiltrating prohibited areas, hiding behind boxes and in air vents. Even hacking minigame from HR is back with some twists. It's really nice to see that they managed to keep everything that was good about HR gameplay and improve it a bit without breaking or making it worse. If you enjoyed previous game you'll definitely like this one too.

The atmosphere of MD is amazing. Big european city turned into totalitarian camp where police is around every corner and nobody can feel safe especially if he or she is augmented. It reminded me of C17 in Half-Life 2 which probably imfluenced developers in some way. While playing the game you will find more and more info about the city and situation which makes it feel even more realistic. The game has only one hub-world but it's bigger then Detroit in HR and more detailed.

The side-missions in the game are very well made. And during most of them players will have to make different choices with different outcomes. What really impressed me if you don't rush during the quest you can find more info and get better ending. These kind of things became very rare in modern games and having them here made me happier.
Now time for negatives.

Without spoilering anything I have to say that main quest line is very promising at the beginning but it turns out to be shallow and has no proper ending. Does anyone remember that horrible mobile port called Deus Ex: The Fall? Mankind Divided has absolutely the same issue regarding the end of main story. You know there should be more to it but you only get end credits. I really want to hope there is more on the way. Some sort of Expantion or even the 2nd chapter because currently the game lacks of something that can close the story.

Even though Michael McCann is back the music in MD is very mediocre and has no interesting tracks. It mostly consists of ambient themes to make you feel the atmosphere even more but nothing beyond that. After playing the game for 20 hours I can't actually remember anything from the soundtrack. Maybe someone will not agree with me here but opinions can be different and there is nothing wrong with that.

People complain a lot about this side of the game currently. To be honest I have almost no issues here because of running in on gtx 1080 with 85-90 fps. Everything is maxed out excluding MSAA which is only x2. Because if I try to go a bit further I'm going to lose half of the frames with almost no visible changes. The game is really really demanding but again if you look at the screen shots it doesn't look like a next gen at all. MD has also problems with lipsync and animations in cut scenes. And there are also some bugs and crushes. I experienced a couple crushes but managed to solve the issue. But in current state the game requires at least one patch to deal with those things.
And there is one more thing that bothers players.
Yes, the game has them and you can purchase ingame currency or praxis points with real money. But do you need them to complete the game or get better combat experience? Absolutely not. So I don't see any big deal here but someone can feel otherwise and it may definitely be a problem for him. But the choice is up to the player in the end.
To sum it up. The game has its flaws one of them being a disappointing ending. It also requires to be patched so bugs will not interrupt your gameplay. But despite all that if you like Human Revolution you'll probably like this one too. At least I did and looking forward to more story-related content if it happens of course. 7 out of 10.

Had my eye on this since it was announced way back when. Have a friend that I watched the show and discussed stuff regularly with, and we'd been debating getting the game for awhile. The summer sale was when we decided to take the plunge. It was...alright. Pretty fun actually. We both felt that Yang and Blake were kinda meh, and Weiss' ability to freeze things, along with Ruby's combos were crazy strong. Character customization, or specialization I guess, was pretty barebone, but ah well, it's Early Access right? We actually didn't even have any problem with the character models. Not the second ones, those were awful. But the ones that came after? Meh, good enough.
Then they announced the game's full launch. I honestly wasn't thinking much on it, but I browsed the various RWBY places (Here and reddit) to see what the word on the street was, so to speak, and people brought up some good points. 'How could this be close to a full launch? There's nothing here. This is barely a beta! There's no way there's enough to justify a full release!' Those are the things I heard and it got me thinking. And kinda worrying. But hey, no sense in judging so soon, I say. Let the game speak for itself! Then you can talk about it. After you've SEEN it for yourself!
Then I saw it for myself. Man. I'm not gonna complain about Team JNPR or anything like that. It's still the gameplay I enjoyed with my friend, and Yang even kinda felt stronger than she was before. But...the game just feels so so barren. Like one of those games you see that use those, like, asset packs. The models are fine. I like them. They look enough like the main four for me that whatever their reason for changing the original models, no big deal. The rest of the game though, not so much.
Other random things that bugged me.
The UI feels flat, the music isn't super exciting, the amount of invisible walls was and is still frustrating, the EXP being based on killing blow is frustrating (yes the assist EXP is here now, but man, it's totally possible to just hog EXP for the characters with devastating AoE attacks), and the subtitles, oh man. It may sound weird to complain about, but it just feels so LAZY the way they just drop a literal huge chunk of text at the bottom of the screen. Is timing individual lines super difficult or something? And they shrunk the text down to fit too.
Bottom Line, I guess. It's fun. I enjoyed playing with my friend. But, it doesn't feel like a complete game. It doesn't feel like a professionally made game. It doesn't feel like a game that costs $24.99 is the bottom line I'm getting at. I could recommend it at $10 or maybe $15, but not $25, not for what it is. And the "DLC is coming!" thing doesn't fly with big name devs, so it's not gonna fly here, not with me anyways.
Disclaimer about product for free: My friend and I are goofs, and we just bought each other the game when it was on sale. This is technically free, but I paid for my friend's copy. If that matters at all, I mean.
Just finished the game, LOVED IT! Loved the final boss! :) Can't wait for horde mode and Team JNPR!

The villain is obvious and predictable to say the least, checking a fair amount of cliches from the cliche villain list. You can sense a lot of ambition behind this game, but as it's a low-budget indie title, it's not at all surprising to see that so many corners had to be cut and that it still needs a lot more polish. Despite the full-release, it's still a work in progress, but I can feel a good game trying to get out.
The game is about killing waves upon waves of the same Grimm with the same attacks over and over, but the combat is fast, flowing, and it feels very good when four players are present. There aren't a lot of combos but the characters all play radically differently and, between the animation and sound effects borrowed from the show, feel like they hit hard. I actually really enjoyed fighting the final boss, even if he was pretty simple. Also, this game is not meant for long sessions. You'll probably get bored if you don't play it in bursts.
The characters don't look like glossy barbie dolls anymore. They no longer make me cringe, but they're still far from the original models. I'd probably still be frustrated about this if Kami Peppers wasn't so good at making retexture mods. The dev team's top priority should be to make this game feel like an interactive episode of the show, as that is its main selling point. The look and feel of this game IS important.

The original  Rise of the Triad  is a relic of the early ages of PC gaming. It didn't ask you to aim up or down, quick save every few minutes, or worry about fiddling with graphics settings. It did, however, beg you to explode, shoot, and instagib everything.
Interceptor Entertainment's 2013 remake is an earnest love letter to the original—warts and all. There are no quick saves, for example. There's no regenerating health. The game doesn't even have actual cutscenes aside from the intro. What it  does  have is an undeniable charm. This is Quake on steroids. Things move faster, explosions are bigger, and the giblets are greater.

You play as a member of H.U.N.T., a Special Forces unit sent to a nondescript island to investigate cult activity. The cultists, it seems, are also some sort of military force? And have rocket launchers? Honestly, it doesn't matter. You're not going to play RotT for its story, but for its retro shooter sensibilities.
RotT is a hard game that follows in the footsteps of classics like Doom. The challenge isn't in killing enemies, but in managing your health and ammo. Running out of rockets is akin to bringing a knife to a gunfight—which is funny, since the melee attack is super effective. This isn't your modern, hide-and-shoot, cover-based game. Instead, you run and jump around corners with guns blazing. If you aren't covered in gore, you're not doing it right.
Multiplayer makes great use of the game's super fast pace. Having 16 players jumping around a map at hyperspeed while picking up power ups that let them fly across the map is amazing. Oh, and I'm now 100 percent sure that text-to-speech should be in every game. RotT reads out anything that anyone types into the chat, rendering multiplayer matches a mixture of chaotic fun and laugh-until-you-explode-because-you're-still-in-game action.
The most important thing about a game like this is the gunplay—it's fan-freaking-tastic. Ignore the basics like pistols and the submachine gun, and you've got an awesome selection of weapons at your disposal. A staff that shoots lightning, a flak cannon that chains explosions, a rocket launcher masquerading as a gatling gun and more.
For better or for worse, RotT isn't afraid of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. Breakaway floors? Check. Indiana Jones-style giant rolling balls? Check. Bosses that just won't die? Check. This game has all of the things that make old school games nearly unplayable today, but they're the reason that Rise of the Triad is an annoyingly amazing game.

Pros
--Nonlinear level design with plenty of routes and plenty of secrets.
--Fun toolset, especially the water moss arrows and especially rope arrows.
--Light and sound fully accounted for in stealth, Non dousable lights in a marble hallway leads to a swift detection.
--Higher difficulty means more enemies and less supplies, aswell as stricter and more mission objectives enemy health scaling isn't relevant when you can oneshot most enemies, you should be avoiding them anyways.
--Cool as hell cutscenes.
--Maps are part of the game's world, not just a screen in the pause menu. You can write notes on them and they reflect Garret's knowledge on the mission.
--Difficult in places. ( Difficulty is always a good thing. )
--Can boreder on horror at times ( Constantine's manor best level. )

Cons

Thief Gold is a first person stealth game by Looking Glass Studios ,in fact it is actually the first of its kind. You play as Garrett, a wise cracking and all around great thief. I must say that I love Garrett. He is a thief through and through and just loves what he does, his voice actor is excellent as well.
The core gameplay of Thief Gold revolves around maneuvering large and complex levels stealing various artifacts. The level design is very good for any lover of exploration. However, these levels can feel just gargantuan in size especially on your first playthrough; you can easily be lost for thirty minutes or close to an hour on some. That aside, sneaking around is quite fun. Garrett possesses many tools for the job: a sword, blackjack (for knocking people out), arrows, water arrows (for extinguishing torches), flash bombs (flash bangs essentially), rope arrows (for vertical movement), lock picks, mines, etc. Yet there is one unique contraption that is paramount in this game. It is a yellow gem that appears at the bottom of the screen. This gem will indicate how much you are vulnerable to being seen. Bright yellow = very vulnerable. Slightly dark = keep your distance from guards. Very dark = you are almost invisible. Keeping track of this gem is essential in order to not get caught and have to deal with the awkward combat system. Garrett is not a solider. So be prepared to run or sometimes reload a previous save if you get caught. In addition to this, there is a heavy emphasis on the noise you will make when you walk on different surfaces. Carpets = very quiet. Tiles = not a lot but be careful when guards are close. Metal = can be loud. Overall the gameplay is very fun but it can drag some times.
The story in Thief Gold is very intriguing. I will not spoil it, but I will say that it will capture your interest. However, I will spoil the atmosphere. The atmosphere this game creates is simply excellent. It really does draw in to the world. I could write an essay on how good it is. The sound design in this game released in 1998 is better than most games made today. To put it simply, this game feels like a horror game. It has that particular feeling in the air that something is amiss.
The only real complaint I have with this game is its higher difficulty levels. There are two higher difficulty levels: Hard and Expert. These difficulties add new objectives such as having you steal another artifact or do not kill any servants/innocents.  Those are fine additions. What I dislike is the addition of objectives asking to steal 1000 gold worth loot or whatever number it asks. The problem I have with these objectives is that they can be really tedious sometimes. This problem can magnified immensely depending on the level you are playing. I will fully admit that I have given up on some levels on Expert for this reason. I just cannot find that last 50-100 gold pieces worth of loot. HINT: If this happens to you hold Ctrl, Shift, Alt, and End to skip to the end of a level.
Despite that complaint, I would highly recommend Thief Gold to any stealth fan.

The definitive save scum experience!
Along with Metal Gear Solid, helped define the stealth genre, and it still holds up pretty well even today. The sound design is especially amazing - since the HUD is so minimal, you have to listen very closely to track enemy position, which works very well. I highly recommend installing the OpenAL patch(which I think is part of NewDark), since you get some nice reverb effects with that. My gripes are that the worst enemy in the game is ladders*, which I never did figure out how to consistently dismount safely, & the level design is labyrinthine, especially with regards to the optional objectives on higher difficulties. If you miss something, prepare to consult a walkthrough to find out where the hell it was, or run around the level at random trying to find what you missed. There's also a mission with an uncharacteristically cryptic switch puzzle - the game is normally pretty good about dropping hints in the form of notes or NPC chatter, but in that level it's basically nonexistent, so have fun studying every nook & cranny! Other than those gripes, this game is a blast, and if you enjoyed stealthing about in Deus Ex or Splinter Cell, you can see where the genre began.
*Other than loud, tiled floors, that is.

I can't really recommend this game to low-income players, but I can't give it a bad rating either, as it is QUITE fun once you get into it. Sims 3 is probably the best life sim I've ever seen/played. If you like life sims, than you really should get this game. If the idea of helping a person, or persons, through daily life sounds tedious, then it's not the game for you. The basic game comes with two towns you can mess around with, one of which is a free download. You get to build your player's lot up any way you'd like within the limits of the games included inventory.
You help a character you create, and motivate to make big (and small) desicions regarding their entire life, from schooling, to Careers, to Hobbies, to whether they brush their teeth or not after eating garlic dishes. The interactions within the world can get crazy intricate... Or you could make it your business to create a Sim with the right motivations, and just let them do what they wish. This usually doesn't end well, but many have tried it.
I will caution you about the mircro/macro-transactions that Sims offers it's players. If you are not satisfied with the content provided, you can get more, but it almost always costs extra real money for your video-game objects. If you want additional towns, for example, you'll need to be willing to part with another 20-30 dollars to purchase it. You can also buy some pretty cool furniture sets with real money too anywhere from a few cents, to $25 for some of the truly premium stuff. While this is fine for folks with money, this can be problematic for younger players, or people with limited income. Once you've bought the furniture, you CAN use it in any future saves; so at least you don't have to pay through your teeth multiple times for individual things.
If you get this game, try to be determined to stick with the limited content you start with, or you will find that you've forked out over a hundred dollars in no time. Otherwise have fun with it. It's really quite entertaining sometimes.

TL;DR: Generic story, fun combat, varied skill tree, some interesting mechanics, psuedo-open-world, and worth it, at the very least on sale. Oh, and it has spiders. But anyway, Steam gives refunds. If you've got the money, why not try it for less than two hours, and then decide on playing it through or not?
Let me start off by saying the game IS rather generic in its story, so if you want something for story purposes, I'd advise against this.
The map consists of various small, closed-off areas that are generally not connected by actual loading screens, but small corridors from area to area. I like that system, and am fine with the not-really-open-worldness of it.
So, onto the combat. It doesn't lie when it says it's a hack'n'slash, so your basic attacks are most of what you'll be using, but with the three skill trees and Destiny system (More on that later), it's plenty fun as a hack'n'slash. There are nine weapon types, each with some special moves, and three armor types (More depth on those later.) The three trees are Might, Finesse, and Sorcery, corresponding to the Warrior, Rogue, and Mage archetypes for the most part. Every time you level up, you get three points to put into the trees almost completely at will. Higher-tier abilities in a tree require more points in said tree to get, but you can mix trees as much as you like, as long as you remember that you won't be getting the most... Interesting and/or overpowered abilities, if you spread your points out too much.
Now for Equipment. Each tree has its own armor, with Warriors having the most actual Armor stat and increased block efficacy, Rogues having the middleground and increased critical chance, and Mages have the lowest Armor stat but with extra mana-related things (I think mana regen specifically). Each tree has three weapons. Warrior weapons are generally slower, more powerful, and melee. Rogue weapons are generally faster, less damaging, and melee except for the bow. And finally, Mage weapons are primarily Elemental damage (Fire, Lightning, or Ice), an average speed, and generally ranged aside from the close-ranged, cone/AoE (in general) staff/stave (The game seems confused on what to call it).
The Destiny system has seven groups, Sorcery, Might, Finesse, Might/Sorcery, Might/Finesse, Finesse/Sorcery, and Might/Finesse/Sorcery. Each has about five or six Destiny tiers, with each providing better bonuses and having higher requirements relating to its intended tree(s). To unlock a given Destiny, you must put X points into a specific tree, or group of trees. Some Destinies replace your dodge roll with a short-range "teleport" that CAN deal damage, with certain Destinies, and some Destinies involve special passive bonuses relating to equip requirements or your professions.
And now onto the aforementioned professions/whatevers! There's a fair few, including one that reveals most of the secrets (Hidden caches of loot, fake walls that are actually doors, etc.), and Blacksmithing, which makes all Unique weapons and armor completely and utterly obsolete, sadly. They're pretty generic, the normal Lockpicking, Alchemy, Stealth, that stuff.
The game's story is basically you can unweave the threads of Fate, and do so with every single action you take, since Fate doesn't really have a plan for you, because you already died. Meaning you're the only one that can win a battle fated to be lost, and have to save the world from the Tuatha. Which, if the Tuatha sound familiar, it's because a LOT of the game's story seems to be taken from Irish mythology, which I find to be pretty interesting, but you might see as laziness.
The graphics are stylized and have aged pretty well because of that, and the game has some utterly beautiful areas, especially with the Gallow's End DLC.
The game also has a fair few player homes, as many RPGs seem to have now, and one of which you can sacrifice to not fight a small army of spiders. I, like many people (I assume), have never returned to that home, or the town it's within, because we gave it up to not fight spiders.
Almost finally, the quest Her Righteous Fury can break her game. It's in the desert area of Detyre, and isn't mentioned in the TL;DR because I demand effort! I demand work! I demand research! But anyway, you can easily find a guide to get through it, or just remember to make the lowest-damage-daggers you can, with as much Poison damage as you can, or just let the NPC that tags along deal with the enemies. And SAVE before you start the quest, of course.
Finally, I have concluded that you should buy the game and get a refund if you dislike it, which I don't think you will if what I have just spent time describing is enjoyable.

This game will always be tied to the Curt Schilling and Rhode Island controversy, which is a shame because it could have been one of the greatest games of all time, and despite everything still manages to be a really good game.
It sports a massive, rich and varied game world that strikes just the right balance between open world freedom and linear narrative development, gives a rich world to explore without feeling repetitive or tedious, and in general delivers a lot of fun simply with how much content there is, how much you can do. It won't give you the feeling that you're living and breathing in the world as the Elder Scrolls series do, so don't expect that, but there's plenty of immersion in feeling that you're adventuring through a rich, wonderful world. It was never a technological marvel, but the graphic design works well, the environments look wonderful, the cities are vibrant, the dungeons are varied and interesting, and there are a number of quite memorable sequences. It's absolutely an AAA-grade production, which is probably why the company went bankrupt in the first place.
Yes, there are quite a few bugs, some of which are rather annoying and almost unavoidable, and you can only hope that they remain merely a nuisance rather than break the game outright. The studio did not survive long enough to release the patches this game needed, and unlike the Elder Scrolls series, you're going to have to play the game as is; you won't be able to count on community patches to fix the issues or mods to expand the gameplay.
All that shouldn't prevent you from going for this game if you enjoy RPGs with vast open worlds, interesting setting, and plenty of adventuring and crafting to do. It's a worthy game that deserves more attention for its own merit than it did.

As you can see from my profile, I don't write many reviews, but I found this too important.
I'm a big fan of the DX universe. I thoroughly enjoyed DX:HR: one of the few games I've played several times.
DX:MD has a lot of what made HR really great: great story, more choice, etc.
At the same time, I feel like the developers really stopped caring about the PC (and in general) release, and also seem to have really wanted to screw their customers for 2 reasons. Despite my love for DX, I have to give this a negative review:
(for the record, writing this did not make me feel good...I really wanted to enjoy this game...)
1. Performance issues: I'm sorry, but to say that people with the greatest of rigs can't play a game at more than 58fps on a 1080 4k resolution because the game is 'demanding' is absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and they know it. If we want to talk 'demanding', I've been to NASA multiple times and seen what 'demanding' is on computer systems. This is a game (that's supposed to be) DESIGNED TO BE PLAYED...not designed to do the complicated math algorithms. Saying this is an 'optimizing issue' is an attempt to make your customers feel like absolute morons. Admit to the mistake and fix it...for your own reputation at least...
2. 'Non-durable' DLC which was not advertised as 'non-durable': What an absolutely ridiculous, shady, attempt to try and get people to spend even more money on your game. Great attempt at microtransactions. Did you really think people would enjoy DX:MD if you put in some ridiculous 'freemium' with consumable items? What on earth were you people thinking? This is a clear attempt at swindling people out of even more money! An utterly shameful act that seriously stains your reputation. Everyone who didn't fight this decision should be ashamed.
People ARE paying attention. You may be ok with ruining a franchise like DX, but we will remember this when you ever try to come up with an original IP...

Played through once, going for a stealth run. Like stealth runs usually go, I didn't use many of the shiny new toys they had, opting to crouch and tap-q my way through the game. A shame, since all the trailers featured the new augments being used. Other upgrades also seemed extraneous to the classic first-time stealth run and I had plenty of biocells, crafting parts and money never used. Still, part of the value for money for dude sex games comes from experimentation with different playstyles so at least I had the ingame items to do so.
The game itself seems a bit too short to fully enjoy and experiment with new augments but the content and quests offered are quality. Clocked in at around 25 hours as only a part ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at games so not completely all of that time was spent savescumming. No fetch quests etc and there's plenty of dialogue, pocket secretaries, and computers to hack into for lore. The game also does a reasonable job at acknowledging the choices you make. Gameplay wise it feels much like DXHR. Levels accommodate players deciding to tackle a problem differently adequately.
Lore and story-wise, it doesn't really build up to it's end. The last level does throw you a slightly unique challenge but it's just not the same sense of urgency players received in DXHR, where they strap into a rocket to fly to a great big hole in the ocean fighting pseudo-zombies. There's also less of a personal hook to the story compared to DXHR- HR has a bunch of people make an enemy of you right at the start and there is a cohesive theme. tl;dr: It leaves you feeling like you just played the underwhelming pilot episode of a spin-off series on the blockbuster that was Human Revolution.
===============================
Damnit... my heart has just been broken...
[(partial) SPOILERS]
Just spent 20 hours playing the game, thrilled to be back in the Deus Ex universe, waiting to be awed by all the pretties and shinies that we've come to expect from this studio. Unfortunately, to my shocked surprise, the game simply ends with the most depressing slideshow of "micro-documentary storyline wrapups" since fallout 3 after defeating an apparently minor henchman in the first bossfight of the game (and what felt like at most 1/3 of the storyline).
They got the gameplay right, same as Human Revolution, just wonderfully smooth. And save for the forgivable minor buggyness here and there, it plays like a charm.
But everything that made the that game tower out above all others at the time for me:
- The sweeping globalised storyline unravelling before your eyes
- The incredibly rich locales, befitting this brand new reality
- Futurism and incredible tech pouring from ever nook and cranny of the world
... is utterly absent from Mankind Divided, making the environments positively dull.
All of the game is set in the same grey slum they label Prague (not the Prague I've visited, I'll tell you) with next to no unique, awe-inspiring, or interesting locations to be found. The sidequests are mostly running around in this drab place, and almost none of the amazing places you hear about (or even see in the distance) all over the freaking place are visited. (hint hint: DLC, expansions, sequel material coming up! Yay.....)
The main storyline starts off reasonably ok (a bit slow and running simulatorish) but only really gets going after hours and hours of introduction, and then just cuts off on a horribly jarring note as mentioned. A dozen storylines all over the place are just dropped or sloppily explained away in the horrifically cheap ending cinematic, leaving you with a complete sense of "What...? That's it...?".
Hence, it leaves you feeling like you just played the underwhelming pilot episode of a spin-off series on the blockbuster that was Human Revolution.
===============================
I want to recommend it as the gameplay is still perfectly solid, as in the last game. But knowing that they are capable of so much more than this is what decides it. Living up to the hype is impossible and living up to Human Revolution is right next to that, I fully get that. But this was just so... so much less..
Just wait till the next sale I guess, give it a try, maybe the DLC will save it in some minor way.

I'm editing this review because I was able to get the game running and here's how:
If you're crashing after the initial splash screens but before the actual start menu like I was, try running a utility called DDU from
. Its a free program that completely strips display drivers off your machine, including any fragments left in the registry from previous updates or cards. I also deleted (all files, including leftovers from Steam uninstall) and reinstalled DXMD.
After, install the latest drivers for your card and give Deus Ex another shot.
This worked after I had run all the other options, including DLC on/off, turning all settings to lowest possible, updating drivers (before using DDU), running the DXMD.exe as admin, disabling steam overlay, verifying cache, redownloading and more.

Windows 7 Home Premium 64-bit

This has been a long time coming. Ever since the first iteration of Super Smash Brothers on Nintendo 64, I've been hoping and waiting for a PC version with online support. Now my personal Brawlhalla is finally here and it looks smashing already. Since this game is in early access right now, access is limited but I had no trouble getting in within a few hours of signing up. If you're interested in this game, definitely go and sign up for the closed beta right now.
Gameplay:
It is time to Brawl on PC! Since everyone and their dog has probably already played a version of Smash Brothers, you'll find this game easy to pick up and play right away, Hit an enemy enough times so that your next stronger move sends them flying off the arena, taunt with a nice pose, repeat. The familiar mechanics are all there in a very similar way. Light attacks, smash attacks, a distinct move set for every weapon and an unarmed moveset for when you have none. While in the air you also have access to a triple juimp (because double jump was apparently too mainstream). The dodge move is much more powerful than in this game's ancestor: You can dodge in EVERY direction, even up, down or diagonally. In the air as well. OP much? Not at all, since everyone can use it.
Graphics:
The graphics are okay. Not great, but far from bad. Some animations could use some more fluidity and the artstyle isn't really distinct enough to be memorable, you'll probably thoroughly enjoy what there is already. The health bar isn't really informative yet, unlike the % number in Smash Brothers you'll only get a colored indicator that lets you know about how far you'll knock back the enemy.
Sound:
While the sound design is nothing to write home about - it really isn't memorable and lacks impact - the music is FANTASTIC. You'll get the soundtrack stuck in your head even after the first match and find yourself humming along as early as the second. Here's hoping the sounds will get a bit crunchier as development progresses.
Free to Play aspects:
From what is there so far, it looks like cash shop purchases are cosmetic only. If this stays this way, I will gladly drop a few dollars here and there just to get the saltiest taunts and sexiest skins. As of right now there doesn't seem to be a way to earn currency by playing.
Early Access Notes;
For an early access release, this game is remarkably solid already. There's a nice variety in characters, average variety in weapons and a few usable items already. Stages are alright so far, those that exist are pretty distinct from each other. Netcode is okay, though the servers lump everyone together at the moment, as it seems, so expect some teleporting enemies every now and then.
For now, I can thoroughly recommend this game to everyone who likes Smash Brothers or fighting games in general. It is that good. Not just a clone or cash-in on the "I want Smash for PC!" audience but an actual possible contender-in-the-making for the genre throne. We'll see how this changes as development progresses, I'll keep updating this review as patches come in.

First and foremost I should note that before playing this game that it's mandatory to install T-Fix, as it upgrades the game to run on NewDark (an updated version of the game's engine that's used in the digital release of System Shock 2), gives options for improving the graphics (something I'm not too fond of doing myself), and restores the cutscenes so they actually work.

I can also reccomend installing the Gold To Dark mod for first time players, which converts Thief Gold into Thief : The Dark Project, for reasons that will be stated later in this review.
Now on to the review.
I never really played that many stealth games before Thief Gold, I mean I did dabble around with Bioshock Infinite's DLC (which is a stealth game) and I did play the Thief Reboot, but I never really thought I'd be one who would be really into the stealth genre, that is untill I played Thief : The Dark Project (or the GOTY edition known as Thief Gold). In Thief : The Dark Project, you play as Master Thief Garret, who goes around stealing♥♥♥♥♥♥from places, or at least that's what the game centers around at first. I won't spoil what happens, but the gameplay does take a shift near the end of the game. While the game mostly involves breaking into places, and stealing a ton of loot, some missions feel more akin to Tomb Raider, which to me isn't entirely a bad thing, as these missions are (in my opinion) much more relaxing than the standard theiving missions, and are a nice break from the stealing aspect of the game. The crontrol in this game isn't the best, mostly due to the fact that this is a Dark Engine game, but you will get used to them after playing for a while, and once you do, they can be quite enjoyable at times while climbing up stuff, and feeling like a stealth god. The combat on the other hand isn't all that great. It's clunky and unresponsive, and extremely akward to use at first, but you aren't really supposed to get into combat, and you can learn the neuances of it. The atmosphere in this game is exelent. Before each mission, you're breifed with an intro video, explaining what to do in the mission from Garret's perspective, which is exelently voice acted if I might add. In game, Garret will occasionally mutter something entertaining or somewhat helpfull, while being well done and believable. The voice acting carries across to all of the characters. Standing around and hearing the guards chatter is not only entertaining, but sometimes extremely usefull, as they often point out key infromation needed to progress. But the guards are just one part of the atmosphere, the soundscape is just freaking awesome, and even somewhat tense at times. However there are some things that I don't like about the game. Level design is exelent and complex, but sometimes way too complex for their own good, at times takeing over an hour for first time players. I mentioned earlier that there is actually a mod that converts Thief Gold to Thief : The Dark Project, and that's because Thief Gold adds 3 new missions. Now while that sounds good on paper, these missions are some of the most assinine missions in the entire game (and debatably the series), taking upwards of an hour and a half to complete for first time players. The Gold missions consist mostly of long empty hallways, and require a metric butt ton of backtracking, to the point where I'm not even sure that I'd reccomend Thief Gold over Thief : The Dark Project. Overall though, Thief : The Dark Project is a great start to an exelent trilogy of games, and while it may not be my favorite in the series (Thief 2 holding that title), it's still an exelent game in its own right. What are you waiting for you taffers?

I had never played any games in the Thief Series, despite being a huge fan of the stealth genre. I decided I would give this a go after seeing it on sale in the Humble Store, but I didn't expect a lot from it because of the release date. I was so wrong.
The gameplay overall is very solid. The combat is a little frusterating at times, but this isn't a game where you should be engaged in a lot of combat anyway. The controlls are total garbage unless you customize them, but that's an easy fix.
Where this game really shines is the stealth, which feels so satisfying. Looking at maps and trying to plan out infiltration routes, studying gaurd patrols, hiding in shadows, pickpocketing keys and gold, it all feels so good. It holds up better than some more recent stealth games I've played (which now days play more like action third person shooters than stealth games). The different types of tools at your disposal are another huge plus. I'm particularly found of the gas and water arrows, because I prefer to move through a level with no kills and minimal knockouts.
The level design is great. It surprises me to see that some people complain about it, because I think it's one of the highlights of this game. The maps are huge, with tons to explore and see. I love that. There were times when I was wishing I could download a mod that removes all enemies because I thought that the maps were so genuinely well designed and fun to explore that I wanted to be able to see every inch of them.
The story is good so far, but I haven't beat the game yet. But very intruiging premise. I like that steampunk medieval cross, it's very cool and gives the game a unique feel. Garretts character is pretty likeable, which is good for any protagonist.
Overall I would say this is a phenomanal game. It hasn't aged nearly as much as you may think. You should buy it.

Would I play this game forever? Not really, but it's a good game for the casual hack n slashers  and/or RWBY fans out there. This game takes a step in the right direction and hopefully more content will be provided.
PS: I noticed that the developers spent♥♥♥♥♥♥loads of time playing through this game (like over 2000 hours), so give them some credit for trying their best on the game.

PROS and CONS below,
but first with my suggestions for a better, personal experience as a game.
I really think this game missed the opportunity of giving immersive experience that only a medium as immersive and personal as a game can provide.
Controlling the characters felt like I am no more than a random guy clicking and pressing the keyboard,
making me feel completely irrelevant to the World of Remnant, the world that I really would love to dive into.
There just isn't enough opportunity for interaction between the characters and the player.
Fighting the grimms gave me a glimpse of what it is like to fight along our beloved huntresses, but not enough.
My suggestion would be making the player to be one of the professors directly managing the team, assigning missions, teaching them skills, upgrading their equipment, healing or aiding them when they are hurt or in trouble, changing their costumes (which effects their abilities), and many more things that can make the whole experience much more personal and allow the player and characters to shape the campaign story together. It would also be great if the characters have dialogues towards the player.
I want to be engaged and connected to the characters, feeling like I am actually contributing to the team RWBY, and perhaps other teams too.
This is not possible with an anime, but very doable with a game.
That is why I think it is a massive missed opportunity.
Having said that, I still think this is a must have for RWBY fans.
Now the PROS
- The action mechanic feels easy yet very satisfying to use.
Clicking in rhythm is cool, especially with Weiss, making steps and moves in orderly fashion.
Turning the camera around with the mouse movement to aim the enemies feel natural and quick.
- Also the visual of the game is pleasant to look at.
Scenery is beautiful and character models are right from the anime.
- Sound effects are just about right. Nothing too noisy or quiet.
And of course, the sound track is awesome.
CONS
- Some parts of the story didn't make sense to me, such as why Dr. Merlot let the team into his lab so easily. Bad move on his part, and I just don't get why he had to make such a foolish decision. Perhaps just for the sake of the progression of the game levels?
- The campaign could be longer. Much much longer.
The overall campaign does have replay value, playing with others and leveling up each characters.
But there just isn't enough content to enjoy for a longer period of time.
People may get into collecting achievements and leveling up gems, but it feels very repetitive overall.
Now, I personally think the price is pretty reasonable.
I also know that there are more to come in the future.
But that future is not here yet, meaning we have only a half of the game, making it hard to call it a 'full release'.
I really enjoy the game, and I look forward to future updates,
I also really hope that Rooster Teeth realizes the full potential of this game as a medium.
It could be so much more.

I still do recommend this game. I bought within the three hours it came out and have had it ever since. While it has been given negative reviews lately, I still believe that they have come a long way from when it first came out.
First, I don't know what this is about the character models downgrading the actual performance of the game, but for me, somebody with a two-year-old Toshiba, which was a Windows 8 ( now a Windows Ten because it's the only option I had ), with an Intergrated Intel 4 graphics card, it works.. actually quite nicely, even with the 'full release' ( I'll cover this later ).
Could they refine the new character models a bit more? Yes, they could. However, I find the new ones to be much easier on my eyes, despite the 'doll like' faces. The beginning models had a bright glowing to them that was kind of obstructing the features of the models, anyways. Maybe if they removed the glowing characteristic, they could have kept the old models. It was definitely a good change for people who have sensitive eyesight and couldn't sit down to play the game for more than thirty minutes without their eyes becoming sore or a headache. I would like to see an option to switch between the new and old models , though. Mostly so people would stop giving the game negative reviews ( and yes, people are doing this ) just because of the models not looking as 'nice' as they used to. Other than that, the graphics are quite stunning to look at, even if you're playing on 'potato' quality, as the game calls it. They could continue to improve these.
Now onto the 'full release' aspect of this.
I don't think this game was quite ready for a full release and the $25 price. I think they should have kept it at $20, as the range of most early access games coming-out-of-early-access are anywhere between $15-20. I do think they should have waited a few more months, or at least have brought it gradually, instead of all at once in one giant pile. I wasn't able to attend RTX, so the people who did go might say otherwise as they got to see more of the content, but as for how my standing is right now, the ending feels somewhat rushed and the enemies towards the end... well, unbalanced.
As far as the co-op portion goes, the only real issue would be the kill-EXP stealing. If EXP was shared equally when monsters were killed, this would not be an issue at all. However, usually, the person who kills the monster, gets the exp. Unless you're playing with friends, this can be quite an issue, and can force you into single player. That and it feels kind of crappy to have somebody steal your kill after you just pulled off a flashy combo. Obviously you'd still have your Wave MVP EXP which might somebody ahead, but that's usually a component in most team-based games to begin with, and it's not that big of a difference.
Camera could use some more refinement for controllers, I believe. The camera for the keyboard-mouse playing option seems to be alright for me, however. I have played both methods and the one that's more awkward, for me at least, is the controller one due to the camera angles being quite irritating at key points.
Other than this, the game's actually pretty good. I'd recommend it ( and have been recommending the ever living hell out of it since it came out ) to my friends and people who are part of the show. It's definitely got some ways to go, but at least they're trying to handle all of this at once as best as they can.
This is purely my opinion, however, and others may have different opinions as we are humans and we're not all entirely the same. I am grateful that this community is at least somewhat respectful of everyone's opinions and that its.. 'innocence' so to speak hasn't entirely left it. And I hope it stays that way, because we all know what happened to several other games once the squeakers got a hold of them.

I became accustomed to all of the options and possibilities, however, and now it is my favorite version of the Sims! Although I like the new Create-a-Sim Mode on Sims 4 that uses click-and-drag to determine Sims' looks, I miss all of the options for hair and eye color in Sims 3. The Sims 3 also had the Create-a-Style option which allowed the player to personalize virtually anything in the game by selecting patterns and colors for it. I once made an entire house with everything inside it entirely in plaid, just because I could! And it was fun!
Another reason I love the Sims 3 the most is how the map is continuous and you can watch your sim travel from destination to destination in their car, instead of having a load scene while switching lots.
The Sims 3 also has the most career options, which I appreciate. Sims 4 really lacks variety in this area. It doesn't even have a medical career track, which was even in the first version of the Sims! The stuff packs and expansions of Sims 3 are also really fun if you have enough money and space to accommodate them. A con of the Sims 3 is that it takes more power and storage space to run it than the other versions.

In a nutshell: Single-Player World of Warcraft with great action combat, flexibility, and choice, marred by too many shallow sidequests, a lot of backtracking, and far too much running through vast fields of nothing, and a fast travel system that needs serious overhauling.
I really like Kingdoms of Amalur. I wasn't expecting much from this series seeing as I was already badly burned from so many other RPGs I've tried that just didn't "click." Then, after I created a spear made of everything a giant cave troll was and ever will be then shoved it straight into its skull, I thought to myself:
"Damn, this was a really good buy."
And it is!
The Combat is very fun, with the variety in enemies, the responsiveness of the controls and how good it feels to murder the crap out of everything, plus the many different choices you get for how you want to destroy them make it all the sweeter. Though some weapons get too lazy and overpowered for my taste (Chakrams, for Sorcery classes, which is a shame because they look so cool), all of them look fantastic, handle well, and are extremely fun to use.
Granted, spinning round and round like a record with a giant, flaming sword as big as you are rarely isn't incredibly entertaining.
That you can mix and match your styles up without much cost, with little to no consequences, and you're actually encouraged to mix and match it up with the "Destinies" mechanics that allows you to specialize (and get cool titles at that) really helped.
Tired of blowing everything up with magic? Unbind your Destiny, and stab the ever loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them instead.
However, for however fun the combat is, the game suffers from a serious problem of "content dillution." Like "Mad Max" the videogame, it DOES have hours and hours of content and a huge world to explore... unfortunately, it's just constantly rehashing the same tasks over and over again, "Fetch This," "Kill That," "Talk to this Person." There's so many of them and they're oftentimes so disconnected that it makes everything a blurry stew of "I did this and gained XP."
They really should have done like the Witcher 3 and made fewer sidequests with much richer content and storytelling, that filled it up with so much busy work.
Speaking of content dillution, this world is also too damn large--or rather, there's no convenient, fast way to get around. You're forced to go on foot and unfortunately there's a LOT of points in the main questline where your next point of interest is halfway across the world, and you'll have to run on foot before you can fast-travel there.
This game seriously needs mounts or a better way of transportation, it just feels like all this spreading out of the world fills like filler to artificially extend gameplay, and the "no fast traveling in dungeons even after you've murdered the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everything" mechanic REALLY needs to go.
I also can't end this review without saying my piece about the skill/upgrading system. Rarely is an RPG an RPG without growth and leveling up, and unfortunately the system also suffers from that dillution problem, and artificial extension for the sake of padding out gameplay. I often found myself spending points in useless skills just to try and get to the more advanced spells, and spending precious skillpoints on things I'll never use because what I need is locked behind a level and investment wall.
It keeps me from making a ridiculously overpowered class straight from the get go, yes, and I can understand the decision, but sometimes you just gotta let your players become massively OP early and let them wreak havoc, rather than force them to spend and invest in things they don't want or will never use (like poorly designed skills like "Quake") to get what they really want.
To finish up the cons, lockpicking is far too simple with the "five quadrants" rule and the skill being a waste of precious points (though I do appreciate the lack of arbirtary "can't pick this, above my skill level" gating with the "difficulties"), and dispelling, while interesting at first and with great consequences with the "explode and curse for failure" mechanic, quickly just becomes a matter of timing and reflex than any sort of thinking.
Does this game have problems? Yes, plenty.
But is it still really ♥♥♥♥ing fun? Yes, VERY.
Get Kingdoms of Amalur, maybe now, probably on sale so you don't feel too bad about the "price/quality" thing.
It'll be worth it when you're running around with your preferred combination of Fighter/Mage/Thief, killing the ever loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everything, before executing giant monsters and unfortunate enemies with their Fate, such as smacking gnomes through stained glass windows with a giant hammer.

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is probably one of the most underrated and dismissed games of all time.  After 38 Studios, the developer behind the game went bankrupt, the game itself seemed to have just disappeared into the fog of gaming forever.
The game itself is a 3rd person action-roleplay game, centering on loot, story driven questlines and attack fluidity.  Lots of people are comparing it to Fable and Elder Scrolls, which is a fair point.
The game is done very well, with the combat being its strongest suit, followed closely by the story itself.  The story, written by R.A. Salvatore, is engaging enough to keep me interested, but it's the combat that really hooked me.  Playing as a classic Rogue class, it is extremely fun jumping from enemy to enemy while ripping them to shreds.  There are a few unique classes of weapons in the game, the most obvious being Fae Blades and Chakrams, with both having very cool attack animations.  They're very fun to use.  Otherwise, all of the classic weapons can also be found, swords, shields, daggers, staves, etc.  I have yet to play as a pure caster-type, but I may try that in a future playthrough.  The loot system is similar to the standard WoW coloring system.  White items are trash, green, blue, purple and finally yellow, with those being set pieces.  Armor sets work as they do in Diablo III, with a full set granting certain traits - NOT abilities, but traits.
The game does have a crafting system, but be prepared to read up on it, as it isn't too obvious what needs to be done.  The class system is good, with character creation leaving a bit to be desired, but still workable.  Skills are good, with the ability to make hybrid builds.  This can lead to some replayability.  This is a fairly long game, so as long as you get into the story and enjoy it, expect to spend many many hours in it.
The game is obviously no longer being worked on, as the creation studio(s) have gone belly-up.  Do not expect any fixes or tweaks.  It is literally "as is".  There are some minor issues that would have likely been patched - such as the game crashing if too many items are put into or taken out of your loot chest too quickly.  There are also a few areas that were clearly earmarked for more work, but it was never completed (ie; the twin locked doors in Castle Gastyr with no way to open them.)
The visuals, while still colorful and full of flavor, are slowly succumbing to time.  Sometimes certain areas look very very good, while other areas and small items look a little "blocky".  That shouldn't be a reason to not get the game though, as they are easy to overlook and move past.
All in all, if you can catch this game on a sale, which it appears to be on fairly regularly, it's a steal and will offer multitudes of hours of play.  Dollar for time, it has a high value.
The two DLC packs are worth it, but again, get them on sale.  I spent in excess of 10 hours in each one, with Dead Kel logging a bit more time than Teeth of Naros.  Still, overall a fun game and glad that I played it.

This is a great, fun game that will be sure to entertain you for a while and keep you on your toes, but it is definitely not without its flaws. But we'll start with a simple list:
Pros:
* Beautiful open world, artwork and soundtrack
* Story is interesting and entertaining
* Characters are well-voiced and implemented
* Combat is very versatile, customizable and enjoyable (similar to fable, darksouls) You can create pretty much any build you want and play however you want to play without losing any viability.
* Map is large, plenty to explore, plenty of things to do.
* Steady and smooth progression through story and character development
* Variety of different skills you can use to enhance your playthrough, such as the ability to discover treasure more easily, create powerful equipment and potions, price rates, etc.
Cons:
* The game gets very easy, very quickly. Even with hard mode enabled.
* The leveling system for equipment in chests, NPC difficulty, vendor stock and some other loot actually gets locked the moment you first enter a zone - meaning if you enter too early, you could essentially ruin any chances of getting the higher level items, and eventually make leveling up your character very difficult due to the low exp you get from the npcs in each zone. Furthermore this likewise means that once you get higher level gear from the vendors, you will completely crush those enemies and remove any aspect of difficulty from the game. (this is why I personally stopped playing)
* Bosses do not respawn, you'll need to reload your save if you want to farm them for specific items
* The forced camera angle betrays the beauty of the game and flow of the combat. It takes a lot of getting used to.
* Exploring the world there isn't really too much you can interact with except for treasure, gathering spots and other npcs
* You can't jump or climb, making some travel extremely irritating - one example from my personal experience is having my quest goal almost within arms reach, but there was a 2ft ledge between me and the target. I had to run around the entire cliffside for about 2 minutes until I could actually get to the marker.
Overall, I'd recommend this game - it's a good passtime, fun and interesting if you don't mind the flaws too much. I'd rate my experience overall, having completed the story and all dlc, about a 6.5/10

I know I'm a couple years late, but oh well.  In a word: overrated.
I think one of the reasons I waited so long to play this games is that I had heard too many people sing it's praises.  I had seen some of the gameplay and didn't understand why it was thought to be so amazing.  Having finally played it, I think my suspicions were confirmed.  It is certainly not a bad game, but I found it to be merely decent.
The game is not visually stunning.  There are many examples of games out there that deliver much more visually than this one.  There are various benches where you can sit and take in the scenery, but those feel somewhat forced and still don't thrill me.
The game world is interesting, but underdeveloped.  I want to know more about the strange creatures that inhabit the game world.  Slight spoiler: At one point you navigate the aftermath of a battle between titans, but you have no idea what really happened there or why.
The unique controls are not especially captivating.  Very few times are you really required to handle them truly simultaneously.  I suspect this is because it's not very intuitive and overuse of this may have worn people out.  I know that for me personally, whenever the left stick brother was on the right side of the screen and I was moving both brothers, my brain would short circuit a bit.  There are times when the brothers work together by holding onto the same object, like the very beginning of the game, but at these points it's more like controlling one entity from two points.
Like I said, I think the general premise of the story is compelling and it does arc nicely, but for me it fell a little flat.  Going back to the lack of dialogue, I think this would have helped flesh out the story.  I feel like the sort of simspeech in the game was almost done just to be "artsy."  It seemed like they were saying "We don't need dialogue to tell our story."  Sure, you don't need dialogue, but I think that's a self-imposed handicap.  I would rather a story that is more compelling with dialogue than one that manages to get by without it.  Again, this might just be me.
If you don't buy the hype and just go in expecting a pleasant little interactive story with some interesting mechanics, then you will enjoy this game.  If you want a visually stunning puzzle game, play Trine 1 and 2.  If you want a longer game with a more engrossing story, play the Last of Us.

I never played Rise of the Triad (ROTT) when it was released back in 1994. I knew that this game was one of the pioneers of FPS PC gaming. It was very simple in concept: shoot to kill and the plot would take a backseat to the action. It required players to hone their FPS skills and adjust to the fast paced nature of the game.
ROTT is a remake of the original classic game. For better or worse, the game has no cutscenes after the introduction, it’s fast paced as everything moves very fast, the explosions are big, and there are plenty of giblets. I remember seeing my frame rate running at 100+ constantly from start to finish.
The game offers a selection of characters, male and female, for playing against an organization known as The Triad. You are a member of an organization called H.U.N.T., a United Nations taskforce. The Triad members have set up their base of operations in San Nicolas. It is up to you to stop them, but it will not be easy. The game is so fast that the enemies will constantly challenge you while your health and ammo for explosive weapons will need replenishing. Explosive weapons include rockets, heat seekers, and firebombs.
Two things become clear in this game: it is not about taking cover and shooting and the story is not that important. You go into every room guns blazing, jumping around corners avoiding gunfire, and avoiding the many traps that have been set up. There are no concerns about reloading the basic weapons like the pistols and machine guns since they contain infinite ammo. The explosive weapons contain finite ammo and using up all the ammo on these weapons can be disastrous against tougher enemies, especially bosses. This challenge also applies to the staff that fires lightning and the excalibat, a baseball bat that shoots deadly green balls. The explosive weapon that feels really powerful is the firebomb. Man, that firebomb can sure make a difference in boss battles since it causes multiple explosions upon impact. Just don’t be close to the impact of those explosions.
There are some frustrating experiences you will go through in the single player campaign. The game was released without quicksaves, but a patch has added quicksaves to quell some of the frustration that comes with playing certain levels of this game. A checkpoint can be placed at the beginning of a dangerous puzzle and if you die in the middle of solving the puzzle you will be forced back to the checkpoint. Many puzzles tend to include moving spike traps that require you to learn the pattern of the movements so that you can move on unharmed and without losing your life. Another frustration that sometimes comes into play is the tendency to get stuck in some corners and it can be hard to remove yourself from those corners.
The enemy A.I. is generally average. Some guards will strafe from left to right or right to left, but that is as intelligent as they can be. You can kill one guard while a nearby guard will react like nothing happened. I found the enemies to be nothing more than sitting ducks during combat. The difficulty you face against these enemies is their numbers. Sometimes an enemy will throw a net to neutralize and the only way to escape from the net is to use your knife to cut through it. Each episode ends with a boss and each one is predictable as long as you can find the attack pattern.
ROTT does add quite a bit of sense of humor, especially if you find secrets and secret levels. There are secrets scattered around every level. The secrets contain coins, ammo, and the occasional surprise such as pictures of the game’s developers.
I think the graphics of ROTT are decent, but the gameplay mechanics feel outdated. The gameplay mechanics such as no need to take cover during a shootout, no need to reload conventional weapons are outdated since today’s game emphasize the need to take cover and the need to reload when ammo is out. I understand that the selling point of this game is to relive the past using modern day graphics, but you may want to look elsewhere if you are seriously into FPS games with modern gameplay mechanics.
At a price of $15, this game is worth buying for nostalgic fans of the FPS genre. It will appeal to deathmatch fans who want both the single-player campaign and the multiplayer matches. I think that ROTT is a respectable game that pays homage to the old school first-person shooters of the 1990s.

Alright, well, I haven't played much yet as you can see, but I have played enough to see just about everything the game has to offer. (There isn't too much content right now, but I let that slide seeing as how it's clear this game is still in its infancy)
PROS:
~ Dragons with lazer beams on their backs!
~ Fun and easy to understand gameplay, no real tutorial is needed unless you have a hard time understanding very simple game mechanics.
~ This game has a CRAPLOAD of potential, and I hope to see that potential realized as they update the game.
CONS:
(Note: These cons are about the game in it's condition at the time of the review, cons are subject to change in future updates)
~ You cannot select specific maps or servers that you would like to play on, you select a game mode and it puts you in a random match, so you only have a "Quick Match" option essentially.
~ No party system, this makes playing with friends nearly impossible, your friends also cannot join your match via the Steam Overlay
~ All of the Dragons have different stats and abilities but feel exactly the same in the end. What about adding a dragon that can stabilize itself on the ground and do mortar fire at the cost of mobility. Or a dragon that can "Snipe" with a zoom in ability. Until things like this are implimented, all of the dragons feel exactly the same.
~ DNA is useless for the time being. Essentially you earn "DNA" points as you rank up, but all you do with it is unlock dragons... which there aren't very many of at the moment. I imagine in the future it will be used to unlock weapons, upgrade dragon specific abilities and such. But for now its next to useless.
In the end I can say this, as long as the devs continue to make improvements, and don't RUIN the game with said improvements, I will recommend this game and would spend money on it.
NOTE FOR THE DEVELOPERS: Should you guys decide to implement a Microtransaction system for the game... there is only ONE way to do it without making players angry or making your game Pay to Win. The purchasable content can ONLY be cosmetic items... ONLY cosmetic items... such as dragon skins, weapon skins, etc. Customizable items will still make you money without making the game Pay to Win and thus losing and angering your player base.

tl;dr: It leaves you feeling like you just played the underwhelming pilot episode of a spin-off series on the blockbuster that was Human Revolution.
===============================
Damnit... my heart has just been broken...
[(partial) SPOILERS]
Just spent 20 hours playing the game, thrilled to be back in the Deus Ex universe, waiting to be awed by all the pretties and shinies that we've come to expect from this studio. Unfortunately, to my shocked surprise, the game simply ends with the most depressing slideshow of "micro-documentary storyline wrapups" since fallout 3 after defeating an apparently minor henchman in the first bossfight of the game (and what felt like at most 1/3 of the storyline).
They got the gameplay right, same as Human Revolution, just wonderfully smooth. And save for the forgivable minor buggyness here and there, it plays like a charm.
But everything that made the that game tower out above all others at the time for me:
- The sweeping globalised storyline unravelling before your eyes
- The incredibly rich locales, befitting this brand new reality
- Futurism and incredible tech pouring from ever nook and cranny of the world
... is utterly absent from Mankind Divided, making the environments positively dull.
All of the game is set in the same grey slum they label Prague (not the Prague I've visited, I'll tell you) with next to no unique, awe-inspiring, or interesting locations to be found. The sidequests are mostly running around in this drab place, and almost none of the amazing places you hear about (or even see in the distance) all over the freaking place are visited. (hint hint: DLC, expansions, sequel material coming up! Yay.....)
The main storyline starts off reasonably ok (a bit slow and running simulatorish) but only really gets going after hours and hours of introduction, and then just cuts off on a horribly jarring note as mentioned. A dozen storylines all over the place are just dropped or sloppily explained away in the horrifically cheap ending cinematic, leaving you with a complete sense of "What...? That's it...?".
Hence, it leaves you feeling like you just played the underwhelming pilot episode of a spin-off series on the blockbuster that was Human Revolution.
===============================
I want to recommend it as the gameplay is still perfectly solid, as in the last game. But knowing that they are capable of so much more than this is what decides it. Living up to the hype is impossible and living up to Human Revolution is right next to that, I fully get that. But this was just so... so much less..
Just wait till the next sale I guess, give it a try, maybe the DLC will save it in some minor way.

I'm editing this review because I was able to get the game running and here's how:
If you're crashing after the initial splash screens but before the actual start menu like I was, try running a utility called DDU from
. Its a free program that completely strips display drivers off your machine, including any fragments left in the registry from previous updates or cards. I also deleted (all files, including leftovers from Steam uninstall) and reinstalled DXMD.
After, install the latest drivers for your card and give Deus Ex another shot.
This worked after I had run all the other options, including DLC on/off, turning all settings to lowest possible, updating drivers (before using DDU), running the DXMD.exe as admin, disabling steam overlay, verifying cache, redownloading and more.
