Review - Holdfast : Nations At War
Before i bought this game, i have this state of doubt whether to buy it or not to buy it. Because not only it's an early acces game, but i'm afraid if the gameplay is too repetitive. And after play it for 24 hours, here's my review of the game.
[ Graphic ]
The graphic of the game is very nice. I am stunned by how beautiful the map is. And i really love that there's a dynamic weather system in the game, like it can sometimes be snowy, and the snow is kinda build up on the ground by time. The vfx is very nice.
[ Gameplay ]
The gameplay is the one that surprised me. At first, i thought the game will be somehow like M&B : Warband multplayer, where the player just run around go for the kill. But no. Even on non-event and non-regiment battle, it is very possible that there will be someone who take the lead and lead a whole regiment complete with line infantry, musician, doctor and such. Each game played differently, even tho we played at the same map. I really don't feel the repetitive feeling too much.
The game has class system where you choose your role. I like the fact that there's a class for Flag bearer, musician, carpenter, surgeon, officer, etc. The dev make a good job by adding those and really make most of them fuctionable and has their own system on how to get points without killing enemy (as they are support unit). Why most ? because some of them are now exist just to be there. Like, surgeon didn't get heal point at the moment. The chance where you need a healing from a surgeon is very low, making the point of having one is optional because when you get shot, you will most likely died instantly. And carpenter is just there for now, i know the dev are still developing them but this is an early acces review.
The thing that is not good yet is the combat system. The shooting i find a bit weird sometimes. Like i can occasionally get a 80m shot while the other time i miss a guy 8m infront of me even tho i aim exactly in the center. Probably caused by movement, but the system of the hit box is still weird a bit. The melee is not the best. To get a kill with melee for now required understanding on where to hit and luck.
The speaker system is great. It really add more atmosphere to the game.
[ Player Base ]
Player base is one of the most important aspect of multiplayer game like this. By far, what i can say about the player base that is currently in the game is pretty nice. As i mention earlier, the players will likely group up as a team and attack together if only someone dare to take the lead. And there are also regiments where people can be an official member of one regiment and play together as a regiment on events, experience events in a very coordinated but fun play. Well, expect a few jerk that run around, using their speaker to play some random loud irritating music, but you can mute them anyway. And for now, you can at least find a room full or 3/4 full every time throughout the day.
[ Server ]
I play this from SEA area, and as i expect the dev doesnt really have a server on this area (or if there is, not enough player playing on it) and i can get ping from 180-300 sometimes. Even tho with that ping, the game still runs well, i can still get kills and rarely have a lag issue.
[ Conclusion ]
The game is very nice, even tho at it current state.
Do i recommend the game for it's price ? Yes. Kinda. I mean its not too good not too bad.
I really hope that the dev add more feature to the game very soon like cavalry unit, refine the melee system, and things like that.
And also i hope the dev do a marketing on it, so that they can get more players to play. Because without players, this game will die.

Before its release to Steam, I played hours upon hours of Kingdoms of Amalur for the Xbox 360, and I can tell you my experiences with this game had me loving it more and more each time I played it. KoA is a fresh take on the RPG Adventure games we're so used to playing, this one in particular giving us a very unique character that develops based upon your choices and decisions. Instead of listing the pro's and con's of this game in a bullet layered format, I'll instead give an in-depth analysis of what this game has to offer for you potential buyers!
Main Story:
Right off the bat, the main story line leaves you in suspense as you traverse further to figure out 'Who you really are', and 'What really happened.' I will refrain from giving out spoilers, but the entirety of the main quest line has an interesting plot, in which the character has many ways of going about, all leading up until that moment where you fulfill your goals and get your questions answered! The questline is not generic in any way, other than the fact that you find yourself broken, defeated, and lost in a world in which you have to learn, once again, about where you came from, and what it is you're meant to do. All of this becomes apparent as you meet new key characters along the way that help guide you on your path without giving you too much to lean on in the beginning of the game. That being said, delving into the questline in order to find the truth was truly captivating to me, and I enjoyed each and every quest from start to finish.
Side Quests:
While the side quests are always completely optional, I can't stress it enough that actually taking the time to do them is both fun and rewarding! Several factions are mapped out across The Faelands that have their own unique and interesting questlines, not to mention the incredible rewards each has to give! These Factions are not the only side quests given within the game, as there are other civilian and non-dynamic character quests that are given throughout the entire game. Some quests can be tedious, but unlike other games, these tedious quests truly do reap great rewards for the character. Not only will completing a quest leave you with a bit more gold in your pocket, or an extra item to equip, but completing these side quests will increase your relationship with other npc's, sometimes so much so that they will be willing to share a few items of their own with you. All in all, the side quests are incredibly refreshing, and add a bit more flavor to the game when you're not so interested in just following the main story line.
Dungeons:
This is something that I can't really express much love or hate for, as the dungeons in Kingdoms of Amalur were honestly satisfactory, for me at least. Each dungeon, while very different, had extremely generic layouts and areas that had no unique flavor setting them apart, other than perhaps the loot acquired from each of them. Don't get me wrong, the layout is beautiful and it does give you that dungeonesque feeling, but when it comes down to it, I just don't feel like they added enough diversity. Other than the aesthetics, the rewards given in each dungeon speak of their own value, as you'll never be left empty-handed for completing one.
Combat system:
I've finally reached my favorite aspect of the game... the combat. I absolutely love the combat to this game, possibly due to the fact that, well, its insanely unique! There are no set combos or time frames that it takes for your character to swing or attack. YOU attack when YOU want to attack, and this aspect of combat really gives you a sense of control and realism with your character. The different weapons and unique patterns of attacks offered for each type of weapon is absolutely awestriking. My first time using the chakrams and seeing how flashy and insane the moveset was really set that weapon apart from the rest. Not only do you have the ability to create your own combinations, you can tie your combination in with two different weapons, making the number of combinations unexhaustable. A staff and a sword, or a chakram and a great hammer, a wand, a greatsword, faeblades, a bow, so on and so forth! This all ties in well with the fact that you are not limited by your imagination to throw magic, or any spells in the mix. This truly gives your character a sense of value, as you are, within reason, your own, indistinguishable person.
Gear/Crafting:
I really enjoyed some of the gear sets in the game, and you always have that excited feeling when you pick up a piece that has better stats, and just looks plain awesome! Starting out, your gear will obviously be mediocre, but that doesn't take away the fact that these sets 'get the job done.' Each new piece of gear is unique in its own way, and when we add gem sockets and enchants to the mix, you will find an entirely different craft all together. The crafting system works in a systematic way where you'll need to acquire several pieces of equipment that have 'matching qualities' before you can create your new weapon or armor piece. Of course, this goes without saying, the better equipment you have and the higher your skill, the better your gear will be when you make that fresh new piece. Adding gems to gear in order to give your character some type of buff, whether it be increased mana, or extra burn damage, etc, is always satisfying, and lets not forget to mention... You can name a piece after you craft it. I don't know about you, but I love giving names to gear of my craft to give it that unique and one of a kind feeling. All in all, the gear in the game is not sorely lacking, but I will say that there was room for improvement on the aestheitc aspect of it, such as maybe adding more flair to a crafted piece or unique piece, but that aside, the gear in the game, as well as the crafting system, is rather balanced.
Skill Tree/Perks:
Could I go ON about how I love the skill tree in this game... While there are not an infinite number of talents, there sure seems to be an infinite number of ways you can build your character. With the three main skill trees, (Might, Finesse, and Sorcery) you can literally build your character any way you want. There are multiple different fate cards for each type of build, so there is never a scenario where you'll feel unrewarded for going into this tree, that tree, and the other. You will always be compensated for the way you spec, so much so that you'll recieve your own unique buff while you traverse farther down your own unique spec. The perks, too, have very rewarding qualities to them, giving you a plethora of options for how you want to build your character so they fit to your liking. Whether it be increased chance to lock pick, or finding hidden treasures with ease, all of these different perks really are rewarding in their own way.
There are many other aspects of this game that can be talked about, but I believe that the true value of this games comes within the eye of the beholder, so I'll stop this review here. If you're looking for a fun, refreshing game, Kingdoms of Amalur brings the package to the table. The cartoonish graphics and unique gameplay give this game its own unique flair, and the story only becomes more exciting with the DLC content as you explore different and unique areas to the game with their own interesting storylines and rewards! I hope this basic review helps you decide whether or not you want to take a peek at KoA: Reckoning. With that being said, I wish you luck, fateless ones!

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is focused on its combat sections which have you pressing roughly 3 buttons repeatedly. It's boring, repetitive, and really isn't fun. You always melee and only use your gun part for either parts of combos that are preset or for the incredibly weak enemies. Enemies are meat sponges that eat up most of your hits and the later levels really like spamming the tankiest enemies. Combine that with the lack of really interesting combos to shake up the gameplay, and you've got yourself something really, really, really bland. And keep in mind there are 10 levels to play through, which means a lot of button mashing. Honestly really disappointing since the RWBY series is known for its combat scenes.
Subpar. The game looks nice on occasion but there are many moments when you see some questionable textures and images. I suppose it doesn't really affect gameplay, but sometimes some things just don't look right.
Performance was subpar. The graphics aren't exactly amazing but I still got a little bit of frame drop at lowest settings. It feels more like a "me" problem, but I swear this game just doesn't seem well optimized. I recommend a good look at the recommended settings.
It's a pretty good soundtrack but sort of disappointing for what it is, considering it's RWBY. Jeff Williams, as usual, comes in to make a rocking set of songs which are nice to the ears, but gets a bit clouded when you keep on listening to them for a while (and trust me, with how drawn out some levels are, you'll really be hearing the songs). There isn't really much to the soundtrack itself though. A part of me feels like it could have had more done but I suppose that's just me.
It's really, really questionable to be buying this game, especially at full price. $24.99 for the game really doesn't cut it when the game is just the same gameplay repeated 10 times, for 10 levels. It'll probably be fun for one campaign run, and then you'll never play it ever again, with very little replay value.
I wouldn't recommend this game, even if you are a big RWBY fan. The RWBY series is nice and the game market for it has a lot of potential, but RWBY: Grimm Eclipse simply doesn't take that potential to heart.

Now, I love the RWBY series. I like the story and mythos. However, I cannot recommend the game currently. For starters, I got this game during the summer sale and I only played about 85 mins. It was about $10 when I got it and I notice something pretty weird. Previously, this game started as $15. After an update, it went to $20. Now it is $25. Hopefully this is its final stand but it is pretty strange to rise your price over time when other games from early access stayed the same price at full release. Now other than that, lets go over the pro's and con's of this game. Note: This is quite lengthy, so I will make a short review on it at the bottom.
Pro's:
1. Models: So far, the models have reverted back to their early state, which is very similar to the show models. That is an improvement considering the small controversy on the model change upon the first major update, making the models look a bit dated and weird.
2. Combat: The combat in this game is more of a hack and slash, so if you are not into hack and slash, this will get boring fast. However, the combat animations are on point and show off the characters movesets. Each have their signature style of combat and it shows the amount of effort put in to work on the combat animations to resemble those from the show.
3. Graphics: The looks and art style of the show are here in the game. It is bright, colorful. While most are recycled and quite dull at times, it is obvious the developers want you to feel like you are in the shows universe.
4. Voice-acting: The voice acting is great. Some points, not so much, but mostly well spoken and similar to the show.
Con's:
1. Lack of content: Now as I said, this is a hack and slash and it does get quite samey. You got repeated monsters and not much variation than mash buttons to win. However, not much has really changed from its early access to its release. So far, only more maps were added to the story. So if you wanted more characters other than team RWBY, you are out of luck.
2. Price: The price point of this game is ridiculous. For $25, this will feel shallow unless you are planning multiple playthroughs with all 4 members of RWBY and can withstand the grind. Other than that, this game feels like a $15 game than a $25. I would hold on to your money and wait for either more content or till the price drops.
3. No new characters: Now, on the news, it is stated that upon the full release new characters will be added. Where are they? There is still the same team RWBY available. Now I understand that making the models and animations are tough but when you advertise and promise to have new characters upon launch, I expect it. Because of this, some consumers are more wary of the developers and holding off when they cannot withhold the promises they made upon launch. Now they did state that more characters will be added for free later on but I cannot accept the fact that no new characters were available on launch.
4. Combat upgrades: Now, it is no suprise that the game has a level up system in it to upgrade whichever character you play, however, the pre-requisites are out of proportion. 300 range kills? 150 ult kills? Now, this may not seem like a lot to others but when you are playing 4 player co-op, with everyone running off like headless chickens taking your kills, it becomes a chore to get there. Sure, you can play with friends and ask them to let you take the last hit kills to level up but in random matches, it is quite difficult to accumilate. "But the game has singleplayer cross-connection. Wouldn't that mean you can level up in singleplayer as well to get the level ups?" Yes but not that the game raises the difficulty the more players there are in the match, and by raising the difficulty, it means spawning more things. So in singleplayer, you may only accumulate about roughly 60-70 kills at bestor you can join a 4 player co-op and rack up 200-250 kills (that is if you get most of the kills itself). So you will need to grind hard and make sure you are not spamming the attack buttons to try get the unlocks itself because for most new players, it will become quite difficult to not mash the attack button just to get 1 more range kill.
5. Story: Story is mediocore at best. It is in between season 2 and season 3. It is quite dull and you will not care much about it at all later on as it becomes obvious and see plot lines from miles away.
!TL:DR!
Pro's:
good models
great voice acting
has the feel of the universe
good hack and slash combat
Con's:
bare content
ridiculous price
no Neopolitan (I cry everytime ;~;)
grindy upgrades
meh story
All in all, its not a terrible game, not in the long mile but it is quite lacking. Its like drinking soda. You can drink as much as you want but you will always feel a bit lacking or wanting more by the end. Overall, I would say it is about 5/10 at the current state. It's not groundbreaking standards but not♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I would save your money and wait till it hits a sale for about $15 or $10 or wait for more content to release. Thankfully, most of the updates will be free but this is most likely like Titanfall, you will power it up only to play about 1-3 matches at best.

Let me start out by saying I love this game. While there may seem to be some bias, I'll try to keep it as factual as possible.
While most games you see today have incredibly advanced gameplay, graphics, and complex strategies, Shoppe Keep is a game that can be offered to everyone because it is none of that. When I say that, I mean it in the sense that it's easy to understand, has simple graphics that still look good, and contains strategies that can be as complex or simple as you make them.
The beginning of the game starts you out as the owner of a brand new shop. After having paid a lot of money for the shop space, you now only have 60 gold to start with. From there, the world is your oyster as you take a few pedestals and some health potions and turn it into an expansive shop serving many different classes. Cater to Warriors, Mages, Rogues and Druids who all have their own unique tiered weapon and armor sets that are unlocked with upgrade points. Upgrade points can also unlock different kinds of furniture and perks that can help you sell more items, deal with pesky thieves or barbarians, or earn you more gold.
Selling items is not the only activity you do. To keep it short, you can repair furniture, kill thieves and barbarians, sweep up bodies and dirt on the floor, track the store's inventory and order more items, use alchemy to unlock and brew special items, grind down items for resources, send out a champion to dungeons and discover epic loot, farm your own crops to sell, and search trash bins outside in the village to find goodies. That's keeping the list short, and the developers have plenty more ideas to add to the game.
The developers are some of the most active I have ever witnessed for any game here on steam. Most discussions they will reply to if they have something to add to the discussion, usually within 24 hours. Some bugs that I submitted got answered within 30 minutes, and the developer who worked with me when dealing with an exploitation bug I discovered was very polite and courteous in our private discussion. They always have something nice to say, and speak in a mature manner. You can also tell that they're very passionate in this game by how much time the developer Arvydas puts into patching bugs and releasing hot fixes quickly after any update to address game-breaking bugs. (Every update to any game has bugs, let's face it.)
To top it all off, the community is very active and offers many suggestions and guidance in the threads players post. To put it in perspective, in the past week, the Shoppe Keep community has been one of the most active of any game on Steam. The community grows larger every day, with more and more people willing to give insight on problems and potential additions alike.
In the end, even though many people dislike the game for how simple it is, I personally enjoy a break from fast-paced action games. Here's some pros and cons:
Pros:
- Simple yet complex
- Simple graphics that still look good
- Easy to understand controls
- Takes patience to progress through the game
- Many different activities to partake in besides just selling items
- Order from a vast catalogue of armor, weapons, and other items
- Expand your shop to add an array of different furniture to display your items to be sold
- Responsive developers to help you with troubleshooting
- Engaged community to criticize and praise suggestions or offer assistance in understanding the game
Cons:
- Graphics and customer AI feel like they were made for the MVP (minimum-viable-product) and haven't been changed since
- Lack of consistent controller support (devs are constantly working on solving the problems, however the fixes are leading to technical bugs in keyboard versions)
- Some UI incompatibility where text is hard to read or blocked by other text
- Certain mechanics make no sense, however they will most likely be updated in the future (notably farming, where crops grow in 30 seconds it seems)
- Issues with GFX and FPS (most often solved by changing various graphical settings, but could still not exist as a whole)
Would you recommend this game?: Yes. For the $10 cost, this game is great and has a lot of potential to become even better.
Highly recommended.  Came for Jack Black and stayed for the awesomeness.

If you are buying this game for a good singleplayer experience, it is the game for you.
If you are buying it to have some great fun online, do not buy this game.
The singleplayer itself is very good, with a really nice storyline that revolves around three characters. You get to see what happens in their lives individually, and see them come together on missions. It is not a quick storymode experience if you plan to 100% the game. You are a bit limited to what you can do in the storymode however, which is the only turn off. You cannot change the main character's cars, you cannot share money with each character (so you are unable to 'main' one character), it isn't very easy to make money towards the end of the game. You do however make a large amount at the very end, but it goes quick and is not easy to make back up again.
The multiplayer isn't the worst thing I have ever seen, but it definitely is something to look past when purchasing this game. From high-leveled, rich players killing you constantly, a broken matchmaking system that takes forever to fill up, extremely long loading screens in the online menus if you don't have a SSD, players in your group doing something stupid and then you fail the mission, or even the constant grind to get anything very good. It is clear that the developers are digging a hole for themselves as they add more and more expensive stuff to multiplayer, expecting people to put 100s of hours into the game just to buy something. Of course, you can always buy one of those microtransactions. You know, the thing that EVERY SINGLE GTA V player asked for when they spent 30-60 dollars on this game. "Yes Rockstar Games, I would love to spend more money on in-game currency after buying your $60 game that is nowhere near worth $60."
Pick up the game when it is on sale. It isn't worth more than $30.

The story is excellent albeit perhaps a smaller scope than Human Revolution. The locations are packed wth more things to find and more interesting side missions. The world is fuller. The graphics are beautiful. There are multiple options for tackling everything and many tough decisions with harsh consequences but no clear right and wrong to choose from. I'm enjoying this as much or more than Human Revolution and as someone who played the original Deus Ex way back when, I think it carries the torch well.
Ignore the cries about microtransactions. Yes they exist. But they are totally unnecessary. If I hadn't seen the whining, I wouldn't know they existed. They are hidden away in the front menu and never brought up in-game. As for pre-order perks. Who cares? Apparently some of the items are a one-time unlock. So if that truly bothers you (and nothing in the pre-order perks is really that game changing), do a run through using none of the perks and that will unlock the hardest difficulty. Then start a new game on the hardest difficulty, take all the perks out of "storage" and save the game before doing anything else. Voila! You can now come back to this saved game with all the perks and do any sort of run through you like on any difficulty you like.
This game is just slightly shy of a masterpiece. I'd like to have seen the world expanded a bit wider, but the locations are so dense, it's hardly a drawback. It's a compelling a worthy sequel and brings a lot of good to the franchise. If you liked Human Revolution, I think you'll like Mankind Divided.

I came into Brothers expecting something along the lines of a pretty little by-the-numbers platformer. What I got was a game with a truly unique central mechanic (the simaltaneous 2 character control scheme) and an emotionally captivating adventure built around it. The experience is only around 3 hours long, but many 20+ hour games struggle to contain as many memorable moments as this one. Beautiful.

Pros:
The game overall is gorgeous - possibly one of the most beautiful games I've played.
Likewise the music is extremely well done as well and boasts one hell of a soundtrack I'll have to pick up.
There's also a powerful story here.
Possibly one of the best uses of the dual analog sticks I've seen.
Cons:
While the dual analog sticks are a must keeping track of both brothers movements at the same time can be a challenge in itself. Fortunately very few if any of the games mechanics rely on QTE that requires you to move both at once in a confusing way.
Also the game isn't the most intuitive with what it wants you to do at times and, for me, got me killed on occasion which took my mind  out of the game.
--
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a game that tells the story of two brothers who are on a quest to find a tincture to save their sick father. The two brothers go out into a world and go through caves, giant castles and other fantasy/fairy tale vistas in their travels.
Having recently gone through Journey on my PS3 for a second time I can't help but feel that the two games try to accomplish much the same thing. Both try to get you into the game with a minimum of distractions and both are fairly short. This one chimed in at just shy of 4 hours for me. Both are gorgeous and with great music.
Brothers, in its defense is a bit more complex and has a lot more going on in that you control two brothers who must overcome various challenges and should you fail in the process the consequence is often death followed by automatically taking you back to a recent checkpoint. None of the challenges are difficult as the game, like Journey, wants the focus to remain on the narrative/story than on any sort of real challenge. They even go so far as to giving you only a few different things to use to control the game. The left and right bumpers will rotate the camera (when possible), the dual analog sticks control the older and younger brother while the left and right triggers function as an "interact" button for the older and younger brother respectively. Personally I think I might have preferred a second interact button for them. Oftentimes the game has you press the Interact button only to quickly release it and jam on it again in order to jump from one ledge to another. I feel that pressing and holding one while tapping on a secondary button might have been easier and certainly would have made me feel more comfortable in the process. As well, the game doesn't do a very good job at explaining what needs to happen at a couple critical times. I'm not comfortable spelling this out as I would consider these spoilers but needless to say it wasn't intuitive and for one of those I actually had to look up what I needed to do because anything else did not make sense logically to me. When someone has to do that in a game whose focus and desire is to keep you immersed for the duration of the game I can't help but feel it fails a bit as a result.
In the end the game mostly accomplishes its task of telling this tale. With a touch more focus on communicating to the player at what needs to be done at certain moments this would be a nearly perfect game. As it stands, I'd give it an 8.9/10. It's a damn good game but falls short of blowing me away nor is it one I'll remember much of a year from now.

You can spend this money to hire recruits and warriors who also level up into greater units as they survive alongside you. Pick and choose your battles, what towns to pillage and loot, what factions to make truces with, and how you develop your name whether it be positive or negative.
What captures my heart and makes this the greatest gave I've ever played is the fact that you make your own choices at every turn when it comes to character development and your relations with utterly countles NPCs. These relationships are valuable, as everyone's destiny seems to be intertwined on some level or another. Personally, I complete tasks for specific factions while looting the towns of their enemies in order to build safe havens of reputation to prosper in while having a large and well defined enemy. You might run into a skirmish between two factions and join right in, choosing a side to help and earning you prestigue with the faction you aid. While the battles are presented simply, don't let the graphics fool you. Skill points and the user's own dexterity come into play as you battle in real time, hearing arrows fly past your head and men scream as they charge you. You'll come up with your own tactics of combat the more you get the feel for how the intuitive combat system plays.
The best part that keeps me playing each day - I get to befriend Noble races while slaughtering arabs. Nothing thrills me more than pillaging an arab town, killing their villagers, raizing the village as I leave and returning to Noble cities to sell and trade the loot. Nothing tops the freedom to slay dirty mussies.

Early Access Watcher Re-Reviews RWBY: Grimm Eclipse
Full Release Edition
Full Edition Play-through:
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer prior to full release and was previously reviewed once.
Team RWBY finally reaches the end of the line in their between season excursion and also locate the exit from Early Access to full release. It has been almost eight months since the all-star team from Beacon Academy entered the program and seems to have struggled a bit after some major facial work. They have grown over the course of their training, however, with a reinforced combat system eliminating some of the mundane motions of engagements. Should this 2.5 adventure have stayed in the archives a little longer though? Grab a bowl full of giant fish and embrace the Yang puns as the crippling truth behind this adventure come to light.
Once I was done running through the campaign on multiplayer, I realized this was all there was too offer. I managed to complete the ten chapters in two hours and fifteen minutes without any real trouble difficulty wise. The campaign is suppose to be played multiple times, but the routine is exhausting after awhile and ends up becoming an endurance test instead of a skill-based encounter. I think this fatigue system adds to the overall problem of the content argument. Originally, in the Early Access plan description on the store page, they mentioned three campaigns with four levels each as the final product. I honestly believe this would have been a better idea, due to the fatigue being easier to manage in shorter dosages. The newly added RANKED system works in the same way as Call of Duty's Prestige Mode and grants your character a rank for completing challenges at the cost of resetting progress. This makes the appeal of replaying the campaign increase or decrease depending on how you feel about progress wipes. As it stands now, the campaign is just to short to qualify the current price and might prove monotonous for many to attempt retreads.
Combat has changed for the better since the first review, but it still lacks the same problems that make playing this game for more than thirty minutes a chore. Each character has a set of light/ heavy attack combos, one ultimate, a ranged attack and aerial moves. While it is better than the single button spam originally available, the lack of progress in attack variety gives little uniqueness to the combat system or needed growth to keep everything fresh. The current upgrade system (max level of 10 with a point per level for skills) allows you to change the properties of your current attacks or increase your recovery times from critical damage. This means you will be using the same three combos and never progress from it. This can make combat dull rather quickly, even if some of the ultimates do feel satisfying to watch.
Sound design is a hit and miss scenario with the majority being done properly. Music levels and voice acting were audible at decent levels, except for a couple of lines during Forever Fall that were almost silent. Music did suffer some strange fallout during Technical Difficulties, sounding as if it lost the partial audio production. Sound effects for basic attacks and special moves were fine, destruction feedback was great, and the only real audio imbalance seemed to be from the new spike traps that drowned every other sound out with high pitch metal scraps. If I had to give one award to any attribute for this game, it would definitely be the audio work.
I have been following the issues concerning the remodeling of the RWBY team and I agree they looked better when I reviewed this game the first time. The character models do not have the shine they use to, looking more plastic in movement and look. The color scheme is also much duller, which is the opposite of the vibrant palette used for the attack effects, ultimates, and the newly redesigned Mutated Grimm that have a pristine shine to their aura. Environments share the same lovely detail with beautiful looking forestry and sterile labs. It is a shame the levels are linear with very little clutter (boxes and chess pieces that provide experience). Enemy designs are typical Grimm that hold a very close appearance to their show counterparts. Two robot variations were also added with this release and they both look wonderful. I should mention the game looked better when I reviewed it the first time, but it still looks good. It is a shame some technical issues hold back the graphical appeal.
Frame rate issues are present in the world of Remnant and it isn't just a computer hardware issue. The obvious issue is the underground segment of Mountain Glenn when the vast surge of Grimm decide to take center stage and protect a bomb. The stuttering here could be a cause of the sheer numbers involved, which might also explain why the rationing system is used when releasing Grimm during Wave segments. Another example, but with greatly reduced numbers, is the lab serum segment in Chapter 9 and could be a result of the consecutive explosions. I also noticed random dips during Wave segments across most levels and during transitions into cutscenes. It feels a little more time spent optimizing the game might have fixed some of these issues.
Plenty of random issues plague the game from long start up issues to failed team attack executions. Achievements also seem to be flailing up even if you hadn't earned it, or just won't give you the achievements you did earn. Counter attacks can fail to execute and will end up teleporting you to the enemy instead. I personally have not experiencing anything else, but there are reports of glitches in terrain, reviving command not registering, and screen freezing. I recommend taking these claims with a grain of salt, but only due to my play rough not showing anything I just mentioned.
I am usually not a stickler for story, but I will admit the overall story provided was rather disappointing. I will try to keep this as spoiler free as possible, but the evil character's motivations were not fleshed out nor was the character itself. The whole experience felt more like a random episode of a 80s cartoon show and wrapped up with little closure. The final boss also left something to be desired. There was no real danger established by the events of this little adventure and nothing is really added to the canon of the series. I cannot judge the use of the story or really penalize the game for it, but it is good to know what you are getting into if your a fan of the series.
I managed to watch all three seasons of RWBY before reviewing this game and was rather pleased with how well the show grew in terms of graphical refinement, voice acting and story. While I am far from a fan, I know when to give credit to a studio for putting out a quality project. Unfortunately, that same level of detail found in the show is just not found beneath the layers of this endeavor. Content suffers from a short campaign and a lack of additional distractions, which does not warrant the current asking price. Technical issues have also been left to fester without the optimization needed to control them. Team RWBY would have greatly benefited from a couple more months honing their skills in Early Access, but as it stands this group of students have bit off more than they could chew. The final verdict for RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a standard pass. Let this be a lesson that Early Access should never be judged by the potential it might posses, but by the merits it holds at the current moment. What was yesterday, is destined to be different tomorrow.
Pros
- Environments and effects look great
- Music and voice overs hit their mark most of the time
- Combat is engaging in small doses
Cons
- Content is complete around the 2hr mark
- Combat fatigue sets in very quickly
- Loading screen issues, Start-up issues
- Frame rate issues

First off, the UI is definitely great, The bars and the character icon is upgraded and it shows the other user's level but I had one thing on my mind, why didn't they just add a health bar and ultimate bar there? Surely it would be useful, or otherwise, they had other plans...
Second, Sound is great except some of the effects sounds...okay, I think.
Third, Models....the models, can you fix the clipping (SLIGHT clipping), and the faces?
Fourth, Combat is extremely good, I can reach high combos with all of the 4 characters.
Fifth, I think you're missing one feature, not the Horde mode...*ahem* Where's the semblance? I know that Weiss's and Blake's semblances are present but where are Yang's "damage-absorption" semblance, and Ruby's "ultra-speed ricochet hit something somthing" semblance?
Sixth, I think random monster spawning is not present here, it should be ULTRA RANDOM, like the game where you got inpiration from, Left 4 Dead 2's zombies was extremely random and that was the reason that it had high replayability.

This is my first review on Steam. I've seen a number of reviewers miss what I consider to be the point of a Deus Ex title, so I'm going to lead off with what I feel are the two main things that make Deus Ex, Deus Ex:
- An intricate game world, emphasizing thorough exploration and allowing for a wealth of player choice.
- A nuanced, conspiracy-heavy storyline told as much through email snippets and newspapers as through cutscenes and voice-acted dialogue.
On both these counts, Mankind Divided succeeds. The level design is a step up from Human Revolution, and is arguably on par with the original Deus Ex. The main storyline is serviceable, and well-augmented by an array of emails, newspapers, and more. Blazing through this title in 15-20 hours does it a tremendous disservice, which is a large part of why so many negative reviews are showing up.
That being said, Mankind Divided has a variety of flaws, mostly around the edges. The graphics engine is poorly-optimized, and the game is prone to crashes. The immersion is harmed by insanely stupid unforced errors, such as throwing a microtransaction store into the main menu, or linking the mobile Deus Ex GO into the primary single-player campaign. Interacting with NPCs or your inventory feels clunky, and it's very clear the development team built the control scheme around gamepads.
These are absolutely flaws, but the quality lying at the core of Mankind Divided shines past them. I urge anyone wanting a true Deus Ex experience to give this title a shot. It's not perfect (though a couple of comprehensive patches would go a long way, so the game's not far off), but it's worth the price of admission.
8/10.

Ever wondered what an RPG shopkeeper does when you visit their shop? Then this game answers that question!
Shoppe Keep is a game developed by three people under the name of Strange Fire and published by Excalibur Publishing and Merge Games
The first time this game was announced and I saw the publisher who was publishing this game, I did not have high hopes for the game as the publisher has been known for publishing some bad games and seeing this game in early access, I did not want to purchase it as it didn't look that interesting
Now that the game has come out in full release, I must say that the game is fun and entertaining
You as a shop keeper have the objective of selling items to people whilst keeping your shop free of theives and Barbarians. Over the course of selling items in the game, you will gain XP as well as upgrade points
The game not only offers a builder where you build stalls to display your item, but you also have combat and quests and also cleaning dirt from the worthy customers. I must say that for the simple gameplay, the game is fun to play
The graphics are like that of Borderlands and the graphics are simple. The music is nice yet does tend to repeat after a while. The game runs in days, in those days you have a morning, afternoon and evening cycle where customers flock to your shop
The game is fun however the game can get boring and repetitive after a while since all you do is stay stuck in your shop all the time and cannot do anything else. Thankfully you can leave your shop and enter your home but nothing else, after you unlock the champion, you can send your own champion on adventures but all you do is stay stuck in your shop selling armor, swords and weed... yes weed
The differences I've noticed between Early Access and the full release is huge. The graphics have improved and some mechanics have been improved greatly, however, there are some stuff which have either been removed or changed. Some mechanics such as tax have been removed and the Menu UI and the UI looks ugly and out of place
Overall, Shoppe Keep is an interesting game and very fun to play. If you love simulation/management games, then Shoppe Keep takes that genre to a different unique level

I'm recommending "Rise of the Triad" even though, personally, I find it borderline.  That's really a reflection of my tastes more than anything about the game.  ROTT is more of a hard-core shooter than I'd prefer, and there's a bit too much platforming in it for me.  But, looking at the what the game advertises itself to be, it does its job well.  For the most part, the game mechanics (even the platforming) work just fine and the graphics are great.  And, considering it took me a bit over 42 hours to finish the game on Normal (Medium) difficulty with each level 100% complete, I can't complain about the dollars-to-hours ratio:  the game is well worth the money.
There are some issues with the game, though.  First, even moving away from my preferences, there's still too much platforming in it simply because it's classified as an old-style First-Person Shooter.  Most people buying such a game are not going to be the same people interested in a platformer.  So, there's a bit of audience alienation.  Still, most of the platforming is fine:  some jumps, some bounces, etc..  However, there are some levels that just have too much platforming (most of episode two comes to mind and one of the secret levels is entirely hard-core jumping).  Even worse, in several cases, there were jumps I could not do without making changes to one of the ini files.  Looking at the comments in the discussion area, though, I seem to be the only one suffering from that.  So, it might be something with my system.
Second, there's only one QuickSave spot.  All the rest of the saves are actually checkpoints (three or four per level).  Along with the normal problem with checkpoint systems, there's also the issue that when you hit a checkpoint, you're barred from going back to previous areas (a door will close, or you'll have dropped down to an area you can't jump out of).  And, even worse, there are a few areas where choosing to do things differently than expected will prevent you from getting everything in a area.
Third, QuickSaving, itself, will sometimes cause things to not work correctly.  So, you'll reach the end of a level where you've been QuickSaving for safety, and find that even though you've done everything the game's given you, you're still short a coin or a kill or a secret area.  So, back you go to redo the whole level.
And, finally, the secret areas need to be more findable.  My methodology was to play every level without help first, and looked for all the secrets.  I NEVER succeeded in completing a level 100% on my own (and I'm SLOW -- I've seen comments that one full playthrough should take 15-20 hours (and there's an Achievement for doing it in less than 4 hours):  I took 42 hours).  I absolutely HAD to watch YouTube videos to find everything.  There really needs to be more hinting to make these findable.
Even so, the game is fun enough and long enough to be worth the buy.

Happy about the great success of Torchlight, Torchlight 2 was made and a good competitor to the failed release of Diablo 3.
Almost looking like the first game, they tried to change a lot that went wrong in the first game:
The classes:
Babarian (melee), Outlander (ranged), Embermage (caster), Engineer (dafuq???)
The story:
The alchemist (playable character from the first game) went crazy from the presence of the evil overlord they killed in the first game and starts to lay waste on the world, searching for a cure.
On your way you will encounter 4 villages and 4 different areas, with countless dungeons and open regions. Unlike the first game, it is not a continuing endless dungeon, but a world, with regions and borders. The dungeons are still random generated, but no longer endless.
Every major region you will encounter several bossfights and events.
First being let down by the beta, I tried the game again and saw, that they changed most of the issues that made it from the first into the second game:
- Attributes are now more easy to understand and you always know now, what you are skilling for
- Skilltrees are more logical and you can mix easily abilitys (and more important passives) like you want
- Skills and classes are more balanced, no class is an alone ranger anymore
The endless dungeon is replaced by the map systems, similar to the maps from the first game, where you activate a random short dungeon. Now, every dungeon has a endboss, and every map has prefixes, like + loot or + damage.
Also it has a New Game+ function, where you can restart the campaign on a higher level. You can do that several times until you are at the max enemy level of 105 and your own level of 100.
The problem again is, that you can powergame again with abilitys, that use % of weapon damage. While most abilitys have a fixed damage, those will scale with your weapon and can make insane amounts of bonus damage, outranging all other abilitys. Big looser again, is the Mage with nearly none % abilitys. Big winner is the engineer, that literally can clear the whole screen with one attack.
Having full steam workshop mod support, the game is customizable and fun for longer playing.
(I dont recommend it for achievment hunters, because several achievments are bugged and locked)
very fun if you were disappointed with diablo 3 and want to find a good dungeon crawler, this is the game.

Overall the experience is great and the game offers a lot. Must buy if it's on sale, but you also can't do wrong if you pay the full price.

I bought this game for about five dollars during the summer sale (ignoring wallet funds I obtained through Steam alone to help purchase it). That money was gathered as a precaution; I had watched and read plenty on the Early Access of the game and felt that, even with big improvements, it wouldn't quite be worth ten dollars.
I've completed the full release of the game and unfortunately I still don't think it is, let alone the full twenty-five.
The campaign is about 2.5 hours. It's 10 chapters long, but thanks to the handful of enemy types - most of which have similar attacks and can be killed with the exact same strategy - uninspired level design, and a grand total of one boss, it feels like 3 chapters stretched obscenely far.
All characters play more or less the same. Changing from one to another barely requires different inputs and certainly doesn't require different tactics.
Speaking of inputs I couldn't find any way to rebind my keys. It's to be expected of any full release.
The skill tree seems very small. What's worse is that it feels pointless. There are skills you'd be a sucker not to buy, like one that allows you to revive a teammate in just about one second, and another that lets you store two ultimate attack charges, both of which cost a single skill point.
I can't imagine why I'd ever use a build other than the first I decided on.
Given that the animated series focuses so much on team dynamics, I was hoping for a more engaging system for team attacks. What this game offers is a simple key press to automatically perform one, so long as one of your partners happens to (semi-randomly) trigger the prompt by attacking.
Requiring specific positioning and timing, a more challenging input (that changes depending on who sets up the team attack, perhaps?), combining ultimate attacks for more devastating ones, any of these could have improved the feeling of attacking as a unit.
Leveling your character can be sped up by finding EXP orbs and relics. These are hidden in such a way that you'll probably find all of them on your first run.
Parrying enemies stuns them, interrupting their attacks and causing them to take more damage for a time, but it's almost never preferable to just attacking continuously. On top of this, level up Blake's ranged attack once and suddenly you can stun entire waves of enemies at your leisure.
If you're playing as a big fan of the show you might be disappointed by how little this resembles it. The character models were replaced before release and are extremely rough. On top of this, the characters and environment look like they're from two entirely different video games. This is easily seen by standing next to an urn or crate and moving the camera closer to a wall so that it zooms in.
Yang's arms clip through her hair when she runs. I was certain this would be corrected for the full release. It wasn't. Looks very sloppy.
Shadows, buildings, scenery etc. appear and disappear before your eyes now and then as you're running around.
Most of the sound effects are good. The game uses plenty of music from the show for battle sequences, even the track from Dance Dance Infiltration that kicks♥♥♥♥♥ All characters are voiced by the proper actors.
The only gripe I have is that Blake repeatedly mentioned "floor 1" on a particular chapter, at every floor.
Very dull. The new villain has very little presence. His motivations are a bit of a mystery as well.
This genre doesn't lend itself to storytelling. I think a much simpler plot, focused on chasing down a rival character or team, then fighting them on the last stage would have been more engaging
better for replay value. (Since uncovering a mystery is rarely enjoyable in repetition)
I was hoping to like this game, but I can't recommend it to anyone. Not even big RWBY fans. The price tag is absolutely insulting given the amount of content in the game and the level of depth or polish.
I don't doubt that you worked hard on this game. I hate to imagine how frustrating the negative feedback coming in must be, especially since some design decisions probably weren't yours to make. I hope things work out better for any future projects you end up on.

Full disclosure: I purchased this game while it was in Early access, so it was cheaper when I bought it. That said, most of my points would still stand, even if they hadn't raised the price.
Positives:
Very pretty game. Aesthetically similar to the show it's based on.
Lighting and character models are also good.
Well animated and voiced.
Enemy variety is fairly good, though enemy compositions in individual fights was often repetitive.
Negatives:
Short. I was able to complete the campaign solo in 3.4 hours, and I am not particularly fast in these games.
Levels were extremely linear. With a single exception halfway into the game, there were no branching paths of any kind. Certain levels featured segments where you can go slightly off of the beaten path, but you always have to return to where you went off from. There were also several noticable invisible walls.
Gameplay was generally repetitive. Go to point A, defeat waves of enemies. Go to point B, defend objective while fighting off waves of enemies, rinse and repeat.
Only two boss fights (which is disappointing considering the show it is based on). One was a larger version of a regular enemy with wider-reaching attack patterns. The other was unique, but easy to defeat (it is a melee-based opponent who cannot move while attacking).
Progression system artificially extends the game's life with inflated requirements (most unlocks require 300 kills with a specific attack. Some of these attacks are weak on their own, and are used to start an attack sequence, not finish them. Several require that you repeat the process for each character).
Low level cap means you will never be able to experience the entirety of your character's skill tree at once.
Combat system is basic. You have a melee combo, a charged melee attack, and a ranged combo. You also have an "Ultimate" that is charged by damaging enemies. These Ultimates all take the form of a radial attack that damages enemies around you at the point of casting. Finally, you can parry certain enemy attacks to leave them vulnerable, and counter-attack them for a good amount of damage. This was unreliable in my experience, as pressing the respective buttons for those moves simply teleported me to the enemy in question, without performing the parry/counter-attack.
Movement system lacks smoothness. Jumping and dashing were very "janky".
Enemies tended to be on the damage-spongy side, and all but the most basic ones can block your light attack. Since the light attack combo doesn't do much damage by itself anyway (almost a full combo just to take out a single basic enemy), you will find yourself ignoring it in favour of the heavy charged attack, which bypasses blocks and can be upgraded to open enemies up to counter-attacks.
Finally, the story was lackluster. You find mutant Grimm creatures, talk with the person responsible, and he never explains why he was mutating them. The game also lacks a proper ending. You leave the bad guy's lair on an airship, then... credits. No real resolution of any kind. You don't even get to meet the main antagonist face-to-face.
Hardware-based (these may be different for those with different setups):
The game was largely bugless, but it also had severe performance issues (even on the lowest graphics settings). I lack a framerate display, but I'm fairly certain that it never went above 30. This was compounded by the fact that the options menu was severely lacking. You have 4 graphical presets (from "Potato" to "Ultra"), Ambient Occlusion, and Glare. That's it.
There was also a small amount of input lag. Given the timing-sensitive nature of the parry prompts, this was aggravating.
My computer may not be top-of-the-line, but it's no slouch either. It can run Crysis on maximum settings better than this on the minimum settings. Make of that what you will.
Conclusion: This game is not recommended, even to fans of the show. The gameplay is dull, the story is unsatisfying, and outside of the novelty of playing as team RWBY and visiting some of the locations from the show (which are, admittedly, very nicely rendered. Even on the lowest settings), there really isn't much here. Certainly not enough to warrant 25$/£19/your region's equivalent.
It is unfortunate that Rooster Teeth's first entry into the industry that catapulted them to fame should be so lacking.

To preface, I would have given a negative review in response to the microtransactions and preorder/season pass content, but those two things don't really affect the experience at all.
This game is solid.  This game is a pure sequel to Human Revolution and perfects nearly every aspect of it's predecessor.  The cover system, in my honest but seemingly unpopular opinion, has been improved, save for the bug that occurs when you save a game while in cover.  The hacking minigame is harder and now forces you to find other ways to overcome a situation if your hacking skills aren't up to par.  Your aug upgrades have more meaning to them, and will specialize you for different situations.  Combat and AI is better and more viable for those who want to go in guns-blazing.
In terms of story, this game has a better one than HR, EXCEPT for the ending.  The experience leading up to the ending will definitely differientate from player to player, I've taken about 27 hours, though some have taken 12 and others 40+.  I would suggest taking your time.  The exploration has improved, and the world-building emails and ebooks that defined HR are all there.
Side quests are the real meat here.  Much more than there was in HR, and also more interesting.  If you don't do them, or do a minimal amount of them, I guarantee you will leave the game very dissappointed.
The soundtrack is top-notch.  More stellar work by Michael McCann and newcomer to the series, Sonic Mayhem(Sascha Dikiciyan).
Of course, the game has problems.  Some of the non-hub levels feel short and rushed if you don't explore them, and the main story, while pretty good at the start, really drops in the final hours.  I was able to overlook these issues, though.
If you loved HR, you will love this.  If you are reading this and have not played HR, it's worth picking up before this.  It's rather cheap on sale and will give you a good taste of what to expect here.

This is a brawl style game like Super Smash Bros. and that Sony spin off that nobody remembers. What sets Brawlhalla apart is the little things they do to make the game more of a challenge to defeat your opponents. First off, there is no shield, only a dodge. And it is a heavy 2 second dodge that will leave you vunerable in the wrong situation. Secondly all characters have the ability to triple jump! If you expend your jumps you will fall to your doom. That is ofcourse if you dont manage to grab onto a wall. That's right! The fourth thing that sets it apart is that all characters can cling onto the walls and wall jump. Once you cling onto a wall your jumps get reset. The 5th and final thing is that your opponents cannot use your weapons that you might accidently drop/throw.
Gameplay 8/10 (higher when lag issues are resolved)
Graphics 10/10 (Can't see em getting better or any need to get better)
Music 7/10 (It's good and can't wait to the addition of more tracks)
Weapons 8/10 (I believe there are 6 to 7 wepons so far. 4 equippables and 3 useable. Each equippable has there own unique flavor. Adding more weapons could improve the game or take it a step back)
Characters 8/10 (Each character has their own stats and play style.)
Replayability 10/10 (Great game to play with friends and can only improve)
All in all this is looking out to be a very good fun game that can only get better. And one that is worthy of your support.

I'm writing this as the Sims 4 is out, but this one is still worth your while or if you are considering getting into the SIms, just read the review for the story so far.
SIms allows you to create and guide the lives of a Sim single, or family through the course of their daily life. You can build homes for them, decorate, manage their daily activities like work and play and develop skills that help them in their life.
The Sims for the most part are autonomous meaning that they will act in the interests of their own self preservation if left alone (and they have the sufficient skills to take care of themselves). Guiding them during the game play slowly equates to developing good habits they need to survive in life although there are some of the real life missing elements like trolls and troll groups, the challenges there provide a good foundation for learning much need life skills and balance of the basic elements in life. It also encourages creativity in your own real life (for instance it might get you thinking that a night out to dinner and a movie every once in while is imperative to your health at some important social level).
All in all it encourages healthy lifestyle decisions without constraining one to "conformity" and rewards them.
One of the best and most fun aspects of the Sims line of games is designing your Sim. During this process you can choose the physical, mental and emotional characteristics of your Sims even giving them a background story. This can really flesh them out and once again what a wonderful tool for character exploration.
In Sims 4, they've really added some new features to the Sims you can create which allow for intelligent emotional lives as well. Sims 3 still holds its ground if you're on a limited budget and want to try a game from the Sims franchinse.
There's an online store as well that you can make purchases for your Sims and from time to time they offer free seasonal items for the holidays that you can use to decorate your Sims dwellings for that time of year.
One of the nice things about Sims is that if your looking for a change in pace from the action genre, this one would be a good start as its pacing is anything but tense and stressful bar trying to wake your Sim up in time to get ready for their day. Still challenging and magnetic gameplay that will keep you coming back.
When you return to your action game, it will have a bit of zest put into it by the change in pace. You might even consider that the baddies you're blasting away have simulated families somewhere who are depending on that baddie to get rid of you and make it home safely. You might end up developing a bit of a complex and conscience about it. Read Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥s "Do Androids Dream Of Electric Sheep?" aka Bladerunner and you'll get what I mean.
These Sims are pretty darn convincing in ways, but don't put them through the Voight-Kampf or Turing test.
You might spoil the illusion.
Highly recommended.

DISCLAIMER: This is my first ever review. Please forgive me if my spelling or grammar is incorrect.
Let me start by saying that this is not a 10 hour game experience.
This game is roughly 2 to 3 hours of playtime.
It is a story of two brothers who make a long journey, trying to find a cure for their sick father.
It is mostly a casual game trying to pass some very deep meanings and emotions in way that sets it aside from the norm (breaks many cliches).
I am not gonna spoil anything. I'm just saying that if you are willing to give this one a try, have a pair of tissues in close proximity.
I am not going to grade any of the aspects of the game, because I believe that numerical grading is a flawed way of sharing your experience. Instead, I am going to put my experience into words as best as I can.
The graphics are very stylish and, along with an excelent sound design keep the the ambience of the game constant and fluid. The soundtrack is also top notch and well executed.
The controls are as simple as they get (not much to say here), though they are not the core of the game. Rather, they are a guide for helping you experience the feeling and tension of the game.
The story( which is the meat of the game) is  simple yet deep and compeling. Almost like reading a very good short novel. You want to finish it in one go (which is what I did)
All in all, I find Brothers: A tale of two sons to be an excelent game. I haven't regretted a single euro of my purchasing of this game, even though it's a short one.
A really good game, a beauty to look at, and a bittersweet storyline.  Although it's fairly short it's a journey I'm glad I've taken.

I haven't played enough of the game yet but I cannot wait to write the review since this game is simply fantastic. I wish they would have created a sequel and this time fix a few of the issues that people didn't like with the original game.
+MASSIVE World, especially with DLC. I cannot stress this enough.
+Quests, quests, quests, quests, and even more quests. Too many quests honestly.
+You can make your character look bada**. And I mean real bada**. Not from the middle or near the end, no, right from the beginning itself. You can make him/her look batshit crazy.
+Complete customisation. You aren't bound by any rules. You can play your character the way you want to play him. You can even change your class midway through the game if you didn't like the class you're playing with and are too lazy to restart.
-Darn repair system. This ruins it for me, although some might like how it helps keep the player looking for new gear. It gets real annoying when you have to keep repairing your armor/weapons and find new repair kits over and over again.
-Scaling. The game has a really weird enemy level system. Supposing I enter an area at level 2, all enemies in that area, every single one, will be level 2 for the rest of the game. This is why it gets extremely easy in higher levels when you return to old areas.
-Invisible walls. If you're going in expecting complete freedom to roam everywhere in any way you want, you will find other games more appealing than KoAR. There's always that one invisible wall that doesn't let you jump down stairs, ledges, clear open spaces etc.

This game is definitely worth the price because of two reasons:
1. The Combat
2. The time it takes for completion  $5 = atleast 5 hours but in this case you get 200
PROS +
AMAZING COMBAT - Its combat is truly amazing it has great fluidity and just overall is extremly fun without getting boring. I just wish there were more skills for me to try.
GRAPHICS - Although this game was released in 2012 its graphics still look good with a really colourful environment.
OPENWORLD - Just a really nice touch for an rpg.
LOOT - One thing that has always attracted me to rpg's is the loot/ special items you can find in them. KOA Reckoning does a phenominal job with having tons of  rare accessories, weapon and armor sets.
TIME PLAYED - You can play this game for hours because of the sheer amount of quests and the size of its world.
FACTIONS - You recieve special stuff when working with factions. The idea of factions is really cool and even though I like how you can work with all of them there isnt much story for them.
REQUIREMENTS - Works great and doesnt require a top end gpu.
CONS -
STORY - Its story.... well all I can say is that it has one. The story is pretty lack luster and generic in my opinion and the npc's aren't really memorable either.
CAMERA - You miss out on a lot of the beautiful environment because the camera angle is facing downwards on your character.
RNG/BUGS - I've played through this game so many times looking for all armor sets but due to some unlucky bugs that make chests impossible to open I always quit halfway through due to frustration.
BOSSES & Difficulty - The bosses in this game aren't really different from the monsters you fight regularily while playing through the game and the game itself is too easy even on the hardest difficulty.
_______________________________________________________________________________
Overall this game is just great and  really fun to mess around in! I just wish that somehow, someway they can make a sequel to this game.

Tekken 7 finally enters the PC gaming and even though this chapter might not be the strongest title in the franchise it's still the king amongst fighters. Major difference to the rest of the games in the series is the introduction to rage arts and rage drives, features encouraging clutch gameplay. It's a nice new addition and definite game changer as it has effect on both pacing and fighting itself but not everyone might see it as good thing. I, as a matter of fact, don't like the feature but objectively I have to say it's a matter of preference and not necessarily bad thing. Just a different, new thing. I've broken my no pre-order policy for this occasion and once again there were no regrets about buying a Tekken game. Here's the list of good and bad:
+ smooth and enjoyable gameplay, hallmark of Tekken series
+ learning curve, easy to jump in
+ outstanding visuals and animation
+ great optimization and performance
+ big roster, variety of different fighters
+ variety in moves, different martial arts and ways to play
+ practice mode
+ decent customization
+ decent netcode (not ideal but compared to consoles it's heavenly)
+ great work on both port and launch of the game
+ it's Tekken on PC
- many basic features are missing (proper tutorial, replays, quick rematch in player match)
- many elementary modes are missing (no time trial, no survival, no tekken force (!), no team battle (!!)
- some legacy characters absent (Wang dead, Zafina MIA, no Jaycee/Julia/Michelle, no Mokujin (!), no Lei (!!)
- DLC content and politics have been pure♥♥♥♥♥♥so far (season pass owners not getting all DLC and discounts instead, Tekken Bowl)
- short on Story modes and single-player content overall
- Jukebox mode is Playstation exlusive
The absence of elementary features, game modes and fighters that have been part of the game for two decades now is very surprising and quite unpleasant. I can very well understand and live with three 2D characters in the roster but not at expense of missing irreplacable character (or move-set if you will) of fighters like Lei or Julia. Even less I can understand the absence of some very basic and easy to implement offline game modes. I was hoping for Team Battle getting it's online debut and it's not in the game at all for the first time in 20 years, since Tekken 3. In fact, every numbered Tekken game had much more content than Tekken 7... considering how long we had to wait for the port from arcades it just leaves a bitter taste in mouth. That being said, even as hurt as a Tekken fan I am, I still would recommend this game to anybody, especially players that couldn't play Tekken all those years due to the console exclusivity. Unless Tekken 6 or Tekken Tag Tournament 2 gets ported, there will be a long wait until the next Tekken game so you might as well enjoy playing this one till then because despite its flaws, at it's core it's still Tekken, the King of the Iron Fist.

Not only is Tekken 7 the best iteration in the franchise to date, it's also the best fighting game in the current generation of fighters (SFV, KoFXIV, GG:Xrd, MvC:I, MKX) and has the largest PC player base of them all (approximately 60% larger population than Street Fighter V).
If you're looking to sink your teeth into a fighting game, whether you're an absolute beginner to the genre or you're a seasoned veteran of a previous entry or a different franchise, this is the game to get right now.
Alternatively, hold out for the upcoming Dragon Ball FighterZ which has shown significant promise based on what we've seen so far.

I'll preface this review with this: If you're expecting this game to have comparable story depth to Human Revolution, you're currently wasting your time.
I'll start with some quick pros and cons after finishing my first playthrough, around 20 or so hours of playtime.
Note: I've completed the main story,
(EDIT: I've progressed considerably, completing or on the way to completing the remainder of side quests available)
Pros:
+ Visually the game is gorgeous, even at mid-tier settings and the poor PC optimization (update your drivers btw)
+ Gameplay surrounding augments is somewhat more fleshed out with the introduction of new abilities (some useful, some not), and the new additions are fit into the story somewhat, despite the mission surrounding it hitting something of a dead-end at the end of the game
+ Prague is fun to explore, giving much more to find and do than Detroit in the previous game. This is one of the games strongest points: Prague is very carefully designed and each nook and cranny has purpose to it, and give you a little tidbit of personal story for someone that may have lived in an apartment, all the way to a stray corpse in the sewers.
+ Non-lethal and Ghost play styles are given much more love in the level designs
+ Elias Toufexis is always a joy to listen to
+ tfw no Eliza Cassan gf
++ Side missions are incredibly well written and involve compelling characters (most namely Johnny Gunn in SM10) that briefly take Jensen into a better story than the one that surrounds him
Cons:
- My biggest complaint: story depth come the end of the game just drops, unsatisfying conclusion that only just barely expands on the overarching antagonist that Human Revolution spent building, the scope of the ending sequence shrinks exponentially as the narrative progresses, likely because the ending sets up the confirmed story DLC (be ready to pay for a full ending)
-
(EDIT: To my knowledge this has been effectively patched, huzzah)
- Mankind Divided has 2 open hubs to do side quests in, Prague (with its 3 variations: daytime, nighttime and Martial law) and Golem City. While Prague is exciting to explore, Golem City has very little to do in it aside from advancing a single story mission and a small handful of side objectives.
- Microtransations in a single player game, that just goes without saying
Mankind Divided in its current state is a very heavy disappointment as a continuation of Human Revolution, a very inconsequential story that leads to an "ending" that only exists to serve the upcoming DLC and/or sequel installment, held up by pretty graphics and somewhat enjoyable gameplay mechanics that all in all left me wanting, both a better game and another playthrough of Human Revolution.

Game is incompetent at day 1 proper management; Mouse issues, framerate issues, and DLC content issues abound- any pre-order items you may have gotten are entirely one-time use, leaving you high and dry without any such features should you start up a second play through.
The game has RMT (Real Money Transactions) in it. This by far is the WORST step and the most atrocious I've seen since Dead Space 3. And of course, one of the reasons why the game is no longer an IP worth investing into. So if the companies decision was to completely destroy this game series, they've done it.
Patching locks you out of the game, and when the game requires a patch, it takes over EIGHT HOURS for the patch servers to come online for you to even get it. Until then? Sucks to be you; You won't be playing this game at all during that time.

Ontop of that it suffers horrible performance issues even running on an overclocked I5 6600k and overclocked GTX 980 it chugged quite often on "High" settings. For the most part, this game looks promising. I really like the concept of being able to control dragons that have lazers beam and missiles and fighting them to the death. I'm sure you've already read this in other reviews, but just in case: The only reason there are so many negative reviews is because there were some issues at launch. And people found that a good enough reason to riot.

After playing for only about half an hour, I can already see where this game is most likely going. I can see a bit of meta forming, and each of the dragons clearly has their own playstyle and purpose. I can't say for sure if this game is going to get better or worse over time - but as is, it's worth an hour or so of your time. It's incredibly easy to pick up (you don't even need to know what any of the keys do the first time you jump into a match. You'll be fine.)

I like how your starting dragon is a bit of a heavyweight. Not the bulkiest of the bunch, I assure you, but they have enough HP so that you'll survive a few of the hits you're no doubt going to be taking while you improve. They're enough of a middle-ground so that you can jump into any of the other dragons with enough basic experience under your belt to know what you're doing.

Though I have only played a few games, I'm noticing that I only see about one of a type of dragon per team, which is nice. It's a good indicator that there isn't a clearly broken dragon to play as. Yet.

The airplay is a little frustrating at times and momentum doesn't seem to work exactly as it should (I would love to see an update where it's possible to build up a lot of speed and then ram right into them. With recoil, of course. Right now, the dragons don't really feel like they have weight to them.) but it's a solid starting point.
That seems to be my all-around opinion on this game, actually. It's hit the ground running with a solid start in it's development and I'd love to see where the devs take the game from here. It's definately possible for this to fall flat, but who really knows? Best of luck to you, devs.
