If there's one game that did more than any other to define my gaming childhood, it's Apogee's Rise of the Triad (1994). Originally envisioned as a full sequel to Wolfenstein 3D, it morphed into a standalone game that gathered a cult following despite its bad fortune to be released in the shadow of Doom 2. For years it dwelled in relative obscurity until a couple of years ago when Interceptor Entertainment and a resurgent Apogee announced a remake of the beloved but oft forgotten game.
This new Rise of the Triad was released last year to moderate fanfare. After the utter farce that was Duke Nukem Forever, it's fair to say there was scepticism about how an old Apogee/3D Realms classic could be revived. ROTT 1994 is a game I still play from time to time to this day, so I was curious to see how ROTT 2013 stands up just a year later, once the mists of nostalgia had faded. Put frankly, ROTT 2013 is one of the most satisfying shooter games I've played in recent years. It had me tearing my hair out at times, but the joy and insanity of the original has transferred over and makes for a hugely enjoyable game.
ROTT always was a always strange beast. Using a modified Wolfenstein 3D engine, its 90 degree walled levels betrayed its origins and the limitations of the technology were always apparent. The look and feel of the game also betrayed its more Nazi-iferous beginnings with the Triad enemies having a distinct whiff of the jackboots about them. On the other hand it was also a game in which ridiculously powerful rocket weapons were always on hand, you could become a god, a dog or just get high on shrooms and bounce around trap filled rooms with elastic super powers. It was slightly unhinged and it revelled in its own stupidity. ROTT 2013 brings all of this back.
Shooting a firebomb round into a clustered group of nasty fascists and getting a ludicrous gibs bonus is as fun today as it was in 1994. ROTT 2013 knows what people want and it gives it to you; big dumb guns and squishy meat sacks to fire them at. It's brutal, over the top, bloody and very satisfying. Every classic gun from the original is faithfully recreated and handles just as in the original. As are the enemies. The over-patrol throwing a net at you, the lightning guards nicking your bazooka to use against you or begging for their life and playing dead when injured, it's all there from the original and fits into the action perfectly.
The game is punishingly hard at times, definitely adhering to the old school rules of difficulty. There is absolutely no hand holding, it throws you into the action and expects you to come out gunning, or exploding. It may well be one of the quickest games around. The speed of the gameplay is at first a little disconcerting if, like me, you'd got used to the slower pace of modern shooters. Once you get into the groove, you'll find yourself stringing together ridiculous mid air rocket manoeuvres and jumping around shooting all over the place. Admittedly I'm not the best player, but even an unskilled player like me can be made to feel like a bazooka shooting goddess.
That is until you hit a section where the frame rate decides to go on holiday and leave you in the lurch. ROTT 2013 is hardly the prettiest or most technologically advanced game out there (just like the original in that way too), but it manages to mangle the Unreal Engine it's built on and create an unpredictable beast that can have the performance go up and down wildly. It's a horribly optimised game, terrible even. Parts of the game I could play with maximum graphical settings, others it would struggle with medium settings for no apparent reason. What's worse is that you can only change graphics options from the game launcher, so experimenting with the long list of graphics options means restarting the game. Interceptor Entertainment have patched the game and improved performance since the initial release, but it's still pretty unstable and wildly unpredictable.
Performance issues dampened my enjoyment of the game but they were more an annoyance than anything, what did cause me to groan in pain was some of the naïve level design on offer. The levels are all remakes of the levels from the original and for the most part are really well done and fantastic arenas and shooting galleries, but then you hit upon a terrible jumping puzzle or platforming section that is incredibly frustrating and leaves you thinking “Why?”. I came across numerous places where I got stuck behind props or bad geometry in the environment. If you are making a high-precision platforming section where you have to travel from jump pad to jump pad over an insta-kill death pit of doom but you have ledges to get stuck on and cause you to fall to your death, it's going to annoy players. Getting stuck by a tiny box in the middle of a fire fight with an army of baddies is going to frustrate people. Finding that a flight of stairs won't let you pass because of misaligned geometry makes players want to scream. Yes, ROTT 2013 was made on a small budget with a small team, but such clunky design is pretty disappointing.
These are far from the only problems with the game. The enemy AI is very basic, with some baddies just standing around until activated when I was almost right next to them. Character models and animation were equally basic and the colour pallet meant that enemies frequently blended into the brown surroundings. I'd often find that I was being shot by someone unseen and I'd have to stand in the middle of a room and scan around slowly, squinting to see who was left alive and still audacious enough to carry on shooting at me. Clipping issues and bad hit-boxes abound, unavoidable death traps are used to sucker punch the player far too much and the checkpoint saves are spotty at best.
If it sounds like I'm being harsh on the game, it's only because I care so much. And I know I'm not the only one. Interceptor Entertainment obviously put an awful lot of love into this remake. They are clearly fans of the original and must have doted over it a long time to get the remake to feel so faithful. There are plenty of nice touches to see, Easter eggs and references. They even give you a choice of the classic level music or the newer heavy metal covers. There are plenty of new one liners for each of the five playable characters (it's not the wittiest of dialogue, but enjoyably silly) and briefings to listen to for each level. Multiplayer mode is chaotic and frequently exhilarating.
The remake of Rise of the Triad is pretty messy in places, for certain, but the fact is that throughout most of my time playing it, I've had a huge grin across my face. It remains faithful to the original whilst tweaking the gameplay enough to make it relevant to modern audiences. If you're a fan of the original, everything will be familiar and just as fun as you remember. If you're new to ROTT, you'll find one hell of a silly good time. It's a shame it didn't receive more polish and forethought with some sections but I'm so glad that this game exists. ROTT is ludicrous, deranged, challenging and very, very fun.

Rise of the Triad is a reboot of a cult classic from the 90's, an over-the-top, arcade-like fast-paced first person shooter game in the spirit of games like Doom, Quake, and Duke 3D. What really set apart ROTT from other FPS games of it's era, was that bullet weapons had infinite ammo and all of the other weapons are variants of rocket launchers, flamethrowers and magical weapons. It was also one of the first games where you blew up humans instead of monsters, but of course more enemies are encountered throughout the game like robots. The game also had many traps and obstacles to get passed, like flame walls or fireballs, crushers and more. There was also a scorebar for those who liked to make high scores.
This reboot brings back everything you loved about the original ROTT and other games in it's era. It keeps everything you loved about games in the 90's. Long non-linear levels using the colored-key door style system with plenty secrets to be found (and secret levels!), boss fights at the end of each episode, weapons scatterd everywhere and many enemies needing to be blown up. Just like the original, there's also lots of fun obstacles and small platforming segments, now improved since this version has jumping. The 4 different characters all with different stats that you can play as also comment on things going on in the world which adds a nice little touch. There's a story, but the gameplay isn't stressed upon it. Basically, the H.U.N.T team is sent out to clear out the Triads from any trouble they are causing, until they find out that they are being ordered by something much bigger than they first thought; El Oscuro.
The graphics are really good, especially for a UE3 game. That being said, it may favor Nvidia cards a little more than AMD cards. It looks better than many other UE3 games in my opinion. Sharp particles, huge detailed environments and many pretty lights, and an insane amount of gore. Animations, specifically the first person weapon animations are sexy, got that badas­s mo­fo feel to them. Add on to the fact that the music is some shredding metal remixes of the originals, it even enhances that badas­s effect.
The devs are very responsive to their customers and keep a close eye on their forums. Many people have suggested features throughout the game's development and many of the things that the community wanted most, they were able to implement into the next patch, such as more multiplayer levels, a new weapon which was the shotgun, new player models for MP, and a classic quicksaving feature which they admitted to being an oversight not being in 1.0 in the first place. Not to mention they're just cool dudes to talk to and play with.
The multiplayer community isn't huge, but it is very active. The community makes new MP levels very often, some SP levels have started to rise up recently too.  Every Saturday the community gets together and plays all of the most popular custom maps, and the developers often join in too and it's a lot of fun. This is the only game I have ever pre-ordered, and it was worth every penny.

Short version: Awful.
Long version: On my spectrum of crappy shooters it's worse than Command & Conquer: Renegade and slightly better than Serious Sam 3.
Technical: Only one save, occasionally crashes and frequently changes the difficulty level without permission. Horrendous bouts of lag. E4M2 respawns every enemy in the map when you quickload. It took me 45 minutes to get out of the starting hallway. Not even joking.  3/10
Graphics: Passable, but so is a kidney stone.
AI: Endless waves of generic looking Not-Nazis, robots and sorcerers. Human enemies frequently rush you then glitch backwards ten feet. Since they blend seemlessly with the brownish environment you won't know who's shooting at you most of the time. 0/10
Weapons: You move faster while using ironsights. Think about that. Also: What's with all the rocket launcher variations? I only need ONE to get the job done. That's why it's a rocket launcher. Bullet weapons have unlimited ammo and never need to be reloaded. Yet, pressing R *initiates a reload animation*. 0/10
Items: You can turn into a dog and bite guys in the nuts, because it was in the original. Other "power-ups" reverse your controls and turn you into a pinball, or make everything psychadelic. 3/10
Level Design: You find keys. You open doors. You shoot bad guys. Traps weren't cool in 1995 and they make even less sense in 2014. 0/10
Story: You are part of a spec-ops team sent to infiltrate a make-believe island off the coast of Los Angeles that has been appropriated by a mysterious terrorist cult for nefarious purposes. In other words, there is no story. 0/10
Humor: "Oh, I get it, you only THINK you're John Woo." 0/10
Characters: You get to pick from four caricatures who fart frequently and utter ridiculous "catch-phrases" during gameplay. How this pays homage to the original is anyone's guess. Each player has individual strengths, ranging from running faster, to running A LOT faster. Seriously, that's it. Since the default movement speed is already ludicrous, this was a cryptic design decision. 0/10
Music: You can pick between the original remastered tracks or modern heavy-metal renditions of said tracks, and they both sound awesome. 10/10
Gameplay: This is a game that is trying to be "old-school". Unfortunately, it's not old, it was made in 2012, so it just comes off as "bad-school". It's energy is a 10. Had the developers showed some restraint and cranked it back to 7, they could have had a fun, modestly-paced Return to Castle Wolfenstein clone. Instead, the character speed is so fast and the mouse sensitivity so amped it's hard to hit even basic enemies. This also makes it almost impossible to make precision jumps, which is poison considering most of the secrets and puzzles involve moving platforms and jump pads. 3/10
Replayability: The final boss is so tedious I actually opted to nuke L.A. and get the "bad" ending just so I wouldn't have to fight him. Lastly: Every time you die-- and you will die often, cheaply-- the mission-briefing guy tells you how much you suck. Who is this person? How does he know what I'm doing? And why should I care what he thinks? 0/10
Overall: This game is so bad it made me want to cut myself. There is so little substance beyond endless gore and depravity that I actually sympathized with politicians who try to ban violent video games. The reason modern shooters tend to include regenerating health, cover systems and checkpoints isn't because gaming is dumbing down, it's because those things WORK.

Once you get over the initial (and I have to be honest) clumsy UI this game becomes good fun. Once you tweak the graphics, read the tutorials and adjust the UI slider so you can read anything, this game becomes fun. Once you get past the fact that despite having opened a shop you have to walk the streets to sell your Health Potions to get started, this game becomes fun....
Anyone who has ever owned a business or even made sales via eBay knows the thrill of getting your first, then second then third customer. and this game does that nicely.
There are a lot of upgrades (poorly presented mind) and tiered products that open up your offerings. From leather to plate to wood to Stealth to Wizard.... There is a reasonable number of shelving and display options, also requiring unlocking.
Progression is nicely balanced. Your items become unlocked as your furniture becomes unlocked, and your automated bot systems become unlocked and your earnings allow you to open the shop up... See where I'm going... It's a nice smooth path.
Hire a "Champion" and it can be made to do missions to bring back items, some rare. You can grind up unwanted items, loot, even thieves and Barbarians and turn them into higher level, unbuyable items via the cauldron and associated grinder.
You can plant beets, shrooms and weed and sell them for good coin. You need to repair your furniture, sweep your floors, put in dividers, plants, floormats etc. Upgrade your sword, your hammer and your broom. There are Quests, essentially linked to what you're selling and these unlock "K" points - the currency to gain the unlocks.
There's a lot to do and you'll be busy...
BUT.....
A relentless thief mechanic. You spend a large part of your time chasing thieves, killing innocents and generally upgrading to make your store thief proof - but still they come. Even with all kinds of enhancements and weaponary and markups at 135% you'll be spending 10 minutes of everyday chasing after, killing, picking up and cleaning up thieves. Yep, first few are funny, after that a tedious, mindless chore.
Barbarians. Why? In 56 hours not a single loot drop and not a single reason for them even being in the game. They scare off all your customers, your automated weaponary doesn't kill them (but a thief with a $12 potion is insta-popped) and you can't leave your store running without being there in case they turn up. We can feed them meat to stop them, sure. IF you have a Champion or go trashdiving to find some.
K Points are associated with the game, not the store, so every upgrade you earn in Shop 1 also applies in Shop 2 if you start a second shop. If you reset, both stores lose the points.  If you want multiple players with seperate saves (like my 3 kids) then each have to share the K points earned. This is a damn silly thing and clearly multi-store save was added as an afterthought and the problem wasn't even considered.
Once you reach the point where your Champion is bringing back the rare items to craft the fancy armor/weapons, the number of missions and effort required to make those items makes the point of doing it meaningless. eg: To get a Dragonbone Armor Set made requires a lot of work and good luck and once you do, the value of the sale is about 1/10th the effort. Yep, bump up the price you say? Then the thieves become worse and customers whine and... and... I couldn't be bothered after the first set. Poorly tacked on "feature" hardly worth your time once curiousity is sated.
The game drops off. No... It totally and utterly flatlines. Once you've opened all rooms, set up all your displays and got the bots to restock (too damn tedious doing it manually - trust me) the entire day is
- Open doors. Stand there watching customers who talk but you can't hear.
- Fight off Barbarians once a day. Why, why, why? Make it worthwhile dammit!!
- Continuously clean up the dead thieves your bots kill (forever and a damned day!)
- Once door closes, let bots restock, then restock bots, manually repair all furniture and...
- Rinse and Repeat.
But hey, if you're feeling adventurous, find and empty trash cans and you may get some classy loot.
(NOTE: Title is by a single coding dev, 18 months of work. I wish him well and hopefully his next title will be designed with the END product in mind. Allowing customer generated feature creep and starting with a loose design principle from the getgo is bad mmmmkay?)

Shoppe Keep (or Medieval Shop Owner as I like to call it), is a business/management simulation that takes the setting of Medieval times, where you are a humble shopkeeper in a place with no name, trying to make a living by selling various items to customers (adventurers) who are looking for gear, potions, weapons, and, above all, magic stuff (the weed). Yeah, it's serious business.
Basically, it's like what you would expect in a possible business simulation game: you own a shop, you decide what you want to sell, you decide how you price it, and you wait. Shoppe Keep is just that. However, the difference with this game between other simulations is that it is First-Person POV, which for some simulations, it's usually Omniscence/overhead view, and of course, it is Medieval times, making this game not only a rare sight, but perhaps genuine in its nature.
In this game there are business three phases during business: Morning, Day, and Night, each creating their very own "hot items" that, if found in your store, will bring in more customers (or drive them away if ridiculously priced). Of course, before business, you have to prepare, so that's why you have three preparation phases: the Shopkeeper phase, Build phase, and Clean-up phase.
In the Shopkeeper phase, you can order items off of your catalog, and then place those items on shelves, tables, weapon racks, armor racks, whichever you decide at your discretion (in accordance with the game rules).
In the Build phase, it is just like the name implies: you build shelves and tables to stock your store with goodies to sell.
And with the Clean-up phase, you clean-up your store, repairing your furniture as well as making sure your store is nice and tidy (nuff' said).
In addition, your store can be attacked by barbarians and you will often get thieves, that's right, this game is not all that innocent, which is why there's the Attacker phase. In this phase, you have a sword and spell out (default is a longsword and lightning spell). With these two weapons of destruction, you stop those thieves by incinerating them or stabbing them; the same applies to barbarians. However, be careful, for if you kill an innocent individual, you lose gold (life insurance expenses).
Aside from all of that, the game also takes on the role of an RPG-esque game with a leveling system and an ability tree system, where the ability points are K points, which are earned by doing "Quests" and selling items to your fellow patrons. The ability tree consists of six columns of abilities (apparently), all of which I will not name because there are many abilites in this game I wish not to uncover in this review.
If you dislike a form of grinding with a simulation game that literally resembles an RPG in its nature, do not get this game.
During the business phases, different pieces of music play in each respective phase, which is fine, only if it wasn't so repetitive in every single phase of the game (you would want to mute this music after a while, trust me).
Graphics are decent, in fact, are actually quite good for a game made by three people. Mechanics are stable, and long-term gameplay is very-well established.

Thief: the Dark Project, one of the most influential stealth titles out there, is a must play for stealth gamers.
Thief Gold is pretty much the Dark Project with a few missions added to it.
Positives:
+ Great stealth gameplay. Use darker areas to your advantage to sneak by enemies, aided with a wide arsenal of arrows and your trusty club, blackjack. The light crystal, unlike other similar objects in other stealth games, shows you the degree of how hidden you are, rather than show you if you're visible or not.
+ Large, non-linear level design.
+ Difficulty. Prepared for a challenge? Expert will test you if you're a professional thief. No killing, more loot.
+ Your state of mind after listening to hammerites whistling that DAMNED tune for hours.
+ Stephen Russell's voice as Garrett.
Negatives:
- Outdated looks. This can be fixed to some degree with graphical mods.
- Large level design can get you stuck at times.
- New players could find the controls to be uncomfortable. Profiles can be found online for a more "modern" control scheme.
- Thieves' Guild. The worst mission in the entire series (not counting the missions in the press-space-to-win reboot). When you get to this point, good luck.

People are regularly saying that the game is not translated into english and that the graphical fidelity is poor.
The only thing that hasn't been translated has been the VO dialogue, which really isn't a big problem.
As for graphical fidelity, the models are obviously done by a small team doing the best they can; don't expect AAA graphics.
However, there is a small issue with the animation framerate which makes the game feel much less fluid than it should (animations are running at 30fps but game engine is capped at 60fps) But, this is a minor issue and can be related to either the netcode or the physics implimentation.
It is a small game with limited weaponry, but that makes balanicng much easier (take BF4's 100+ weapons that all need to be balanced and there are still multiple carbines in that game with are absurdly OP) And focuses on skill-based combat, rather than who has the higher damage output.

Where to begin...
I have sunk more hours into this game then I probably should have. I have been watching this game develop for quite some time and I have seen big improvements made too it. However, it seems with each step this game takes forward it makes two back.
For a free to play game the game is not necessarily pay to win, but more pay to unlock. The grind in this game is ridiculous, I mean ludicrously long. And the worst part is they constantly make it longer, and are constantly increasing the prices on weapons and vehicles. Yes, though it is good for drawing in hardcore players, it does knock back most casual gamers. Which is not what the focus of a game should be. Because of this ridiculous grind, it basically gives you no other option then if you want good gear, you are going to have to cough up the cash (which I can say I have sadly fallen for). Which I think is absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t for casual gamers playing a free to play game. I know that the game must make money somehow, however I personally would rather get rid of the free to play, and pay $20 to maybe even $30 US to purchase the game, scrap the "repair system" and the "gold system" reduce the grind and make everything level and credit based.
Other problems.
This game used to pride itself on being a free to play game that anyone with any set up could play. However, every update that comes out seems to create more and more optimisation problems and severe drops in fps for people on low end gaming computers and or laptops. Forcing many players such as myself to give up the game as it has become unplayable on their machines. It seems the focus of Reto has gone from making it a game for everyone, too making that tree in the far corner of the map that no one will see pretty. Gameplay over graphics Reto, that is what drew me to the game.
Tanking
The tank combat system in this game is simplified at best. Yes, there is strategy too it, however it’s not about, "I'll go here to get the jump on this guy" it's more like "I'll hide hear for 20min of the game being useless while I wait for this AT (anti-tank) ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on a bike buggers off to hell." The tank combat in this game though simple, is difficult. I don't quite mind playing as medium or light tank, however, heavy tanking in this game is near on impossible. You are slow and huge thus easy to spot, and are often swamped by AT before you even get a chance to support the infantry, get to a good vantage point, or let alone fire upon an enemy tank. There needs to be large improvements that could be made to the anti-tank system in this game. Such as AT charges should be needed to be placed on set points of a tank and not just anywhere.
Teamwork
The game is heavily based around teamwork, and matches can be won or lost very quickly depending on how well the team communicates. I like this aspect of the game; however it is hard to communicate through the type chat system quickly. I would recommend that if you do play this game with friends to use discord or TeamSpeak when playing this game.
Now I know I have basically just blasted the crap out of this game, however there is one undeniable fact that I haven't mentioned.
It is Fun.
A lot of people say it is frustrating. Yes, it can be, however when played with friends this game is a great killer of time and even enjoyable.
The game is challenging and good at hooking you in for hours of a time.
There is a lot in this game that needs improvement, and it is not finished yet. Though they update it regularly and has not been abandoned by its developers.
I look forward to the prospect that one day it, it will be finished. I hope the Reto team takes this feedback with open minds and moves forward with the goal to listen to the community and fan base, and make improvements where they are needed.

This game deserves a 10, but I can see people arguing a 9.5.
*I have considerably more hours into this game than a vast majority of people who wrote reviews.
-First two hours of the game are slow.
-Do not play this if you can't stand dialogue because there is a lot in this game.
-Bugs-as with every game. There was one bug where I was stuck in one place, tried everything to move but it didn't work. I restarted, loaded that previous save, and I was still stuck. Important: THIS IS WHY YOU SHOULD HAVE MULTIPLE SAVE POINTS-which is what I thankfully had, in addition to autosave.
There's another bug with the House of Sorrows quest line (which is like a faction). If you leave the castle before accepting all of the quests (including the main faction's quest), you'll get locked out. I googled it for a solution after being locked out and people suggested keeping the heartstone key. If you destroy it, you're screwed. Luckily, I kept the key in my stash. Unfortunately, that solution didn't even work. iIeven tried equipping it-nope. Locked out of that questline still. My most recent save to where I'm able to access that questline is like five hours back from where I currently am. So I'm forced to choose between sacrificing five hours of gameplay just to be able to access that storyline, or foregoing it altogether to keep/maintain those five hours of gameplay.
-When buying in bulk, it doesn't show you the total dollars. This is basic in rpg games. It only has a slider for the quantity you want to buy, not the total amount in gold/dollars.
+Bang for your buck. Remarkably, there is so much content in this game. I thought this was going to be a 20-30 hour game-tops. Steam counter has me at 85 hours (not counting 6 hours offline)-and I haven't even completed many of the side or even main quests or even the "Legend of Dead Kel" dlc.
+The most beautiful scenery I've ever seen, and I've played Skyrim. There were multiple moments where I was amazed.
+The dialogue is so good and reflective/philosophical and poetic.
+The story line is original (ex: The story of Edgar Aron in Apotyre (the underdog going against the giant Motus Mining corporation) goes almost the opposite with it).
+The weapons are cooler than I expected.
+Impressively fast loading screens (compare to many other games) to the point where you can't finish reading the hint texts on the screen.
+Variety in play style. You don't have to choose between being a rogue (finesse), a mage (sorcery) or a warrior (might), in the "destinies" section, you can actually be a hybrid of the two if you select talents from your two favorite play styles.
+Voice acting which 90% of rpg players ♥♥♥♥♥ about wanting, despite how expensive it can be for game studios to include.

2) Scary PR. Untold millions price tag+not enough initial buyers to break even, let alone make a profit (needed 2-3 million buyers)=developing company (38 Studios) goes bankrupt=perception of a horrible game=throwing money away.

Charlie's Adventure is a relatively short two-dimensional platformer from indie developers, Just1337 Studios.
In Charlie's Adventure you play the titular Charlie, a young boy who, upon finding a strange box in his sand pit and opening it, unwittingly causes zombies to invade the world. Never fear, though, the same box seems to have given Charlie various strange powers with which he can combat the undead horde.
Graphics are mostly fairly bright and colourful. Character sprites are relatively simple, but nicely drawn, with smooth animations. Level backgrounds progress through a few different themes and include animations, some of which tend to distract from the main action. Cut scenes are hand drawn and possess a certain charm, with crude animations that remind me of nothing more than Beavis and Butthead, but maybe that's just me.
Background music is nice, with a spooky theme that fits the game well. It's not the sort of music you'd by a soundtrack for, but it's good enough. Sound effects are mostly good, but there's an annoying evil laugh sound that I didn't like much, and I'm still not sure if it's supposed to be from Charlie or one of the zombies. The star-collecting sound reminds me of a Mario game.
Charlie's Adventure plays like a typical 2D platformer. Using keyboard or controller you can move left and right, jump, double-jump, and dash, as you make your way around the various platforms, collecting stars, avoiding traps, and killing zombies. Falling off the bottom of the screen kills you, putting you back to the last-visited checkpoint.
Charlie has a fairly impressive arsenal for a little boy. Having found a 'phazer' he can shoot zombies with that, or charge it up for mega-damage shots. He can also slam zombies from above when jumping over them, or charge into them as part of his dash, which also makes Charlie briefly invincible to zombie and trap damage. All of these moves use some of his magic energy reserves, though, so keep an eye on the meter in the top left when you're in a fight, as running out at an inopportune time can leave Charlie in a bit of a pickle.
Each level is divided up into a number of areas marked by checkpoints. Kill all of the zombies in one area to unlock the checkpoint to the next, and then reach the checkpoint in order to have Charlie reappear there upon death. Charlie's final ability can help in some of the more convoluted areas, too: find zombies. This ability shows little arrows pointing from Charlie to each of the remaining zombies in Charlie's current area.
Each area has a number of gold stars that Charlie can collect by running into them, as well. Collect enough of these and Charlie becomes 'enraged' for a short time, increasing speed and damage. Watch out, though; even though Charlie's more of a bad♥♥♥♥♥when enraged, he still takes the same amount of damage from traps and zombies.
There are 12 levels in Charlie's Adventure. I haven't completed them all, but I've played for about two hours, including some alt-tabbing to take notes for this review, and I've completed over half of them. That suggests the game is relatively short, although you can always go back and play again at one of the other difficulty levels if you're really keen. I expect only die-hard achievement hunters will both with that, though, as the levels are all very similar, both to each other and many other games in the genre, so there's nothing here to really grab your attention and drag you back to play again.
I found the keyboard controls a bit awkward, and they seemed to not be configurable. Controller support was good, but I found it a bit less precise than the keyboard, so neither was quite perfect. In both modes my most frequent cause of death was pressing the shoot button when I meant to press the dash.
I encountered a couple of frustrating problems in Charlie's Adventure. Firstly, on one level it was frustrating to collect a star close to the bottom of the screen because just touching that area of the screen caused Charlie instant death. I had to try that one multiple times before I managed to grab it without touching the 'death zone'. Secondly, on one occasion I managed to knock a zombie backwards behind a part of one level that Charlie was unable to get to, meaning that I had to kill Charlie off and restart that area. Neither of these was too problematic, though, and the game seems very stable; I didn't encounter any other bugs or crashing. I did see a few grammatical errors in the game, though. Oh, and some of the achievements don't seem to quite work right, so any achievement hunters might want to keep an eye out to see if they drop.
Pros:
+ A certain sort of charm to the character sprites and animations, and the cut scenes
+ Solid platforming action
+ Spooky music
+ Steam achievements and trading cards
Cons:
- A bit boring; doesn't do anything out of the ordinary
- A couple of small problems make it more frustrating than it should be
- Short
Charlie's Adventure is a solid indie platformer that fans of the genre should enjoy. It doesn't bring anything revelatory to the genre, but it gets the basics right.
Note: I received this game for free for review purposes. This did not influence my review.

Awful game. I hoped this was going to be Ace of Spades done properly, but I'm surprised to say it's even worse.
Movement and controls are clunky, so don't expect to be running and jumping and shooting skilfully. This (and the target audience) is probably why most matches are just sniper wars.
Plenty of things don't have sounds, which is actually a big deal because it makes things feel unresponsive. Even taking/capturing/returning the flag doesn't have sounds, only a small message. This makes it very difficult to tell what's happening.
Even with those things fixed, the gameplay just isn't balanced. As expected, the sniper dominates. CTF is poorly done - nobody really wants to take the flag because of snipers, and because you have to walk the flag back on foot, unable to use any weapons. The flag returns quickly enough that you often can't get back to it in time after dying, and sadly most of the team don't try to help.
There is a building system too, but it's redundant. Nobody has time to build things because the controls are too cumbersome and will get them killed. Anything other than stairs and bridges are useless anyway.
In short, this is a game that had potential but plays like an alpha, which is unforgiveable given the amount of time it's been on Steam.

The new Rise of the Triad is an attempt to capture old school shooter arcade action with updated graphics. It aims to capture the run and gun feel of the originals with things like health pickups, armour, and no cover system while ignoring modern shooting conventions like regenerating health/shields. All this seems well and good, but the problem is that game just isn't very good. First, let me just say that this game is incredibly buggy. I got stuck in walls and rocks ever 10 minutes or so, and often had to load an old game because there was no fixing it. This was a much more persistant problem than it should be. Second, the AI in this game is abysmal. I understand that old school shooters had less tactical AI, but the new Rise of the Triad AI is downright stupid. It gets stuck, it doesn't know how to go around corners, and the only reason its chalenging is their aim is 100% accurate, all the time. The controls feel rediculous. Instead of captuing the raw smooth quality of classics like doom and Duke nukem, everything moves so fast and over responsive that it is jarring to move throughout the world. The voice acting in this game is almost unbearable. It doesn't feel like a so "cheesey its good" vibe either. It sounds like the dev team got their friends to do it, and none of them know how to sell a line. The level design is uninspired and boring, and sometimes its easy to get lost. The levels are often too easy, and the bosses too hard. Most of the bosses unleash rediculous amounts of damage and there aren't any defensible positions for you to hide. Many of the bosses can kill you in about 3 literal seconds. You will be replaying the boss fights from the begining quite often. Why? you ask, since Rise of the Triad has a save system. Well, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who made this game thought it would be a great idea to remove the save feature duing boss fights. There is no reason other than to frustrate the player. "You know that game feature we've had all game? Yeah, its gone now, because we don't know how to make the game challenging through creative means." The final complaint I have with this game comes from the fact that despite it wanting to be an old school shooter, it gets rid of one of the best parts about old school shooters: Holding tons of weapons. In this game you have a worthless pistol, a weak machine gun, and then you can carry one big gun at a time. Later in the game you can also cary one mystical object at a time. I wanted to be able to switch between 4 or 5 big guns during boss fights, but no luck. The boss rounds have very few good guns lying around, but plenty of bad ones. In the end, you just got frustrated and didn't want to play any further. The final boss battle also lets you use a powerup (flying) that you really didn't have access to earlier in the game (outside of secrets). This means players have to get used to a whole new type of gameplay during the final boss. Couldn't they have used it earlier so players were more familiar? This is seriously a terrible game.

In depth.
The worst thing about this game is how horrendously poorly it starts off and presents itself. In that first hour of play, I was VERY tempted to claim a refund. I didn't feel any satisfaction in being a shop keeper, I had no idea what I was doing, there was very little in terms of tutorial (a note, text on pages will never be a good tutorial - give me prompts when starting out and you'll convey how to play the game more quickly and easily to the user), and I only had 3-4 customers coming by to buy health potions in the first few days.
Then the second hour hit. Then the window of a refund closed, and funnily enough, so did my desire to claim one. Then the third hour hit. Apparently the fourth has also hit but I have no awareness of that, I was too busy sweeping and restocking. Now it's far too late and I want to sleep, but not before praising the game.
If you ever wanted to be a retail worker who can brandish a sword and slaughter a thief or even just a rude customer, this is for you. The game is exceptionally good at simulating the busy shop nature. I have to stock so many of these items, but suddenly someone is stealing something, then some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ customer throws a shield, dirt is accumulating, my chest pieces are now out, my delivery of swords is in but all of a sudden no one wants swords they want armor, oh someone else is stealing, oh I thought someone was stealing but they were just running after I murdered the first thief now I'm an actual murderer, oh but the gloves are out as well...
Things get hectic. And it's pretty fun gameplay.
As I implied above, the biggest things to improve are:
• Tutorials that aren't trash. It's so commonplace to put a tutorial at the beginning that having a separate section handle it seems alien. Also a dozen pages of texts does not make a great tutorial. It was enough to get my feet wet but I'd much prefer button prompts in the first day. "Push 1, now left click on the table to place your health potions" etc. It might not feel important, but with the 2 hour window for refunds, you should strive to set a better first impression. Throwing the user into the fray is a game mechanic for some games, but this isn't Dark Souls: Shop edition.
• Better UI. It's a bit of a mess when looking at all the skill pages. Part of the reason starting off needs a better tutorial is the skill pages overwhelms a new player a bit. There's a ton of crap all over the place. It should just be one page.
• Better overall interface. The game feels pretty amateurish. If you've played Town of Salem or some other browser game now on steam, that's the vibe I get. I don't expect triple A menus, design, etc. In fact, I don't expect the devs of this to do anything about it in this game. But it's something for the next game. And I can already tell they have talent mixed with creativity, so this is just a place to improve on.
As I keep playing, my list of cons grows shorter. But these three are pretty constant for me thus far.
All in all, this is a great game for a great price. $10 is ideal, but I could see $15-20 for this, granted at that much I'd likely shy away from the game just at a glance. Having played it now and knowing what I'm getting into, I can see a higher price point.

A touching story
"Brothers" is a fairly simple game, definitely on the easy side, but I applaud the storytelling, especially as it doesn't have any dialogue that I can tell (All characters are speaking either a simlish kind of madeup language, or one I am entirely unfamiliar with).
Instead, all of the story is told through the events and the scenery. It's a minimalist decision that I rather enjoyed, and it fit rather nicely with this fairy tale adventure through its beautiful world.

This game is a masterpiece and single handedly proves that games can definitely be a powerful artform. Everything from the perfectly matching soundtrack and vocals, absolutely and unique gorgeous vistas, and impeccable use of controls (gamepad is a must) for controlling both brothers all culminates in one of the best emotional stories I have ever experienced. The game is short, but worth every penny even for its full asking price.

Holdfast: Nations At War is a great napoleonic game, it competes with the mods for the Mount and Blade series and even the likes of rising 1800s games like War of Rights. Now, those two games are good and I am not gonna throw dirt on them and all im saying is that this game can be up there with the likes of them. First of all, the Army Battlefield is probably the most fun gamemode, though I would like to see a longer respawn time for it. Most of the time in gamemodes like that, there are a TON of chokepoints which is realistic, but if your into arcade like shooters I do not reccomend that type of gamemode. I will not talk about army siege because nobody plays it that much. As far as the Naval Battlefield gamemode goes, I love it because of the teamwork you find there that cannot be found anywhere else but a competitive group. However, If you want to be the guy who just ventures off in a rowboat mid battle to play a violin song for the enemy.. that's ok! it is really fun and nobody normally judges me for it. The only downside is that the grapeshot's aren't in the game yet which dissapoints me. To talk about classes the riflemen will always be full because they are fun.. why?.. they have better accuracy and actually hit the target. The carpenter will always hit the target at close range and is good for firing a shot at a passing ship in naval battlefield and the musicians are just there because they like the songs and support roles every other class is either not played much (ex: Surgeon, even though he is good in melee encounters) and classes that are just used competitively (ex: Officer) or just a class that has a musket and is used either when the riflemen are full or an event is happening (ex: Musketman and Guard) point said. Overall I would recommend this game because it is fun and more and fun stuff is coming, like Prussians, hopefully.

Small warning: Don't give this to under-aged children before playing it yourself.
All the images show a beautiful scenery and make the game look fantastic, but this game also has a very dark side. There is a surprising amount of blood and death in this game, so I would recommend you not give it to any young kids.
That being said, Make sure you play this with a controller. You can without one, but unless you hold your keyboard in your hands and it vibrates, you won't get the same immersion. Trust me on this one, the game is not as good without a controller.
Regarding the puzzles, they were really easy for me to solve. I expect all other long-term gamers can say the same, but if you give this game to somebody that is new to gaming, it might take them some time.
Overall, the game is cute. Not the best game ever and definitely not worth the 15 euros they are asking, but if it is on sale, it might be worth your time. I personally got it for my wife to try out, but I'll probably have to help her out from time to time.

This is my first review, so don't judge too harshly!
The Gameplay: Heroes and Genrals is an action packed FPS, with amazing quality for a FTP game. The infantry sections are meh, but the Tank and Aircraft sections are GLORIOUS (especially with the new updates!)
The Strategy Element: Alongside the FPS section, there is a mini RTS game. You send assault teams on different areas on a map of Europe during WW2. The RTS game is pretty simplistic, so if this is why you want to play the game don't bother. It also takes a long time to get to it, I haven't even gotten to it! And, you can see my playtime.
The Community: This is where the game falters. I play as America, and we have stereotypes for the other nation's players. We have "German pansies" and "Russian ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t."The Germans usually rush you in an infantry situation, and they usually one shot you with their starter rifles. The Russians camp the same area, usually with a tank or vehicle if they have them, and they snipe you from the same position as you try to get a waypoint. The Russian planes were also OP before the latest update. You can see why I wanted to play as Aircraft since I first got the game.
The PTW aspect: This game is heavy on it's pay to win aspect. There is a currency called gold, which is the Preminum currency. With it you can buy everything in the game AMAZINGLY quickly. If you have a couple hundred to spend, you could level up your infantry men to have the best auto gun in the game, with the best mods, the best ribbons (perks) and the best grenades without playing a single round. For the rest of us, though, we have to spend literally WEEKS, maybe even MONTHS on grinding just to get the next gun or vehicle. In short, the PTW aspect is♥♥♥♥♥♥
Overview: Even with all it's flaws and falters, the game holds a unique charm. I actually unistalled the game, but once they updated it and fully completed it, I came right back in. I am in fact writing this review as I wait for the next game to que up. Or at least I was, till the game I was playing started it's Russian ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

This is a Deus Ex game alright. The gameplay is a big step up from HR and it's actually really good. I played on Deus Ex difficulty.
+ Most zones available from the get-go. Your skills are the only limit, so go ape
+ You get to rob a freaking bank, like, waltz through laser pits into the C-suite and clear out the safes
+ Lots of secrets. For instance, major plot point in the completely optional Tarvos corporate vault
+ Even weak enemies are deadly good. AIs work together (but could stand to be a bit more aggressive)
+ Seamless transition into zero-consequences tutorial mode and back
+ Unique weapons are back
+ Stun gun is now a mid-ranged nonlethal with EMP
+ Pistol and cloak still OP
+ Silenced shotguns (wtf)
+ Titan + EMP / flash shielding = god mode
+ Cover mode is actually useful for takedowns and remote hacking
+ Main NPCs are memorable
+ New game+ (Items, augs all carried over)
+ Great performance for a port (GTX780M), although some folks had major problems
- The main thing holding this game back is the writing. Like many others have said, it's too heavy-handed and shoves line after line into your face like you can't interpret things at all. The only good thing is that it really keeps you guessing about who you can trust throughout the game. The game also ends immediately after the pace starts to pick up, like where you would normally expect an "insert disc 2". It will likely give those who have been closely following the narrative a big wtf.
- various cross-platform CTD preventing progress at launch
- UI bugs, occasional control / context loss
- Asset loading problems. Taking out or switching to a weapon shouldn't take 5 seconds sometimes
- Vendors forget you after you come back to town
- Loading the game with spacebar in cover mode will launch you out into the open. Whatever happened to playtesting?
- Scraps are way too scarce to fully upgrade more than 1 or 2 weapons
- The only boss fight is a pushover
- The game feels like it is part one of something bigger, and it could have stayed for 3 more months in the oven because a lot of the bugs and the writing is immersion-breaking.
Despite its problems, I thoroughly enjoyed it while it lasted, but the ending was very disappointing.

I've played all Deus Ex games when they launched and will be writing this short review with this intention in mind.
Performance; Out of the box, there can be plenty of mouse lag and the default mouse sensitivity was incredibly high. The mouse sensitivity is a non issue after configuration. The mouse lag can be fixed in the same way you do almost any PC game with this issue: set maximum pre-rendered frames to 2 in your graphics control panel, mess with windowed fullscreen versus exclusive fullscreen, try enabling triple buffering in your graphics control panel if you want to run vsync. After the usual messing with configuration, the mouse lag situation does get fixed.
There are some really nice looking graphics features that will let the game visually age well. Those features do carry a heavy impact on your graphics card, so yes you will have to find which configuration works best for you just like Crysis 1 when it launched. DE:MD does absolutely have graphics features that are very advanced compared to other recent game titles. I'm very pleased with them, they look fantastic and run fine on my hardware.
Gameplay; DE:MD is an absolute joy and an improvement over all previous Deus Ex installments. The amount of detail put into every space is astonishing at times and refreshing. Sometimes it can almost be disorienting from all the things to interact with. This is probably what it feels like to be a kid in a candy shop all over again. The story is good (not a bestseller), has tons of great animation and audio. Side quests expand the stage but do not necessarily deepen the main arc.
Support; Eidos appear to have taken a rather impressive approach by stopping feature development and solely focusing on player reported bugs for the launch week. In 4 days, we have seen 2 patches that focus only on bugs. I would have prefered quality assurance to have caught the bugs before launch but their approach is a really positive one.
21:9/3440x1440 support; Launch had some quirks which hurt my initial impression of the game. Fast forward to 8/26, those issues have been patched. Glorious!
Difficulty; Pick the hardest difficulty available to you when you start, it isn't hard.
DLC; I've always prefered expansion packs over DLC for PC games. Though I am aware of DLC, there is absolutely nothing missing from the main campaign experience when you play it like you aren't a manchild. The overall experience exceeds all of the predecessor Deus Ex installments.
Should you buy? Resounding yes. DE:MD is a very good game and delivers outstanding content. It is not for fans only and does have an excellent recap video you can choose to watch to set you up in the Deus Ex universe.

I'm following the Deus Ex series since the first game years ago and it's really nice to immers myself again into that world. Unfortunatelly there are few things that are holding me back from a true immersion.
1. glitches - game has lot's of them, from very simple ones like characters T-posing in the view when they are spawned to more serious ones like blockers in quests that require rewinding to previous savegames (if you lucky to have one). Nothing I can't handle and nothing so far on the main path but since this is not an open world game and I would expect better.
2. conversation choices - not enough for me, game seems dumbed down. The "choice wheel" on PC should be replaced with proper list of options.
3. UI - feels like cheep console port. Especially the "Hold" action is not very common on PCs and should be replaced with a proper key bindings. The inventory screen should be improved, took me 20h to notice tha theres a "Storage" button in the inventory :). The context menu for the items sucks as well, console influence again. On PC could be much nicer and more functional. Also its impossible to put a custom marker on the map - WTF guys -.- ?
4. Lipsync - omg. What kind of software did you use for this? In most of the dialogs this totally ruins otherwise very nice impression of characters. Some more important dialogs are much better but probably all due to manual work of some poor animator...
5. Sounds - game is lacking here. Feels flat. Ambients are decent but the rest of the sounds feels like from a game 10 years ago. The sewers and vent ducts could use some more reverb. You are loosing a LOT of mood here.
6. Not enough interactivity with the world. I know it's cheaper to have static geometry in the world but seriously, a little bit more rigid bodies here and there should not kill your engine. Also, there are no complex physical objects to interact with (cloths, chains, ropes, water). No physical puzzles either. You can baerly stack two boxes on each other.
Exceptional things:
1. Level Art - love it. Especially the ARC area. Locations are memorable and detailed. Level design itself could be a little bit more challenging, sometimes it's too easy.
2. Characters Wardrobe / Augmentations - love it, it's not over the top, looks belivable and stylish. I like the details in the character clothing that actually make sense. Great work there.
3. One of few games I have a real choice in how I want to play the level.
All in all, it's obviously not a perfect game but it's a solid and memorable title worth playing. 8/10.

Mount & Blade: Warband is a very extraordinary game. Made by some rather random dev that no one had heard of, a sequel to a game that didn't have a particulalry large following, this game nonetheless has become a rare gem, and one that I can say we have never seen the likes of before, and frankly I doubt we ever will. And just a warning: if you do buy this game, you will see days fly by without even noticing them because there's always that one last battle to win, always that one last city to capture.
This game sets its stage on the fictional continent of Calradia, where six kingdoms battle for supremacy. You as the player can do many things within this land. You start off as a nobody, and are free to forge your story as you please. You could be a merchant, travelling all across Calradia selling your wares in every city from the eastern coasts of Swadia to the western deserts of the Sarranid Sultanate. You could be a famous sellsword, serving the highest bidder. You could be a feared warlord, leading your warband wherever the loot is best, slaughtering anyone who gets in your way. You could perhaps even become a noble, a vassal to whichever faction you choose. Or, if you don't wish to follow others, you could strike out on your own, and instead command others as you rule your kingdom from your throne or at the front of your armies.
This game has pretty much infinite replayability. No two wars will ever be the same. The political landscape of Calradia is always shifting and changing, and is forever unpredictable. One day, your Kingdom may be the grandest in all of Calradia, and the next your armies are wiped out, your cities in ruins, and your story nothing more than a legend told by drunken men in taverns late at night. This replayability is further built upon by a very dedicated and very talented modding community, with gems like Gekokujo, which sets Warband in Feudal Japan, to Nova Aetas, which pushes Warband forward to the Renaissance era, to A Clash of Kings, which puts you in the middle of the Game of Thrones universe!
There is so much diversity in these mods, as well as the base game itself, that it tailors itself to a great many players. Fancy yourself a strategy man? You can command your troops into formations and battle lines, and watch the battles play out as a general. Or are you one that likes wet his blade in the blood of his enemies? You can do that too! You can lead your troops into battle, at the forefront of every charge, fighting and dying alongside those you are honored to call your brothers in arms.
Furthermore, Warband has two amazing DLC, namely Napoleonic Wars and Viking Conquest Reforged.
Napoleonic Wars is esentially exactly what the name says. It's the wars in Europe during the time of Napoleon. Be warned this is not a singeplayer DLC!!!! It is mutliplayer only, but by god is that multiplayer glorious. It is probably one of the most refined multiplayer games I've ever played. There is so much attention to detail, and just so much to do. You can be anything from a frontline Rifleman, to a soldier playing a musical instrument for morale support, to a commander giving orders and leading his troops to victory!
Viking Conquest on the other hand is the game developer's attempt at making a more story based and single player experience. You play during the time of the vikings, and the game is set around what is now the United Kingdoms, and the territories east of them. It is very interesting to play, and the story is very extensive and very interesting to play.
This game is amazing, and is overall probably one of my top 3 games of all time, if not my favourite game of all time. This game is worth every penny even when not on sale. What are you doing still reading this review?! Go buy the game already!

It's got its fair share of issues with story, difficulty, and general pacing.  I also think the level design is boring.  But Kingdoms of Amalur does the important stuff really well.  For one, fighting anything in this game is an incredible experience.  I actually want to kill things in this game.  This is a big plus, because Western RPGs with combat systems this fun are hard to come by.  I feel like a total badass fighting off hordes of monsters in real time, with real hitboxes and sword swings.  On top of that, the world building is rock solid.  I skipped through all of the dialogue and cutscenes in the beginning to get to the gameplay, thanks to the devs for giving me the option to do that.  After getting immersed in the world for a few hours and actually caring about the game world, I found myself talking to NPCs and quests givers for info, and saw that the developers actually wrote up a ton of thought-out lore and history for this game.  Props to them again, for that.  And to top it all off, there is a metric buttload of content in this game.  There are new towns, dungeons, forests, and all sorts of locales everywhere, and dozens of quests to go with each.  This game can keep you busy for a while.
If you're a fan of Action RPGs or Western RPGs in general, this game is worth your time to check out.  You'll have to overlook a few big flaws, but Kingdoms of Amalur is undeniably fun and engaging.  It's a lot like The Elder Scrolls or Dragon's Dogma, if you want an easy comparison.  Those are some of my personal favorites, so this game is getting a full recommendation from me.

This game is the pure essence of "Fantasy Action Adventure".
Set in the fairytale-style world of Amalur (obviously), you are thrown into a conflict between mortal Humans and Immortal Fae.
The story isn't too inovative but neither is it boring. No one aspect of the game is truly amazing, but they all work really well together to make a solid adventure that will have you hooked for many many hours. The best way to describe it quickly would be to imagine World of Warcraft, but with single player, a more direct combat system and a more involved crafting system. There are many areas in a pre-scripted world. Some things are persistent while others respawn. It really pays to explore every nook and cranny, as the next corner could hold an interesting quest or even a dungeon.
Pros:
+ fast-paced combat system where your reaction times and movement matter just as much as tailoring your stats to your playstyle.
+ lots of game time. I played it for 50+ hours and aren't close to the end yet.
+ a good crafting system. It isn't overly complicated but still allows you to make a large array of items that you can tailor to your specific play style. (also, custom names which I personally love.)
+ respeccing is possible, so you don't have to worry about building your character into a corner.
+ clear separation of battle skills and crafting skills, so you never wonder "is this going to help me kill things better?"
+ Fully voiced, high quality dialogue with a diverse range of voices. This is actually really impressive because of the sheer number of characters and interactions.
+ Player owned realestate which can also be customized to your liking to aid you with crafting and storage.
+ no DLC ads in-game, no struck content, no micro-transactions. Just buy the game and play it till you get bored.
Cons:
- no multiplayer whatsoever.
- no mods or add-ons as far as I can tell.
- pre-scripted world. Much like in most MMOs, once you explore 100% of the game once, you won't be surprised again.
The game really doesn't have many negative aspects. Anything you think is bad will probably come down to personal preference.
Do you want to go on a big adventure in a vast fantasy world? Then this game is definately for you!

Thief Gold, an expanded version of Thief The Dark Project, is one of the stealth genre's most successful titles.  Although the game is dated, the gameplay is immersive and the level design is immaculate.  Each mission is designed in a way to allow you the use of all of the tools available to you.  Loot is hidden around each mission, interesting sights and text that provides flavor may also be found simply through the exploration of a level.
*****One problem with this version*****
The game advertised is not the game you are buying.  You end buying the original Thief The Dark project and -not- Thief Gold.  Thief Gold had added missions and they are missing from this download.  Something else that is missing are the cut scenes between missions.  Not only are the scenes entertaining, but they help to make you care about the game world and characters while furthering the narrative of the story.  Without these cut scenes, someone knew to the game won't understand everything right away and we are all missing an important part of the experience.

I reccomend this to any fan of late 90's games and especially to anyone who likes the stealth genre.

This game is in Alpha, keep this in mind.
-It has terrible, terrible melee compared to its 'predecessor' Mount and Blade Napoleonic Wars.
-Its naval combat is okay, but Blackwake is a much better purchase if you are looking for the Naval side of things.
-Only two nations, with 126 max per server. (Compared to NW's 250)
-Carpenter has no building capacity, making them useless.
-Shooting is even more hit and miss than NW, sometimes unrealistically so.
-No team chat, must have a mic to coordinate with team.
After reading this, you may be wondering why I am thumbing this game up.
The game is breathing new life into the community surrounding games like NW, which has lasted throughout the years, slowly shrinking and shrinking, until at some points, the only server to play on was Minisiege (Which is Disgusting). Many of my favorite servers, be it the 63e siege server, Toon Roleplay, and so on, had been abandoned.
And this new game is bringing hundreds of new players back into the wars of the Napoleonic Era.
And the beauty of this game, with its new, and farily good community, is that is doesn't have to have good melee, or good shooting. (Though keep in mind if the Devs fixed these things it would be glorious.)
The beauty of this game is the moments you create with other players, be it by joining a regiment, or playing on the public servers and experienceing some of the most hilarious experiences that you have ever experienced in gaming. Most of my time in both NW (Over 600 hours) and Holdfast, have been in public land battles. They are some of the most chaotic and at the same time relaxed things I have ever experienced in gaming. (Yes I will keep using the word Experience) You will have officers, trying to rally public players into lines, and get them to use tactics. There are cannon balls flying everywhere, shots landing left and right, and you stand in this horde of men, formed into the smeblence of a line. You can stand and play the flute if you want, f*ck if I know. In one match, we were playing as the British on the farm villa map, and the entire objective for both teams was to secure the piano, and get someone on it to play. Hundreds lost there lives in that room and around it, and eventually the French (Frog Eating Surrender Monkeys) claimed victory after one last suicide charge by me and 12 other british solders, into a line of 50 french guns, to secure the piano. As you can see, the value of this game is the moments you create with the community, not your K/D, or even PTFO.

This game is great, it is very historically accurate to the way combat would have been fought during the time period with the correct units aswell as a community that seems to work together unlike any other community that I have personally encountered in the past. This game has plenty of "wow" momments that will keep you on your feet and wanting to come back. Starting on a low note and ending on a high note once again, lads. Because with Desu Ex: Mankind Divided, there's a lot of low, and a lot of high.
Right, first off, although it doesn't really affect the game itself (well actually it does) the developers are absolute jews. Just. Jewish. I'm one of the guys who pre-ordered, and incase you haven't heard by now, the pre-order bonuses are all consumables, which means you can only use them on ONE save. After that, they're gone. This wouldn't be too bad unless Square Enix hadn't edited "CONSUMABLES" onto the pre-order bonus right after release. Jewish trick number 1.
Next up, the microtransactions. You can buy yourself to overpoweredness and make yourself a real Deus Ex Machina by paying. Devs (and complete ♥♥♥♥tards) would justify this with "It's there so people who want to complete the game quickly or who struggle with the game can complete it easier." Literallywhat happened to cheats. If the devs were worried about people struggling with "muh difficulty", they could easily add a few cheat codes or anything like that, but that way, they don't get any of the emone. Jewish trick number 2.
Now, as for the other pre-order bonuses, the extra mission, I'm glad I ♥♥♥♥ing got it. Because that♥♥♥♥♥♥is actually pretty central to the story. I played through the entire game making assumptions about who was behind one particular event, purely because a mission that would explain that perfectly was sat on the main menu screen waiting for me to play it. This mission is actually, properly ♥♥♥♥in' relevant the storyline, but ♥♥♥♥ you if you decided you didn't wanna pre-order or splash out a good 80 bucks in order to experience the full story. Jewish trick number 3.
Continuing with the bad, the game's not optimized too well. I can run it at 60 on medium on a GTX 970, although crucial textures, like signs, are blurry af tbh fam and generally the game just looks♥♥♥♥♥♥ You've probably heard already, but make sure to turn MSAA right down, and keep volumetric lighting and contact shadows at the "on" setting.
And to make matters worse, the story is kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's got quite a few plotholes and a plot device that's completely unecessary and satisfies more than a few tropes just by merely existing. The plot itself is interesting enough, with a lot of twists. One problem though, is that it leaves a lot of questions completely unanswered, and these questions all arise from plotholes. The story at its most basic level isn't exactly a life-changing experience, and all the important questions I wanted answered are probably going to be answered in the inevitable sequel, because that ending is definitely sequelbait. Mankind Divided's story just feels like part 1 of a much bigger story.
Also, and I know I say this about every game, but it's a lil too easy. I played on the hardest difficulty and the only times I ever died were when I explicitly decided to attack the cops and get half the city chasing after me. Once you get a stun gun, you can blitz through the game entirely non-lethal and still full combat without much trouble. Like Gandhi crossed with Duke Nukem.
Now for the good. The gameplay is ♥♥♥♥in' A top-tier♥♥♥♥♥♥ And I mean that in a good way. Stealth is fluid, combat is a little less than fluid but still works pretty well, and the level design tops it all off. There are a few levels which are just better than any other levels in the series altogether. They live up to the Desu Ex standard pretty well.
The level of detail is just like any other Desu Ex game. Emails on every computer, with seemingly irrelevant characters fleshed out really well. The game is 50% side missions, but all those side missions are entirely different and really ♥♥♥♥in' detailed. Even the most minor characters are still elaborated on through emails. Reading emails is also pretty fun with all the subplots throughout them.
Then the main quest, it's a lil bit disjointed, to be honest. It's like you're given one task by your superior, but then you do something completely different and everyone's just like "K, let's go with that then." It leaves you flying around the city not really sure of what's happening next.
The game's also got a little side feature called "Breach", which is basically like Metal Gear Solid VR missions except they try to have a story thrown around them. Not exactly riveting stuff, but it's basically a core rundown of the mechanics.
Also, the game can be completed with no kills, alerts or augments. Wew for that.
It's pretty good. I still prefer Human Revolution, but I think Mankind Divided is a pretty solid sequel. Also, it lasts a good 30 hours or so if you do a few side quests as well, and a few of the characters are memorable.

I really want to like Brütal Legend.  It's an ambitious game with lots of obvious love and care invested in it.  Unfortunately, it's a bit too ambitious and winds up screwing itself over about halfway through the game.  It's got a really strong first impression, but once you hit the halfway point, it breaks down, and breaks down fast.
The game starts off strong, with an extremely stylistic, lovingly crafted world; appreciable and exquisitely well voice-acted characters; and strong game design.  It manages to blend open world action-RPG, RTS, and car-combat excellently, much better than any previous game that's ever tried anything similar (Giants: Citizen Kabuto comes to mind), and that's something I tremendously appreciate.
Unfortunately it falls apart as soon as you're no longer fighting the clone-of-your-own faction.  Drowning Doom and Tainted Coil have numerous advantages over your own faction, Ironheade, and you have few ways of fighting back.  This is largely due to a multiplayer-focused patch that was intended to make Ironheade less of a gamebreaker, but whose changes apparently propagated into single-player, breaking the game balance in the process.  There comes a point where roving packs of enemies are so strong, that you absolutely cannot leave your car except to play Solos or talk to NPCs, because doing so invites almost certain death.
As a result, the latter half of the game is an unfun slog, where you dread every single fight on foot while traversing the open world because you know you're outmatched and there's a very good chance you're going to die and wind up back at the nearest Motor Forge.  Sure, there's no penalty for dying otherwise, but there's also no fast travel system to mitigate the long transit times of walking or driving from point-A to point-B, especially if you need to, say, go from the Jungle all the way back to Bladehenge.  This is a beautifully-crafted world you made, Double Fine!  Why not let me enjoy it without having to fear killer baby carriages that throw unavoidable life-sucking dolls?
Stage Battles (the RTS aspect of the game) are particularly harmed, because any tactics you have totally break down when faced against any faction but your own.  They become zerg rushes, where you desperately attempt to keep the enemy from snowballing, scavenging to get whatever units you can out on the field to soak a few hits while you die repeatedly trying to keep enemies away from your Stage.  When your foes seem to have functionally endless resources, and you find yourself overwhelmed by not only numerical but game-mechanic superiority, the clunkiness of the game's RTS mechanics really come to the fore.  It doesn't help that the game lacks a "retry now" function so that you can give up on a losing fight and start over fresh.
Final verdict: If you pick this up, don't play past Lionwhyte.  You'll have a lot more fun and a lot better of an opinion of the game.  Instead of playing past Lionwhyte yourself, look up a Let's Play from before the Ironheade nerf, or find a cutscene compilation video.  This way you can enjoy the story, characters, setting, and voice acting, which remain beautiful throughout the game, without the tear-jerkingly unfun gameplay of the second half of the game.

After finally finishing a playthrough of the game I have to give it a thumbs up.
Kingdoms of Amalur has a rich world with a metric ♥♥♥♥ ton of lore to go through, characters to meet, dialogue to go through, side quests to complete, several faction options with their own quests, and of course a main quest which is engaging and pretty well considered and designed. There are three ability trees which you can mix and match to produce one of seven classes which all seem to be different enough to warrant more playthroughs if you have the stomach for it. Several skills, including three crafting options, also offer subsystems and gameplay changes that give you more room to explore and get comfortable with the game. It is just an overwhelming amount of content to go through so if you have the time and desire? It will find ways to use them.
Unfortunately the game is marred by severe camera problems, balance issues, repetitive enemies, strange interplays between systems, and an end game that comes too early and offers no challenge. Crafting seems segmented as they do not benefit one another beyond being able to smith gems into weapons (but not slots for more than one gem or the highest class of gem) leaving alchemy in the dust where it is more or less useless. If you are using a controller then your skills are limited to four at a time despite being easily able acquire many more active skills than that and the keyboard controls are finicky, especially sensitivity if you have a mouse with more than 2 DPI so you must choose between smooth gameplay or combat options. Not that you'll need those options because by the time you hit level 20 unless you deliberately try to handicap yourself the difficulty of the game approaches zero and by the time you're at level 30 upgrading equipment mostly becomes a 'when I feel like it' thing.
Crafting makes your equipment so much better than what you can find naturally that it further trivializes the game and the built in slow time mechanic means you can usually dispatch a boss in a few seconds if you use the tools at your disposable (and consumables stack so you can dish out LUDICROUS damage if you want.) The only problem is stunning which the game relies on to keep you from curb stomping reality itself but since you can also stun your opponents or parry attacks it's kind of moot. If you have even a modicum of skill Amalur is going to require you to up the difficulty and opt for suboptimal equipment that just looks cool to keep things within six miles of the word 'challenging.'
Another prominent drawback is that much of the lore and content are unoriginal and highly repetitive, while every NPC has several dialogue options (all of which are fully voice acted) you are going to hear the same things repeated to you over and over. This will pad the game length out to an absurd degree if you want to listen to it all which I can't recommend but thankfully you can skip it, line by line, but not entire scenes unfortunately. The game has A LOT to tell you but it also seems to be convinced you didn't pay attention so it will tell you each thing six times which makes it feel more tedious than it otherwise would.
Minor issues also abound like finite storage space that is more finite than it needs to be, inconveniences with inventory management, a strange menu that I won't call BAD but the wording and subcategory arrangement is baffling at times, and nowhere near enough player models to the point where there seem to be 4 kinds of NPC and even if they have different names you'll be hard pressed to remember who is who.
Kingdoms of Amalur isn't a bad game for all those faults however and the time I spent playing it was pretty damn enjoyable, especially for the price, but this is a flawed game and if you aren't willing to overlook them as they come then I can't expect you'll enjoy it. If you meet it on it's terms and play through the VAST amount of content though you'll find a real gem in there.
